0.title: In the Beginning Was the Word
0.overview:
The Gospel of John is the most theological document ever written. Where Matthew presents Jesus as the King of Israel, Mark as the Servant-Son, and Luke as the Saviour of the world, John presents Jesus as the eternal Word of God who became flesh and dwelt among us — the visible form of the invisible God. John wrote last, having lived longest with the mystery of the incarnation, and every sentence carries the weight of that lifelong meditation.

John's purpose is stated with unusual precision at the end of the book: "these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name" (20:31). Two things — belief and life. Not mere assent to facts, but faith in a person; and not mere existence, but the eternal life that is knowing God and knowing Jesus Christ whom he has sent (17:3). The entire Gospel is an extended argument for this faith, structured around seven signs and seven "I AM" declarations.

The seven signs escalate in power and publicity: water to wine (private), healing the official's son (at a distance), healing the invalid (Sabbath controversy), feeding five thousand (crowd), walking on water (disciples alone), healing the blind man (Jerusalem), raising Lazarus (public, four days dead). Each sign is a window into who Jesus is; together they build the case that "no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him" (3:2) — and more than that: unless he is God. The eighth and final sign is the resurrection itself, which the prologue has been anticipating from its first verse.

The seven "I AM" statements are the theological spine of the Gospel. Each one appropriates the divine name revealed at the burning bush (Exod 3:14 — "I AM WHO I AM") and fills it with the content of Jesus' saving work: I am the bread of life; the light of the world; the door; the good shepherd; the resurrection and the life; the way, the truth, and the life; the true vine. These are not metaphors about a human teacher but divine self-disclosures of the Son of God. When Jesus says "Before Abraham was, I am" (8:58), his hearers pick up stones to throw at him — they know exactly what he is claiming.

Who wrote it? The Gospel names its author only as the disciple whom Jesus loved, who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things (21:24; cf. 19:35). He was one of the inner circle at the Last Supper, and he never names himself or his brother James, though he names almost every other disciple. The early church, from Irenaeus on, identified him as John the son of Zebedee, writing in old age at Ephesus, probably between AD 80 and 95. Some scholars think the beloved disciple was a Jerusalem follower other than one of the Twelve, or that the Gospel was finished by his community. But the internal evidence fits John, the son of Zebedee, best, and the church’s testimony is early and consistent.

Why is it so different from Matthew, Mark and Luke? John has no parables, few miracles and long discourses; much of his story is set in Judea and Jerusalem, across at least three Passovers; and the great “I am” sayings are his alone. He was not correcting the others but completing them. He chose his material deliberately, so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God (20:30–31), and says plainly that he left out much more than he included (21:25). Where the others mostly give the Galilean ministry, John adds what happened in Jerusalem and what it meant.

Unique to John is the Farewell Discourse (chapters 13–17) — five chapters of intimate instruction given to the disciples on the night of his betrayal. Here Jesus gives his most extended teaching on the Holy Spirit ("another Helper"), on union with him ("abide in me"), on the world's hatred, on the coming joy, and on the prayer that will sustain the church to the end of the age. The High Priestly Prayer of chapter 17 — Jesus praying for his disciples and for all who will believe through their word — is the most sacred text in Scripture. John's Gospel ends not with a great commission on a mountain but with a question on a beach: "Do you love me?" Everything hangs on the answer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Prologue: The Word Became Flesh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before anything existed, the Word already was. He was with God, and he was God. Everything came into being through him, and in him was the life that is light for humanity, a light that darkness has never put out. God sent John to testify about the light so that all might believe, though John himself was not the light. The true light was coming into the world he had made, yet the world did not recognise him, and his own people did not welcome him. But to all who received him and trusted in his name, he gave the right to become God’s children, born not by human descent or decision but of God. The Word became human and lived among us, and we saw his glory, the glory of the Father’s one and only Son, full of grace and truth. John testified that the one coming after him outranked him, because he existed before him. From his abundance we have all received grace on top of grace. The law came through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God, but the only Son, himself God and closest to the Father, has made him known.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Word (Logos) is not an abstract philosophical principle but the personal Son of God through whom all things were made and in whom life and light reside. John's Christology is the highest in the New Testament: Jesus is fully God, co-eternal with the Father, the agent of creation, the source of life. The incarnation does not diminish his deity — 'the Word became flesh' while remaining the Word. Grace and truth come through Jesus Christ; the law came through Moses. The contrast is not abolition but fulfillment: the law pointed to the one in whom grace and truth are personally embodied.

Verse 2 is a safeguard rather than a repetition. Having said the Word was God, John at once restores the distinction — He was in the beginning with God — so that the identification cannot swallow the persons. The Prologue's architecture is carried by its verbs: the Word simply was, while all things were made, and in verse 14 the Word himself became flesh. He never became God; he became flesh.

The new birth of verse 13 is stated in three negatives before its single positive: not by descent, not by natural desire, not by the decision of any human head of a house — and therefore not by anything a person can inherit, produce or decide. Sonship is conferred, not achieved. The right of verse 12 is exousia, a granted legal standing, and the word used of believers in this Gospel is children (1:12; 11:52), while the Son is reserved for Jesus alone — a distinction that protects the uniqueness of Christ and enlarges rather than reduces the gift.

Grace and truth in verses 14 and 17 echo the name God proclaimed over Moses at Sinai — abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exod. 34:6) — which is why verse 17 must not be read as setting Moses against Christ — a reading Jesus himself forbids at 5:46. Moses was shown the glory from behind and told to write it down; the Prologue claims that the same grace and truth have now arrived in person. And verse 18 closes the door natural religion keeps trying: God has never been seen as he is, and the only one who has never left his side has come out and told us — the telling being a life rather than a lecture.
verseByVerse.examples:
The Prologue is the key that opens the entire Gospel: whoever grasps who Jesus is before reading a single miracle will interpret everything correctly. 'The Word was God' (not 'a god') is one of the clearest affirmations of Christ's full deity in all of Scripture. And the Logos would have resonated with both Jewish (the creative Word of God) and Greek (the rational principle of the universe) audiences — John is announcing that the one both traditions were groping toward has arrived in person.

The darkness has not overcome it is the sentence a reader in a dark season needs: the light has never yet been extinguished, however far it has been reduced — and the church's own history is the evidence, since it has been down to a very few candles more than once and has never gone out. The verse does not promise that the darkness will feel defeated; it says the dark did not put the light out, and the shining verb is in the present tense while the failure to overcome is in the past.

The pastoral force of the three denials in verse 13 is usually missed. Because nothing whatever in the new birth was contributed by the one being born, there is nothing in it he can later fail to keep up — which is the answer to the Christian who cannot locate a moment of conversion and has concluded it never happened. No one remembers being born; the evidence of a birth is not a memory but a pulse. John gives the tests himself in his first letter, where believing the Son is the present-tense proof of a birth already completed in the past (1 Jn. 5:1).

verseByVerse.quote: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God.

Meaning first. The Gospel of John was written by the apostle John, the son of Zebedee, the disciple whom Jesus loved (21:20–24), probably in Ephesus late in the first century. John tells us why he wrote: so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name (20:31). His Gospel is different from the other three: it focuses on Jesus’ long discourses, his signs, his ministry in Judea, and above all his identity. The prologue (vv. 1–18) is the overture to the whole book, introducing its themes: Word, life, light, darkness, witness, belief, glory, grace, truth. And the first two verses take us further back than any other page of the Bible, to the Son before the world, face to face with the Father, himself God.

In the beginning. The words deliberately echo the first words of Genesis 1:1. John begins a new Genesis, a new creation. But he goes further back than Genesis. Genesis says what happened in the beginning; John says what already existed in the beginning. Genesis begins at the beginning. John begins before it.

Was the Word. Not came to be, but was. Before the beginning existed, the Word already existed. The tense (imperfect) means continuous existence: there was never a moment when the Word was not. The Word had no beginning.

Why the Word? Of all the titles available to him, Son, Lord, Christ, King, why open a Gospel with a noun that sounds like a piece of grammar? Because a word is the thing that comes out of a person and tells you what is inside him. You can watch a man for a year and learn very little. He says one sentence and you know something about him you could never have worked out by looking. God is not visible. But God has an eternal Word, not a sound he makes but a Person he is, and that Person has now walked into a room and spoken to people who could hear him. A word expresses what is in the mind; Jesus expresses who God is.

A word for Jews and Greeks. The title lands in two directions at once, and John knows it. A Jewish reader hears Genesis: and God said, let there be light, a world that exists because God spoke (Genesis 1:3; Psalm 33:6). He hears the prophets, where the word of the LORD came to a man and rearranged his life, and Isaiah’s promise that God’s word does not return to him empty but does the thing it was sent to do (Isaiah 55:11). A Greek reader hears logos, the reason and order holding the universe together, the thing his philosophers had been reaching for and never quite touched. John takes the noun both of them were straining after and does something neither expected with it. He does not say the Word is a principle. He says the Word had a face, and we ate with him.

And the Word was with God. “With” (pros) means face to face with, turned towards, in relationship with. The Word is distinct from God the Father, in eternal fellowship with him. Two persons, and between them not distance but communion.

And the Word was God. Not a god, not divine in some lesser sense, but fully and essentially God. In Greek, “God” comes first for emphasis (theos ēn ho logos): God was the Word. The Word is distinct from the Father, yet himself God. Here is the foundation of the doctrine of the Trinity: one God, in more than one person. The Trinity is not yet named, but it is already present: two persons in eternal communion, both fully God.

Where Christians differ, and beyond. Jehovah’s Witnesses translate “the Word was a god”, arguing from the absence of the article before theos. Verdict: this is grammatically mistaken. In Greek, a noun before the verb without the article describes the nature or quality of the subject; it does not mean “a god”. John means the Word was fully divine, all that God is, without being the same person as the Father. A “god” alongside God would be polytheism, which John, a Jew, utterly rejected. The church confessed it at Nicaea (325): true God from true God, of one substance with the Father.

The grammar in plain words. That phrase “not a god” is worth more than an assertion, because a reader may well have had it disputed on his own doorstep. The observation about the article is perfectly correct; the conclusion drawn from it is not. John is doing something very precise, and English cannot quite carry it. He needs to say two things at once and not let either swallow the other: the Word is not the same person as the Father (so, the Word was with God), and the Word is nonetheless everything the Father is (so, the Word was God). Had he put the article in, he would have said the Word was the Father. Had he meant a god, he would have written a sentence no Jew could utter, since a second and lesser deity is precisely what Israel’s whole faith existed to deny. And the very next verse closes the door: all things were made through him. Whatever exists that is not God was made through the Word, so the Word cannot be among the things that were made. There is no room left for a created, junior deity. He stands on the Creator’s side of the line, which is the only line the Bible ultimately draws.

Watch the verbs. Read the prologue watching one thing only, and the whole passage opens up. In these two verses the Word simply was, four times, in a tense that describes a state running back with no starting point in view. From verse 3 onward the verb for everything else changes. All things came to be. There came to be a man sent from God, whose name was John (v. 6). Everything that is not God is spoken of with the verb of beginning. And then in verse 14 that second verb is finally used of the Word himself: the Word became flesh. He never became God. He became man. That switch of verbs is the architecture of the entire passage, and it carries more weight than any adjective could.

He was in the beginning with God. Verse 2 appears to add nothing, but it is not padding; it is a guard, set exactly where a reader is most likely to fall. The Word was God, standing on its own, could be heard as saying the Word simply is the Father under a second name, and John has just spent a clause denying that. So he goes back and says it once more with the distinction restored. The with is repeated after the identification, so that neither one can swallow the other. What the church would later spend three centuries learning how to say, one God, and the Son is not the Father, is already here in the second sentence, before a single event has been narrated.

Does this mean there are three Gods? No. Christians believe in one God, as firmly as any Jew (Deuteronomy 6:4). But this one God exists eternally as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, three persons who share one and the same divine being. The Son is not a part of God, or a third of God, or a junior God; he is wholly God, as the Father is, and he is not the Father. No picture from creation captures it fully, and most attempts (water, ice and steam; one man as father, son and husband) end up teaching an old error. It is better to say what Scripture says and stop there: the Word was with God, and the Word was God. We do not believe it because we can picture it, but because God has said it, and because only a Saviour who is truly God can bring us to God.

If Jesus is God, who was he praying to? To his Father. Prayer between the Son and the Father is not God talking to himself; it is the eternal conversation of verse 1, overheard on earth. Before the world existed, the Father and the Son were face to face in love (17:5, 24). When the Son became man, that relationship did not stop; it was carried into a human life, so that the Son now prayed as a man, depended on his Father as a man, and obeyed as a man. The prayers in the Gospels are therefore not a problem for the doctrine of the Trinity. They are one of the clearest windows onto it.

The alternative is silence. It is worth being clear about what the alternative to this sentence actually is. It is not a neutral universe; it is a silent one. If the beginning was matter, then before there was anyone to love there was nothing being loved, and the deepest thing about reality is force: impersonal, uninterested, and very old. Everything warm arrives late and by accident, and will go out. John says the deepest thing about reality is a conversation. Before there was light, before there was time to measure, before there was air to carry a voice, there was a Father and a Son, and they were not sitting in silence.

In a sentence. Before anything existed, the Word already was, in eternal fellowship with God, and the Word himself was God.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test you can run on yourself. Ask what you picture God doing before he made anything. Most of us, pressed, imagine something like waiting: a solitary figure with nothing to occupy him until the world turned up. If that is honestly the God you pray to, then you are praying to someone who needed you, and you will never quite shake the suspicion that you have turned out to be a disappointing return on his loneliness. The God of this verse was not lonely. He did not make you because he was short of company. He made you out of a fullness that was already complete without you, which means his interest in you is not the strained interest of a man with nothing else to do. It is the interest of a Father who had a Son to love before there was a universe, and who has decided to bring you into it. Pray to him like that today.

For worship. Whatever else we do not yet know about God, we may know this much and steady ourselves on it: he was never silent. Before anything existed that could hear him, he was speaking, and what he was saying was a Son. The Jesus we trust is no creature promoted to glory, but the eternal God, who was face to face with the Father before the first morning, who shares all that the Father is, and who has spoken him to us. He is the Word, and he was God, and he is worthy of everything we are.
verseByVerse.note: “In the beginning” deliberately echoes the first words of Genesis. “The Word” (Greek logos) was a term both Jews and Greeks understood: God’s self-expression, through which he created and revealed himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men.

All things were made through him. The Word is the agent of creation. The Father created through the Son (Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2; 1 Corinthians 8:6). The comprehensive scope is deliberate: all things, nothing that exists came into being apart from the Word. This eliminates any eternal matter independent of God; the Word is not one creative force among many but the sole agent through whom the Father creates. If all things were made through him, he himself was not made. He is the Creator, not a creature.

And without him was not any thing made that was made. John says it twice, once forward and once backward, and the second clause is not a flourish. It is a fence. State only the positive and someone will go looking for an exception: some corner of reality, some raw material lying about, some dark thing that got in by another route. John closes the gap before anyone can reach for it. There is no back door into existence. Nothing exists that the Word did not make, and this refutes the ancient heresy (Arianism) that the Son was the first and highest created being.

Everything that was used against him. That means something bracing about the world you woke up in. He made the wood the cross was cut from, and the ore in the ground that became the nails, and the hands that would drive them, and the breath in the lungs of the men swinging the hammers. Nothing was ever used against him that he had not first supplied. That is not a poetic flourish; it is simply what all things means once you follow it into the story this Gospel is about to tell.

Why does my Bible punctuate this differently? The oldest manuscripts carry no punctuation, and some early readers ran the sentence on: without him was not anything made. That which has been made was life in him. Your Bible may carry a footnote to that effect. The difference is real but small: on either reading the Word is the Creator, and on either reading the life is in him. It is a question of where the full stop goes, not of what is being claimed.

In him was life. “Life” (zōē) occurs 36 times in John, and it does not mean the state of not being dead. It is life in its fullest sense, eternal life, the life of God himself. Everything alive has life the way a room has light at four in the afternoon: on loan, from elsewhere, and shortly to be withdrawn. John is saying that in the Word life is not on loan. He does not have it; he is it. The Word has life in himself (5:26), original and self-existent, and he gives it. Every other living thing in the universe is running on something it was handed.

What do you have that you did not receive? Try the test Paul once put as a question (1 Corinthians 4:7). Not your possessions: your heartbeat, your next breath, the fact that your body has again this morning chosen to work. There is not one item on the list that you arranged. That is either terrifying or it is the most restful fact available to a human being, and which of the two it turns out to be depends entirely on what the giver is like. John has twenty-one chapters to show you.

For the one sitting with a diagnosis. Say this carefully to the reader who has been given bad news, or who is watching someone thin out in a bed. The Christian hope at that point is not that life is generally stronger than death; it plainly is not, and pretending otherwise is cruelty dressed up as comfort. It is that there is one place in the universe where life was never borrowed and therefore cannot be called back in, and that this Gospel exists to tell you he has come within reach. He does not offer to extend the loan. He offers himself (11:25).

And the life was the light of men. Then the strange bridge: how does life become light? In this Gospel light is the revelation of God, truth, goodness and salvation, as opposed to darkness: sin, ignorance and death. It is never merely information. It is what lets you see where you are and know what you are looking at, and, less comfortably, it is what shows up whatever else is in the room. That is why the very next sentence is about darkness. In Genesis, light was the first thing created (Genesis 1:3); here the life in the Word shines as light to humanity, and by chapter 8 Jesus will say it outright: I am the light of the world (8:12). The thing to hold on to is that the light is not a body of teaching he brought with him. It is the overflow of the life he is. Nobody is illuminated by studying him from across the room. People are illuminated by being near him.

If he made everything, did he make evil? No. He made all things good (Genesis 1:31). Evil is not a thing God created but the ruin of good things he did create: a creature turning its God-given powers against him. Darkness is not a rival substance; it is what results when creatures turn from the light. That is why the next verse speaks of darkness opposing the light and failing. Nothing the Word made is evil in itself, not the body, not food, not sex, not work, not the material world, and nothing evil is outside his rule. He who made all things is able to remake them, and that is exactly what this Gospel is about to show him beginning to do.

In a sentence. Everything was created through the Word, and nothing exists that he did not make; in him was life, and that life was humanity’s light.

On a Tuesday. Before you eat today, or step outside, or hold someone you love, say inside yourself: he made this. Not only the beautiful things; the ordinary ones too, your hands, your work, the food on the plate. Then let it run the other way: the one who made it all is the one who came to save you, which means the world you live in is not foreign territory to him and your life is not outside his interest. And if you have been looking for life in something he made rather than in him, the career, the relationship, the health you are trying to protect, notice that you have been drinking from the jug and ignoring the spring.

For worship. Everything that lives is borrowing, and he is where it is borrowed from. The hand that shaped the stars, that set the oceans in their beds and wrote the code in every cell, is the hand that was pierced on the cross. The Creator of all became the light of men, and he has life in himself to give. Glory to the Word, through whom we were made, and in whom alone we live.

verseByVerse.quote: "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it. There was a man sent from God, whose name was John."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it. There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.

The light shines in the darkness. Darkness is the world in rebellion against God: sin, ignorance and death. The light is not afraid of the darkness; it shines into it. And look at the tense, because it is the pastoral heart of the verse and it is easy to walk past. The verbs in the opening lines are in the past: was, was made. This one is present. The light shines. Not shone; not will shine. It is the first present-tense verb in the passage, and John slips it in at the exact point where the darkness enters. Whatever else has finished happening, this has not finished happening. It is going on while you read.

And the darkness has not overcome it. The ESV notes that “overcome” can also be rendered “understood”. The Greek (katelaben) means to seize, to lay hold of, to take something and have it. It is used of an enemy overtaking a man on the road, and it is used of a mind finally getting hold of an idea. So the King James read it as comprehended and most modern versions read it as overcame, and both are honest translations of the same word.

Both meanings are true. John almost certainly wants both, and you can prove it from his own book. The darkness in this Gospel does try to put the light out, and that is what Good Friday is, and it fails. Even at the cross, when darkness seemed to win, the light was not overcome. It rose again. And the darkness in this Gospel repeatedly fails to understand what it is looking at: a teacher of Israel who cannot follow a sentence about birth (3:10), men told plainly why they cannot hear (8:43), Pharisees asking whether he means them (9:40). Both meanings come true in the narrative. Do not choose between them; the sentence was built to carry the two.

One verdict already in. The second verb is the opposite of the first: settled and finished. The darkness has not overcome it, one decisive non-event. Put the two together and you have the Christian’s actual position described with unusual accuracy. The dark is real and present-tense, and so is the light; but only one of them has already had its verdict handed down.

What it does not mean. A sentence this confident sits one step from a cruelty. This verse does not promise that the darkness will feel defeated. It does not say the light is bright, or warm, or winning by any margin you can see from where you are standing. It says the dark did not put it out. If you are reading this in a season where God seems to have gone quiet and the light appears to be one candle in a very large room, you are not failing to believe the verse. You are living inside its first clause. The verse does not ask you to feel that the dark is losing. It asks you to notice that the light is still lit, and that this has now been true for a very long time and through much worse than yours.

If the light has won, why is there still so much darkness? Because the victory is decisive but not yet complete. At the cross and the empty tomb the darkness did its worst and lost; its defeat is settled. But God, in patience, has not yet ended the age, so that the light may go on shining into the dark and drawing people out of it (2 Peter 3:9). We live between the decisive battle and the final day, when there will be no night at all (Revelation 22:5). That is why the Christian is neither naive about evil nor despairing in front of it. The darkness is real, it is still dangerous, and it is already beaten.

There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. And then, with no warning at all, verse 6. We have been before the beginning; we are now in a wilderness with a man who has a name. This is John the Baptist. This Gospel never calls him the Baptist, because the only John it needs to name is him; the author never names himself. “Sent from God”: a true prophet with a divine commission. A man, in contrast to the Word who was God. John does not ease the transition, and the abruptness is the point. The verb changes, exactly as it does for everything created: there came to be a man. He has a start date. The Word does not.

The eternal with an address. Notice what has just been claimed by putting these two sentences side by side. The eternal thing has an address. It can be dated, and there are people who can be named in connection with it, and if you had been in the Jordan valley in the late twenties you could have gone and looked. Christianity’s strangest claim is not that God is eternal; most religions will grant something like that. It is that the eternal turned up in a particular decade, in a specific stretch of river, and that a man with a job and a diet and a family was sent from God to point at him. Four hundred years of prophetic silence end in that one line, and the first thing God says after four centuries is: look over there.

In a sentence. The light keeps shining in the darkness, and the darkness has neither understood it nor put it out; and God sent a man named John.

On a Tuesday. Think of the darkest stretch you have come through. Ask, not whether it felt survivable at the time, but whether the light went out. Almost everyone who has walked with God for any length of time discovers that the honest answer is no: that it thinned, that it was hard to see, and that it was there. That is not a small thing to have found out. It is the verse, confirmed in the only laboratory available to you. However dark your circumstances now, the light of Christ is not overcome. Trust it, and do the next thing in its light.

For worship. The light shines, and it has been shining since before the first night fell. It shone in the garden after the fall, in the promise of a serpent-crusher. It shone through the long night of Egypt and the exile and the four silent centuries. It walked into the darkest Friday the world has known and let the dark close over it, and on the third morning the dark gave it back. No night has ever put it out, and none ever will. Blessed be the Light of the world, who shines into our darkness and is never overcome.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “overcome” can also be rendered “understood.” The John of verse 6 is John the Baptist.

verseByVerse.quote: "He came as a witness, to bear witness about the light, that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but came to bear witness about the light."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came as a witness, to bear witness about the light, that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but came to bear witness about the light.

He came as a witness. “Witness” (martyria, martyreō) is one of the load-bearing beams of this Gospel: it and its relatives turn up nearly fifty times. John the Baptist, the Father, the Scriptures, Jesus’ works, the Spirit, the disciples: all bear witness to Jesus (5:31–39). A witness testifies to what he has seen. John is writing something shaped like a trial. There is a claim being made, and a case being assembled, and witnesses called one after another. The reader is not being addressed as an audience. He is being addressed as a jury, and a verdict is expected.

The word that became martyr. It is also the word from which we get martyr, and the drift of that word from testimony to death is not an accident of language. It happened because of what testimony repeatedly cost. The man in this verse would lose his head for it (Mark 6:27).

That all might believe through him. “Believe” (pisteuō) occurs about 98 times in John, but the noun faith never. For John, faith is an action: believing, trusting, coming, receiving. The goal of all witness is belief (20:31). John’s entire ministry is defined by what he is not, and the purpose of his witness establishes from the outset that faith is the response the Gospel calls for. All the signs, discourses and encounters in this book are designed to produce belief.

Through him. Then a preposition worth staring at. God could have arranged for people to believe by direct broadcast, without an intermediary, and he did not. He appointed a man with a strange diet and a rough manner, standing in a river, and routed faith through him. That is God’s ordinary method and it has not changed (Romans 10:14). Almost certainly you can name the person it came through for you, and almost certainly they were not impressive, and almost certainly they knew it.

He was not the light. Why would that need saying? Nobody reading a Gospel is at risk of confusing a desert preacher with the Son of God, except that people were. There were still disciples of John the Baptist decades later and hundreds of miles away; Paul ran into a dozen of them at Ephesus who had received John’s baptism and had never so much as heard there was a Holy Spirit (Acts 19:1–7). Some may have thought John was the Messiah. This flat denial is not a rhetorical flourish. It is a correction being issued to a live movement, by an author who knew it was still going on. The Gospel firmly puts John in his place: a witness, not the light. John himself said so (v. 20; 3:28–30).

The signpost. John’s whole identity here is stated in negatives: not the light, and in a moment not the Christ, not Elijah, not the Prophet. That looks at first like a diminishment. It is the opposite. A witness is not a lesser version of the thing he testifies to; he is a different kind of thing altogether, and the value of his work depends entirely on his not being confused with it. A signpost that people admire and stop at has failed. A signpost that they walk straight past, on their way to where it pointed, has done the whole of its job.

I am not a preacher. Am I a witness? Yes. A witness is not someone with special training but someone who tells what he knows to be true. You may not be able to explain the Trinity or answer every objection, but you can say who Jesus is, what he has done, and what he has done for you. That is what John did, and it is what the man born blind did with almost no theology at all: one thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see (9:25). Witness happens over a kitchen table, in a hospital corridor, in an honest answer when someone asks why you still go to church. And the results are not yours to produce. A witness is responsible for the truth of his testimony, not for the verdict of the jury.

In a sentence. John came as a witness to testify about the light, so that all might believe through his testimony; he was not the light himself.

On a Tuesday. Here is the test, and it is a hard one. Think of someone you have taught, or discipled, or raised. Now imagine them going on to know Christ better than you do, in a church you have no connection with, and rarely thinking of you again. Does that land as joy or as loss? The honest answer is a fairly exact reading of whether you are being a witness to the light or quietly setting up as a small light of your own. Like John, you are not the light, but a witness to it. Point people to Jesus, and be glad when they walk past you to him.

For worship. John will give his own answer to that test in chapter 3, and it is one of the loveliest sentences in the Bible: he must increase, but I must decrease (3:30). He is not the light. He never once sounds disappointed about it. And how could he? The one he pointed to is the true Light, the Lord of every witness, who is worth every life that has ever been spent in testifying to him, and who stands at the end of every finger that points his way.

parallels.desc: he was a burning and shining lamp

verseByVerse.quote: "The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him.

The true light. “True” (alēthinon) means genuine, real, as opposed to imitations and shadows. It is a favourite word in John: the true bread (6:32), the true vine (15:1). Jesus is the reality to which all other lights point. Every human experience of light, beauty, reason and goodness is a dim reflection of the one who is the source.

Which gives light to everyone. Every human being receives some light from the Word: the light of reason, conscience, and the knowledge of God through creation (Romans 1:19–20; 2:14–15). Not that everyone is saved, but that everyone is accountable. This is the general illumination of common grace through which all people have some knowledge of God and of right and wrong.

Was coming into the world. The incarnation. Your Bible may differ here from the one in the next pew. The phrase coming into the world can attach to the light (the true light was coming into the world) or it can attach to everyone, which is how the older versions read it: the light that lights every man that comes into the world. The Greek allows both, and the difference is not doctrinally serious. It is a question of which word a phrase leans on, not a dispute about what is true.

What it does not mean. Gives light to everyone has been made to carry a great deal: that all people are already savingly enlightened, that every religion is a road up the same mountain, that no one really needs to be told anything. But gives light can mean to shed light on something as much as to switch a light on inside someone. And John himself settles the question in the very next breath, which is why the two verses sit in one entry: the light shone on the world, and the world did not know him. Whatever universal illumination means here, John states plainly, one line later, that it did not by itself produce recognition. The sun rising over a city is not the same thing as the city waking up.

Enough to accuse, not enough to save. What the verse does secure is real and worth having. There is no human being who is simply outside the reach of this light. Every flicker of conscience, every ache after beauty, every stubborn refusal to believe that cruelty is merely a preference: all of it is light, and it is his, and it is falling on people who have never heard his name. Paul says the same thing in Romans 1 and draws the same conclusion: it is enough light to leave a man without excuse, and not enough to save him. Which is precisely why somebody has to go and tell him.

So what about people who have never heard of Jesus? They are not without light: creation and conscience speak to them of God, and they are accountable for what they know (Romans 1:20; 2:14–15). But that light, by itself, has never saved anyone, because the human heart suppresses it. Scripture teaches that salvation comes through conscious faith in Christ, for there is no other name by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12), and faith comes from hearing the word of Christ (Romans 10:14–17). That is not a reason for despair but for mission. God is not limited; he has sent his gospel to the ends of the earth and saves people in every nation through it. The right response to this question is to pray, to give, and to go.

He was in the world, and the world was made through him. He came into the world he had made. John says world three times in a single sentence, and each time it turns the knife. He was in the world. The world was made through him. The world did not know him. There is no villain named, no plot described; the tragedy is done entirely with a repeated noun.

Yet the world did not know him. “The world” (kosmos) appears about 78 times in John. Here it means humanity in rebellion against God. The creatures did not recognise their Creator. Isaiah had already found the image for it, and it is more humiliating than anything John could have invented: the ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s crib, but Israel does not know (Isaiah 1:3). An animal in a stall recognises the man who feeds it. A dog knows its owner’s step on the path before the door opens. What John is reporting is a failure of recognition beneath the level of an animal’s: the creation standing in the presence of the one who specified every atom in it and registering nothing at all. Not mere ignorance, but wilful non-recognition.

Before any hostility. And notice that this is said before any of the hostility begins. There is no persecution yet, no trial, no cross. The first thing said about the world’s response to God arriving in it is not that it fought him. It is that it did not notice.

Would I have known him? Almost certainly not. That is the plain sense of the verse, and it is meant to land. The people best equipped to recognise him, the ones with the Scriptures, the calendar, the prophecies, the daily sacrifices, are precisely the ones this Gospel will show missing him. If recognising God depended on being religious, well taught or sincere, the record of the first century is against you. Which is exactly why the next few verses do not go where you expect. Having established that nobody recognised him, John does not turn round and urge the reader to look harder. He says something else entirely, and it arrives in verse 13: those who did receive him were born of God. Recognition was never going to come from the side of the ones who could not see. It had to be given.

In a sentence. The true light that gives light to every person was coming into the world he had made, yet the world did not recognise him.

On a Tuesday. The world still does not know its Creator. Do you? Ask where in the last week you were in the presence of his gifts and registered nothing: the meal, the sunrise, the friend’s kindness, the conscience that stopped you. Then thank him for them by name. And when you meet someone who does not know him, remember that the light is already falling on them. Your task is not to switch it on but to tell them whose it is.

For worship. The Maker walked into his workshop and the tools did not know his hand. The Lord of the world entered the world as a stranger, and he did not turn back. He came anyway, knowing he would be unrecognised, and he came for the very people who looked straight at him and saw nothing. And then he did what no creature could do for itself: he opened blind eyes. Praise the true Light, who was not known, and who came to make himself known.

verseByVerse.quote: "He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him. But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him. But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God.

He came to his own. Literally to his own things: his own home, his own property. The Greek here is sharper than any English version can quite manage, because John changes the gender of a word halfway through the sentence and the whole tragedy is in the change. He came to his own: that phrase is neuter and plural. His own things, his own place, his own home. “His own” is Israel, God’s own people, to whom he had given the law, the prophets and the promises.

And his own people did not receive him. Now the word is masculine. His own folk, the household. So the sentence runs: he came home, and the family would not let him in. The verb is the one used for welcoming somebody in off the road and giving them the spare room. He was not turned away at a border by strangers. He was left standing at his own door by people who knew the address because it was theirs too. This is the deepest rejection, and the whole Gospel records it, climaxing at the cross.

They were not badly prepared. This is the point that stings. They had the Scriptures, the promises, the temple, the calendar, centuries of longing and a national hope built entirely around his arrival. Nobody on earth was better set up to recognise him. The failure did not happen for want of information.

When your own family will not receive him. Say a word here to the reader for whom this is not history. Some who follow Christ pay for it at home: a father who stopped speaking, a family who treat the faith as an embarrassment to be managed, a husband or wife who did not sign up for this. If that is you, notice that this verse puts you in company you did not expect. He knows what it is to be the odd one in his own house, and he knows it from further in than you do, because his own people were not merely unsympathetic; they eventually killed him. Whatever it has cost you at home, you are not walking a road he sent you down and never took himself. Keep loving them, keep praying, and keep the door open from your side (1 Peter 3:1–2).

But to all who did receive him. Then but, and the sentence turns. Some did. “All”: whoever they are, Jew or Gentile. The receiving is not confined to a subset of Israel; anyone, from anywhere, who receives him is included.

Who believed in his name. To receive him is to believe in him. The receiving and the believing are the same act described from two angles. “His name” means who he is, as he has revealed himself.

He gave the right to become children of God. Three words in this half-verse deserve to be slowed over. First, the right. The word is exousia, and it does not mean power or ability. It means authority, privilege, legal standing: the right recognised by whoever gets to recognise such things. It is a legal word, not a moral one. God does not merely make it possible for people to be his children; he confers the standing, and the standing holds because of who conferred it. That is worth having on a day when you do not feel like anybody’s child. Your standing was not issued by your feelings and is not withdrawn by them.

Children. Across this Gospel, Son is Jesus’ title alone; believers are children. It looks at first like a demotion and it is exactly the opposite: it is the safeguard that lets the gift be as large as it is. Jesus is Son in a way nobody else will ever be, by eternal right. We are children in a way we never were before, by gift. Both are kept whole, and neither is diluted to make room for the other. We are not children of God by nature; we become his children by adoption, through faith in Christ (Galatians 3:26; 4:4–7; Romans 8:14–17; 1 John 3:1). It is the greatest privilege in the universe.

Become. Not discover, not realise, not remember. The verse does not say people found out they had been God’s children all along. Something happened to them that had not previously happened. There is a real truth in which God is the Father of all: he made everyone and sustains everyone, and his kindness falls on everyone (Acts 17:28). But this is not it, and John will not blur the two. By creation everyone is his. By this, some are his in a way that requires a birth.

Is believing then my contribution? A careful reader will feel the pressure here, and ought to. If the right is given to those who receive and believe, has the believing not just become the qualifying act, the one contribution that is finally mine? Verse 13 exists to shut that door, and John shuts it before anyone can get a foot in it. Those who believe are those who were born, not of the will of man, but of God. Faith is truly yours: you believe, and you are commanded to. But it is never a payment you hand over. It is the empty hand of a child who has already been given life. Read on before you decide.

In a sentence. He came to his own people and they rejected him, but to all who received him by believing in his name, he gave the right to become God’s children.

On a Tuesday. A test, for anyone unsure whether this has happened to them. Ask what word rises first when you think of God, and be honest, because the polite answer is not the true one. Judge. Employer. Landlord, keeping an eye on the state of the property. Distant relative. Or Father. Not whether you can defend the word Father theologically, but which one your stomach reaches for at four in the morning when something has gone wrong. That reflex is telling you something about what you actually believe you have been given, and this verse is what it needs to be corrected by. When you pray today, begin with Father, and mean it.

If my own father failed me. Say the plain thing to whoever needs it: if your own father was absent, or frightening, or simply never much interested, you are not disqualified from this verse; you are its natural audience. The word Father is not being defined for you by the man who taught you to flinch at it. It is being defined by the Son who is going to spend twenty chapters showing you what his own Father is like.

For worship. He came home and was shut out, so that we who had no home could be brought in. The Son who was rejected by his own household opens the door of his Father’s house to strangers and calls them children. If you believe in Jesus, you are a child of God, by the gift of the only one who has the right to give it, and nothing can revoke it. Blessed be the Father who adopts, and the Son who makes us his brothers and sisters.

verseByVerse.quote: "who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.

Who were born, not of blood. John does not simply say the new birth is God’s work. He says it three times in the negative first, and each denial closes a specific door that people have actually tried to get in by. Not of blood: and the Greek is plural, bloods, which sounds odd until you know that in the thought of the time a child was reckoned to come from the mingled blood of both parents. So the first door shut is descent, not because of who your people were. Being born a Jew, or into a Christian family, does not make you a child of God. This is aimed first at anyone leaning on Abraham, an argument Jesus will have to have out at length in chapter 8, but it lands just as squarely on a Christian home. A godly mother is one of the great mercies of God, and she is not a birth certificate. Grace does not travel down a bloodline. Every generation is converted from scratch or not at all.

Nor of the will of the flesh. The second door is natural desire, the whole biological machinery of wanting and conceiving and producing. Not by human desire or effort. Nothing in the ordinary equipment of being human generates this.

Nor of the will of man. Here the word is not the general one for a human being but the specific one for a male, a husband, a father. That is deliberate, and in that society it was pointed. The head of the house decided whether a newborn was acknowledged and taken into the family at all; a word from him settled it. John says: not that either. Not by any human decision, whether a husband’s, a parent’s, or one’s own. No head of any house can decide you into God’s family: not your father, not a priest, not a minister, not a church membership roll, and, though it is the hardest one for us to hear, not you. The decisive vote is not yours to cast.

But of God. Three closed doors and then one open one. Becoming God’s child is a new birth, and its source is God alone (3:3–8; James 1:18; 1 Peter 1:3). It is the same fence-building John did back in verse 3, where he said all things were made through the Word and then said it again backwards so nobody could hunt for an exception. He is not being repetitive. He is sealing the room.

Where Christians differ: faith and new birth. Arminians teach that a person, enabled by grace, chooses to believe, and is then born again; on that view “not of the will of man” rules out only natural descent and human effort as the source of life, not a free human decision to believe. Verdict: Reformed theology reads verses 12–13 together: those who believe are those born of God, not of the will of man. The new birth is God’s sovereign work, which produces faith (1 John 5:1, where “everyone who believes … has been born of God”, perfect tense). We believe because we have been born of God, not the reverse. Yet we truly believe, and are commanded to.

Then why should I preach, or call anyone to believe? Because God gives the new birth through his word (James 1:18; 1 Peter 1:23). The same Jesus who says no one can come unless the Father draws him (6:44) stands and cries out, if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (7:37). The call is sincere and it is for everyone. We do not know who God is bringing to life; we only know that he does it as the gospel is spoken. A sovereign new birth is not a reason to keep quiet. It is the only reason to expect anything when we speak, because we are talking to people who cannot raise themselves, and we know who can.

When you cannot find the moment. There are Christians who read a verse like this and go cold, because the language of being born again makes them go looking for a date, and there is no date. No aisle, no night, no thunderclap. They have believed as far back as they can remember, or the thing crept up on them over years, and they cannot point to the hour. And they conclude, quietly and for a long time, that whatever happened to other people has probably not happened to them. Read the verse again and notice that it says nothing whatever about your being able to locate it. It tells you who did it. That is the entire content. It is a statement about the agent, not about your memory of the event.

Nobody remembers being born. That is exactly what you would expect, on the analogy John has chosen. Not one person alive has a recollection of the most decisive physical event of their existence, and nobody treats that as grounds for doubting it happened. You do not establish your birth by memory. You establish it by breathing. So the evidence is present-tense, and John gives it, not here, but in his first letter, where he wrote for exactly this reader: we know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers (1 John 3:14). Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God (1 John 5:1). The tense in that second sentence is the whole answer: the believing is present and the birth is already completed. He does not say believe and you will be born. He says that if you are believing, you have been born. The birth is behind the faith as its cause, not in front of it as its reward.

A pulse, not a feeling. Then run the honest test, which is not a memory test at all. Do you find yourself wanting things you did not use to want? Is there sin you once enjoyed that has gone quietly sour on you? Do you pray when nobody would know if you did not? Have you had every reason to walk away from Christ and found that you could not? None of those is a feeling. All of them are a pulse. And keep the guard on the other side, because this must not be turned into a blanket. The answer to a person with no evidence of any kind is not that they were probably born long ago and simply forgot. It is that this verse tells them where to go and who can do it. If nothing in that list is true of you, the news is not that you should look harder for a memory. It is that God gives births, and that people ask him for them.

And the Word became flesh. This is the heart of the prologue, and of the Christian faith. Here the verb finally arrives. Through the whole opening the Word simply was, while everything created came to be; and now, for the first time, the verb of beginning is used of him. He never became God. He became this. The eternal Word, who was God, became flesh: a real human being, with a real human body and soul. Not merely appeared to be human, as the Docetists taught (1 John 4:2–3). Not changed into a man, ceasing to be God. He took human nature to himself, while remaining God. This is the incarnation: genuinely becoming what he was not while remaining what he was.

Flesh. Look at which noun John picks. He does not write that the Word became a man, though that is true. He does not write that he took a body. He writes sarx, flesh, which is the crudest, weakest, most mortal word available to him. It is the word for what a man is when you consider that he gets tired, gets hungry, gets thirsty, bleeds when cut, and dies: human nature in its weakness and mortality. John, who has spent thirteen verses climbing to the highest claim in the New Testament, sets the two words side by side without a cushion between them: the Word, and flesh. Every heresy about the person of Christ in the next four hundred years is an attempt to soften that collision, and John’s own letters show him already fighting it (1 John 4:2–3).

Make it concrete. It is meant to be. It means he had to be taught to walk and fell over doing it. It means teeth coming through, and splinters in a carpenter’s hands, and sweat, and the particular kind of tiredness where you fall asleep in a boat in a storm. It means that at some point somebody changed God’s nappies. If that sentence is uncomfortable, it is doing its work. God did not send a message, or a projection, or an appearance. He arrived in a body that could be hurt. God became what we are, so that we could become what he made us to be.

Did he stop being God when he became man? No. The Word became flesh by taking human nature to himself, not by setting aside his divine nature. He did not exchange one for the other, and he did not blend them into something in between. He is one person, truly God and truly man, the two natures joined without confusion and without separation (Westminster 8.2). As man he grew tired and wept and died; as God he upheld the universe throughout (Hebrews 1:3). He laid aside his glory’s display, not his deity. That is why his death can save: it is the death of a real man, in our place, and the life of the one who dies is the life of God.

And dwelt among us. “Dwelt” means literally pitched his tent (eskēnōsen), tabernacled. This is not a decorative verb. John reaches back to Exodus and expects you to come with him. Stage it. Israel is in the wilderness with no land, no city, no temple and no address. They build a tent to God’s specification, and when it is finished the glory of the LORD comes down and fills it so completely that Moses cannot go in (Exodus 25:8; 40:34–35). That is where God chose to live: not in a palace, not on a mountain-top out of reach, but in a portable structure of goat hair and dyed skins in the middle of the camp, pitched where they pitched, struck when they struck, moved when they moved. From the outside it was the least impressive dwelling imaginable. Inside it was unbearable with glory.

This time the tent was a body. John is telling you that this happened again. The plain, unremarkable exterior that nobody in Nazareth found worth a second look; the glory inside. God once more choosing to camp in the middle of his people rather than to summon them somewhere. God’s presence in the tabernacle, and later in the temple, is now in the flesh of Jesus. He is the true tabernacle, the place where God meets his people. And it is a tent, not a house, which is honest about what the incarnation was: thirty-odd years is a short pitch. But do not draw the wrong conclusion from the temporariness. Later in the Gospel he says he is going to prepare a place (14:2), and the Bible ends with the same word coming back one last time: the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them (Revelation 21:3). The tent was temporary. The camping among us was not.

And we have seen his glory. “We”: John and the apostles, eyewitnesses who gazed at it with their own eyes and kept looking (1 John 1:1–3). This is an eyewitness sentence, written by an old man who is claiming he was in the room. “Glory” (doxa) is the visible radiance of God’s presence, which filled the tabernacle. It was seen in his signs (2:11), and supremely at the cross, which John calls his glorification (12:23; 17:1). Here John does something you would not predict: he never even narrates the transfiguration. The glory these men saw was chiefly a man dying badly in public. Hold on to that when you next find yourself looking for God’s glory only in whatever is going well; John looked hardest at it in the one place nobody would think to.

Glory as of the only Son from the Father. “Only Son” (monogenēs; older versions, only begotten) means unique, one of a kind, the only one of his kind. Not only begotten in the sense of having a beginning, but unique in his relationship to the Father: he is the Father’s Son as no one else is, sharing his nature (v. 18). The church confessed this against the Arians: begotten, not made.

Full of grace and truth. This phrase unlocks the verses that follow, so do not read past it as a pleasant pair of nouns. Go back to Sinai. Moses asks the one enormous thing: please show me your glory. He is told that no man can see God’s face and live, and he is put in a cleft of the rock and covered with a hand while God passes by. And what God proclaims as he passes is his own name: the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exodus 34:6). The last two words in the Hebrew are hesed and emet: covenant love and covenant faithfulness, mercy and reliability, the two things you most need to be true about anyone you are going to stake your life on. John writes: we have seen his glory, full of grace and truth. The God who passed by Moses is now seen in Jesus. What Moses asked to see, and was given a fraction of, from behind, through a crack in a rock, they watched eat fish on a beach.

Why does grace come before truth? Because that is how God revealed himself on Sinai: steadfast love first, then faithfulness. In Jesus they are never separated. His grace is not soft on sin, and his truth is not hard on sinners. He tells the woman caught in adultery that he does not condemn her, and then that she must go and sin no more (8:11). Grace without truth would be sentiment that leaves us as we are; truth without grace would be a sentence we could not survive. In him we receive both whole, and we are meant to carry both into how we treat one another.

In a sentence. God’s children are born not by human descent or decision, but of God; and the Word became flesh and lived among us, and we saw his glory, the glory of the Father’s unique Son, full of grace and truth.

On a Tuesday. When you picture God, not the doctrine but the picture that actually shows up when you pray, what is he like? Most of us are carrying something assembled out of guesswork, temperament, and whatever our own father was like. John’s answer to all of it is that you are no longer permitted to guess. God has been seen. He has a face, and it has been described by men who were standing near it. Take one of the Gospel scenes this week, Jesus with a leper, a widow, a thief, and let it correct your picture. And when your own body is tired, sick or ageing, remember that God has worn a body too, and does not despise yours.

For worship. Consider what had to be true for that sentence to be written. The Word, who was in the beginning, through whom every atom that exists was spoken into place, who had never in all eternity been anything less than God, became flesh. Not visited it. Not wore it like a coat and took it off again. Became it. He took a body that could be tired, and hungry, and frightened, and killed; and he pitched it in the middle of a camp of people who would not know him; and he did all of it without ceasing for one instant to be what he had always been. Moses asked to see the glory and was hidden in a rock. John says: we saw it, we heard it, and we ate with it. Glory came down into a tent again. This time the tent had a face.
verseByVerse.note: “Dwelt” means literally “pitched his tent” — God’s presence among his people, as in the tabernacle.

parallels.desc: that I may dwell in their midst
abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness
born of the Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: "(John bore witness about him, and cried out, 'This was he of whom I said, "He who comes after me ranks before me, because he was before me."') For from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace."
verseByVerse.commentary:
(John bore witness about him, and cried out: this was he of whom I said, he who comes after me ranks before me, because he was before me.) For from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace.

John bore witness about him, and cried out. “Cried out”: loudly, publicly, like a herald. Two things about the way this verse arrives. First, John cannot leave the Baptist out even here. Twice now the great poem about the eternal Word has been interrupted by a man with a name and a location. That is not clumsy editing. It is this Gospel refusing, from the first page, to let the Word float free of history. Every time the language lifts off, a witness is put back in the room. Second, John the Baptist has been dead for sixty years by the time this Gospel is written, and the testimony is still ringing in it.

He who comes after me ranks before me, because he was before me. The riddle packs three different time-words into one sentence. Later in arrival. Ahead in rank. Earlier in existence. The middle claim is explained by the third, and the third is the one no one else in Israel could have made. Jesus came after John in time, but ranks above him in dignity, because he existed before him, eternally (8:58).

An older relative’s claim. Here is the detail that gives it its edge, which you only get by reading Luke alongside. John the Baptist was born about six months before Jesus (Luke 1:26, 36). They were relatives. He was the older man. So what is actually being said here, out loud, in public, is a man pointing at a younger relative he has known about his whole life and saying: he existed before I did. Not merely he outranks me, which anyone can say of a superior. He was there first. There is no polite way to hear that sentence. It is either the claim of the prologue or it is madness, and the man saying it has staked his reputation, his following and eventually his head on it.

For from his fullness we have all received. The word is plērōma: the whole contents, everything that is in him, nothing held back in reserve. It is the complete abundance of grace and truth in him (v. 14; Colossians 1:19; 2:9), an inexhaustible supply. Picture the sea filling every vessel that is dipped into it. And the word that governs it all is all. Not the apostles, not the mature, not those who have been at it for thirty years. The oldest saint you know and the person converted last Tuesday are drawing from the same supply, and neither of them is drawing on a smaller tap.

Grace upon grace. Literally grace in place of grace, and the little preposition underneath it is worth having, because the English can be read as merely quantitative, as if the point were simply that there is a lot. The Greek word normally means instead of, one thing taking the place of another. So the picture is not a heap. It is a succession: grace giving way to grace, each one replaced by the next, the way waves arrive. No wave is the last one, and no wave is the same wave. Some read it as the grace of the new covenant in place of the grace of the old (v. 17). Either way, endless grace.

Am I running out of grace? Most of us, somewhere in the middle years, quietly start doing arithmetic: I have confessed this same sin so many times now, I have had my share, whatever I was given at the beginning must be getting thin by this point. That is the arithmetic of a fixed quantity, and it is the wrong arithmetic entirely. The grace you are living on this morning is not the grace of your conversion, stretched and rationed and going grey at the edges. It is a new one. The old one did its work and was replaced, and this is what has been happening every day since, whether or not you noticed a single one of them.

What it does not mean. Grace that keeps arriving can be misheard as grace that does not mind. It is not indulgence; a wave is not a shrug. What is being described is a supply that outlasts your failures, not one that is indifferent to them. The man who reads this and concludes he may now sin comfortably has not understood the sentence. He has understood the size of the supply and missed entirely whose fullness it is coming out of (Romans 6:1–2).

How do I actually receive grace? By coming to Christ himself, again and again, with empty hands. Grace is not a substance stored up in sacraments or earned by effort; it is the favour and help of God given to us in his Son. We receive it as we trust him, and God has given us ordinary means by which he keeps feeding that trust: his word read and preached, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, baptism, and the fellowship of his people. None of them is magic, and none of them is optional for a hungry soul. Go to them not to earn anything but to receive, the way a child goes to the table.

In a sentence. John testified that the one coming after him ranks above him because he existed before him, and from his fullness we have all received grace upon grace.

On a Tuesday. A test you can run this week: at the end of a day you would call a bad one, short-tempered, prayerless, the same old thing, ask whether your instinct is to stay away from God until you have improved, or to come and draw again. The first instinct assumes a fixed allowance you have overdrawn. The second is the only one this verse leaves standing. Come tonight, and draw.

For worship. Nobody is on their last grace. There is another one behind it, and behind that one a fullness that has not been touched. The Son who was before John, before Abraham, before the world, holds in himself all the fullness of God, and he has opened it to the poorest of us without reserve. Wave after wave it comes, and the sea is not lowered. Glory to Christ, from whose fullness we have all received.
verseByVerse.note: John was born about six months before Jesus; “he was before me” points to Jesus’ existence before his birth.

parallels.desc: in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell

verseByVerse.quote: "For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known.

For the law was given through Moses. The law was a gift of God, good and holy (Romans 7:12). It revealed God’s will and exposed sin. Watch the two verbs, because they are not the same verb and John chose them carefully. The law was given: a passive, and Moses is named as the channel it came through.

Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. The Greek here is the prologue’s own verb of arrival, the same one used three verses earlier when the Word became flesh. The law was handed over. Grace and truth walked in. That is the contrast: not a bad thing replaced by a good one, but a description delivered and then the thing itself turning up in person. Not that there was no grace in the law, but that the fullness of grace and truth came in Jesus. The law could command but not give the power to obey; Christ brings the grace that saves.

Moses is not the villain. There is a mistake that has done real damage: reading this verse as though Moses were the villain of it. There is a decisive reason not to set the two men against each other, which is that Jesus in this very Gospel forbids it: if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me (5:46). You cannot use John 1:17 to demote Moses without running straight into John 5:46. Moses is not the opposition. He is a witness for the defence. And the clinching point is the one already planted in verse 14: grace and truth echoes what God called himself on Sinai when Moses asked to see his glory (Exodus 34:6). So the sentence is not saying Moses got the rules and we got the kindness. Moses was shown the grace and the truth, from behind, through a crack, in a proclamation he was told to write down, and John’s claim is that the same grace and the same truth have now come up the road on two feet. Moses had the account. We have the person the account was about.

Does this mean Christians can ignore the Old Testament law? No, but we read it through Christ. The law still shows us God’s holy character and our sin, and its moral heart, summed up in the Ten Commandments, still describes how love for God and neighbour behaves (Matthew 22:37–40; Romans 13:8–10). What has changed is our relation to it. We are not justified by keeping it, because Christ kept it for us and bore its curse (Galatians 3:13). The ceremonial laws of sacrifice and cleanness were shadows, and Christ is the substance (Hebrews 10:1). And now the Spirit writes the law on our hearts, so that we obey from love rather than fear (Jeremiah 31:33).

Jesus Christ. A small thing worth noticing in passing: this is the first time the full name Jesus Christ appears in the Gospel, and one of only two places John writes it. He has spent seventeen verses on the Word, the light, the life, the only Son, and then, at the moment the eternal meets the historical, he puts down a man’s name and his title, as if to say: this one, the one you have heard of.

No one has ever seen God. God in his essence is invisible (Exodus 33:20; 1 Timothy 6:16). Even Moses saw only his back (Exodus 33:23). A reader who knows his Old Testament will object immediately, and he should. Moses and the elders went up the mountain and saw the God of Israel and ate and drank (Exodus 24:9–11). Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up (Isaiah 6:1). Jacob said he had seen God face to face and lived. So what does John mean? He means that nobody has ever seen God as he is in himself, unmediated and unveiled, and that every genuine sighting in the Scriptures was accommodated, screened down to what a creature could survive. But he means something more startling than that, and he says it himself later in the book. Of Isaiah’s vision in the temple, John writes that Isaiah saw his glory and spoke of him, meaning Christ (12:41). The Old Testament sightings of God were not exceptions to this verse. They were early appearances of the one this verse is about.

God the only Son. The ESV notes the readings “the only One, who is God” and, in some manuscripts, “the only Son”. The best manuscripts read monogenēs theos, the only God, or God the only Son. That is a genuine difference in the manuscripts, and it is worth knowing why your Bible may differ from your grandmother’s here. Either way the sentence teaches the same thing: the reading with Son still says he is at the Father’s side and has made him known, and the whole prologue has already said he is God in verse 1. And the older manuscript evidence points, if anything, to the higher reading. The prologue ends as it began: the Word is God (v. 1).

Begotten, not made. The word begotten has confused generations of readers into thinking it means Jesus had a beginning. It does not. The Greek word means one of a kind, the only one of its sort; Isaac is called by the same word in Hebrews 11:17, though Abraham had another son. It speaks of uniqueness of relationship, not of origin in time. This is exactly why the Nicene Creed insists on the strange-sounding phrase begotten, not made: whatever the Son’s eternal relation to the Father is, it is not the relation of a creature to its Creator. He was not produced. He is, and always was, the Father’s own.

Who is at the Father’s side. Literally in the bosom of the Father: tucked into his side, the place of closest intimacy, eternal fellowship. Keep that image, because John is going to use it once more and only once. At the last supper, one of the disciples is lying at Jesus’ side, and it is the identical phrase, the same word, the same posture (13:23). The position the Son eternally occupies with the Father is the position John found himself given with the Son. He is telling you that he knows, from the inside and from one evening at a table, what kind of nearness the sentence describes.

He has made him known. “Made known” (exēgēsato), from which comes exegesis: explained, interpreted, revealed. It means to lead out, to draw out into the open, to narrate something in full; it was used of guides taking you through a place and of priests unfolding an oracle nobody else could read. What is striking is that in the Greek the verb has no object at all. The sentence ends: he has explained. Full stop. Not explained a doctrine, or a subject, or an aspect of God. He has done the explaining, and he is what the explaining consists of. Jesus is the exegesis of God. To know what God is like, look at Jesus: whoever has seen me has seen the Father (14:9).

If Jesus shows us God, what about the hard parts of the Old Testament? They are not a different God. The same Lord who drowned Pharaoh’s army wept over Jerusalem; the same Jesus who welcomed sinners overturned tables in the temple and warned of hell more than anyone in Scripture. Jesus does not cancel God’s holiness and judgment; he reveals them at their most intense, at the cross, where God’s wrath against sin fell on his own Son.
