Names are declarations of intent. Here is one of the great comforts of the Christian life: the names God gives people are not descriptions of their performance. They are declarations of intent. Gideon is addressed as mighty man of valour while he is hiding in a winepress threshing wheat in secret because he is frightened of raiders (Judges 6:11–12). Abram is renamed father of a multitude while he is childless and old. In every case the name arrives first and the man walks toward it, usually badly, and usually for years. That is exactly where most Christians live. You have been told you are a child of God, a saint, a new creation, and the daily evidence is a man or woman who lost their temper before breakfast. The gap is not proof that the name is false. The gap is the normal condition of everyone God has ever renamed, and Simon is in this Gospel partly to prove it.

What it does not mean. A promise is not a permission. The name did not make Peter’s failure unreal or unpainful. He went out and wept bitterly, and this Gospel takes him back to a charcoal fire in chapter 21 and asks him three times whether he loves him, once for each denial. The name did not spare him the reckoning. It meant the reckoning was a restoration rather than a dismissal.

Does naming Simon the rock make him the first pope? Roman Catholic teaching reads this with Matthew 16:18 as the founding of an office passed on to the bishops of Rome. The name is real and prophetic; Peter did become a foundation stone of the church. But Scripture says the church is built on the apostles and prophets together, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20), Peter calls himself a fellow elder (1 Peter 5:1), and nothing in the New Testament speaks of his office passing to successors. Peter’s foundation work was done once, through his preaching and his letters, and we stand on it whenever we believe the gospel he preached.

In a sentence. Andrew brought Simon to Jesus, who looked at him and said that he would be called Cephas, meaning Peter, rock.

On a Tuesday. Ask what name you would give yourself this morning, honestly, from the evidence. Now ask which one God has actually used of you in Scripture, forgiven, child, saint, beloved, and notice that he issued it knowing every single thing you would since do with it, including the part you have never told anyone. He was not misinformed when he named you. When you fail today, do not rename yourself by the failure. Confess it, and walk on toward the name.

For worship. Jesus sees not only who you are, but who his grace will make you. He looked at Simon the way he looks at all his people, and then he said what he intended to make, and he made it. The Lord who renamed the unstable fisherman Rock is the Lord who finishes what he begins (Philippians 1:6). Praise him who calls things that are not as though they were, and then makes them so.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that Cephas (Aramaic) and Peter (Greek) both mean “rock.”

verseByVerse.quote: The next day Jesus decided to go to Galilee. He found Philip and said to him, "Follow me." Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day Jesus decided to go to Galilee. He found Philip and said to him: follow me. Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.

The next day Jesus decided to go to Galilee. North, from the Jordan to Galilee. And before the content, the calendar, because John has been counting, and this is where the count becomes visible. He has marked off successive days since the delegation arrived: the next day (v. 29), the next day again (v. 35), and now the next day once more. And then, at the start of chapter 2, on the third day there was a wedding at Cana. Add them up and John has laid out something very close to a week, which is difficult to read as an accident in a book that opened with the words in the beginning.

A new week of creation. The exact arithmetic is debated, and it is honest to say so; commentators reach six days or seven depending on how the last interval is counted. But the shape is unmistakable, and so is where it lands. A week that begins with a man announcing that the light has come into the world ends at a wedding, with water turned into wine, and the sentence: this, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory (2:11). Genesis 1 is a week that ends with a man and a woman brought together and God looking at what he has made. John’s week ends at a wedding too. He is not merely illustrating the creation account. He is showing that the same person who made the world is now at work making it new.

He found Philip. Here Jesus takes the initiative, and the verb turns round. Everyone so far has been finding somebody: John points, Andrew finds Simon, and in a moment Philip will find Nathanael. Here, for the first time, Jesus himself does the finding. Nobody fetched Philip. Nobody had prayed for him as far as we are told. Jesus went to Galilee and found him. Ultimately it is always Jesus who finds us (Luke 19:10).

Follow me. The call to discipleship, and the first Follow me in this Gospel. Two words, no explanation, no terms offered, no indication of where. It is also, and this is worth carrying to the end of the book, the last thing he says to Peter on the last page, on a beach after breakfast: you follow me (21:19, 22). The first Follow me and the final one are the same. Everything in between is what it looks like to obey it.

Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter. Bethsaida was a fishing town at the north end of the Sea of Galilee. Mark says Peter and Andrew lived at Capernaum (Mark 1:29), perhaps having moved there. And the geography is doing more than colour. Bethsaida is one of the towns Jesus later names in a lament: woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago (Matthew 11:21). Hold those two facts together, because they will not resolve into anything comfortable. Three of the twelve apostles came out of Bethsaida. And Bethsaida, as a town, is the object of one of the severest sentences Jesus ever spoke. The place that supplied the most did not itself believe.

A comfort and a warning. That is a real comfort and a real warning in the same sentence, depending on where you are standing. If you have come out of a family or a church or a town where the gospel was heard for years and did nothing, you are not carrying its verdict; three men walked out of Bethsaida and followed him. And if you have grown up inside a great deal of exposure to Christ and have never actually moved, this verse says that the exposure is not the same thing as the following, and that being near where God is working is a more dangerous position than being far from it, not a safer one.

If Jesus finds us, do I have any part to play? Yes, a real one, but it comes second. You respond: you hear his call, and you follow. The call does not wait on your seeking, but it does summon you to act. When Jesus said follow me, Philip did not stay where he was and wait to be carried. Yet the order matters for your peace. You did not stumble on Christ by your own wisdom or hold on to him by your own strength; he came looking for you, and he will not lose what he has found (10:28). So follow him gladly, and when you feel your grip weakening, remember whose grip it really is.

In a sentence. The next day, about to leave for Galilee, Jesus found Philip, from Bethsaida like Andrew and Peter, and told him to follow him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is the one who seeks and finds. Respond to his call: follow me. Ask what following him would mean in the specific decisions in front of you this week, a conversation, a temptation, the use of an evening, and take the step. And if you were raised near the gospel and have never truly moved, do not assume closeness is enough. Answer him today.

For worship. Two words, to a man who had not asked. It is still, by a distance, the most life-altering sentence anyone has ever had addressed to them. The Creator who began the first week by speaking light has begun a new week by speaking to a fisherman from Bethsaida, and the same word that made the world is now making disciples. Blessed is the Shepherd who goes looking for his sheep and calls them by name.
verseByVerse.note: Bethsaida was a fishing town at the north end of the Sea of Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: Philip found Nathanael and said to him, "We have found him of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip found Nathanael and said to him: we have found him of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.

Philip found Nathanael. Philip has been a disciple for perhaps an hour, and the first thing he does with it is go and find somebody. He was found by Jesus in one verse and is finding a friend in the next. Nobody has taught him to do this, and nobody has told him he is allowed to. Nathanael is not named in the other Gospels; he is often identified with Bartholomew, who is paired with Philip in the lists of apostles (Matthew 10:3). He was from Cana in Galilee (21:2).

We have found him of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote. That is not vague piety; it is a claim with contents, and it is worth refusing to leave it fuzzy. The whole Old Testament points to Jesus (5:39, 46; Luke 24:27). Moses had written of a seed of the woman who would crush the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15), of the offspring of Abraham in whom all nations would be blessed (Genesis 22:18), of a ruler from Judah to whom the obedience of the peoples belongs (Genesis 49:10), of a star coming out of Jacob (Numbers 24:17), and of a prophet like himself whom Israel must hear (Deuteronomy 18:15). The prophets had written of a virgin’s son called God with us (Isaiah 7:14), a child on David’s throne called Mighty God and Everlasting Father (Isaiah 9:6–7), a servant pierced for our transgressions (Isaiah 53:5), a ruler from Bethlehem whose origin is from of old (Micah 5:2), a king coming humble and mounted on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9). Jesus himself will later put it as a standing accusation: you search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me (5:39). And on the Emmaus road he does exactly what Philip has just done, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets (Luke 24:27).

Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph. How people knew him, and in two respects incomplete. He was not from Nazareth in the sense that mattered prophetically; he was born in Bethlehem, which is the very thing Micah had specified and which the crowd will throw at each other in chapter 7 as a reason he cannot be the Christ (7:41–42). And he was not the son of Joseph by birth, as the Gospels insist (Matthew 1:18–25; Luke 1:34–35). Philip did not yet know of the virgin birth. John’s readers know more (1:14). John does not correct him. The mistakes stand on the page, and Nathanael comes anyway, and by the end of the conversation he is confessing more than Philip knew how to say.

What if I get it wrong when I talk about Jesus? Sit with this if you have ever kept quiet because you were afraid of getting it wrong. The first missionary sentence in this Gospel is incomplete twice over, and God used it to bring in an apostle. Philip’s grasp of Christ was partial, second-hand, an hour old, and expressed inaccurately. What he had was true enough to be worth passing on, and the passing on is what he was asked for. Accuracy grows. Nobody is waiting for you to be finished. Say what you know, admit what you do not, and point the person to the Gospels, where Jesus can speak for himself.

A chain of friends. There is a shape here that will not stop repeating. John points at Jesus and Andrew goes. Andrew fetches Simon. Jesus finds Philip. Philip finds Nathanael. Not one link in that chain is a sermon, and not one of them is a stranger. Every single one is somebody telling somebody they already knew.

In a sentence. Philip found Nathanael and told him they had found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, Jesus of Nazareth, Joseph’s son.

On a Tuesday. Read the Old Testament as Philip did: it is about Jesus. When you read it this week, ask of each passage what it promises, what pattern it sets up, or what longing it leaves open that Christ fulfils. And think of one friend you already know, not a stranger, to whom you could say simply: I have found someone you should meet.

For worship. The law and the prophets were never a closed book of rules and riddles; they were a long finger pointing to one man. Every promise, every sacrifice, every king and prophet and psalm was saying his name before he was born. And now he has come, and has a hometown, and is being talked about by a fisherman to his friend. Glory to the Christ of whom all the Scriptures speak.
verseByVerse.note: Nathanael is not named in the other Gospels; he is often identified with Bartholomew, who is paired with Philip in their lists.

parallels.desc: Nathanael of Cana

verseByVerse.quote: Nathanael said to him, "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" Philip said to him, "Come and see." Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said of him, "Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nathanael said to him: can anything good come out of Nazareth? Philip said to him: come and see. Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said of him: behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit!

Can anything good come out of Nazareth? The remark is funnier and smaller than it sounds, and knowing why makes it land better. Nazareth was an obscure village, a hamlet of a few hundred people at most, up a hill off the main road. It is never named in the Old Testament, nor by Josephus, who lists dozens of Galilean towns and knew the region as a commander. There is no prophecy attached to it, no history, nothing, and the Messiah was expected to come from Bethlehem (7:41–42). And Nathanael, we learn at the very end of this Gospel, was from Cana (21:2), the next village along. This is not lofty prejudice from a man in Jerusalem. This is one small place being rude about another small place a few miles away, which is a thing small places have always done.

The ordinary form of unbelief. That makes the objection more useful than a grand one would be, because it is the ordinary form of the thing. Most people do not reject Christ after weighing the evidence. They decline to look, on the grounds that nothing worth having has ever come from that quarter: that sort of church, that kind of person, those people, that book. It is not an argument. It is a reason not to have to make one.

Come and see. Philip does not argue. He invites Nathanael to meet Jesus himself, using Jesus’ own words (v. 39), now travelling: the invitation is being passed along the chain exactly as it was received. He could have pointed out that the Messiah was to be born in Bethlehem and started a debate about origins, and he would have lost, because he had his facts slightly wrong. Instead he refuses the terms and offers the man a look. The best answer to objections is often an encounter with Christ.

What it does not mean. Come and see is regularly quoted as if it meant stop thinking. It means nothing of the kind. This is the Gospel that says at its close that these things were written down, from a much larger body of evidence, precisely so that you might believe (20:30–31); the whole book is a case being made. The invitation is not to suspend your judgement. It is to bring it closer, because there are some things about which no amount of discussion at a distance is worth one look from nearby.

So should I avoid giving reasons when people object? No. Peter tells us always to be prepared to give a reason for the hope that is in us, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15), and Paul reasoned in synagogues and marketplaces. Learn what you can, and answer honest questions honestly. But arguments are not the goal. Philip’s instinct is right: the aim of every answer is to bring the person to Christ himself. So when the objection is really a reason not to look, do not get stuck defending Nazareth. Invite them to read a Gospel with you, to come to church, to see for themselves.

Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit! A true Israelite, honest, sincere, without guile. There is a wordplay in it that a Jewish ear would catch instantly. The word for deceit is dolos, and it is the word used in the Greek Old Testament at Genesis 27:35, when Isaac, shaking, tells Esau what has happened to his blessing: your brother came deceitfully, and he has taken away your blessing. So: here is a true son of Israel, a man descended from Jacob, with none of Jacob in him. Jacob, whose name was heard as deceiver, got everything he wanted by deception and spent twenty years running from the consequences (Genesis 27:35–36). Jesus looks at Nathanael and says: not this one. Psalm 32:2: blessed is the man in whose spirit there is no deceit. And having opened with Jacob, he will close the conversation four verses later with the night Jacob slept on a stone.

Honest, not sinless. Notice what it does not mean. It does not mean Nathanael is sinless, and it does not mean he is nice. The last thing out of his mouth before this was an insult about Jesus’ home town, and it is precisely for that, in a sense, that he is commended. Here is a man who says what he actually thinks. There is no gap between what is in him and what comes out of him. Even his objection was honest. He was rude, and he was honest, and Jesus prefers that to smoothness by a wide margin.

For the awkward one. That is worth saying to the Christian who has always felt himself to be the awkward one: too blunt, too doubtful, the person who asks the question everyone else is too polite to ask, and who has quietly concluded that the smooth people are the spiritual ones. It is not a smooth man that Jesus stops to praise here. It is the sceptic from the next village who said the wrong thing out loud.

In a sentence. Nathanael doubted that anything good could come from Nazareth, but Philip told him to come and see, and Jesus greeted him as a true Israelite with no deceit.

On a Tuesday. Honest doubts can be brought to Jesus. Come and see. If you have questions about the faith, do not hide them or pretend; bring them to him in prayer and to his word, and ask a Christian you trust. And check your own Nazareths: the kinds of people or churches you have decided nothing good could come from. Ask whether that is a judgement or just a reason not to look.

For worship. Good did come out of Nazareth: the best that ever came out of anywhere. The Lord of glory grew up in a place no one thought worth naming, so that no one could say he came only for the important. And he greets an honest sceptic with praise before the man has said a kind word to him. Blessed is the Lord who is not offended by our honest questions, and who answers them with himself.
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth was an obscure village; it is never named in the Old Testament. “No deceit” may contrast Nathanael with Jacob, the deceiver who became Israel.

parallels.desc: your brother came deceitfully
in whose spirit there is no deceit

verseByVerse.quote: Nathanael said to him, "How do you know me?" Jesus answered him, "Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nathanael said to him: how do you know me? Jesus answered him: before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.

How do you know me? Surprise. They had never met. Nathanael’s question is already halfway to a confession; he suspects something extraordinary.

Before Philip called you. That is the order, and it is stated deliberately. Before the human contact, before the invitation, before Nathanael had the first idea that anything was happening, he was already the subject of attention. Everything Philip did was second. There is a whole doctrine in the preposition, and nobody in the scene uses a single technical word for it.

When you were under the fig tree, I saw you. Here it is worth being disciplined, because this is a verse people fill in. We are not told what he was doing. Sitting under one’s own fig tree was a picture of peace and security in the messianic age (Micah 4:4; Zechariah 3:10): they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree, and no one shall make them afraid. The rabbis also used the shade of a fig tree as a place to study and pray. Preachers have supplied the scene for centuries: that he was studying the Scriptures, or praying, or, most attractively, reading Genesis 28 about Jacob at Bethel, which would explain the answer Jesus gives three verses later. Any of those may be right. The text says none of them, and the honest thing is to say so rather than to invent a scene and preach it as though it were reported.

What the effect proves. What we can say is what the effect proves. Whatever happened under that tree was private enough that being told I saw you turned a sceptic into a confessor inside a minute. A man who had been mocking Nazareth moments earlier now says, Rabbi, you are the Son of God. Something was said or thought or wept under that tree that no other human being knew about, and it had just been referred to by a stranger. Jesus saw him, supernaturally, and knew what was in his heart (2:25). A man under a fig tree is a man in the one place he feels unobserved.

For the one who feels unseen. The verse needs handling on both sides, because it comforts one reader and undoes another, and both of them are in the room. To the one who feels unseen, the years of praying in a room nobody knows about, the caring for someone that nobody is counting, the faithfulness that has produced no visible result and no acknowledgement: this is the verse. He saw you. Not deduced you, not was informed about you: saw. And notice he does not say what he saw, then or now. He simply lets you know that the private place was never as private as it felt.

For the one with something to hide. To the one who has something under his own fig tree that he would very much rather were not seen, and most of us do, the same sentence lands as exposure, and it is no use pretending otherwise. He saw that too. But look at what he does with what he saw. He does not use it. He does not name it. He mentions the tree and stops, and the whole weight of the encounter is not accusation but welcome. The one person who has complete access to your private life is the one who came to take away the sin of the world, and he does not use what he knows to shame those who come to him. He uses it to prove he knows who he is talking to.

Does Jesus know everything about me now? Yes. He knew what was in man (2:25), and as the risen Lord he searches minds and hearts (Revelation 2:23). He knows your thoughts before you speak them, your sins you have hidden, and your sorrows you have never voiced (Psalm 139:1–4). For an unbeliever that is a solemn truth, because nothing will be hidden at the judgment. For a believer it is the ground of deep rest: you never have to pretend before him, and you cannot surprise him into rejecting you. He took you knowing everything. Bring him the truth, because he has it already.

In a sentence. When Nathanael asked how Jesus knew him, Jesus said he had seen him under the fig tree before Philip called him.

On a Tuesday. A test, and it is a fair one: how do you feel about being fully known? Not by God in the abstract; by this man, in detail, on the specific matters. If the answer is dread, the problem is not that he sees. It is that you have not yet believed what verse 29 says about him. Take the thing you would least like him to see, and tell him about it today, and then remember that the Lamb takes away sin.

For worship. He had been watching Nathanael before Nathanael had heard his name. That is either the most frightening sentence in the chapter or the most comforting one, and which it is depends entirely on the face of the one who was watching. And we know that face now: it is the face of the Lamb of God, full of grace and truth. Jesus sees you when no one else does, and knows your heart. You are fully known and loved.
verseByVerse.note: Sitting under one’s own fig tree was a picture of peace and security.

parallels.desc: every man under his vine and under his fig tree

verseByVerse.quote: Nathanael answered him, "Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!" Jesus answered him, "Because I said to you, 'I saw you under the fig tree,' do you believe? You will see greater things than these."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nathanael answered him: Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel! Jesus answered him: because I said to you, I saw you under the fig tree, do you believe? You will see greater things than these.

Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel! A great confession, the fullest so far in the Gospel, and it comes from the sceptic. Son of God and King of Israel were both messianic titles (Psalm 2:6–7). Nathanael believes Jesus is the Messiah. He may not yet understand all that Son of God means, but it is true in the fullest sense. Both titles are larger than Nathanael can possibly know.

King of Israel. This is not a devotional phrase. It is a political claim, and in an occupied country it is the kind of claim that gets people killed. Follow it through this Gospel and watch where it goes. A crowd will shout it at him with palm branches on the road into Jerusalem (12:13). And then Pilate will have it written out in three languages and fixed above his head, and the chief priests will object to the wording, and Pilate will refuse to change it (19:19–22). The title Nathanael gives him in a field in Galilee is the title that ends up on his execution notice. He is right, and he has no idea what he is saying, and the man he says it to knows exactly what it will cost.

Because I said to you, I saw you under the fig tree, do you believe? Not a rebuke, but a promise. His faith was based on one small sign. It could be read as a mild reproach, that faith resting on one impressive moment is a thin foundation. But nothing in what follows sounds like a rebuke. Jesus does not tell Nathanael his faith is inadequate. He tells him it is small compared with what is coming, which is a different thing entirely and much kinder.

Jesus does not despise small faith. That distinction matters, because Jesus in this Gospel is notably unfussy about where faith starts. He will tell a royal official that people will not believe unless they see signs and wonders, and then heal his son anyway (4:48–50). He will invite Thomas to put his finger in the wounds (20:27). He never once turns away a small faith for being small. What he does, repeatedly, is refuse to let it stay that size.

You will see greater things than these. The signs of the Gospel, and the glory of the cross and resurrection. Not different things; greater. The direction is set: whatever brought you in is the smallest thing that will ever happen to you. And the honest word on the other side, which the verse also requires: the greater things promised here were not more private words of knowledge. They were a cross and an empty tomb. What Nathanael actually went on to see included the worst week of his life. Greater does not mean more pleasant. It means more of who this person is, and there are parts of who he is that can only be seen from somewhere painful.

What if my faith has gone flat since the beginning? Some Christians have a moment they have been living off for thirty years: a conversion, an answered prayer, a week when God seemed close, and everything since has felt like a slow decline from it. The moment has quietly become a museum rather than a beginning. This verse says the moment was never meant to be the peak. It was the fig tree. It was the thing that got you to look up. Jesus promises greater things, chiefly a deeper sight of himself, and he gives them through his word, through suffering, and through the long faithfulness of ordinary years. Ask him to show you more of himself, and go looking where he has promised to be found.

In a sentence. Nathanael declared Jesus to be the Son of God and King of Israel, and Jesus said that he believed on account of a small thing, but would see greater things.

On a Tuesday. What is the most recent thing you learned about Christ: not remembered, learned? If the answer is some years old, that is not a reason for guilt. It is a reason to take this sentence as addressed to you: he told a man who had believed for about four minutes that the good part had not started yet. Choose one Gospel and read it this month asking a single question: what does this show me of him that I had not seen?

For worship. Whatever you have seen of Christ so far, there are greater things to come. The King of Israel wore his title on a cross, and then rose to wear it on a throne, and the Son of God has more of his glory to show his people than all their years will exhaust. Nathanael saw a stranger who knew his secret. He went on to see the Lamb slain and risen. We will see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

parallels.desc: my King, my Son
the King of Israel, the LORD, is in your midst

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to him: truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.

Truly, truly. Amen, amen: a double truly found only in John (25 times), and this is the first. A solemn introduction to an important statement. And the word itself is strange enough. Amen is what you say to somebody else’s statement: it means yes, that is reliable, let it stand. It is the congregation’s word, said after the prayer. Jesus puts it in front of his own sentences, twice, before he has said anything. He is endorsing his own words with the word designed for endorsing somebody else’s, which is either a piece of extraordinary presumption or a claim about who is speaking. He never argues for his authority in this Gospel. He simply talks as though it is not in question.

I say to you, you will see. The ESV notes that “you” is plural: the promise is for all the disciples. Everything to this point has been addressed to Nathanael personally: I saw you, do you believe. Here the you goes plural. He turns from the one man to the whole group, and by extension to everybody reading. The fig tree was for Nathanael. This is for all of us.

Heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending. Genesis 28:12, Jacob’s dream at Bethel: a ladder set up on the earth, reaching to heaven, and the angels of God ascending and descending on it. Stage it, because the power of the allusion is entirely in the circumstances, and they are not respectable ones. Jacob is running. He has just cheated his brother out of the blessing by dressing in his clothes and lying to his blind father’s face, and Esau has announced his intention to kill him, and he is escaping north with nothing. Night catches him in open country. He takes a stone and puts it under his head and sleeps in the middle of nowhere, alone, guilty, and about as far from a holy place as a man can be. And that is where heaven opens over him: a stairway with the traffic of God going up and down it, and the LORD himself standing above it, promising to be with him and bring him back.

Surely the LORD is in this place. Jacob wakes up afraid and says the sentence that names the place: surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it. This is the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven (Genesis 28:16–17). Read that against verse 26 of this chapter, where the Baptist tells the delegation from Jerusalem: among you stands one you do not know. It is the same discovery, centuries apart, in almost the same words. God turns out to have been present in the place where nobody thought to look for him.

On the Son of Man. Jesus is the ladder. He is the meeting place of heaven and earth, the true Bethel, the house of God, the gate of heaven. The way between God and humanity is open through him alone (14:6). Nathanael, the true Israelite (Israel was Jacob), will see what Jacob saw, fulfilled in Jesus. And there is even a translator’s question in Genesis that Jesus may be settling here. The Hebrew says the angels were ascending and descending on it, or on him; the word is ambiguous, and the ancient rabbis discussed both. Jesus says: on the Son of Man. Jacob thought he had found a place. Jesus says the point of contact is a person. “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself, from Daniel 7:13, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and is given everlasting dominion.

Ascending first. Notice the order, which is odd in Genesis and odd here: ascending first, then descending. Angels are presumed to live in heaven; you would expect them to come down before they go up. They start at the bottom. Wherever the ladder’s foot is, that is where the traffic begins, and Jesus has just said where the foot is standing.

The ladder has legs. That is the whole point, and the reason this verse is the right end to the chapter. Jacob stumbled on the gate of heaven by accident, in the dark, and marked it with a stone and poured oil on it and called it Bethel, house of God, so that he could find it again. Every religion since has been trying to do the same thing: locate the place, secure the access, mark it so it can be returned to. A temple. A shrine. A practice. A state of mind you were in once and have been trying to get back to. Jesus tells a man who has been a believer for about five minutes that the ladder has legs. The meeting-point between heaven and earth is not a site you have to find and not a condition you have to achieve. It is a person who walks about, and who found Philip, and who saw Nathanael under a tree before anyone called him.

Does this mean I will see angels? Not necessarily, and you should not go looking for visions. Jesus is not promising the disciples a literal sighting of a stairway; he is telling them that in him the traffic between heaven and earth is now open, and that they will see it in what he does: the signs, the cross, the resurrection, the ascension. Angels do serve those who will inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), usually unseen. But the wonder of the verse is not the angels. It is that you have access to the Father through the Son, right now, in ordinary prayer, wherever you are, because heaven is open over him and you are in him.

In a sentence. Jesus solemnly promised that they would see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.

On a Tuesday. Wherever you are today, the kitchen, the office, the hospital, the place you feel far from God, say what Jacob said and mean it: surely the LORD is in this place. Then pray, not as someone trying to climb up to God, but as someone for whom the way has been opened in Christ. You do not need a holy place. You need the Son of Man, and you have him.

For worship. The chapter opened in eternity with the Word who was with God. It closes with a promise of heaven standing open over a man from Galilee, and between the two, a week has gone by, several people have been fetched by their friends, and God has begun the whole thing again. And the ladder is a person. Not a place, not a rite, not a mountain, not a season of unusual devotion: a man with a name, who gets tired and sleeps in boats, and up and down whom the whole traffic of heaven runs without pausing. Jacob found the gate of God by accident in the dark and was terrified of it. This one goes looking for men under fig trees, calls them by name before they have been introduced, and invites them to come and see. Heaven is open. It is open over him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “you” is plural: the promise is for all the disciples. “Truly, truly” is a solemn formula found only in John.

parallels.desc: Jacob’s ladder, angels ascending and descending

1.title: The Word Made Flesh
1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.<sup>2</sup>He was in the beginning with God.<sup>3</sup>All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made.<sup>4</sup>In him was life, and the life was the light of men.<sup>5</sup>The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it.<sup>6</sup>There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.<sup>7</sup>He came as a witness, to bear witness about the light, that all might believe through him.<sup>8</sup>He was not the light, but came to bear witness about the light.<sup>9</sup>The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world.<sup>10</sup>He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him.<sup>11</sup>He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him.<sup>12</sup>But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God,<sup>13</sup>who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God.<sup>14</sup>And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.<sup>15</sup>(John bore witness about him, and cried out, “This was he of whom I said, ’He who comes after me ranks before me, because he was before me.’”)<sup>16</sup>For from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace.<sup>17</sup>For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.<sup>18</sup>No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known.<sup>19</sup>And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, “Who are you?”<sup>20</sup>He confessed, and did not deny, but confessed, “I am not the Christ.”<sup>21</sup>And they asked him, “What then? Are you Elijah?” He said, “I am not.” “Are you the Prophet?” And he answered, “No.”<sup>22</sup>So they said to him, “Who are you? We need to give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?”<sup>23</sup>He said, “I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness, ’Make straight the way of the Lord,’ as the prophet Isaiah said.”<sup>24</sup>(Now they had been sent from the Pharisees.)<sup>25</sup>They asked him, “Then why are you baptizing, if you are neither the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?”<sup>26</sup>John answered them, “I baptize with water, but among you stands one you do not know,<sup>27</sup>even he who comes after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie.”<sup>28</sup>These things took place in Bethany across the Jordan, where John was baptizing.<sup>29</sup>The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!<sup>30</sup>This is he of whom I said, ’After me comes a man who ranks before me, because he was before me.’<sup>31</sup>I myself did not know him, but for this purpose I came baptizing with water, that he might be revealed to Israel.”<sup>32</sup>And John bore witness: “I saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove, and it remained on him.<sup>33</sup>I myself did not know him, but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me, ’He on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.’<sup>34</sup>And I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of God.”<sup>35</sup>The next day again John was standing with two of his disciples,<sup>36</sup>and he looked at Jesus as he walked by and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God!”<sup>37</sup>The two disciples heard him say this, and they followed Jesus.<sup>38</sup>Jesus turned and saw them following and said to them, “What are you seeking?” And they said to him, “Rabbi” (which means Teacher), “where are you staying?”<sup>39</sup>He said to them, “Come and you will see.” So they came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day, for it was about the tenth hour.<sup>40</sup>One of the two who heard John speak and followed Jesus was Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother.<sup>41</sup>He first found his own brother Simon and said to him, “We have found the Messiah” (which means Christ).<sup>42</sup>He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, “You are Simon the son of John. You shall be called Cephas” (which means Peter).<sup>43</sup>The next day Jesus decided to go to Galilee. He found Philip and said to him, “Follow me.”<sup>44</sup>Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.<sup>45</sup>Philip found Nathanael and said to him, “We have found him of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.”<sup>46</sup>Nathanael said to him, “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” Philip said to him, “Come and see.”<sup>47</sup>Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said of him, “Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit!”<sup>48</sup>Nathanael said to him, “How do you know me?” Jesus answered him, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.”<sup>49</sup>Nathanael answered him, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!”<sup>50</sup>Jesus answered him, “Because I said to you, ’I saw you under the fig tree,’ do you believe? You will see greater things than these.”<sup>51</sup>And he said to him, “Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”
1.overview:
John opens not at Bethlehem but before creation. The prologue (vv. 1–18) is the overture to the whole Gospel: the Word who was with God and was God, through whom all things were made, has become flesh and lived among us, and in him we have seen the glory of the Father’s only Son, full of grace and truth. The great themes of the book appear here first: life and light, darkness that cannot overcome the light, witness, the world that does not know him, his own people who do not receive him, and the gift of becoming God’s children through faith, by a birth from God.

The narrative then begins with a week of witness. John the Baptist tells the Jerusalem delegation that he is not the Messiah, not Elijah, not the Prophet, only a voice preparing the way. He points to Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, the one on whom the Spirit came and remained, the Son of God. Two of John’s disciples follow Jesus; Andrew brings his brother Simon, whom Jesus renames Cephas; Philip finds Nathanael, who doubts that anything good comes from Nazareth until Jesus shows he knows him, and then confesses him Son of God and King of Israel. Jesus promises greater things: heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man, Jacob’s ladder fulfilled in himself. One title after another is given to Jesus in this chapter: Word, God, Light, Lamb, Son of God, Rabbi, Messiah, King of Israel, Son of Man. The rest of the Gospel shows what they mean.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Wedding at Cana: Water into Wine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three days later there is a wedding in Cana of Galilee, and Jesus’ mother is there; Jesus and his disciples have also been invited. When the wine runs out, his mother tells him they have no wine. Jesus answers, addressing her as “woman”, that this is not their concern, for his hour has not yet come. She tells the servants to do whatever he says. Nearby stand six stone water jars used for Jewish purification rites, each holding twenty to thirty gallons. Jesus tells the servants to fill them with water, and they fill them to the brim. Then he tells them to draw some out and take it to the man in charge of the feast. He tastes the water that has become wine, not knowing where it came from, though the servants know. He calls the bridegroom over and remarks that people normally serve the best wine first and the cheaper wine once the guests have drunk freely, but he has saved the best until now. This, the first of his signs, Jesus does at Cana, revealing his glory, and his disciples believe in him. Afterwards he goes down to Capernaum with his mother, brothers and disciples, and stays there a few days.
verseByVerse.theology:
John calls the miracles of Jesus 'signs' (semeia) — they are not mere wonders but pointers to a deeper reality. The water-into-wine sign points to who Jesus is (the one who brings the new wine of the kingdom) and what his mission accomplishes (the transformation of the old into the new, abundance replacing scarcity, joy replacing labor). 'His hour had not yet come' — the hour of the cross, the hour of glorification, which will be the ultimate sign to which all others point. The disciples see the sign, believe, and their faith is the intended fruit of every sign in this Gospel.

The material of the sign is the point of the sign. The six jars were there for the Jewish rites of purification — the physical apparatus of a whole system for dealing with uncleanness — and Jesus does not replace the vessels but fills them. The water of ceremonial cleansing becomes the wine of a wedding feast: not the destruction of the old order but its transformation into joy. The quantity settles the tone. A hundred and twenty to a hundred and eighty gallons, at a village wedding, is not a measured response to a stated need; the disproportion is itself the message.

Semeion is established here as this Gospel's word for a miracle, and the choice is deliberate: John never uses the Synoptics' dynamis (mighty work). A sign is a signpost, valueless if you stop at it, and the crowds of chapter 6 will do exactly that. Seven signs are selected, and 20:30-31 states the purpose. He manifested his glory pays the claim of 1:14 — and the first instalment of that glory is a wedding present given anonymously in an unknown village. And his disciples believed in him, though they had already believed (1:41, 45, 49): faith in this Gospel grows and is tested rather than being settled once.
verseByVerse.examples:
The abundance of the provision — six jars of twenty to thirty gallons each — is a sign of the inexhaustible generosity of the kingdom. Jesus honors the institution of marriage by performing his first miracle at a wedding. And 'the best wine last' is the pattern of the gospel: the world offers its best first and then disappoints, but Christ gives his best at the end — the resurrection, the new creation, the eternal feast.

The pastoral register of the first sign is lower than readers expect and deliberately so. Nobody is ill and nobody is dying; a family has run out of drink and will be humiliated for years in a culture where hospitality was an obligation with teeth. The first miracle of the incarnate Son was performed because somebody was going to be embarrassed — which sets the threshold for what may be brought to him far below where most praying puts it. Mary's four words state the trouble and propose nothing: They have no wine.

You have kept the good wine until now is the gospel's shape against the world's. Everything else front-loads — the advertisement better than the product, youth spent early, the decline negotiated afterwards. But the promise must be guarded: it is not an assurance that circumstances improve, and it should not be handed to a suffering Christian as though it were. Plenty of lives get harder. What is promised is a better end, not an easier road — which is precisely why it speaks to the reader who has concluded his best years are behind him.

verseByVerse.quote: On the third day there was a wedding at Cana in Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. Jesus also was invited to the wedding with his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the third day there was a wedding at Cana in Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. Jesus also was invited to the wedding with his disciples.

Meaning first. John 2 shows Jesus beginning his public work in two scenes that belong together. At a village wedding in Cana he turns the water of Jewish purification into an overflowing supply of the best wine: the first of his signs, revealing his glory, the joy of the new age arriving. Then at Passover in Jerusalem he drives the traders out of the temple and says that if they destroy this temple he will raise it in three days, meaning his body. Together they say who he is: the bridegroom who brings the wine of the kingdom, and the true temple where God meets his people, whose death and resurrection will replace the whole old order of cleansing and sacrifice.

On the third day. After the call of Philip and Nathanael (1:43). Before anything else, finish the sum John has been quietly doing since the delegation arrived from Jerusalem. He has marked the days off one at a time, the next day, the next day again, the next day (1:29, 35, 43), and now he writes on the third day. Counting the days from 1:19, this is the seventh day of a new creation week. Commentators reach six days or seven depending on how the last interval is counted, and it is honest to say the arithmetic is not certain. What is not in doubt is that a book which opened with the words in the beginning has just laid out a week and arrived at the end of it. And the third day hints at the resurrection, when his glory would be fully revealed.

Where the week lands. Genesis runs six days of making and ends with a man and a woman brought together, and God looking at what he has made and calling it very good. John’s week ends at a wedding, with more wine than anyone could drink, and the sentence: this, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory (v. 11). He is not decorating the creation account. He is saying that the same person has started again, and that this time the week ends not with a garden but with a feast.

A wedding at Cana in Galilee. Cana was a village in Galilee, a few miles north of Nazareth, small enough that we would not know it existed but for this Gospel. And it is worth remembering who came from there. At the very end of the book John mentions, almost in passing, that Nathanael was of Cana in Galilee (21:2). Which means the man who had asked, a few days earlier, whether anything good could come out of Nazareth is now standing at a wedding in his own village watching Nazareth’s carpenter make the best wine anyone there had ever tasted. Jesus told him he would see greater things. It did not take long.

What a wedding was. Weddings were the great celebrations of village life, lasting up to a week, with the whole community invited. Not an afternoon: a week. The whole village came, and stayed, and the groom’s family was responsible for feeding and supplying all of them. Hospitality in that culture was not a courtesy but an obligation with teeth, and the celebration was often the largest thing a family ever did.

And the mother of Jesus was there. John never names her; she is always the mother of Jesus. Perhaps she was helping, as a relative or friend of the family. Notice the order of the guest list, because it is not what you would expect: she is named first, and simply present. Jesus also was invited, and his disciples with him. He is the add-on. It is worth admitting the obvious possibility, though the text does not press it: a party of half a dozen extra men arriving at a village wedding may be part of the reason a household ran out of drink.

Two scenes, one thread. John, who names Nathanael and Nicodemus and Lazarus and Malchus the servant whose ear was cut off, calls her only the mother of Jesus. Apart from a passing mention (2:12), she appears at only two scenes in the whole book: here, at the first sign, and at the cross, where she is standing when the hour finally arrives (19:25–27). Both times he addresses her the same way: Woman. This scene and that one are the two ends of a single thread.

Jesus also was invited to the wedding with his disciples. Jesus’ first sign is at a wedding. He honoured marriage by his presence (Hebrews 13:4). He was not an ascetic; he came eating and drinking (Luke 7:34), sharing in human joy. And that leaves the plainest fact of the chapter, the one most likely to be walked past. The eternal Word who was with God before there was light spent one of his first recorded days as an incarnate man at a village party, and stayed long enough to notice the drink running out.

Are holiness and enjoyment at odds? Say this to anyone who has quietly come to believe that the serious Christian is the one who does not much like anything. There is a kind of piety that would have been more comfortable if the first sign had been performed in a synagogue. It was performed at a wedding, for a family who would have been embarrassed, and it produced more than a hundred gallons beyond what the occasion strictly required. God gives us richly all things to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). Food, friendship, music, marriage and laughter are his gifts, and receiving them with thanks is not worldliness but worship (1 Timothy 4:4–5). What turns a gift into an idol is not enjoying it but loving it more than the Giver.

What does this say about marriage? That God honours it. Marriage was his idea from the beginning (Genesis 2:24), and Jesus chose a wedding for the first display of his glory. Scripture will go further: marriage between a man and a woman is a living picture of Christ and his church (Ephesians 5:31–32), and history ends with the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9). So a Christian wedding is not merely a private celebration; it is a small sign of the great one. And if you are single, widowed, or your marriage is hard, the deepest wedding is still yours: the Bridegroom has come for his bride, and you belong to her.

In a sentence. On the third day, Jesus, his mother and his disciples were invited to a wedding at Cana in Galilee.

On a Tuesday. Picture Jesus arriving at the last celebration you were at: a wedding reception, a birthday, a table of people laughing too loudly. If the honest image is of the room going quiet, ask where that picture came from, because it did not come from this chapter. He was invited to this one. He went. And he was the reason it did not end early. Jesus is at home at a celebration. Invite him into your joys as well as your sorrows, and thank him for them aloud.

For worship. The Lord of glory went to a village wedding. He who would walk the road to Calvary first walked the road to Cana, and sat among ordinary people on the happiest day of their lives. He is not a stranger to our joy. He made it, he blesses it, and one day he will crown it at his own wedding feast, where the celebration will never run dry. Glory to the Bridegroom, who was glad to be a guest.
verseByVerse.note: Cana was a village in Galilee, a few miles north of Nazareth. A wedding feast could last a week.

verseByVerse.quote: When the wine ran out, the mother of Jesus said to him, "They have no wine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the wine ran out, the mother of Jesus said to him: they have no wine.

When the wine ran out. To feel the verse you have to feel the size of the failure, and by our standards it looks like nothing at all. Nobody is ill. Nobody is in danger. A family has run out of drink at a party. But in a culture built on honour and shame, running out of wine would have shamed the family publicly. Hospitality was a sacred duty, and a wedding host was expected to provide generously. The whole village was present, and the shortfall would be discussed for years: the wedding where the wine ran out. Some have suggested the groom’s household could even face a legal claim for failing their obligation; that may be pressing the evidence, but the direction is right. A social disaster for the bridegroom, and a humiliation with a long tail.

An embarrassment, not a tragedy. So it belongs to a category most of our troubles belong to and most of our praying does not. It is not a tragedy. It is an embarrassment: the sort of thing that will be noticed, and remembered, and told about you, the shortfall, the thing you could not provide, the moment everyone saw you had reached the end of what you had. And that is exactly the register the first sign is performed in, which is not an accident. Jesus could have opened his ministry by raising a dead child. He opens it by rescuing a family’s reputation at a party. Whatever else that tells us, it tells us the threshold is far lower than we assume.

They have no wine. Mary states the problem. She does not tell Jesus what to do. No request. No suggestion. No argument for why he should act, no reminder of who she is, no proposed method. She brings the need to him, states the situation and stops, trusting him to act. A model of prayer.

What it does not mean. That is not a technique, and it should not be turned into one. There is nothing wrong with asking God for specific things; the Psalms are full of people telling him exactly what they want, and Jesus told us to ask (Matthew 7:7). But there is something worth learning in the restraint. A great deal of praying is really the presentation of a plan for approval, and the anxiety in it comes from the fact that we have already decided what the answer has to look like and are now negotiating for it. She lays the problem down where he can see it and leaves the method with him, which turns out to be wise, since what he does is not remotely what anyone would have asked for.

Faith in his character. And notice the direction she faces. There is no evidence she had ever seen him do anything of this kind; John says plainly in verse 11 that this was the first of his signs. She has thirty years of knowing him and no track record of miracles at all. What she has is a settled conviction about what he is like, and she takes a problem to him on the strength of it. Her faith is in his character, not in his compliance.

The deeper meaning. In the prophets, abundant wine is a sign of the messianic age (Isaiah 25:6; Joel 3:18; Amos 9:13–14). Running out of wine may picture the emptiness of the old order: Israel’s religion had run dry. Jesus brings the new wine of the kingdom.

Is it really all right to pray about small things? Yes. Paul says, in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God (Philippians 4:6), and everything includes the small. The God who numbers the hairs of your head (Matthew 10:30) is not bored by your car, your exam, or the awkward meeting on Thursday. Praying about small things is not trivialising God; it is acknowledging that nothing in your life is outside his care. And it keeps you honest, because the person who only prays about emergencies has quietly decided he can manage everything else on his own.

In a sentence. When the wine ran out, Jesus’ mother told him that they had no wine.

On a Tuesday. Name something currently going wrong in your life that you have decided is too small to pray about. Most people can produce one inside a few seconds: the awkward conversation, the thing at work, the shortfall nobody knows about yet. Now notice that you did not really classify it as small. You classified it as unworthy, which is a judgement about God rather than about the problem, and it is precisely the judgement this chapter exists to overturn. Bring that need to Jesus today, simply, and trust him with the answer.

For worship. The first miracle of the incarnate Son of God was performed because somebody was going to be embarrassed. That is the kind of Lord he is. He bends to the small shames of ordinary people and covers them with his kindness. He who will one day bear the great shame of the cross begins by lifting a little one from a bridegroom in Cana. Nothing that troubles his people is beneath his notice.
verseByVerse.note: Running out of wine would have shamed the family publicly.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Jesus said to her, 'Woman, what does this have to do with me? My hour has not yet come.' His mother said to the servants, 'Do whatever he tells you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus said to her: woman, what does this have to do with me? My hour has not yet come. His mother said to the servants: do whatever he tells you.

Woman. A respectful form of address in the first century, not a rude one. Jesus uses it from the cross, tenderly, as he entrusts her to John (19:26). But it is not the word a son would usually use for his mother. It creates a gentle distance and signals a change: his relationship with her is now that of Lord, not son under parental authority.

What does this have to do with me? Literally what to me and to you?, a Hebrew idiom meaning: what do we have in common in this? This is not your business to direct. Jesus acts on his Father’s timing, not his mother’s, however well meant (Luke 2:49). In English it can sound like a brush-off, and coupled with my hour has not yet come it seems to be a refusal, after which, puzzlingly, Jesus goes ahead and does exactly what the situation required. Did his mother change his mind? Did he decline and then relent?

Why does he refuse and then act? Two things dissolve the difficulty. First, the idiom’s force depends entirely on tone: it can be a rebuke, as when demons cry it at Jesus (Mark 5:7), or it can be the gentle this is not for you to arrange of one who is about to act on his own footing. Paired with the courteous Woman, the softer sense is plainly meant. Second, my hour everywhere in this Gospel means one thing, the hour of the cross and the glory that follows it. So my hour has not yet come is not I will not act now; it is the hour of my full unveiling is still ahead. That is exactly why the sign is done so quietly that only the servants know how the wine came to be. This is a veiled foretaste, not the public hour itself.

My hour has not yet come. “The hour” in John is the time of Jesus’ death, resurrection and glorification (7:30; 8:20; 12:23, 27; 13:1; 17:1). Everything in his life moves toward that hour, set by the Father. The full revelation of his glory, and the abundance of the messianic age, will come through the cross, when the wine of his blood will be poured out.

The two ends of his ministry. He calls her Woman here, at the first sign, and says his hour has not yet come. She appears in only one more scene in this Gospel. It is at the cross, when the hour has arrived, and she is standing near enough to be spoken to, and what he says is: Woman, behold, your son (19:26). The same address at the two ends of his ministry: once when the hour was still ahead, and once when it had come. He does not stop being her son; he arranges her care with almost his last breath. But from the moment of this verse he relates to her as the one whose hour is coming, and she has to learn to know him that way, which is the hardest thing any mother in history has been asked to do.

Do whatever he tells you. Mary’s last recorded words in the Gospels, and the best advice she ever gave. She does not take offence. She does not argue or explain. She trusts him, and directs others to obey him. And the sentence has a precedent, and once you see it you cannot unsee it. There is a famine in Egypt, and the people cry to Pharaoh for bread, and Pharaoh says: go to Joseph. What he says to you, do (Genesis 41:55). The same shape exactly: a shortage nobody can fix, a crowd turning to the wrong authority, and the answer being to go to the one man who has what is needed and do what he says without asking how.

Where Christians differ: Mary’s intercession. Roman Catholic devotion has seen Cana as a picture of Mary’s power as intercessor, obtaining favours from her Son. Verdict: the passage shows the opposite emphasis: Jesus gently declines her direction, acts in his own time, and Mary points away from herself to him: do whatever he tells you. She is a model of faith and of pointing to Christ, not a mediator between us and him. There is one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5).

Honouring Mary rightly. This one scene has been made to carry a great deal of weight, and it will not carry the load either way. It is no snub of Mary: he honours her faith and grants the need. Scripture calls her blessed among women and favoured by God (Luke 1:28, 42, 48), and Protestants have often been too shy of saying so. But neither does this scene show her directing him. Her last recorded words point not to herself but away from herself, to him. That is the truest thing Mary ever said, and it is the right word over every life: not do what I tell you, but whatever he tells you. The way to honour her is to take her advice.

Obedience before understanding. Notice what it costs the servants to take it. In a moment they will be told to fill six enormous jars with water when the problem is a shortage of wine, and to carry a cup of it to the man in charge of the catering. There is no explanation offered at any point. They are simply asked to do a series of things that make no sense in the direction of the need, and the wine appears somewhere between the drawing and the serving, which is to say, after they had committed themselves and before they had any evidence. She does not tell them to understand him. She tells them to do what he says.

How do I know what he is telling me to do? Chiefly from Scripture. Jesus’ commands are written down, and most of what he asks of us is already plain: love God, love your neighbour, forgive, tell the truth, be faithful in marriage, give, pray, gather with his people, make disciples. Begin there; most of us have more than enough to obey before we need any further guidance. In decisions Scripture does not settle directly, such as which job, which house, whom to marry among believers, ask for wisdom (James 1:5), take counsel from mature Christians, and choose what best serves Christ and others. You do not need a voice. You need to do what he has already said.

In a sentence. Jesus told his mother that this was not her concern to direct, for his hour had not yet come, but she told the servants to do whatever he said.

On a Tuesday. A great deal of what Christ asks is like carrying water to a wine steward: it does not look connected to the thing you are actually worried about, and you will not know whether it worked until after you have done it. Keeping a promise that costs you. Forgiving someone who has not apologised. Telling the truth when a small lie would ease things. Name one such instruction in front of you this week and do it, before you see how it helps.

For worship. Mary’s word is for you: do whatever he tells you. And the one who tells us is worthy of it. He moves at his Father’s hour and no other, and his timing has never once been wrong. He is not ours to direct, but he is ours to trust, and those who do what he says find, sooner or later, that the water has become wine. Blessed is the Son whose hour came at last, for us.
verseByVerse.note: “Woman” was a respectful form of address, not a rude one. Jesus’ “hour” in John is the time of his death and glorification.

parallels.desc: “Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do”

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were six stone water jars there for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding twenty or thirty gallons. Jesus said to the servants, "Fill the jars with water." And they filled them up to the brim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there were six stone water jars there for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding twenty or thirty gallons. Jesus said to the servants: fill the jars with water. And they filled them up to the brim.

Six stone water jars there for the Jewish rites of purification. Everything in this sign turns on what the water was for, and John tells us in the same breath as the measurement. Picture the jars. Stone, not pottery, deliberately, because stone jars did not become ritually unclean the way earthenware did, so they were used to hold water for ceremonial washing (Mark 7:3–4). Large, waist-high, standing where guests would come in. Their entire function was to hold water for washing: hands before eating and during the meal, vessels, the removal of whatever defilement a person might have picked up in the course of an ordinary week. Six: perhaps a hint of incompleteness, one short of seven. The old order of ritual purification.

The machinery of cleansing. That is the raw material of the miracle. Not a well, not a spring, not a wine jar standing empty. The water of religious cleansing, the physical apparatus of a whole system for dealing with the problem of not being clean enough to come near God, is what he asks them to fill, and it is what comes out as the best wine anyone at that wedding had drunk. The sign is not that Jesus can produce a drink. The sign is that the machinery of purification has become the wine of a wedding feast. What people had been using to try to get clean has turned, in his hands, into the thing you serve at a celebration. And nothing was thrown away to do it: he does not smash the jars and conjure new vessels. He fills the old ones. The washing-water is not condemned; it is fulfilled and turned into joy.

Was the Old Testament law then a bad thing? No. The purification rites were God’s own gift, given to teach Israel that he is holy and that sinners need cleansing before they can come near him. They were good, and they were temporary, like a signpost that is meant to be passed. They could make the body ceremonially clean but never cleanse the conscience (Hebrews 9:9–14). What they pointed to, Christ provides: the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7). So we do not despise the jars. We thank God for them, and we drink what they were waiting for.

Each holding twenty or thirty gallons. Literally two or three measures: about 75–115 litres each. Together, somewhere between 120 and 180 gallons (450–680 litres). Call it something close to a thousand bottles, for a village wedding, late in the feast. It is worth doing the arithmetic, because the number is not decorative. Nobody needed that. The need was for enough wine to get through the evening without disgrace, and what arrives is a quantity the family could not have consumed if the wedding had run a month, and it is theirs to keep. It is not proportionate. It is not a measured response to a stated need. It is lavish, and the lavishness is the message: this is what the kingdom is like, and it does not deal in exactly enough.

Fill the jars with water. An ordinary command. No explanation.

And they filled them up to the brim. Obedience, as Mary had said. Full: no room for anything else to be added, so what follows is not a trick. And it is a small phrase doing real work. They could have half-filled them; it would have been less effort and no less obedient in the letter. The detail is recorded because it is the human contribution to the miracle, and it is the only contribution available. They could not make wine; they could only fill jars, and they filled them until the water was level with the rim.

Does the size of the miracle mean God will always give me more than I need? Not in the sense of more money or easier circumstances. Paul knew hunger and need as well as plenty (Philippians 4:12). What the sign promises is the character of God’s grace: it is never measured out grudgingly. In Christ he gives forgiveness that covers every sin, a Spirit poured out without measure, an inheritance that cannot fade, and a love that surpasses knowledge (Ephesians 3:19). Your circumstances may be thin. His grace to you is not, and it is always more than enough for what he calls you to bear (2 Corinthians 12:9).

In a sentence. Six large stone jars for ritual washing stood there, holding about twenty or thirty gallons each, and Jesus told the servants to fill them with water, and they filled them to the brim.

On a Tuesday. Think of the last thing you knew you were being asked to do and did adequately: the visit made but kept short, the apology offered with a qualification attached, the giving that was calculated to be defensible. None of that is disobedience. It is simply not to the brim. Nobody at the wedding would have criticised a servant for filling a jar three-quarters full, and nobody would have got a hundred and eighty gallons of wine either. Obey Jesus in the ordinary instructions, all the way. Miracles often begin with simple obedience.

For worship. Six jars of water for getting clean, filled to the top by men who did not know why. It came out as the best thing anybody there had ever tasted. That is what Christ does with everything that pointed to him: he fills it to the brim and turns it into joy. The long centuries of washing and sacrifice end not in a smaller religion but in a feast. Praise the Lord whose grace runs over the rim.
verseByVerse.note: Stone jars did not become ritually unclean, so they were used for purification water. The ESV notes that each held two or three measures — twenty to thirty gallons: well over a hundred gallons in all.

parallels.desc: the washings of the Jews

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast." So they took it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to them: now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast. So they took it.

Now draw some out. No prayer, no touch, no word over the water. Just a command to draw it out. This is the moment of the sign, and John refuses to describe it. There is no gesture, no shimmer on the surface of the water. He said fill them; they filled them. He said draw some out and take it to the man in charge; they did. Somewhere in that sentence the water became wine, silently, by his will, and the text does not say where. That is characteristic of this Gospel. John is far more interested in what a sign means than in how it looked.

And take it to the master of the feast. The master of the feast was the guest put in charge of the celebration, the head steward, responsible for the food and drink. He is the man whose job it is to know what is being served and to stop anything unsuitable reaching the guests.

So they took it. More obedience. They took a risk: what if it was still water? Consider what they were being asked to do. They are to walk up to the steward, in front of the party, and hand him a cup of what they personally drew out of a washing jar a moment ago. If nothing has happened, they are not merely mistaken; they are presenting the master of ceremonies with a cup of hand-washing water at a wedding. They had no evidence. They had watched the water go in. Nobody had told them anything had changed. The only thing standing between them and public humiliation was a sentence from a guest, and a woman’s instruction to do whatever he said.

The proof comes after. Note the order, because it will not reverse. They do not taste it first. There is no version of this story in which the servants get to verify the wine in the kitchen and then decide whether to carry it out. That is not a defect in the arrangement. It is what trust is, and every other arrangement is something else wearing trust’s clothes.

Does faith mean acting without any evidence at all? No. The servants were not leaping in the dark; they had a word from Jesus and the testimony of someone who knew him. Christian faith rests on solid grounds: the eyewitness record of his life, death and resurrection, the fulfilled Scriptures, the changed lives around us. What faith does not have is a guarantee in advance of how each step of obedience will turn out. We trust the person, and then we act, and the confirmation often comes after. That is not irrational. It is how every relationship of trust works.

In a sentence. Jesus told the servants to draw some out and take it to the master of the feast, and they did.

On a Tuesday. Faith obeys before it sees the result. Is there something you know Christ is asking of you that you are holding back from until you can see how it will work out? Carry the cup anyway.

For worship. He never touched the water. He told some servants to move it, and they did, and that was the miracle. The Word who spoke the world into being needs no ceremony to change water into wine. He wills it, and it is so. And he chooses, out of sheer kindness, to work through the hands of servants who trust him. Blessed be the Lord who lets us carry what he has made new.
verseByVerse.note: The master of the feast was the guest put in charge of the celebration.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the master of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and did not know where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew), the master of the feast called the bridegroom and said to him, 'Everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the poor wine. But you have kept the good wine until now.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the master of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and did not know where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew), the master of the feast called the bridegroom and said to him: everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the poor wine. But you have kept the good wine until now.

The water now become wine. A real miracle of transformation. Not grape juice, but wine.

And did not know where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew). The humble servants knew; the important master did not. Those who obey Christ see his works. The steward tastes it and cannot account for it. The bridegroom gets the credit and has no idea what for. The guests drink it and never learn anything happened at all. The only people in that building who understand what has just taken place are the ones who were carrying the jars. That is not a random touch. It is a statement about how this knowledge is distributed. It went to the people who did what he said: not to the man with the office, not to the one being honoured, not to the room full of people enjoying the result, but to the servants, who obeyed a strange instruction and therefore found out (7:17).

Where from? The word is pothen, where from, and it is going to follow Jesus through the whole book. The crowd in Jerusalem will say they know where this man comes from and that settles it (7:27). A blind man will tell the authorities that the remarkable thing is precisely that they do not know where he comes from (9:29–30). And at the very end, Pilate, out of his depth in his own judgment hall, will ask him straight out, where are you from? and get no answer at all (19:9). The first person in this Gospel to taste what Jesus has done and be unable to account for it is a wine steward at a party, and he will not be the last.

Everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the poor wine. Normal practice: serve the best first, when people can taste it, and the cheap wine later.

The bridegroom praised by mistake. An irony John surely enjoyed. The steward, having no idea where the wine came from, calls over the man he assumes is responsible and congratulates him. The bridegroom is being praised for the one thing at his own wedding he had nothing whatever to do with. And within a chapter John the Baptist will use that exact word about Jesus: the one who has the bride is the bridegroom (3:29). The real bridegroom is standing in that room.
