Every item on that list may be worth doing. Not one of them is a birth. Bring the list to God, and ask him first for what only he can give.

For worship. If you see the kingdom of God, it is because God has given you new birth. Praise him. You did not climb into his family; you were born into it from above. The God who said let there be light has shone into your heart (2 Corinthians 4:6), and the eyes that could not see now see the King.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “again” (Greek anōthen) can also be rendered “from above.” Nicodemus hears one sense; Jesus means both.

parallels.desc: born of God
born again to a living hope

verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus said to him, "How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother's womb and be born?" Jesus answered, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus said to him: how can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born? Jesus answered: truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.

How can a man be born when he is old? Nicodemus takes it literally, or perhaps means: how can someone my age change completely? A whole life of religious habit cannot be undone. You cannot start over. His question is not absurd; it is the honest bewilderment of natural reason confronting something only God can do. He takes Jesus seriously enough to push back.

Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born? Impossible. Exactly right. A person cannot cause his own birth. That is the point.

Unless one is born of water and the Spirit. Water and Spirit together recall Ezekiel’s promise of cleansing and a new heart: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean from all your uncleannesses … And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you … And I will put my Spirit within you (Ezekiel 36:25–27). Water: cleansing from sin. Spirit: new life. One birth, with two aspects. Nicodemus, the teacher of Israel, should have known this (v. 10).

Ezekiel 36 seen, not only cited. Israel is in exile. The temple is rubble, the land is lost, the name of God has been dragged through the mud of the nations by the very people who carried it, and into that, God says: I will sprinkle clean water on you. I will give you a new heart. I will remove the heart of stone. I will put my Spirit within you. Count the verbs and notice who is doing all of them. There is not one instruction in the passage. God is not telling a defeated people what to do about their condition; he is telling them what he intends to do about it, while they are in no position to contribute anything at all. The water and the Spirit were promised together, in that order, six hundred years earlier, to people who had proved beyond argument that they could not fix themselves. Nicodemus is being told that the promise has arrived, and that he is one of the people it was made about.

Where Christians differ: “born of water”. Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and some Anglican teaching take the water to be baptism, and teach that baptism is the means of regeneration (baptismal regeneration). Others take water to mean physical birth, the water of the womb; others take it as John’s baptism of repentance. Verdict: the best reading, in context, is Ezekiel 36: water and Spirit describe one spiritual birth, the cleansing and renewing work of the Spirit. Nicodemus could not have understood a reference to Christian baptism, not yet instituted, and Jesus expected him to understand (v. 10). Baptism is the sign of this new birth, not its cause. The thief on the cross entered paradise without baptism (Luke 23:43).

Then what is baptism for? Baptism is the sign and seal Christ commanded for those who have been born again and believe (Matthew 28:19; Acts 2:38, 41). It pictures what the Spirit has done: washing from sin, burial with Christ and rising to new life (Romans 6:3–4). It is the believer’s public confession of faith and the church’s welcome into its fellowship. So it matters greatly and should not be neglected, but it is not a switch that produces new life. This Gospel says again and again that it is believing that gives life (1:12; 3:15; 20:31). We hold, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, that baptism belongs to those who profess faith, and we honour paedobaptist brothers and sisters who agree that baptism does not of itself regenerate.

He cannot enter the kingdom of God. Not just see it, but enter it. What Jesus presses on Nicodemus is not a rite he has missed but a work of God he cannot perform on himself.

In a sentence. Nicodemus asked how an old man could be born again, and Jesus answered that unless a person is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter God’s kingdom.

On a Tuesday. You cannot make yourself born again. Ask God for the cleansing and new life only his Spirit can give. If you are older and think it is too late for real change, notice that Nicodemus was old too, and the promise was for him. And if you are trusting in your baptism, or your church membership, ask whether there is the life the sign was meant to signify: faith in Christ, a new love for God, a war with sin.

For worship. I will sprinkle. I will give. I will remove. I will put. Every verb is God’s. The Lord who scattered Israel for its sin promised to wash and remake it himself, and in Christ he has kept that promise for people from every nation. Blessed be the God who does for us what we could never do, and gives us new hearts to love him.
verseByVerse.note: Water and Spirit together recall Ezekiel’s promise of cleansing and a new heart.

parallels.desc: I will sprinkle clean water on you and put my Spirit within you
the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.

That which is born of the flesh is flesh. “Flesh” here means human nature, mortal and fallen, working with its own resources. Like produces like. Natural birth produces natural life. The principle is one everybody already accepts everywhere else. An apple tree does not, under any circumstances or with any amount of encouragement, produce a pear. Water does not rise above its source. Human beings, by nature, can only produce more human nature. Religion, morality and effort, however good, are still flesh.

What it does not mean. The sentence is not an insult aimed at the body. Flesh here does not mean the physical as opposed to the spiritual; this is the Gospel that has just said the Word became flesh and meant it as the highest news in the world. It means everything a person is by birth, including the best of it. The intelligence. The moral seriousness. The religious instinct. The genuine longing after God that had a member of the Sanhedrin walking through Jerusalem after dark to find one. All of that is real, and none of it is spirit, and no quantity of it turns into spirit. If the flesh could produce even a little of the life of God, the correct advice to Nicodemus would be to produce more of it, and every religion on earth gives exactly that advice, in one dialect or another.

And that which is born of the Spirit is spirit. Only the Spirit can produce spiritual life. New birth is not the improvement of the old nature, but the creation of a new one (2 Corinthians 5:17). Flesh cannot become spirit by trying. We do not cooperate in our own birth; the initiative and the power belong to the Spirit.

For the one who has tried and failed. There is a hard comfort in this for anyone who has spent years trying and getting nowhere. The reason the effort did not work is not that it was insufficient. It is that effort was never the mechanism. A man standing in a field willing an apple tree to bear pears is not failing through lack of sincerity. Stop trying to manufacture spiritual life, and ask the Spirit to give it.

For the one raised in a Christian home. There is a warning on the other side, for the reader raised inside all this. Nothing transmits. Not the family, not the church, not the years of sitting under good teaching, not the vocabulary you can use fluently. Flesh gives birth to flesh in a minister’s house as reliably as anywhere else. Your parents’ faith cannot be inherited; it must be given to you as it was given to them.

Does this mean nothing good can come from an unbeliever? Not in the ordinary sense. Unbelievers can be honest, generous, brave and kind, and we should thank God for it; it is his common grace restraining sin and blessing the world (Matthew 5:45). But none of it is spiritual life, and none of it can make a person right with God or produce love for him. The flesh can build hospitals and write symphonies. It cannot give birth to a child of God. That is why the gospel is not advice for decent people to try harder, but news for dead people that God gives life.

In a sentence. Natural birth produces only natural life, but birth by the Spirit produces spiritual life.

On a Tuesday. Think of the last genuinely good thing you did that nobody knew about and that cost you something. Now ask where it came from: whether you talked yourself into it, or whether you found, somewhere in the middle of it, that you wanted to. Wanting to is not something the flesh generates on its own behalf. It is the sort of thing that has to be put there. Thank God for it. No amount of self-improvement can make you spiritual. You need to be born of the Spirit.

For worship. Like produces like, and so we could never have produced him. But the Spirit of God produces what nature never could: sons and daughters who love their Father. Every flicker of true love for God in the world is a birth from above, a new creation where there was only flesh. Glory to the Spirit, the Lord and giver of life.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not marvel that I said to you, 'You must be born again.' The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not marvel that I said to you: you must be born again. The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.

Do not marvel that I said to you, You must be born again. “You” is plural: all of you, all Israel, everyone. He is no longer talking only to the man in the room. Through Nicodemus he is addressing the whole religious establishment, and past them, everyone who has ever assumed that being properly brought up, properly taught and properly serious would be enough. “Must”: no exceptions.

The wind blows where it wishes. The ESV notes that the same Greek word (pneuma) means both “wind” and “spirit”. English cannot carry what Jesus does here, and it is worth knowing what is being lost, because it is not merely an illustration; it is a pun, and the pun is the argument. There are not two words being compared; there is one word being used twice. The same is true in Hebrew, where ruach is the wind over the waters in Genesis 1 and the breath in a man’s nostrils and the Spirit of God, all at once. Jesus is saying a thing about wind and a thing about the Spirit in the same breath, and letting Nicodemus feel the join. Perhaps a breeze was blowing as they spoke on a rooftop at night. The wind is sovereign: it blows where it wills. You cannot control it, command it, or predict it.

And you hear its sound. You see its effects: rustling leaves, moving clouds. The analogy is more exact than it first appears. Wind is not vague. It is one of the most powerful forces on the planet; it takes roofs off and puts ships on rocks. What it is not is manageable. Nobody has ever arranged for it, or scheduled it, or made it come. You cannot see it at any point, only what it is doing to everything else.

But you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. Its source and destination are hidden. That is the answer to the question Nicodemus has been circling. He wants to know how. He is a teacher, and teachers deal in method; a method can be taught, examined, transmitted and improved. Jesus gives him weather. Not because the new birth is vague, but because it is not the kind of thing that has a technique attached.

So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit. The new birth is the sovereign work of God’s Spirit. It cannot be controlled, manufactured or explained by human methods. It comes where he wills (1:13). But its effects can be seen: a changed life. This is a foundation of the Reformed doctrine of effectual calling and irresistible grace: the Spirit gives new birth sovereignly, as he wills.

So is there nothing I can do? There is no technique that produces the new birth, but that does not leave you idle. Wind is unmanageable and sailors are not therefore idle: they cannot make it blow, and they can put up a sail, and it makes all the difference whether they have. Reading Scripture, hearing it preached, praying, keeping company with God’s people: none of these produces the wind. All of them are sails, the means through which God ordinarily gives new life (Romans 10:17; 1 Peter 1:23). And it does not mean nobody can know whether they have been born again; John wrote a whole letter to settle that question (1 John 5:13). If you want God, ask him; the wanting is itself the breeze.

In a sentence. Jesus told Nicodemus not to be surprised that all must be born again, for the Spirit, like the wind, blows where he wills, unseen but known by his effects.

On a Tuesday. Think of a Christian whose life plainly has something in it that yours does not: a settledness, a kindness that costs them, a hunger for God you have caught yourself envying. Now ask whether you could account for it: where it came from, when it started, how they got it. Almost always the honest answer is no; there is simply an effect in the room and no visible cause. That is what this verse says it looks like from the outside. You hear the sound. You cannot trace the wind. Pray today, by name, for someone you love who is not yet born again.

For worship. If you are born again, the sovereign Spirit blew on you. Thank him. And pray for him to blow on those you love. He is the wind that hovered over the first creation and breathed into the dry bones of Ezekiel’s valley, and he has never asked anyone’s permission to bring the dead to life. Come, Holy Spirit, and breathe.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the same Greek word (pneuma) means both “wind” and “spirit.”

parallels.desc: you do not know the way the spirit comes
come from the four winds, O breath

verseByVerse.quote: "Nicodemus said to him, 'How can these things be?' Jesus answered him, 'Are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus said to him: how can these things be? Jesus answered him: are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things?

How can these things be? Nicodemus’ last words in this conversation. He fades from view, bewildered. His second how is deeper than his first: not mocking incredulity but genuine confusion.

Are you the teacher of Israel. Jesus calls him the teacher of Israel, a recognised authority, perhaps one of the most respected rabbis. The article is the sting. Jesus does not say a teacher; he says the teacher. This is the man other teachers consulted.

And yet you do not understand these things? The Old Testament had promised the new birth: a new heart and a new spirit (Ezekiel 36:25–27; 11:19), the circumcision of the heart (Deuteronomy 30:6), the new covenant written on hearts, so that no one would need to say, know the LORD, because they all would (Jeremiah 31:33–34), and the valley of dry bones brought to life by the Spirit (Ezekiel 37). All of them say the same thing: Israel’s problem is not information and the solution will not be effort. God will have to operate. He should have known. A man who had spent forty years in those texts had every piece of the puzzle on the table in front of him.

Why he missed it. So the failure is not a gap in his reading. He knows the verses. He can almost certainly recite them. What he has never done is apply them to himself, because the promise of a new heart is only good news to a man who has concluded that his own heart is the problem, and Nicodemus has spent his life being told, accurately, that his conduct is exemplary. Learning without the Spirit leaves even the greatest teachers blind.

I know my Bible well but feel nothing. What should I do? This is a real condition and it deserves to be named rather than scolded. A person can hold correct positions on every disputed doctrine, follow an argument through Romans, spot a bad sermon inside two minutes, and have the whole apparatus running on nothing. The knowledge is not the problem; Jesus does not tell Nicodemus to read less. But the same equipment that lets a man handle Scripture well can also let him handle it at arm’s length, as a subject rather than as a summons. So read it differently: slowly, prayerfully, asking not what it says but what it says to you, and confessing what it shows you. Ask the Spirit to give you a heart that is moved (Psalm 119:18). And look to Christ, not to your feelings; warmth follows sight of him.

The tone of the rebuke. Note the tone, before this turns into an attack on learning. Jesus asks a question. He does not dismiss him, does not end the conversation, and goes on talking to him for another eleven verses, giving this one bewildered official more sustained teaching on the new birth than he gave anyone else in the Gospels. The rebuke is real and it is not a rejection. It is what it looks like when the light shines on somebody it intends to keep.

In a sentence. When Nicodemus asked how this could be, Jesus asked how the teacher of Israel could fail to understand.

On a Tuesday. When was the last time a passage of Scripture went through the defences: not taught you something new, but got past the part of the mind that assesses and landed on the part that hopes or fears? If that has not happened for a long time, the answer is not merely more study. Nicodemus proves that. Theological knowledge is not the same as spiritual understanding. Ask the Spirit to open your eyes, and read today’s passage on your knees.

For worship. The greatest teacher in Israel was out of his depth, and the true Teacher did not mock him but kept on teaching. Christ is patient with our slowness, and he does not leave his own in the dark. He opened the minds of his disciples to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45), and he still opens ours. Blessed is the Lord who teaches the teachers.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus calls him “the teacher of Israel” — a recognised authority who should have known the prophets’ promises.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen, but you do not receive our testimony. If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how can you believe if I tell you heavenly things?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen, but you do not receive our testimony. If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how can you believe if I tell you heavenly things?

We speak of what we know. The plural is genuinely odd, and it is worth naming the possibilities rather than gliding over it. We: Jesus, and perhaps his disciples, or John the Baptist and the other witnesses whose testimony has already been given and refused, or the Father and the Son, or simply Jesus speaking with the authority of heaven rather than for himself. What is certain is that it is eyewitness testimony. He speaks of what he has seen.

But you do not receive our testimony. The ESV notes that “you” in these verses is plural: Jesus is now addressing Nicodemus’ group, or Israel’s teachers, the whole body Nicodemus came representing. And notice what is not being said. He does not say Nicodemus cannot understand; he says he does not receive. The obstacle is not intellectual ability; this is one of the best-equipped minds in the country. Testimony is not the sort of thing you solve. It is the sort of thing you either take from the witness or refuse, and refusing it is not a failure of comprehension but a decision about a person.

If I have told you earthly things. The new birth, which happens on earth, in people’s lives, illustrated by earthly things like birth and wind. Earthly things does not mean trivial things. It means the things that happen down here: a birth, a wind over a field, water and Spirit at work in a man in Jerusalem.

How can you believe if I tell you heavenly things? Truths about heaven itself, God’s plan, the Son’s relationship to the Father, which only one from heaven could reveal (v. 13): a descent from heaven, a lifting up, a Son given, the love of God for the world. If the visible end of it cannot be received, the far end has no chance.

Should I settle the hard questions before I trust Christ? Not necessarily, and Jesus’ order here is wise. People often want to begin with the furthest questions: predestination and free will, those who never heard, the timetable of the last days, why there is suffering. They are real questions and should not be sneered at, and Scripture says much about them. But notice the order Jesus insists on. He will not take a man to the mysteries of heaven who has not yet dealt with the mystery standing in the room, which is that he needs to be born and cannot arrange it. Settle the plain things first: your need, and Christ’s sufficiency for it. Many hard questions look different from inside the family.

In a sentence. Jesus said they spoke of what they knew and had seen, but their testimony was rejected, and if earthly things were not believed, how could heavenly things be?

On a Tuesday. Think of the doctrine you find hardest, the one you circle back to, the objection that has never quite been answered to your satisfaction. Now ask honestly whether the plain things have been settled: whether the reality of your own need, and the sufficiency of Christ for it, are matters you have dealt with, or matters that remain conveniently open while the harder question absorbs the attention. Sometimes an unresolved difficulty is exactly what it appears to be. Sometimes it is a very comfortable waiting room. Believe what Jesus tells you, even what you cannot fully understand.

For worship. The only one who has seen heaven came down to tell us about it, and stooped to explain it in words about wind and birth so that we could begin to understand. He does not demand that we climb to his level of knowledge. He brings heaven down to ours. Praise the faithful Witness, who speaks what he knows.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “you” in these verses is plural: Jesus is addressing Nicodemus’s whole circle.

verseByVerse.quote: "No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man. And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man. And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.

No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven. No human being has gone up to heaven to bring back knowledge of God (Deuteronomy 30:12; Proverbs 30:4). Jesus grounds his heavenly authority in his heavenly origin: he can speak of heavenly things because he has come from heaven. No mystic, no prophet, no visionary has this. Only the Son of Man, who came down from heaven, can reveal heavenly things. He is from above (v. 31).

But were not Enoch and Elijah taken up to heaven? They were taken (Genesis 5:24; 2 Kings 2:11), but they did not go up and come back to tell what they had seen. Jesus’ point, in the context of verses 11–12, is that no one has ascended to bring down knowledge of heavenly things; only the one who came from heaven can speak of it.

The Son of Man. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “who is in heaven”. If those words are original, they point to the Son’s unbroken communion with the Father even while on earth (1:18).

As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness. Numbers 21:4–9. Go back to the desert, because the picture Jesus reaches for is one of the strangest things in the Old Testament. Israel is in the wilderness, nearly at the end of forty years, and they complain about the food, about the route, about God and Moses in the same breath (Numbers 21:5). God sends poisonous snakes, and people begin to die, all through the camp. When the people repented and cried out, God’s answer was not what anyone would design. He does not remove the snakes. He tells Moses to make a bronze serpent and put it on a pole where the whole camp can see it. Anyone bitten who looked at it lived. Not by medicine, not by effort, but by looking in faith at what God provided.

A strange remedy. Consider how much seems wrong with that remedy on the face of it. It is an image, made at the direct command of the God who had forbidden Israel to make images for worship. It is an image of the very thing that was killing them, raised in the middle of the camp like a standard. And it does not require the dying man to do anything at all: not to bring an offering, not to travel anywhere. A man face down in the sand with poison already in him has one thing left that he can still do, and it is to turn his head.

The serpent’s afterlife. The bronze snake had an afterlife, and it is worth knowing. Israel kept it. Centuries later Hezekiah found them burning incense to it, called it Nehushtan, and broke it in pieces (2 Kings 18:4). Even the instrument of God’s mercy will be turned into an idol if it is kept long enough. The look was never meant to land on the bronze.

So must the Son of Man be lifted up. “Must” (dei): divine necessity. Not may, not will choose to. Given what God had determined to do about sin, and given what sin is, there was no other route. The cross is not a tragedy that overtook a good plan; it is the plan, and it was the plan before there was a wilderness or a serpent or a nation to be bitten (Acts 2:23; Revelation 13:8).

Lifted up. “Lifted up” (hypsōthēnai) has a double meaning, and it is used three times in John (also 8:28; 12:32–34). It means to raise something physically off the ground, and also to exalt, to lift to honour. By now this is plainly John’s method: the darkness did not overcome, or understand, the light (1:5); a man must be born again, or from above (3:3); and now this. John does not leave it to be guessed at. He explains it in his own voice: he said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die (12:33). Lifted up on the cross, and lifted up in exaltation and glory. The cross is his glory. The throne is the cross. He is never more visibly the King than when he is nailed up with a placard over his head announcing it.

What hung on the pole. As the serpent, a symbol of the curse, was lifted up, so Jesus, made a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), would be lifted up on the cross. God’s remedy for a dying camp was to lift up an image of the very thing that was killing them, and to ask nothing but a look. Centuries later the Son of Man was lifted on a Roman cross outside the city, and what hung there was our sin. Not his own; he had none. All of it, laid on one body, in daylight, where the whole camp could see (2 Corinthians 5:21). And those who look to him in faith will live.

What does it mean to look to Christ? To look is to trust: to turn away from every other hope and rest your whole weight on Christ crucified for you. It is not a feeling you must work up or a degree of understanding you must reach. The dying Israelite did not need to understand bronze or theology; he needed to believe God’s word and turn his eyes. So it is for you. Look to Christ when you first come to him, and keep looking: when guilt accuses, when temptation bites, when death comes near. Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth (Isaiah 45:22).

In a sentence. Only the Son of Man, who came from heaven, can reveal heaven, and as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up.

On a Tuesday. If you feel that your sin is the thing killing you, you are not being melodramatic; it is what the passage says is happening. The instruction to you is not to fight the snake, or to explain how you came to be bitten, or to demonstrate improvement first, or to feel the right degree of horror. It is to look. That is the whole of it, and it was deliberately made the one thing a dying man can still manage. Today, when the old guilt bites, look again at the cross.

For worship. He became, in our place, the curse that was killing us, so that looking at him would be the end of it. Look to the crucified Christ and live. That is all the dying Israelites had to do. Lifted up in shame, he is lifted up in glory, and from the cross he draws all who look to him. Glory to the Son of Man, our lifted-up Lord.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “who is in heaven.” In John, “lifted up” means both the cross and his exaltation.

parallels.desc: the bronze serpent on a pole
he said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die

verseByVerse.quote: "that whoever believes in him may have eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That whoever believes in him may have eternal life.

Whoever believes in him. As the Israelites looked at the serpent, we look to Christ in faith. “Whoever”: anyone. Verse 14 has just set the terms and this verse keeps them. Not whoever understands; Nicodemus is proof that understanding is not the entrance. Not whoever qualifies. The dying Israelite did not have to comprehend the metallurgy of the bronze snake; he had to trust that the God who told him to look meant it.

May have eternal life. This is the first appearance in the Gospel of the phrase that will end up being its whole purpose, and it arrives attached to a snake on a pole, which is not where anyone would have put it. “Eternal life” (zōē aiōnios) is the life of the age to come, the life of God himself, given now and lasting for ever. Aiōnios does mean unending, and the endlessness is not to be quietly dropped in favour of something more sophisticated. But the noun matters more than the adjective: zōē, the word from 1:4, the life that was in the Word from the beginning and was never on loan from anywhere. Eternal life is not primarily a very long time. It is a kind of life, his kind, shared out. Not just endless existence, but knowing God: this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (17:3). Not a location, not a duration, not a reward scheme. Knowing a person.

It begins now. The tense is the thing to hold on to. May have is present. Not will receive at death, not will be awarded at the judgment. This Gospel will keep saying it in the present tense until there is no way to miss it: whoever believes has eternal life (6:47); whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life; he does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life (5:24). Passed. Already. It begins now, at the new birth, and continues for ever. For anyone in Christ, death is not the doorway into eternal life but an interruption in the middle of it.

Where do Jesus’ words end? The ESV notes that some interpreters end Jesus’ words at verse 15, with verses 16–21 as John’s comment. Ancient Greek had no quotation marks. Either way, the words are true. In a red-letter edition the next verse may be printed in red or in black depending on which publisher you happen to be holding. There are reasons for thinking John is now reflecting: the tense shifts to the past, God’s giving of his Son is spoken of as a completed thing, and the phrase only Son is one John uses in his own voice elsewhere (1:14, 18; 1 John 4:9). Others reply that nothing signals a change of speaker. Nothing whatever hangs on it. If John wrote it, it is the Spirit-carried testimony of the apostle who leaned on Jesus’ chest, and it is Scripture. If Jesus said it, it is Scripture. The words are not more true in red ink.

Does eternal life mean I will float in the clouds for ever? No. Eternal life is the life of the age to come, and Scripture pictures that age not as a ghostly existence but as resurrection life in a renewed creation: new heavens and a new earth, where God dwells with his people (Revelation 21:1–4). Believers who die go at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and they will be raised bodily when he returns (5:28–29; 1 Corinthians 15:42–44). At the centre of it all is not a place but a person: we will see him and know him and enjoy him for ever. That knowing begins today.

In a sentence. So that whoever believes in him may have eternal life.

On a Tuesday. Ask what would be true tomorrow morning if eternal life had already started. Most of us, if honest, are living as though the real thing begins later and the present is a waiting room with better or worse furniture. This verse says the substance is already in hand and only the full delivery is outstanding, which changes what a bad diagnosis is, and what a good week is, and what is actually at stake on a Tuesday. Spend some of today simply getting to know him better, because that is what eternal life is.

For worship. If you believe in Jesus, you have eternal life now. Rejoice. The life that was in the Word before the world, the life of God himself, has been shared out to dying sinners who looked. It cannot be lost, outlived or buried. Praise the Son, who is the life, and gives it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some interpreters end Jesus’ words at verse 15 and read verses 16–21 as John’s comment.

verseByVerse.quote: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him.

The best-known verse in the Bible. Martin Luther called John 3:16 the gospel in miniature. And that is its problem, which is not textual at all. It is the best-known sentence in the world, and familiarity has worn it smooth. It is on placards at football matches and on the bottom of paper cups. A verse can be worn out the way a coin is worn out: still legal tender, and the face rubbed off. So it is worth taking the words apart, slowly, as though they had not been heard before.

For God so loved the world. The ESV notes that verse 16 can also be rendered: For this is how God loved the world. “So” (houtōs) means in this way, more than so much. The sentence is not measuring the love and pronouncing it enormous. It is pointing at something and saying: that is how. The verse describes how God showed his love: by giving his Son. And of course the degree comes flooding back in the moment the manner is stated, which is why the traditional reading is not wrong in its instinct. But the size of the love is not asserted. It is demonstrated, and then left standing.

The world. This is the word that has been quietly sentimentalised. In John, the world is humanity in rebellion against God (1:10): the world that did not know him, that cannot receive the Spirit (14:17), that hates Christ and will hate his people (7:7; 15:18–19). That is the object of the love. Not a world that was lovable and therefore loved; a world that was hostile and loved anyway. Take the sentimental reading and the verse says God cared about a rather nice planet. Take John’s own vocabulary and it says God set his love on the very thing that was set against him. The wonder is not that the world is big, but that it is bad. God loved those who hated him.

That he gave his only Son. “Gave”: in the incarnation, and supremely on the cross (Romans 8:32). Not sent, though he did send. Gave. To give a thing is to part with it, and the whole weight of the verse rests on the fact that the giver did not keep what he gave. “His only Son” (monogenē): unique, beloved, like Isaac (Genesis 22:2), and not created (1:14, 18). The Father had one Son, eternally his, his delight before there was a world to be delighted in, and put him into the hands of a race that this Gospel has already described as not knowing him and not receiving him. The cost of love.

That whoever believes in him. The way to receive it: faith. “Whoever”: no one who believes is excluded.

Should not perish. “Perish” (apolētai): be destroyed, be lost for ever. The alternative to eternal life is not nothing, but eternal ruin. The alternative is stated without softening, and modern ears want it softened. Perish is a real word about a real outcome. This is not a verse about improving people’s lives. It is a rescue verse, and rescue implies something to be rescued from.

Does perish mean simply ceasing to exist? No. Some have taught that the lost are finally annihilated, but Scripture speaks of the wicked going away into eternal punishment as the righteous go into eternal life, with the same word for both (Matthew 25:46), and of a destruction that is everlasting and conscious, away from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:9; Revelation 14:11). To perish is to be lost: ruined, cut off from God, under his wrath for ever (v. 36). That is a terrible truth, and it is told here not to frighten us for its own sake but to show the size of the rescue. God gave his Son so that we need not perish.

But have eternal life. Present tense: have it now.

For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world. The purpose of his first coming was salvation, not judgment (12:47). This needs a guard, because it is regularly used to cancel the rest of the paragraph. It is gloriously true, and it is a statement of purpose, not a statement that judgment does not exist, as the very next verse proves, since it says outright that those who do not believe are condemned already. The two sit together without strain. A lifeboat does not go out to drown anybody. That the drowning is real is precisely why it was launched.

But in order that the world might be saved through him. Through him alone (14:6; Acts 4:12).

Where Christians differ: God’s love and the extent of the atonement. Some take this verse to prove that Christ died equally for every individual, making salvation possible for all. Verdict: the verse teaches God’s love for a rebellious world, the gift of his Son, and the promise of life to everyone who believes. It is the foundation of the free offer of the gospel to all people: anyone who believes will be saved. It does not say Christ died in the same way for every individual. Elsewhere John shows that Christ lays down his life for his sheep (10:11, 15), and that those who believe are those the Father gives him (6:37, 44). Both truths stand: the gospel is offered to all, and those who believe are saved by a Saviour whose death secured their salvation.

Can I tell anyone that God loves them? Yes, and you should, with care. God’s goodness and kindness extend to every person he has made (Psalm 145:9; Matthew 5:44–45), and his offer in the gospel is sincere to all: he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but would rather they turn and live (Ezekiel 33:11). So you may say to anyone: God so loved the world that he gave his Son, and if you believe in him you will not perish; come to him, and he will not turn you away (6:37). What you should not do is tell someone that God loves them in a way that makes no claim on them, or that they are safe without Christ. The love of John 3:16 is a love that calls rebels to believe.

In a sentence. This is how God loved the rebellious world: he gave his unique Son, so that everyone who believes in him will not perish but have eternal life; for God sent his Son not to condemn the world but to save it through him.

On a Tuesday. Try saying the verse about yourself, out loud, with your own name where the world stands, and notice whether anything in you flinches. Most people can affirm the sentence as a general truth for years without ever once letting it be true in the particular. It was not written to be agreed with. It was written to be believed by somebody. Then think of one person who needs to hear it, and pray for a chance to tell them.

For worship. The world he loved was not lovely. That is the whole scandal of the sentence. Nothing on this side was the reason for it. The love came entirely from the side of the one who was doing the loving, and it has never needed anything here to keep it going. God loved you, a rebel, by giving his only Son. Believe in him, and you will never perish. Glory to the Father who gave, and to the Son who was given.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that verse 16 can also be rendered “For this is how God loved the world” — the stress is on the manner of his love.

parallels.desc: your son, your only son

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God. And this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God. And this is the judgement: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil.

Whoever believes in him is not condemned. No condemnation, now or ever (5:24; Romans 8:1). The verdict is settled.

But whoever does not believe is condemned already. Everything turns on one word, and it is the word that frightens people: already. Take it slowly, because it is more merciful than it sounds. Not that God condemns them for not believing alone, but that they are already under condemnation for their sin, and by refusing Christ, they refuse the only rescue. They remain where they are (v. 36). The verse is not saying that a sentence is passed on people the moment they hear about Christ and decline. It is saying the sentence was passed long before, and that the arrival of Christ is not what put anyone in danger. He walked into a situation that was already lost. Nobody was standing in neutral territory waiting to see how they felt about him.

A rescue, not an examination. That means the gospel is not an examination that a person might fail. It is a rescue that a person might refuse, and those are entirely different things, though they feel similar from the inside. In the first, Christ increases the risk. In the second, he is the only reason the risk has an exit.

Because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God. Unbelief is the final sin, because it rejects the cure.

How strong must my faith be? This verse does real damage in the hands of the wrong reader. There are people who read condemned already and immediately begin auditing themselves for whether they have believed hard enough or sincerely enough to have crossed the line. Read the sentence again. The condemnation attaches to one thing only: not believing in the name of the only Son of God. It is not measuring the quality of anyone’s faith. It is distinguishing between those who have come to him and those who have not. A weak hand on a strong rope is not the same as no hand at all, and this verse is about which rope, not about the strength of the grip. Weak faith in a strong Saviour saves.

And this is the judgment. “Judgment” (krisis): the verdict, the dividing line. Verse 19 does something startling, and it is easy to read past. It defines the judgment, and the definition is not what anyone would write. Not a throne, not a book opened, not a sentence pronounced.

The light has come into the world. Jesus (1:9).

And people loved the darkness rather than the light. The real reason for unbelief: not lack of evidence, but love of sin. People do not reject Jesus because they cannot believe, but because they will not give up the darkness. The judgment, in other words, is not only something done to people at the end. It is something disclosed about them now. God’s verdict turns out to be the publication of a preference that was already there and already operating. That is why the last day can be perfectly just without anybody being surprised by it: the evidence will be what each person actually loved. And note the verb. Not tolerated the darkness, not drifted into it, not failed to escape it. Loved it.

Because their works were evil. They prefer to keep their evil deeds hidden. Which locates the real difficulty exactly where Nicodemus has been told it is. If unbelief were an information problem it could be solved by teaching, and he of all people would already be safe. It is a problem of the affections. And affections are not argued into place; they have to be born.

What of those who have never heard of Christ? This verse describes everyone apart from him: no one is saved another way (14:6; Acts 4:12). Those who never hear are not condemned for rejecting a message they never received, but for their sins against the light they had (Romans 1:20; 2:12). That is why Paul asks how they are to believe in him of whom they have never heard (Romans 10:14). The answer is not speculation but mission. And we may trust that the Judge of all the earth will do what is right (Genesis 18:25), including with infants who die before they can hear: the Reformed confessions teach that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (Westminster 10.3).

In a sentence. Whoever believes is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is already condemned, for the light has come, and people loved darkness because their deeds were evil.

On a Tuesday. Is there any darkness you love more than the light? Name it honestly: the habit, the resentment, the secret, the comfort you will not give up. Then bring it to Jesus, not to be condemned for it, since he came not to condemn, but to be freed from it.

For worship. The Light came into a world that loved the dark, and he did not come to condemn it. He came to bear its condemnation. For those who believe, the verdict is already in, and it reads: not condemned. Blessed is the Son, in whose name there is no condemnation.

parallels.desc: no condemnation

verseByVerse.quote: "For everyone who does wicked things hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works should be exposed. But whoever does what is true comes to the light, so that it may be clearly seen that his works have been carried out in God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For everyone who does wicked things hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works should be exposed. But whoever does what is true comes to the light, so that it may be clearly seen that his works have been carried out in God.

Everyone who does wicked things hates the light. Light exposes. The wicked avoid it, as thieves avoid daylight.

Lest his works should be exposed. “Exposed” (elenchthē): convicted, brought to light, shown for what they are. It is a courtroom and workshop word. And the instinct it describes is universal and immediate. Nobody has to be taught it. A child who has broken something goes quiet and moves toward the door. The whole apparatus of adult life, the edited version we give at dinner parties, the tone we adopt in an email that is covering for something, the friendships that stay carefully shallow, is a very sophisticated development of the same reflex, which is to stay where the lighting is favourable.

Avoidance feels like busyness. This is where the verse becomes uncomfortable rather than merely true, because avoidance of the light is not usually experienced as avoidance. It is experienced as being busy. It is felt as not having time to pray, or as finding a particular book of the Bible dull, or as a sudden strong preference for reading about the faith rather than sitting still in front of God. The man in this verse is not shaking his fist. He simply does not come.

But whoever does what is true comes to the light. “Does what is true” means lives honestly, sincerely, by God’s truth: literally, whoever does the truth. In Scripture truth is not merely a property of statements. It is something a person can do, or fail to do; it means integrity, faithfulness, being in reality the thing one appears to be. Such a person is not afraid of the light. So the two groups are not the clever and the stupid, or the religious and the irreligious. They are those who will come out into the open and those who will not.

So that it may be clearly seen that his works have been carried out in God. His works were done by God’s grace and in union with him, and the light shows it. Perhaps an encouragement to Nicodemus, who had come by night: come into the light.

What it does not mean. This pair of verses can be read as saying that good people come to Christ and bad people avoid him, which would undo the whole chapter. Read the last clause again: his works have been carried out in God. Whatever is found in the light was put there by the one holding the lamp. Nobody in this passage brings his own goodness to the light for inspection and passes. The new birth stands behind every honest thing a person does, which is exactly why coming into the light is not the terrifying act it looks like from outside. This is not a system of salvation by works, but a description of the direction of genuine faith.

How do I come into the light in practice? By refusing to hide from God or from his people. Begin with honest confession to God, naming what you have done rather than speaking of it vaguely (1 John 1:9). Read Scripture in a way that lets it search you, not only inform you (Hebrews 4:12). Where there is a sin that has a grip on you, tell a mature, trusted Christian, and let them pray with you and ask you about it (James 5:16). Put right what can be put right. None of this earns forgiveness; Christ has done that. It is simply what it looks like to live as a forgiven person who no longer needs the dark.

In a sentence. Those who do evil hate the light and avoid it so that their deeds will not be exposed, but those who live by the truth come to the light, so that it is seen that their deeds were done in God.

On a Tuesday. Notice what happens in the first few seconds after somebody criticises you accurately. Not what you eventually conclude after a day of turning it over: the first movement, before the reasoning starts. If it is a scramble for cover, an immediate counter-example, a mental list of the critic’s own faults, that is the reflex of this verse, and everyone has it. The question this chapter asks is not whether the reflex is there. It is whether anything has been born in you that is capable of overriding it and walking toward the lamp. Come out of hiding. Bring your life into Christ’s light, and let him show what is true.

For worship. The remarkable thing about the Christian life is that it makes exposure survivable. The light that shows everything up belongs to the one who came not to condemn but to save, which means the worst that can be found has already been dealt with at the cross, and there is nothing left in the file that can be used against us. Praise the Light, who exposes in order to heal.

parallels.desc: expose the works of darkness

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–36 — John's Final Testimony: The Bridegroom's Friend
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus and his disciples spend time in the Judean countryside, baptising, while John is still free and baptising at Aenon near Salim, where water is plentiful. After a dispute about purification, John’s disciples complain that everyone is now going to Jesus. John answers that people receive only what heaven gives. He is not the Messiah but the one sent ahead, like the friend of the bridegroom, whose joy is complete when he hears the groom’s voice. Jesus’ influence must grow while John’s shrinks. The one from heaven is over all and speaks what he has seen, though few accept it; those who do confirm that God tells the truth. God gives him the Spirit without limit, and the Father, who loves the Son, has entrusted everything to him. To trust the Son is to have eternal life; to refuse him is to remain under God’s wrath.
verseByVerse.theology:
John the Baptist's final words in this Gospel are also its most concentrated theological summary: Jesus comes from above, speaks the words of God, gives the Spirit without measure, and holds in his hands both eternal life and God's wrath. There is no middle ground: whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him. The Baptist who began by pointing to the Lamb of God ends by declaring the eternal stakes of the decision about him.

Verse 30 contains a word that is usually missed: both verbs carry must. Not I ought to step back graciously but a divine necessity — the same word Jesus used at verse 14 of the Son of Man being lifted up. The rise of one and the waning of the other are a single arrangement, and it was not the Baptist's to negotiate. These are among his last recorded words in this Gospel (some think he speaks on to verse 36); he does not appear again except in the past tense.

The closing verses hold eternal life and wrath in the same frame, and the pairing at verse 36 is deliberately asymmetrical: not believes against does not believe, but believes against does not obey (apeitheo, refuses to be persuaded). The unbelief in view is not doubt politely held but the refusal of a person who has a right to be obeyed.

And the final verb is this Gospel's own great word. The wrath of God remains on him is menei, from meno — the abiding word, whose first appearance was the Spirit coming down and remaining on Jesus (1:32-33), which reappeared when the first disciples asked where he was staying and then stayed (1:38-39), and which carries the whole of chapter 15. Something abides on everyone. On Christ the Spirit rests and does not lift; in his people he himself abides; and on the one who refuses him the wrath he was already under simply stays, because nothing has happened to move it. Nothing arrives — which is the same truth as condemned already at verse 18, said with a different verb, and which is also where the mercy lies: what remains can be lifted, and this chapter has already said how.
verseByVerse.examples:
'He must increase, but I must decrease' is the defining characteristic of all genuine ministry — the minister who builds his own kingdom rather than Christ's has misunderstood the calling. The image of the friend of the bridegroom captures perfectly the joy of the one who serves another's marriage rather than his own: he is not jealous, not diminished, but fulfilled in the fulfillment of the one he loves.

The friend of the bridegroom is sharper than a general lesson in humility once the role is understood. He stood beside the groom and served the wedding. The wedding was in a real sense his project — and the moment the bridegroom's voice was heard inside, his work was finished and his job was to go home. The Greek doubles the joy for emphasis: he rejoices with joy, and the perfect tense of verse 29 says that joy is now standing complete, at the exact moment the crowds transfer. He is not managing a loss. He is at the height of his life. And if Jesus is the bridegroom there is a bride, and she is not the audience at the wedding — she is the one being married.

Verse 30 must not be left sentimental, because of what it cost, as the other Gospels tell it. Within months John was arrested for telling the truth about a marriage, and from that cell he sent to ask whether Jesus was after all the one who was to come (Matt. 11:2-3) — not the question of a serenely fulfilled man, but of one whose decrease had gone further than he bargained for. He was beheaded without trial to settle a promise made in front of dinner guests. And Jesus' verdict, delivered while he was in that cell doubting, was that among those born of women no one greater had arisen (Matt. 11:11).

This is the passage for anyone being replaced — the younger colleague who is plainly better at it, the role handed on, the retirement that arrived before the sense of usefulness did, the body doing less than last year. The world has no account of those except loss. Note where the weight of the sentence actually falls: he must increase is doing all the work, and the second clause is only its shadow. Nobody in Scripture is asked to shrink for the sake of shrinking; the decrease is bearable, and is even a completed joy, solely because of who fills the space.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, and he remained there with them and was baptizing. John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because water was plentiful there, and people were coming and being baptized.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, and he remained there with them and was baptising. John also was baptising at Aenon near Salim, because water was plentiful there, and people were coming and being baptised.

Into the Judean countryside. An early ministry in Judea, before the main Galilean ministry, recorded only in John. And notice who is where. Jesus has left Jerusalem, the temple, the council, the centre, and gone out into the countryside. He was in the capital for a feast, had the attention of a member of the Sanhedrin, and could have stayed and built on it. He goes to the fields instead, where the water is, and works there for months that no other Gospel records.

He remained there with them and was baptizing. John clarifies later that Jesus himself did not baptise, but his disciples did (4:2). The narrator records the fact and then goes back and tightens it. There is no record anywhere in the New Testament of Jesus baptising a single person with his own hands, which Paul echoes when he thanks God he baptised almost nobody at Corinth, precisely so that no one could attach themselves to the man who did it (1 Corinthians 1:14–17).

At Aenon near Salim. The location of Aenon (springs) near Salim is uncertain, perhaps in the Jordan valley, or in Samaria.

Because water was plentiful there. Plenty of water: which suggests immersion. Baptists note this; it is not conclusive. It is first a logistical remark: it tells us why a preacher pitched at that particular spot, with enough water for the crowds who came.

Two ministries, no rivalry. What matters more is the picture of two ministries running at once, in the same region, doing overlapping work, without either man treating the other as competition. Jesus is in the Judean countryside. John is some distance off at Aenon. Both are drawing crowds. The text records no meeting, no agreement, no division of territory, and no comment from either about the other. They simply get on with it. That is not indifference; John will speak about Jesus in a moment with more warmth than anyone in the Gospel. It is that neither of them experienced the other’s existence as a problem requiring management. Where two works are genuinely God’s, they do not need a treaty. The only people in this passage who are worried about the arrangement are the followers, which is how it usually goes.

How should I think about other churches in my town? As fellow workers, where they preach the same gospel. Christ has one church, gathered in many congregations, and the success of a faithful church down the road is a gain for the kingdom, not a loss for yours. Pray for them by name, speak well of them, and rejoice when people are converted there. That does not mean every difference is unimportant; where the gospel itself is denied, love must speak plainly. But most of our rivalries are not about the gospel at all. They are about numbers, style and pride, and those are not worth one moment of the Spirit’s grief.

In a sentence. Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, where they baptised, while John was baptising at Aenon near Salim.

On a Tuesday. When another church in your town does well, or another department, or another parent’s child, what is the first thing that happens in you before the correct response arrives? Not what you say; what happens. These verses describe two ministries running side by side with no anxiety in either of them, and the only unease in the passage belongs to men who were not doing either. God’s servants can work side by side without rivalry.

For worship. The Lord of the harvest works in many fields at once, through many hands, and he is never short of servants or of springs. He does not need us to guard his work from one another. Praise the one Lord of one church, who gives growth wherever his word is sown.
verseByVerse.note: The location of Aenon (“springs”) near Salim is uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: (for John had not yet been put in prison)
verseByVerse.commentary:
(For John had not yet been put in prison.)

For John had not yet been put in prison. The other Gospels begin Jesus’ Galilean ministry after John’s arrest (Mark 1:14). John explains that this Judean ministry came earlier, overlapping with John’s. He assumes his readers know the other Gospels.

An eyewitness filling the gap. It is worth sitting with what this little bracket implies about the writer. He is aware that other accounts of Jesus exist. He knows they open the Galilean ministry after John was arrested, and he knows a reader coming from those accounts will be confused to find John still at liberty and still baptising. So he stops the narrative and puts in a note. That is not the behaviour of a man inventing. It is the behaviour of an eyewitness filling in what the earlier accounts left out, aware of where his readers may trip, and taking the trouble to steady them. This whole stretch, the months when the two ministries overlapped, is a period the other Gospels pass over. John was there for it, and it is the reason we have the finest words on humility ever spoken by a human being.

A shadow across the parenthesis. Not yet put in prison. The reader is being told, in advance and in passing, how this ends. The man about to say the loveliest sentence in the Gospels is a few months from a cell and, as the other Gospels record, not long from an executioner. He says I must decrease without knowing the half of what it will mean, and it turns out he meant it anyway. The words were not spoken from a settled retirement. They were spoken on a downward slope, by a man who could feel the gradient and did not yet know where it went.

Do the Gospels contradict each other on the order of events? No. They complement one another. Each Gospel writer selected and arranged true events for his purpose, and John, writing last, often fills in what the others pass over: an early Judean ministry, several visits to Jerusalem, long conversations. Here he even flags the seam for us. Apparent differences in order usually arise because one writer groups events by theme while another follows the calendar more closely. Reading the four together does not weaken our confidence in them; it gives us a fuller, stereoscopic picture of one Lord, from four eyewitness angles.

In a sentence. This was before John had been imprisoned.

On a Tuesday. Almost nobody gets to say he must increase, but I must decrease from a position of strength. It is said, when it is said at all, by people whose decrease has already started and is not going to be reversed, and that is precisely when it counts. If you are on a downward slope, in health, influence or circumstances, this is your season to say it and mean it. And read the Gospels together: they complement each other.

For worship. God holds the times of his servants in his hand, the free months and the prison months alike. The Baptist did not know what was coming, but the Lord did, and he wrote the parenthesis and the prison and the crown. Blessed is the God who orders every chapter of our lives, and wastes none.
verseByVerse.note: The other Gospels begin Jesus’ Galilean ministry after John’s arrest; John fills in an earlier period.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a discussion arose between some of John's disciples and a Jew over purification. And they came to John and said to him, "Rabbi, he who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness — look, he is baptizing, and all are going to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A discussion arose between some of John’s disciples and a Jew over purification. And they came to John and said to him: Rabbi, he who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness, look, he is baptising, and all are going to him.

A discussion arose … over purification. Perhaps about the value of John’s baptism compared with Jesus’, or with Jewish ritual washings. Notice what triggers the whole thing, because John records it as an aside and it is not an accident. The argument that produces the New Testament’s greatest statement about humility began as a dispute about ceremonial washing: whose water counted, which rite was valid, who had the authority to administer it. This Gospel has been circling that question since chapter 2, when six stone jars for the Jewish rites of purification stood at a wedding and were filled with something else entirely.

He who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness. They do not name Jesus. A hint of resentment: the one you helped is now taking your followers. Every word of it is the language of a threatened camp. He who was with you puts Jesus in a subordinate position, the junior figure who used to be part of John’s operation. To whom you bore witness implies he owes his standing to their master, and is now trading on a reference.

Look, he is baptizing, and all are going to him. Jealousy. John’s disciples are upset that Jesus is more popular. And all is not true, and they know it is not true, since John is still baptising crowds big enough to need a spring. All is what anxiety says. It is the arithmetic of a man watching numbers move in the wrong direction, and it is one of the most reliable symptoms of the disease: nobody who is genuinely at peace about a comparison ever needs to reach for a total. And look, the smallest word in the sentence, gives it away. They are not informing him. They are directing his attention, the way one does when a person is failing to be as alarmed as the situation warrants.

Loyal and wrong. The saddest thing in the verse is that they are being loyal. They are not attacking their master; they are defending him, and they have come to him with what they take to be bad news out of real affection. That is worth naming, because this is how the ugliest instincts in church life usually present themselves. Almost nobody is consciously jealous. They are concerned: about standards, about where things are heading, about a church down the road that seems to be doing rather well. And John will not look at what they are pointing at, because he is looking at something else. They are measuring one ministry against another, which is the only arithmetic available to someone who has lost sight of who Jesus is. John is measuring nothing, because he settled the question at the Jordan and has not reopened it since.

How do I deal with jealousy of other Christians? Name it honestly as sin, not as concern, and confess it to God. Then fight it with truth. Remember that their gifts and fruit were given from heaven (v. 27), so envying them is a complaint against God. Remember that you are one body, so their gain is yours (1 Corinthians 12:26). Thank God for them specifically, out loud, and pray for their further blessing; envy rarely survives sincere intercession. And look again at Christ, because jealousy grows where we have stopped being satisfied in him.

In a sentence. After a dispute about purification, John’s disciples complained to him that the one he had testified about was baptising and everyone was going to him.

On a Tuesday. Notice which facts about other Christians you retain. Most people can recall, without effort and often for years, the numbers, the growth, the invitation someone else received. Facts of that kind do not stay in a memory by accident; they are kept because something in us is keeping accounts. It is possible to be entirely sincere, and loyal, and generous in speech, and still be running a ledger that God never opened. Jealousy of other ministries is a constant temptation. Rejoice when others are blessed.

For worship. While his disciples counted heads, John looked at the Lamb, and there was nothing left to count. Christ is the end of all our comparisons. When he is seen, rivalry looks absurd, because every crowd that goes to him is going exactly where it should. Praise the one to whom all are going, and to whom all should go.

verseByVerse.quote: John answered, "A person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John answered: a person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven.

A person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven. Everything comes from God: John’s ministry, Jesus’ ministry, every gift, every success. It is worth weighing how absolute the sentence is, because the temptation is to hear it as modesty and move on. Not most things. Not the important things. Not one. Jesus’ popularity is God’s gift, so there is no reason for jealousy. And John’s role is God’s gift too, and he is content with it (1 Corinthians 4:7).

Devastating in both directions. Applied to the case in hand, it cuts both ways at once. If Jesus is drawing the crowds, heaven gave him the crowds, so envying him is a complaint against God. If John’s numbers are falling, heaven arranged that too, so the decline is not a failure to be fought but an allocation to be accepted. And if John ever had a crowd in the first place, that was given as well, which removes at a stroke any basis for regarding it as his to lose. That last move is the one that does the work. Envy always requires a sense of ownership somewhere: the assumption that a thing was mine, or ought to have been. Take away the ownership and there is nothing left for the envy to attach to. A man cannot be robbed of what he was only ever handed.

Against taking credit. It also cuts the other way, against the reflex to take credit. Whatever gift a person has for teaching, or organising, or listening well, or making a room feel safe, none of it was manufactured. The intelligence was given. The temperament was given. Even the capacity to work hard, which feels more like an achievement than anything else on the list, was given.

If everything is given, does my effort not matter? It matters greatly, and it too is given. Paul says he worked harder than any of the apostles, and in the same breath, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me (1 Corinthians 15:10). God gives gifts so that we will use them diligently, and he holds us accountable for what we do with them (Matthew 25:14–30). The point of this verse is not that we should be passive, but that we should be humble and content: working hard with what we have been given, without pride when it prospers or envy when others prosper more.

In a sentence. John answered that no one can receive anything unless it is given from heaven.

On a Tuesday. Think of another Christian, or another church, whose fruitfulness has cost you something to look at. Now try saying about them, in plain words and meaning it, that heaven gave them that. Most of us can manage the sentence. Rather fewer can manage it without immediately adding a qualification: although, of course. The qualification is the thing to notice. It is the sound of someone who has not quite conceded that the giving was God’s to do. Whatever role God has given you, receive it gladly. And don’t envy what he has given others.

For worship. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above (James 1:17). The breath in our lungs, the faith in our hearts, the fruit of our work and the work itself: all of it comes down from the Father of lights. We have nothing that we did not receive, and so nothing to boast of except the Giver. Glory to the generous God.

parallels.desc: what do you have that you did not receive?

verseByVerse.quote: "You yourselves bear me witness, that I said, 'I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him.' The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice. Therefore this joy of mine is now complete."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You yourselves bear me witness, that I said: I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him. The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore this joy of mine is now complete.

I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him. John had always said so (1:20, 23). He has been saying it since chapter 1, to delegations and to disciples, and it has never once sounded like a disappointment. The reason he can watch the crowd leave without panic is that he never mistook himself for the reason they came.

The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. In the Old Testament, God is the bridegroom of his people (Isaiah 54:5; 62:5; Hosea 2:19–20). Jesus is the bridegroom; his people are the bride (Mark 2:19–20; Ephesians 5:25–32; Revelation 19:7; 21:2). John is quietly applying to Jesus the role that belongs to the LORD himself.

The friend of the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom arranged the wedding and brought the bride to the groom, like a best man. His joy is to see the marriage happen, not to take the bride for himself. He was not a decorative figure. He stood beside the groom and served the wedding; it was, in a real sense, his project. And the moment the bridegroom’s voice was heard, his work was over.

Who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice. Perhaps the bridegroom’s shout of joy on receiving his bride. The Greek doubles the joy for emphasis in a way English cannot: he rejoices with joy. It is not resignation dressed up. It is not a man being gracious about a disappointment. And it is not the joy of a spectator; it is the specific gladness of somebody whose own work has just succeeded, and whose success takes the form of being no longer required.

Therefore this joy of mine is now complete. John is not jealous; he is overjoyed. People going to Jesus is the fulfilment of his whole life. The tense matters: a perfect, a thing brought to fullness and standing full. Not will be complete one day when I have made my peace with this. It is complete, now, at the exact moment the crowds transfer. He is not managing a loss. He is at the height of his life.

The bride is not the audience. There is a quiet largeness in the metaphor that should not be walked past. If Jesus is the bridegroom, there is a bride, and she is not an afterthought or an audience. The people being baptised in that river, and the ones who would follow for two thousand years, are not the crowd at the wedding. They are the one being married.

What does it mean that the church is Christ’s bride? It means that Christ loves his people with the faithful, exclusive, self-giving love of a husband, and has bound himself to them by covenant for ever. He gave himself up for her, to make her holy and present her to himself in splendour (Ephesians 5:25–27). It means the church belongs to him, not to its leaders; ministers are at most the friends of the bridegroom. And it means our story ends with a wedding: the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9). If you are in Christ, you are not merely a guest at that feast. You are part of the bride.

In a sentence. John reminded them that he had said he was not the Christ, but sent ahead, and like the bridegroom’s friend who rejoices at the bridegroom’s voice, his joy was now complete.

On a Tuesday. If you teach, lead, parent or befriend people in the faith, ask whose voice they are learning to love: yours, or the bridegroom’s? Your task is to bring them to him and step back. The next time someone you have helped grows close to Christ in a way that no longer needs you, let it complete your joy rather than diminish it.

For worship. Your joy, like John’s, is to see people brought to Christ, the bridegroom. And how great is that Bridegroom: the LORD who betrothed Israel to himself in faithfulness, now come in flesh to claim his bride from every nation at the cost of his own blood. We will hear his voice, and our joy will be complete. Glory to the Bridegroom of the church.
verseByVerse.note: The friend of the bridegroom arranged the wedding and brought bride and groom together — his joy was the groom’s joy.

parallels.desc: as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride

verseByVerse.quote: "He must increase, but I must decrease."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must increase, but I must decrease.

He must increase. “Must” (dei): divine necessity. Jesus must grow in prominence, in followers, in glory. These are, on most readings, the last recorded words of John the Baptist in this Gospel (some think he speaks on to verse 36). Whatever else is true of the man, this is the sentence he goes out on, and it is worth reading as a final statement rather than a devotional maxim. It is the same word Jesus used at verse 14 about the Son of Man being lifted up. The rise of one and the shrinking of the other are not two separate events, one admirable and one regrettable. They are a single arrangement, and it was not John’s to negotiate.

But I must decrease. John must fade from view. Not reluctantly, but gladly. One of the greatest statements of humility in the Bible. The motto of every true servant of Christ. Think of the moon: it has no light of its own, its whole business is to shine when the sun is not there, and its fading is not a tragedy but the arrival of morning.

What I must decrease came to. Now the part that turns this from a fine sentiment into something costly. He said it, and then it happened, and not gently. Within months he was arrested by Herod for telling the truth about a marriage. He spent the rest of his short life in a fortress cell. From there he sent messengers to ask Jesus whether he was in fact the one who was to come, or whether they should look for another (Matthew 11:2–3), which is not the question of a man serenely fulfilled, but of a man whose decrease had gone considerably further than he had bargained for. And he was beheaded, without trial, to settle a promise made in front of dinner guests. He was describing, without knowing it, the whole remainder of his life.
