The greatest, wobbling. And Jesus’ verdict on him was delivered while he was in that cell, doubting: among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist (Matthew 11:11). The greatest man who ever lived, on the assessment of the only person qualified to make it, is the one who arranged his entire existence around becoming unnecessary, and who wobbled at the end, and was called the greatest anyway.

Does decreasing mean I must think nothing of myself? No. John did not despise himself; he knew exactly who he was, the voice, the friend of the bridegroom, and he did that work with courage. Decreasing is not self-hatred or false modesty. It is the gladness of seeing Christ honoured more than yourself, and the willingness to be forgotten if he is remembered. The decrease is bearable, and in fact a completed joy, solely because of who is filling the space. Nobody in Scripture is ever asked to shrink for the sake of shrinking. You are asked to make room for him, and in him you will find yourself more truly than you ever could by holding on (Matthew 16:25).

In a sentence. He must become greater, and I must become less.

On a Tuesday. This is the verse for anyone being replaced. The younger colleague who is plainly better at it. The role handed on. The children who no longer ring. The retirement that arrived before the sense of usefulness did. The body that is simply doing less than it did, and will do less again next year. Every one of those is a decrease, and the world has no account of them except loss. Think of the thing you are most afraid of losing: not possessions; standing. Being needed, being consulted, being the one who knows. Now ask what would be left if it went. If the answer is nothing much, the thing has quietly become the self rather than the service. Make John’s words your prayer today: Lord, may you increase, and may I decrease.

For worship. He must increase. That clause is doing all the work, and the second clause is only its shadow. Christ is increasing still: his kingdom spreading, his name honoured among the nations, his glory filling more of the earth until it covers it as the waters cover the sea (Habakkuk 2:14). And there is no loss in being eclipsed by him. Glory to the King who must increase, for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: "He who comes from above is above all. He who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks in an earthly way. He who comes from heaven is above all. He bears witness to what he has seen and heard, yet no one receives his testimony."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who comes from above is above all. He who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks in an earthly way. He who comes from heaven is above all. He bears witness to what he has seen and heard, yet no one receives his testimony.

Who is speaking? Verses 31–36 may be John the Baptist’s words continuing, or the Gospel writer’s reflection. Either way, they explain why Jesus must increase. It is the same question raised at verse 16, and for the same reason: the Greek has no quotation marks. It happens twice in this one chapter, which tells you something about how John writes. He moves from reporting a voice to adding his own without seam or announcement, because in his mind the two are saying the same thing. The authority of the words is unaffected either way.

He who comes from above is above all. Jesus, from heaven, is supreme over all. The first half of the verse states the principle underneath everything in this chapter. Origin decides authority.

He who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks in an earthly way. John the Baptist, and every human teacher. Even the greatest prophets speak as earthly men, with limited knowledge. If it is the Baptist speaking, he is describing himself: the greatest man ever born of women filing himself under earth without complaint. He is not being falsely modest. He is being accurate about the one distinction that matters, which is not between a great man and a small one but between everyone born here and the one who came from somewhere else. That is why Nicodemus at the start of this chapter and the Baptist at the end of it are in the same category. The best teacher in Israel and the last of the prophets are both of the earth. Only one person in the passage came down.

He bears witness to what he has seen and heard. Jesus speaks from direct knowledge of heaven (v. 11), which is more than can be said for any other teacher who has ever lived.

Yet no one receives his testimony. Generally speaking, rejection (1:11). Not literally no one, as the next verse shows: whoever receives his testimony. This is the Bible’s ordinary way of speaking about a general refusal, the same idiom as a man saying nobody came to a poorly attended meeting. It is not a statistic. It is a lament. The testimony is perfect. The evidence is not the problem, and it never has been.

If Jesus is above all, how should I weigh other voices? Every other voice is of the earth, however wise, and must be tested by his. That includes teachers you admire, traditions you love, experts, your own feelings, and the spirit of the age. Many of them say true and useful things, and we should listen with humility. But when they contradict what Christ has said in his word, he wins, every time (Galatians 1:8). That is what sola Scriptura means in practice: not that only the Bible is useful, but that only the Bible, as the word of the one from above, has the final say.

In a sentence. The one from heaven is above all, speaking from what he has seen and heard, unlike those from earth, yet few receive his testimony.

On a Tuesday. Notice which voices shape your thinking most in an ordinary week: news, social media, podcasts, friends, your own anxieties. Ask how much time you give to the one voice from above. Listen to the one who comes from heaven above all other voices, and let his word have the last word today.

For worship. He who comes from above is above all: above prophets and teachers, above kings and councils, above every power and every voice. He came down from that height to speak to us of what he had seen. All authority is his, and all truth is safe in his mouth. Bow before the one who is above all.

parallels.desc: you are from below, I am from above

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever receives his testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever receives his testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true.

Whoever receives his testimony. Not literally no one, then: some do.

Sets his seal to this. To set one’s seal to something is to certify it as true, as a seal on a document certifies its authenticity. A seal was pressed into wax or clay by a signet ring, and it was the ancient equivalent of a signature on a contract: this is mine, I stand behind it, and it can be produced against me later. Setting a seal was not an opinion. It was a commitment.

That God is true. To believe Jesus’ testimony is to affirm that God is truthful, since Jesus speaks God’s words (v. 34). So faith, in this verse, is not first a feeling or even first a benefit received. It is a signature. To believe Christ is to put one’s name to the claim that God tells the truth, and to do it in advance of much of the evidence, since a great deal of what God has said has not happened yet. And to refuse it is to call God a liar (1 John 5:10). That is not rhetorical overreach. If God has testified about his Son and a man declines the testimony, there is no third position available. Which quietly disposes of the idea that unbelief is always a modest, humble posture. It is a verdict, and it is a verdict about somebody’s character.

God’s seal on us. And there is comfort in the same image, on the other side. A seal works both ways in Scripture. Believers are told they were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13). The one who signs his name to God’s truthfulness discovers that God has already signed his name to him.

What if I believe but still have doubts? Then you are like many in Scripture: the father who cried, I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24), the psalmists who asked how long, John the Baptist in his cell. Doubt is not the opposite of faith; unbelief is. Faith is trusting God’s word while questions remain. So bring your doubts to God honestly, take them to his word, talk to mature believers, and keep doing what faith does: praying, gathering, obeying. Your seal is not on the strength of your feelings but on the truthfulness of God, and he does not change when you waver (2 Timothy 2:13).

In a sentence. Whoever accepts his testimony certifies that God is true.

On a Tuesday. Think of a promise of God that your circumstances currently contradict: that he works all things for good, that he will never leave, that the light is not overcome. Now ask which of the two you are treating as the fixed point, the promise or the circumstance. Everybody has one of them as the constant and the other as the thing to be explained. Faith is not the absence of the contradiction. It is which side of it you put your name to while the contradiction is still standing.

For worship. When you believe Jesus, you put your seal on God’s truthfulness. Trust him completely. God is true. He has never broken a word, never failed a promise, never told his people anything but the truth. Let God be true though every one were a liar (Romans 3:4). Blessed be the faithful God, whose seal is on us.
verseByVerse.note: To set one’s seal to something is to certify it as true.

parallels.desc: let God be true

verseByVerse.quote: "For he whom God has sent utters the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he whom God has sent utters the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand.

He whom God has sent utters the words of God. Jesus’ words are God’s words (7:16; 12:49–50; 14:10). Not in the partial, occasional manner of the prophets, but fully.

For he gives the Spirit without measure. God gives the Spirit to Jesus without limit (1:32–33; Isaiah 11:2). Prophets received the Spirit in measure, for particular tasks. Jesus has the fullness of the Spirit. Or: Jesus gives the Spirit without measure to his people. Both are true. The Greek does not supply the subject. It can mean the Father gives the Spirit to the Son without measure, which fits what the Baptist saw at the Jordan when the Spirit came down and remained on him. Or it can mean the Son gives the Spirit without measure, which is what he is said to do from chapter 7 onwards, and what the Baptist announced at the very beginning: this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit (1:33). The two hold together, and the order between them is the point. The Spirit rests on the Son without limit, and out of that fullness the Son gives, which is why what reaches the believer is not a diluted portion.

The Father loves the Son. The eternal love within the Trinity (5:20; 17:24). Before there was anything made, or anyone to save, or a world to be given up for, that was already the case, and it is the oldest fact in existence. Everything in this chapter runs downstream of it. The Son was given because the Father loves the world; all things were put into his hand because the Father loves the Son and would deny him nothing. Mission is always downstream of the eternal love within the Godhead.

And has given all things into his hand. All authority (13:3; Matthew 28:18). Everything is in his hands, including salvation and judgment. The handing over of all things is not an administrative arrangement. It is what love does: the Father withholds nothing from the Son because he loves him. And hold on to the phrase for later in this Gospel. All things into his hand: the same hand out of which, in chapter 10, Jesus will say no one is able to snatch his sheep (10:28–29). What has been put into that hand includes people, and nothing has ever been taken out of it.

Can I be sure I am safe in his hand? If you belong to Christ, yes. The Father has given all things into the Son’s hand, including those who come to him, and Jesus says of them: I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand (10:28). Your security does not rest on the strength of your grip but on his. You will still stumble and doubt, but the one who holds you is the one who loves the Father and does his will, and it is the Father’s will that he should lose nothing of all that he has been given (6:39). That is not a licence to drift. It is the ground on which a trembling believer can stand.

In a sentence. The one God has sent speaks God’s words, for God gives him the Spirit without limit, and the Father loves the Son and has put everything in his hands.

On a Tuesday. Make a list of what is worrying you this week: health, money, children, work, the future. Then, one by one, say over each: this too is in the hands of the Son whom the Father loves. Do whatever duty belongs to you, and leave the rest in his hand.

For worship. The love that holds the universe together is not a policy God adopted toward creatures. It is what was going on between the Father and the Son before there were any creatures, and the gospel is the announcement that it has been opened, and that there is room inside. Everything is in the hands of the Son whom the Father loves. Rest in that, and adore the Father, the Son and the Spirit, one God in eternal love.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.

Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life. Present tense: has it now. The chapter that began with new birth ends with the sharpest possible alternative: eternal life or the abiding wrath of God.

Whoever does not obey the Son. Unbelief is disobedience. Faith in Christ is obedience to God’s command (1 John 3:23). Refusing to believe is rebellion. Note the pairing, which is deliberately asymmetrical: not believes against does not believe, which is what we would expect, but believes against does not obey. The word (apeitheō) means refuses to be persuaded, will not comply. John is not smuggling works into salvation. He is saying that the unbelief in question is not an intellectual position politely held but a refusal of a person who has a right to be obeyed. It is closer to insubordination than to doubt.

Shall not see life. Will not experience eternal life.

But the wrath of God remains on him. “Wrath” (orgē): God’s settled, holy opposition to sin. The only time it appears in John’s Gospel. “Remains” (menei): abides, stays. Not that God becomes angry when someone rejects Christ, but that all people are already under his wrath because of sin (Ephesians 2:3), and it remains on those who refuse the only one who can remove it. We hear wrath and picture something arriving. Nothing arrives. The wrath remains, in the present tense, as the condition already in place: the same truth as condemned already in verse 18, said now with a different verb. Christ bore God’s wrath for those who believe (Romans 5:9; 1 Thessalonians 1:10).

The abiding word. The verb at the end of this chapter is one this Gospel has used before, and the effect of noticing it is sobering. It is menō, the abiding word. Its first appearance was in chapter 1, when the Baptist watched the Spirit come down and remain on Jesus (1:32–33). Its echo will run all the way to chapter 15 and the vine: abide in me, and I in you. And here is the same verb describing what settles on a man who will not have the Son. Something abides on everyone. On Christ, the Spirit rests and does not lift. On those who are his, he himself abides. And on the one who refuses him, the wrath he was born under simply stays where it was, because nothing has happened to move it.

How can a God of love have wrath? Because his love is holy. Wrath is not an outburst of temper but God’s settled, just opposition to evil, the right response of perfect goodness to what destroys his creatures and defies his glory. A God who felt nothing about cruelty, abuse and lies would not be loving; he would be indifferent. And the cross shows the two together: God’s love provided what his justice required, when Christ bore the wrath we deserved as our substitute (Romans 3:25–26; 1 John 4:10). The same chapter that speaks of wrath speaks of a love that gave its only Son. The love is the way out of the wrath.

What it does not mean. This verse frightens people, and some of them are the wrong people. It is not addressed to the Christian who has bad days, or doubts, or a faith that feels thinner than he wishes. The one described here is not struggling with the Son; he is declining him. And the whole sentence turns on a present-tense contrast, has eternal life against remains, which means the two conditions are the two states people are in this evening. If wrath remains rather than arrives, then it can be lifted rather than merely postponed, and this chapter has already said how. It was lifted the way the poison was lifted in the desert: not by the dying man’s exertion but by his looking at something raised up on his behalf.

In a sentence. Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life, but whoever disobeys the Son will not see life, and God’s wrath remains on him.

On a Tuesday. If you have been putting off a decision about Christ, the verse says there is no neutral ground to wait on. Do not stay where you are: look to the lifted-up Son today. And if you do believe, let the seriousness of this verse make you both grateful and urgent: grateful that wrath has been lifted from you, and urgent in prayer and witness for those on whom it still remains.

For worship. The chapter opened with a man who came in the dark because he did not want to be seen. It closes with a sentence about what is resting on people. And between them stands the Son of Man lifted up, and the announcement that God gave him, and the promise that whoever looks will live. If you believe in the Son, God’s wrath has been removed from you, borne by Christ. Thank him for your eternal life, and worship the Lamb who drank the cup so that it would never be ours.

parallels.desc: the wrath of God is revealed

3.title: You Must Be Born Again
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews.<sup>2</sup>This man came to Jesus by night and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him.”<sup>3</sup>Jesus answered him, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God.”<sup>4</sup>Nicodemus said to him, “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?”<sup>5</sup>Jesus answered, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.<sup>6</sup>That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.<sup>7</sup>Do not marvel that I said to you, ’You must be born again.’<sup>8</sup>The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.”<sup>9</sup>Nicodemus said to him, “How can these things be?”<sup>10</sup>Jesus answered him, “Are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things?<sup>11</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen, but you do not receive our testimony.<sup>12</sup>If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how can you believe if I tell you heavenly things?<sup>13</sup>No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man.<sup>14</sup>And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up,<sup>15</sup>that whoever believes in him may have eternal life.<sup>16</sup>“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.<sup>17</sup>For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him.<sup>18</sup>Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God.<sup>19</sup>And this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil.<sup>20</sup>For everyone who does wicked things hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works should be exposed.<sup>21</sup>But whoever does what is true comes to the light, so that it may be clearly seen that his works have been carried out in God.”<sup>22</sup>After this Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, and he remained there with them and was baptizing.<sup>23</sup>John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because water was plentiful there, and people were coming and being baptized<sup>24</sup>(for John had not yet been put in prison).<sup>25</sup>Now a discussion arose between some of John’s disciples and a Jew over purification.<sup>26</sup>And they came to John and said to him, “Rabbi, he who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness—look, he is baptizing, and all are going to him.”<sup>27</sup>John answered, “A person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven.<sup>28</sup>You yourselves bear me witness, that I said, ’I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him.’<sup>29</sup>The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore this joy of mine is now complete.<sup>30</sup>He must increase, but I must decrease.”<sup>31</sup>He who comes from above is above all. He who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks in an earthly way. He who comes from heaven is above all.<sup>32</sup>He bears witness to what he has seen and heard, yet no one receives his testimony.<sup>33</sup>Whoever receives his testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true.<sup>34</sup>For he whom God has sent utters the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure.<sup>35</sup>The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand.<sup>36</sup>Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.
3.overview:
Nicodemus, a Pharisee and member of the ruling council, comes to Jesus at night with a respectful compliment: Jesus must be a teacher from God. Jesus answers with a statement that sweeps away all religious achievement: no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again, or born from above. The Greek word means both, and Nicodemus hears only the first. Jesus explains that this birth is “of water and the Spirit”, the cleansing and new heart God promised through Ezekiel; it is as free and mysterious as the wind. The teacher of Israel ought to have known. The Son of Man, who came down from heaven, must be lifted up as Moses lifted the bronze serpent, so that whoever believes may have eternal life.

Then come the most famous words in the Bible: God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. God sent his Son to save, not to condemn; but those who refuse him stand condemned already, because they love darkness rather than light. In the second half of the chapter John the Baptist, told that everyone is going to Jesus, rejoices like the bridegroom’s friend: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” The chapter ends with the choice that runs through the whole Gospel: whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son will not see life, but God’s wrath remains on him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–42 — The Woman at the Well
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Leaving Judea for Galilee, Jesus takes the road through Samaria and rests at noon by Jacob’s well near Sychar. When a Samaritan woman comes to draw water, he asks her for a drink, to her amazement, since Jews and Samaritans keep apart. He tells her that if she knew who was asking, she would ask him for living water. She objects that he has no bucket; is he greater than Jacob? He answers that well water leaves people thirsty again, but the water he gives becomes a spring of eternal life within. She asks for it. He tells her to call her husband, and when she says she has none, he reveals that she has had five, and her present partner is not her husband. She calls him a prophet and raises the dispute over whether to worship on Gerizim or in Jerusalem. Jesus says the time has come when the place will not matter: the Father, who is spirit, seeks worshippers in spirit and truth, though salvation comes from the Jews. She mentions the coming Messiah, and Jesus tells her that he is the one. The returning disciples are surprised but silent. Leaving her jar, she brings the townspeople to see the man who knew her whole life. Jesus tells the disciples his food is doing his Father’s will, and the fields are ripe for harvest now. Many Samaritans believe through her word, and more through his, confessing him the Saviour of the world.
verseByVerse.theology:
The living water Jesus offers is not a religious program or a moral reformation; it is himself — the inexhaustible source of eternal life. 'The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.' Jesus does not merely point to the source of life; he is the source. The worship in Spirit and truth for which the Father seeks is not worship in a particular location but worship in the reality of who God is (truth) and by the power of God's own Spirit — the worship that the new covenant makes possible through the regeneration that Nicodemus could not understand.

The living water is explained by John himself later in the book. Standing in the temple Jesus cries out about rivers of living water, and the narrator adds the interpretation — this he said about the Spirit (7:38-39). So the gift offered at the well is the indwelling Spirit, the same new birth from above that Nicodemus could not grasp one chapter earlier, now pictured as a spring rather than a well. The distinction matters: a well is a store that must be gone to, lowered into and hauled from; a spring is water arriving from underneath under its own pressure, and the verb for welling up means to leap. What Jesus gives does not merely satisfy the drinker — it turns the drinker into a source.

Worship in spirit and truth is not sincerity set against ritual. Spirit is the Holy Spirit who enables it, and truth in this Gospel is a person before it is a quality (14:6) — so both halves are gifts rather than techniques. What is ruled out is worship that is correct and dead, and worship that is warm and invented: truth without Spirit is a corpse, Spirit without truth is a mood. And God is spirit (v. 24) does not mean God is vague or impersonal — the God described here speaks, seeks, loves and sends — but that he has no body and no location, and therefore cannot be arrived at or run out of.

The decisive clause is the Father is seeking such people to worship him (v. 23). Worship is ordinarily conceived as the search conducted from this end; here God is the one out looking, which is precisely what the chapter has been narrating since verse 4. A woman went to a well to fetch water and found somebody already sitting there who had come by a road many of his countrymen avoided. Note too that salvation is from the Jews is from, not for: the privilege was a channel and never a possession.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus's method with the Samaritan woman is a model of contextual evangelism: he begins with her felt need (water), moves to her deeper need (the living water), exposes the root issue (her relationships), and leads her to the question of worship and the identity of the Messiah. He does not condemn; he illumines. The woman's testimony — 'Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did' — is the most basic form of Christian witness: here is someone who knows me completely and has not rejected me.

The five husbands deserve more care than they usually get. John never calls this woman immoral; Jesus never mentions sin to her, never calls her to repent, and never says sin no more — which he does say to the woman of chapter 8 and the man of chapter 5. A woman could not divorce in that world, so five marriages behind her means five times widowed or five times dismissed, or some mixture — things done to her at least as readily as by her. The town does not behave as a town behaves toward someone it has cast out: she speaks, they listen, they come (vv. 29-30, 39). The honest answer is that we are not told, and it matters that it be said, because women have sat through sermons on this chapter and been handed a shame the passage never assigns. (The old reading of the five husbands as an allegory of the five nations resettled in Samaria in 2 Kgs. 17 should also be resisted: it dissolves a real woman into a diagram, which is the one thing this passage refuses to do to her.)

Her testimony is instructive precisely because it is so poor by our standards. One fact, about herself; overstated (all that I ever did, when he had named one arrangement); no doctrine; and a closing line phrased in Greek to expect the answer no — nearer to this couldn't be the Christ, could it? And the town emptied. What travels is not the completeness of the account but the evidence that something has happened to the person giving it. Notice what her sentence leaves out: she never says and he did not despise me, because that is the tone of the whole remark. Being completely known had turned out not to be the disaster she would have predicted — which is the thing most people are most afraid of.

The harvest section is for the discouraged sower, and there are many. One sows and another reaps contains no promise that the sower sees it; the parent who prayed for thirty years, the teacher whose class drifted, the missionary who left with nothing to report are all inside that saying. The promise is in the verse before: sower and reaper rejoice together. In ordinary farming the reaper takes the visible result; here the arrangement is deliberately made so that neither can celebrate without the other.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John (although Jesus himself did not baptize, but only his disciples),
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptising more disciples than John (although Jesus himself did not baptise, but only his disciples),

Meaning first. John 4 sets two people side by side who could hardly be further apart. In chapter 3 Jesus spoke with Nicodemus: a man, a Jew, a respected teacher of Israel, who came by night. In chapter 4 he speaks with a Samaritan woman: a woman, an outsider, with a broken history, met at noon. Both need exactly the same gift, and only one of them goes home and tells a town. The chapter then returns to Cana, where a royal official takes Jesus at his bare word and finds his son alive. The thread through all of it is this: the Son of God crosses every barrier to find his worshippers, and the faith he looks for is faith that believes his word.

The setting. Jesus has been in Judea with his disciples, and his ministry is growing faster than John the Baptist’s (3:22–30). He now travels north to Galilee through Samaria, the hostile country that lay between, and the whole first half of the chapter happens at a single well outside the town of Sychar, under the shadow of Mount Gerizim.

The Pharisees had heard. Read this straight on from the end of chapter 3 and it stops being a bare travel note. Just before, John’s disciples came to him upset and said that all are going to Jesus. Now the same report reaches the Pharisees, who had already sent men to investigate John (1:24), and John words it with care: the Pharisees heard, and Jesus learned that they had heard. The same piece of news travels to two different sets of ears, and the reactions could not be further apart. In one camp it produces a jealousy their master refuses to share. In the other it produces surveillance.

Making and baptising more disciples than John. It is worth noticing what the news actually was, because it was numbers. Not doctrine, not a healing, not a claim he had made: a count of disciples. The reason given for the Pharisees’ attention is that Jesus was growing faster than the competition. When religious authorities begin measuring ministries by headcount, they have already confused the kingdom of God with an institution in rivalry with others. And John the Baptist had already given the only right response to the same figures: he must increase, but I must decrease (3:30).

Although Jesus himself did not baptise, but only his disciples. The narrator comes back to tighten what he wrote at 3:22. There is no record anywhere in the New Testament of Jesus baptising a single person with his own hands. That is not a trivial correction. It removes, at a stroke, any possibility of a class of Christians who could say they had been baptised by Jesus personally. Paul saw the same danger at Corinth and was relieved to have baptised almost nobody, precisely so no one could form a party around the man who did it (1 Corinthians 1:13–17). Whatever divides the church, it was never going to be a hierarchy of who had the better officiant.

Why did he leave? Not in fear. This is a man who had recently cleared the temple courts in front of these same authorities. He goes because a collision now would be premature, and everything in this Gospel runs on an hour that has not yet come (2:4; 7:30). There is a kind of courage that consists of walking away from a fight you could win, at a moment of your own choosing, because the fight is not the point.

Does it matter who baptises me? No. The power of baptism does not lie in the minister, however gifted or famous, but in Christ, who commanded it, and in the faith of the one who is baptised into him. Jesus deliberately left the water to his disciples so that no one would treasure a baptism for the hand that gave it. If you were baptised as a believer by an ordinary pastor in an ordinary church, you were baptised into exactly the same name as those who were baptised by Peter or by the disciples on the Jordan. Thank God for the man who baptised you, but do not boast in him.

In a sentence. Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard he was making and baptising more disciples than John, though it was his disciples, not Jesus himself, who baptised.

On a Tuesday. Jesus avoided unnecessary conflict. Wisdom sometimes means moving on, not because you are afraid but because this is not the battle God has set before you today. And notice what you measure. If the main thing you know about your church, or your own Christian life, is the numbers, you are reading with the Pharisees’ eyes. Ask instead whether Christ is increasing.

For worship. The Lord of glory did not need the crowds and did not chase the figures. He was content to let his servants handle the water while he went on to a well in enemy country to find one woman. He governs his own hour; no council in Jerusalem could hurry it or delay it. And he is still the one who gathers his church, by his Spirit through his servants, so that the glory of every baptism and every conversion goes to him alone.

verseByVerse.quote: he left Judea and departed again for Galilee. And he had to pass through Samaria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He left Judea and departed again for Galilee. And he had to pass through Samaria.

He left Judea and departed again for Galilee. To avoid a premature confrontation with the Pharisees. The hour of his death was fixed by the Father, and Jesus would not let men force it early.

And he had to pass through Samaria. Samaria lay between Judea and Galilee. Many Jews travelled round it, down the Jordan valley through Perea and up again, to avoid contact with Samaritans; the direct route through Samaria took about three days and saved time. So geography did not strictly require it. Going through Samaria was the quicker road, not the compulsory one. When John writes that Jesus had to go this way, he is not reporting a fact about maps.

The word of divine necessity. The word is edei, it was necessary, and this Gospel keeps using it for things that are settled in heaven. You must be born again (3:7). So must the Son of Man be lifted up (3:14). And now: he had to go through Samaria. The necessity that put him on that road is the same necessity that put him on the cross. There was a woman, and a town, that the Father had prepared to hear him.

The whole chapter is an appointment. A woman is going to walk out to a well at the hottest hour of the day, on an errand she has run a thousand times, and find that the shortest route between Judea and Galilee has been redrawn in heaven so that a tired man would be sitting on the wall when she arrived.

Who were the Samaritans? Their neighbours called them half-breeds and heretics, which is how enemies describe each other rather than a neutral account. When Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom in 722 BC it deported the leading families and resettled foreigners in the land, and the population that resulted was mixed in blood and in religion (2 Kings 17:24–41). By Jesus’ day they held to the five books of Moses and nothing else, no prophets and no psalms, and they worshipped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem. The hostility had recent history in it: in the late second century BC the Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus marched north and destroyed the Samaritan temple on Gerizim. That ruin was visible from the well.

Does every detour in my life have a purpose like this? This verse does not promise that every closed door has a well and a waiting woman behind it, or that you will be told the reason. It does say that the God who arranges routes is not confined to the ones that look sensible, and that at least once in history the pointless-looking detour was the whole plan. Scripture says more broadly that God works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28). So hold your detours with open hands. You may never see the reason this side of glory, but you are not on the road by accident.

In a sentence. Jesus left Judea for Galilee, and it was necessary for him to go through Samaria.

On a Tuesday. Most people can look back and find a detour that made no sense at the time: the job that fell through, the move nobody wanted, the illness that emptied a diary. Today’s route, the unplanned meeting, the queue, the delayed train, may be part of God’s plan for someone you will meet. Go through your day with your eyes open for the person the Father may have put at your well.

For worship. The Son did not drift into Samaria. He was sent there by the same love that sent him into the world. Long before the woman left her house that morning, the Father had set her name on his Son’s road, and the Son walked it gladly, though his own people avoided it. That is the God we worship: not one who waits behind a wall for the clean and the qualified, but one who must go through Samaria, because he will not leave his sheep in enemy country.
verseByVerse.note: Samaria lay between Judea and Galilee. Many Jews travelled round it by the Jordan valley; the direct route went through it.

parallels.desc: Philip preaches in Samaria

verseByVerse.quote: So he came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph. Jacob's well was there; so Jesus, wearied as he was from his journey, was sitting beside the well. It was about the sixth hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph. Jacob’s well was there; so Jesus, wearied as he was from his journey, was sitting beside the well. It was about the sixth hour.

A town of Samaria called Sychar. Probably near ancient Shechem, at the foot of Mount Gerizim, close to the modern city of Nablus.

Near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph. The geography is thick with covenant memory, and John mentions Jacob twice. This is the field Jacob bought outside Shechem when he came back from Paddan-aram, one of the only pieces of the promised land a patriarch ever owned outright (Genesis 33:18–20). It is the plot he willed to Joseph (Genesis 48:22), and it is where Joseph’s bones were finally buried after being carried out of Egypt and round the wilderness for forty years (Joshua 24:32). It is where Israel stood and swore that they would serve the LORD (Joshua 24), and where the kingdom tore in half a few generations later (1 Kings 12). There is hardly a square yard of ground in Israel more layered with promise, oath-taking and failure, and it is in Samaria, in enemy country.

Jacob’s well was there. Jacob’s well is still shown near Shechem at the foot of Gerizim, one of the most certainly identified sites in the Gospels. It goes down something over a hundred feet through rock. Somebody had to lower a vessel a hundred feet and haul it up, day after day, for as long as the family lasted.

Jesus, wearied as he was from his journey. The verb means worn out by labour, the exhaustion that comes from work rather than lack of sleep. He is truly human: tired here, thirsty in verse 7, hungry in verse 8. The Word made flesh (1:14) gets tired. This is the Gospel that opened by saying all things were made through him (1:3). Four chapters in, he cannot walk any further and has to sit down. The two facts are placed in the same book by the same author without any sense that they need reconciling, and any account of Christ that finds one of them embarrassing has stopped reading somewhere. The one who made the stars sat down because his legs ached.

Was sitting beside the well. Literally on the well, on the low stone wall around its mouth. A Jewish traveller has sat down on the wall of a Samaritan well with nothing to draw with.

It was about the sixth hour. Noon, by Jewish reckoning: the sun overhead, the worst part of the day to be walking and the worst part of the day to be fetching water. Women usually drew water in the cool of the morning or evening, and together. A woman coming alone at noon was probably avoiding the others, though John does not say so, and we should hold that guess lightly (see on v. 18).

From this well to the cross. There is a line running from this well to the end of the book. The man sitting here with no bucket is about to offer a stranger water that ends thirst for ever. Fifteen chapters later he will hang on a cross, and almost the last thing he says before it is finished is I thirst (19:28). He ended thirsty. That is how the offer was paid for.

Was Jesus really tired, if he was God? Yes. The eternal Son took to himself a true human body and a reasonable soul (Westminster 8.2), and in that nature he truly grew weary, hungry and thirsty. His divine nature did not become tired, and it was not turned into something less than God; but the person who sat on the well was the Son of God, and his weariness was his own. This is not a weakness in the gospel. It is its glory. A Saviour who only seemed human could not stand in our place, and he could not sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15).

In a sentence. Jesus came to Sychar in Samaria, near the field Jacob gave Joseph, and tired from the journey, sat down by Jacob’s well at about noon.

On a Tuesday. A word to the reader who is simply tired. Not spiritually dry: tired, the kind where the body has stopped cooperating and the day still has eight hours in it. There is no rebuke here and no instruction to push through. The Son of God sat down on a wall in the heat because he could not go on, and the most important conversation in the chapter happened while he was in that condition. Being exhausted is not a lapse in discipleship, and God is not obliged to wait until you are at your best. Sit down if you must, and let him use you there.

For worship. The one through whom the springs were made sat down beside a hole in the ground that a forefather had dug, because he was too tired to walk, and waited in the midday heat for a woman who was not coming to meet him. He knows your weariness, because he carried it in his own body. And the tired man on the wall of the well is the same Lord who neither slumbers nor sleeps, who upholds the universe by the word of his power. Worship him, the Maker who became weary so that the weary might find rest in him.
verseByVerse.note: Jacob’s well is still shown near Shechem (modern Nablus) at the foot of Mount Gerizim. The ESV notes that the sixth hour was about noon — the heat of the day.

parallels.desc: Jacob buys land at Shechem
Joseph buried there

verseByVerse.quote: A woman from Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, "Give me a drink."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A woman from Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her: give me a drink.

A woman from Samaria came to draw water. Alone, at noon, and unnamed. John never tells us her name, and she becomes one of the most remembered people in the Bible.

Give me a drink. Count what is wrong with this scene by the standards of the day, because the list is longer than we feel it. He is a man, alone, speaking to a woman, alone, in an isolated place. Rabbinic caution about this was severe; there were teachers who held that a man should not greet a woman in public. He is a Jew asking a Samaritan for water, which raises a question of ritual cleanness that she will name herself, since the vessel is hers and strict Jews regarded Samaritan vessels as unclean. And he is asking a favour of somebody with nothing, which is not how benefactors behave. He breaks three barriers, sex, race and religion, in four words, and offers no explanation for any of it.

He begins by asking. The first thing the Son of God says to this woman is a request for help. For the length of one sentence he hands her the position of the one who has something the other needs. She is not approached as a case, or a project, or a problem to be addressed. She is approached as the person by the well with the rope. It is a gracious way to open a conversation.

It was not a technique. A favour asked in order to open a conversation is a manoeuvre, and people can smell it. He was genuinely thirsty. He had walked since morning and had nothing to draw with. The request was true, and being true, it did what no strategy could have done.

What he did not open with. Not her history, which he already knew in full. Not her theology, which was defective. Not her nationality. Every one of those comes up later in the conversation, and not one of them is the doorway.

How do I start a conversation about Christ without it feeling artificial? Begin where Jesus began: with honesty and ordinary common ground. Nearly all our discomfort comes from arriving as the one with all the answers, which sets up a transaction where one party is deficient and both know it. This conversation starts from the other end. The most common ground between two human beings is not that one is right; it is that both need things. Be genuinely interested in the person, accept their help when you need it, and let real questions come. Do not hide that you are a Christian, and do not force the subject; pray for the moment and take it when it comes, as Jesus does in verse 10.

In a sentence. A Samaritan woman came to draw water, and Jesus asked her for a drink.

On a Tuesday. Jesus crossed every barrier to reach this woman. Who is on the other side of a line from you: the neighbour of another religion, the colleague whose politics you dislike, the person whose life is visibly in a mess? Ask one of them for something today, a recommendation, an opinion, a bit of help, and mean it.

For worship. He who owns the cattle on a thousand hills and the waters under the earth stood at a Samaritan well and asked a sinner for a cup. That is the humility of the Son of God. He made himself dependent, here on a woman with a rope, and later on borrowed boats, borrowed rooms and a borrowed tomb, so that he might come close to us without crushing us. The Lord who could have commanded the water to rise asked her for it instead, because he had come for her, and not for the water.
verseByVerse.note: A Jewish teacher would not normally speak with a woman in public, still less a Samaritan.

parallels.desc: meetings at a well

verseByVerse.quote: (For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.) The Samaritan woman said to him, "How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria?" (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
(For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.) The Samaritan woman said to him: how is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria? (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)

For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food. So Jesus was alone, and the conversation private. That absence is providential: this conversation could only happen because nobody else was there. And there is a small sign in the bracket: a party of Jewish men buying food in a Samaritan town is already looser about boundaries than the custom.

How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria? Her reply is not a rebuff and it is not bitterness. It is astonishment, and it is worth hearing the arithmetic in it: you, a Jew; me, a woman of Samaria. She names both barriers in one breath, in the order that puts the greatest distance between them. She has spent her life on the wrong side of a line she did not draw, and here is somebody standing on the other side of it asking for a drink.

For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans. John explains the situation twice in two verses, in two brackets, because he is writing for readers who would not otherwise follow. The verb may be narrower than the English: some understand it as do not use vessels in common with Samaritans, which would fit the scene exactly. A Samaritan woman was regarded by strict opinion as unclean, and so was anything she handled. If that is the sense, her surprise is precise: not that a Jew has spoken to her, but that he proposes to drink from her jar. Hatred ran deep on both sides; Samaritan villagers would later refuse to receive Jesus because he was going to Jerusalem, and James and John wanted to call down fire on them (Luke 9:52–54).

The crack through which grace enters. Contempt she could have handled. Contempt is familiar, and there are ways of standing that absorb it. What she has no defence against is a Jewish man asking her for a favour. The wall she had braced herself against did not arrive, the bracing is doing nothing, and she is off balance and talking. Most people outside the faith already know what they expect from Christians; they have an idea of the disapproval and have arranged themselves against it. The single most disarming thing available is not a better argument. It is the disapproval failing to turn up.

John records the rule and lets it stand. Jews have no dealings with Samaritans is stated as a plain fact of the world, without comment. John does not editorialise. He records the rule, then records the Son of God ignoring it, and lets the reader work out which of the two is going to last.

Does this mean Christ does not care about truth, only about kindness? No. In a few verses he will tell her plainly that the Samaritans worship what they do not know (v. 22). He crosses the barrier of contempt, not the barrier of truth. What he refuses is the hatred, the ritual separation and the assumption that she is beneath him. What he never gives up is the truth about God and about her life. The church needs both: no wall of contempt around itself, and no blurring of the gospel. Love that hides the truth is not love, and truth spoken with contempt is rarely heard.

In a sentence. With the disciples gone to buy food, the woman asked how Jesus, a Jew, could ask her, a Samaritan woman, for a drink, since Jews have nothing to do with Samaritans.

On a Tuesday. The gospel breaks down ancient hatreds. Is there a group you treat as she was treated, whose cup you would not share? Notice your instinctive phrases about them, the jokes you allow, the people you would not invite into your home. Ask God to show you where your contempt is the wall that keeps them from hearing about Christ.

For worship. Christ is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility (Ephesians 2:14). It began here, at a well, with a cup. The hostility of centuries between Jew and Samaritan, and between every people and every other, met a man who would not keep it. He went to the cross to make one new people out of enemies, and every church where former enemies share the Lord’s Table is a monument to what he began beside Jacob’s well.
verseByVerse.note: Samaritans were a mixed people descended from Israelites and settlers brought in by Assyria; Jews and Samaritans had centuries of hostility. The ESV notes that the last sentence may mean Jews did not share vessels with Samaritans.

parallels.desc: the settling of Samaria

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered her, "If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, 'Give me a drink,' you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered her: if you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, give me a drink, you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.

If you knew the gift of God. God’s gift: eternal life, the Spirit, Christ himself (3:16; Romans 6:23). A gift is free. It is not earned, bartered or bought at the noon-hour well of ordinary religion.

And who it is that is saying to you. If you knew who I am. Two ignorances are named here, and it is worth separating them. She does not know what is on offer, and she does not know who is offering it. The second is the one that matters, because a gift is only as good as the giver is able, and she is looking at a tired man with no bucket. The theme of the whole conversation is who Jesus is.

You would have asked him. That is all. Not you would have qualified, or made amends first, or got the mountain question right. The only thing standing between this woman and living water, on Jesus’ own account, is that it had not occurred to her to ask, and it had not occurred to her because she did not know who she was talking to. Her difficulty is not that she is unworthy; her history is about to be laid out and it changes nothing. It is not that she is a Samaritan; that barrier has already been crossed. Ignorance, not unworthiness, is what keeps her poor. And he does not lecture her about it. He tells her, in stages, until she asks.

And he would have given you living water. The roles reverse: the one asking for water is the one who gives it. Living water (hudōr zōn) had an ordinary meaning before it had a spiritual one. It meant running water, a spring or a stream, as opposed to the still, stored water of a cistern or a well. It was the better water, the kind everyone preferred. So she hears a claim about plumbing: this stranger with no rope is offering fresh spring water in place of Jacob’s standing well. She is not being dull. She hears the plain sense of the word, exactly as Nicodemus heard the plain sense of born again.

What is the living water? In the Old Testament God himself is the fountain of living waters, whom his people forsook for broken cisterns (Jeremiah 2:13; 17:13). Living water pictures the life and the Spirit that God pours out on his people (Isaiah 44:3; 55:1; Ezekiel 47; Zechariah 14:8). And John tells us in so many words what Jesus means: standing in the temple at the feast, Jesus promises rivers of living water to whoever believes, and John adds that he said this about the Spirit (7:37–39). The gift at the well is nothing less than the Spirit of God dwelling in a person, the same new birth from above that Nicodemus could not grasp, now pictured as a spring. And Jesus gives the Spirit; he is the fountain.

Then why do so few people ask? Because they do not know the gift or the giver. Most people who stay away from Christ are not refusing living water; they think they are refusing a set of rules, a dull institution or a moral lecture. That is why Christian witness must keep pointing to who Jesus is and what he gives. When people truly see him, the asking follows.

In a sentence. Jesus answered that if she knew God’s gift and who was asking her for a drink, she would have asked him and he would have given her living water.

On a Tuesday. If you have been treating Christ as a demand rather than a gift, stop and ask him for the thing you need most: not a better performance, but his Spirit. And when you speak of him to others, lead with the gift and the giver. Tell them who he is.

For worship. The fountain of living waters sat on the edge of a well and asked for a drink. He is the gift and the giver at once: God’s unspeakable gift to the world, and the Lord who pours out the Spirit on all who ask. He gives freely, without money and without price, and he has never yet turned away anyone who asked him for water. Blessed be the Son who is the spring, and the Father who gave him, and the Spirit who flows from him into dry hearts.
verseByVerse.note: “Living water” normally meant fresh, flowing water from a spring, as opposed to still water in a cistern.

parallels.desc: the fountain of living waters

verseByVerse.quote: The woman said to him, "Sir, you have nothing to draw water with, and the well is deep. Where do you get that living water? Are you greater than our father Jacob? He gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman said to him: sir, you have nothing to draw water with, and the well is deep. Where do you get that living water? Are you greater than our father Jacob? He gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock.

Sir, you have nothing to draw water with. Travellers carried a leather bucket and a rope; Jesus had none. Her objections are perfectly sensible, the objections of a competent person stating the facts to a man who appears not to have noticed them.

And the well is deep. Said to be over a hundred feet, about thirty metres.

Where do you get that living water? She takes him literally, as Nicodemus did (3:4).

Our father Jacob. The possessive is the interesting word. The Samaritans traced themselves to Joseph and claimed the patriarchs as their own, which Jews disputed. In one phrase she has answered the boundary she raised two verses earlier: whatever else divides them, they have the same forefather, and she is standing on his land.

Are you greater than our father Jacob? An ironic question, expecting the answer no. The answer is yes. Jacob gave a well; Jesus gives living water. Jacob dreamed of a ladder between heaven and earth; Jesus is the ladder (1:51). John loves this kind of irony. It is exactly the shape of the question the crowd will ask about Abraham in chapter 8, to which Jesus answers that before Abraham was, I am (8:53–58). The Gospel keeps putting the true answer in the mouths of people who mean it as an impossibility. Jacob dug a hole, and it was a good hole, and his descendants were still drawing from it nearly two thousand years later. The man she is talking to made the water.

Her literalism is the staircase. Notice what he does with her objection. He does not correct her about the bucket, and he does not answer the question about Jacob for another fourteen verses, when he answers it far more fully than she asked. He takes the practical difficulty she has raised and uses it as the next step up.

What do I do with objections that seem to miss the point? Take them seriously, as Jesus does. A question that sounds naive or off-target is very often the real question, held at the only end the person can currently reach. Do not mock it or brush past it. Answer honestly what can be answered, and then use it, as Jesus does, to lift the conversation toward who he is. Patient, respectful answers to plain questions have led more people to Christ than clever arguments.

In a sentence. The woman pointed out that he had no bucket and the well was deep, and asked if he was greater than Jacob, who gave them the well.

On a Tuesday. Think of the honest questions people around you have asked about the faith, the ones you shrugged off. Pick one, find a good answer, and go back to them with it this week.

For worship. He is greater than Jacob, greater than Abraham, greater than Moses and every hero of faith, because they were servants in God’s house and he is the Son over it. The patriarchs dug wells and drank from them and died. Christ opened the fountain of eternal life and lives for ever. All their wells were pointing to him. Worship him, the Lord of the patriarchs, sitting on the wall of their well.
verseByVerse.note: The well is deep — said to be over 100 feet.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to her: everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again.

Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again. It is a strange thing to say to a woman with a jar in her hand, and it is worth hearing how mild it sounds and how total it is. He does not say Jacob’s well is bad water. He says that whoever drinks it will be thirsty again. It is a statement about the mechanism, not the quality.

It is simply true. Every good thing available to a human being works on the same cycle: it satisfies, the satisfaction wears off, and the need returns at full strength and slightly sooner than last time. The meal, the holiday, the promotion, the applause, the relationship. None of them fails. They all work exactly as advertised, and then they stop working, and the stopping is not a fault in them. The woman knew this; she had tried five husbands (v. 18). The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing (Ecclesiastes 1:8). Human beings have a thirst no earthly thing can quench, because we were made for God.

Thirst is not the sin. Say it plainly to the reader who keeps going back to the same well and hates himself for it, whether the well is a bottle, a screen, a person he should have stopped calling, or the approval of someone whose opinion he cannot get out from under. The verse does not rebuke the thirst. Thirst is a design feature; the ache is not evidence that something has gone wrong with you. What the verse says is that the well you keep returning to has never once promised what you keep arriving with. It gives what it has. It gives it every time. And the interval between drinks gets shorter, which is the mechanism of every addiction there has ever been.

He does not despise the well. He asked for a drink from it six verses ago. There is nothing in this chapter against ordinary water, ordinary marriage, ordinary bread. The problem was never that people love good things too much. It is that they ask of them what they were never built to carry.

If I am a Christian, should earthly pleasures stop satisfying me? They should satisfy you more truly, not less, because you no longer need them to be God. A Christian can enjoy a meal, a friendship or a holiday as a gift from the Father, give thanks, and let it go when it ends, because his soul is not hanging on it. What changes is not that the gifts taste of nothing, but that their running out is no longer a disaster. The danger comes when we start asking a gift to do what only the Giver can do.

In a sentence. Jesus said that everyone who drinks this water will be thirsty again.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test that needs no spiritual vocabulary. Think of the thing you were most sure would settle you, the thing you honestly believed five or ten years ago would mean you had arrived. Suppose you got it. Did the wanting stop? For almost everyone the wanting moved. It did not shrink; it changed address. That is not cynicism about good gifts. It is evidence, gathered from your own life, about what kind of creature you are. Name the well you keep going back to, and bring that thirst to Christ.

For worship. You have made us for yourself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in you: Augustine’s prayer is the commentary on this verse. God did not make us small enough to be filled by the world. He made us for himself, and then, when we had forsaken the fountain and hewn out cisterns that hold no water, he came himself to the well to offer us the fountain again. Every unsatisfied ache in a human heart is a sign pointing to the God who alone is enough, and to the Son who came to give himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "'but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.' The woman said to him, 'Sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or have to come here to draw water.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life. The woman said to him: sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or have to come here to draw water.

Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. Never: a strong double negative in the Greek, never, ever. It is not a mild reassurance. It is a door closing on the whole cycle described in the previous verse. The deepest thirst of the soul, for God himself, is satisfied for ever.

A spring of water welling up to eternal life. Then the image changes in a way that should stop the reader, because it stops being about drinking at all. He does not say the water will keep her topped up, or that she may come back whenever she runs low. He says the water he gives becomes in him a spring. The one who drinks becomes a source. That is the difference between a well and a spring. A well is a hole where water is stored; it has to be gone to, lowered into, hauled out of, and it is finite. A spring is water arriving from underneath, under its own pressure. The picture is not of a reservoir carefully managed. It is of something that will not stay down.

Welling up. The word (hallomenou) means leaping, springing up; it is used of the lame man leaping in the temple (Acts 3:8). This is the life of the Holy Spirit within the believer (7:38–39), an inner source of life that never runs dry, rising toward its goal: eternal life.

Sir, give me this water. She asks, but still misunderstands. She wants to be spared the daily trip to the well, and perhaps the shame of coming alone at noon. It is easy to smile at. It is better not to. She has heard an offer she does not understand and asked for it anyway, which is more than Nicodemus managed with a far better education. Her theology is wrong and her hand is out. In this Gospel that combination does considerably better than the reverse.

He does not correct her yet. Jesus could have said: you have misheard me; let me define my terms. He lets her ask for the right thing for the wrong reason and goes on. That is worth remembering for anyone tempted to withhold the gospel until a person’s motives are sorted out. Nobody’s motives are sorted out. Everyone who has ever come to Christ came with a tangle of reasons, at least half of them self-interested, and he has never yet sent one of them away to think it over.

Why, then, do believers still thirst for God? The Psalms are full of it: as a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God (Psalm 42:1). The thirst that ends is the thirst of emptiness, the restless search for something to fill the soul. The Christian has found the spring; it is in him. But a spring is drawn on every day, and Jesus goes on inviting his own: if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (7:37). The longing believers feel is not the old emptiness. It is the appetite of those who have tasted and want more, and it will be fully satisfied when we see him face to face (Revelation 7:16–17).

What if I feel dry, not like a spring at all? Feelings rise and fall; the spring is not your feelings but the Spirit himself, and he does not leave the believer (14:16). Dry seasons come to all God’s children, through tiredness, sorrow, sin or simply God’s wise testing. In them, keep to the means by which the Spirit refreshes his people: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of the church. Confess any sin you know of. And keep asking. The promise does not depend on how full you feel today, but on the faithfulness of the one who gave it.

In a sentence. Jesus said that the water he gives becomes a spring within, welling up to eternal life, and the woman asked for it so that she would no longer need to come to the well.

On a Tuesday. If you belong to Christ, the source is already inside you. Begin the day not by hauling up your own resources but by asking the Spirit to rise in you: for patience with the children, for words at work, for joy in a dull task. Then let it overflow to someone else.

For worship. He does not hand out cups; he opens springs. The Lord Jesus does not ration his Spirit or make his people queue at a well. He puts the fountain inside them, so that the life of God rises in ordinary men and women and carries them to eternal life. A woman came with an empty jar and was offered a spring. Bless the giver of living water, who satisfies the thirsty soul and fills the hungry soul with good things, and who will lead his people at last to springs of living water, where God will wipe away every tear.

parallels.desc: like a spring of water whose waters do not fail

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Go, call your husband, and come here." The woman answered him, "I have no husband." Jesus said to her, "You are right in saying, 'I have no husband';"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to her: go, call your husband, and come here. The woman answered him: I have no husband. Jesus said to her: you are right in saying, I have no husband.

Go, call your husband, and come here. The turn is so abrupt that it is worth asking why he makes it. They have been talking about water and eternal life; she has just asked for the gift. Instead of giving it, he says: go and fetch your husband. It is not a change of subject. It is the point at which the conversation stops being about a subject at all. Everything up to here could be had in the abstract: thirst in general, life in general, a gift available to whoever wants one. The moment he mentions her husband, the conversation acquires a particular person with a particular history, and it can no longer be conducted at a safe distance. She cannot receive living water without facing her thirst, and her sin. Jesus goes straight to the wound.

Where the difficulty nearly always lies. It is not hard to be interested in Christianity. Enormous numbers of people read about it, find it beautiful, and are never once cornered by it, because the whole thing is conducted in the third person. The sentence that changes the temperature is never a doctrine. It is always something like go, call your husband: a request that cannot be answered without bringing one’s actual life into the room.

I have no husband. Four words that are entirely true and are being used to hide something. It is not a lie. It is an accurate sentence deployed as a wall, a half-truth to close the subject, and most of us could perform the manoeuvre in our sleep.

You are right in saying, I have no husband. He does not knock the wall down. He agrees with it, and then, in the next breath, says the thing the wall was built to keep out. He takes her words and hands them back with the rest of the sentence attached. He begins with what she got right. Most exposure in human hands leads with the discrepancy; this leads with the accuracy and lets the discrepancy follow. The difference in effect is enormous. It is the difference between a person being caught out and a person being told the truth by somebody who is plainly on their side.

Why does Christ bring up my sin if salvation is a free gift? Because the gift is for sinners, and no one drinks who will not admit they are thirsty. Jesus does not raise her history to make her earn the water, but so that she will know he is offering it to her, the real woman, and not to an idealised version of her. A gospel that never touches your actual life cannot save your actual life. Repentance is not a price paid for grace; it is the hand opening to receive it. When Christ puts his finger on something, it is because he means to heal it.

In a sentence. Jesus told her to go and call her husband, and when she said she had none, he said she was right.

On a Tuesday. Is there a question you are keeping Christ from asking? Most of us have a subject we steer around in prayer, the way she steered around her household. Name it to him today. And when you have to speak truth to someone else, begin, as he did, with what is true in what they have said.

For worship. The Lord deals gently but directly with sin. He is not a surgeon who cuts without anaesthetic, nor a physician who refuses to look at the wound. He does both things at once: he tells the whole truth and he stays on the person’s side. Bless him that he does not leave us comfortable in our half-truths, and that when he opens the wound it is always in order to bind it up.

verseByVerse.quote: "for you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband. What you have said is true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband. What you have said is true.

You have had five husbands. Jesus knows everything about her (2:25). He had never met her and he knows every year, every name, every ending. Whether through death or divorce, she has had five marriages. In that culture a woman could not divorce her husband, while a husband could dismiss a wife for very little. So five marriages behind her may mean five times widowed, or five times sent away, or some mixture: a life of things done to her at least as much as things done by her, perhaps rejected over and over. Jewish teachers thought three marriages the most a woman should have.

And the one you now have is not your husband. She was living with a man without marriage. This is the one irregularity Jesus names outright, and it is a real one: the present arrangement is not a marriage in God’s sight. That is probably why she came to the well alone at noon, shunned by the other women.

How much do we actually know? It is worth being honest about how much the text supplies, because a great deal has been built on very little. John never calls this woman immoral, and Jesus never tells her, as he tells the man at the pool, to sin no more (5:14). The town listens to her and comes out at her word (vv. 29–30, 39), which is not how a town treats a woman it has entirely cast out. There are women who have sat through sermons on this chapter and heard themselves described, divorced not by their choosing, widowed young, or long ago abandoned, and been handed a shame the passage never assigns. What the passage does assign is this: Jesus knew every year of her history before she said a word, asked her for a drink anyway, gave her the plainest statement of his identity in the Gospels, and sent her back to tell her town who he was.

Are the five husbands a symbol? Some have read them as an allegory: Assyria resettled Samaria with people from five foreign cities, each bringing their own gods (2 Kings 17:24–31), so the five husbands stand for false worships and the sixth for corrupt Samaritan religion. It is ingenious, but John gives no hint of it, the numbers do not work cleanly, and above all it dissolves a real woman into a symbol, which is the very thing this passage refuses to do to her. She is not a diagram of Samaria. She is somebody with five marriages behind her and a man in the house now, standing in the heat with a jar.

What you have said is true. Jesus exposes her, but without contempt. He does not condemn or lecture. He simply tells the truth, and in telling it shows her that he knows her completely and is still speaking to her. That is total knowledge joined to total gentleness.

What if I am living in a situation like hers? Then hear both halves of this verse. Christ knows your situation completely, and he does not pretend it is right: living together outside marriage is not what God designed, and he calls you out of it, into marriage or into chastity. But he says it while offering you living water, not while slamming a door. Come to him as you are; he will not send you away. Talk honestly with a pastor about the steps to take. And if your story is one of being left, widowed or divorced against your will, know that this verse does not lay at your feet a shame that belongs to others.

In a sentence. Jesus told her that she had had five husbands, and the man she was living with was not her husband.

On a Tuesday. Many people dread being fully known. They manage what others see, and assume God is doing the same reckoning with less mercy. Bring to God today the part of your history you would least like read aloud, and tell him it plainly. He already knows. The only thing that changes is that you stop hiding.

For worship. He knew all of it before she spoke, every year, every name, every ending, and he had already asked her for a drink. The knowledge came first, and the kindness was not adjusted by it. That is grace. The Lord who searches the heart is the Lord who died for what he finds there. O Lord, you have searched me and known me, and you have not turned away: there is no one else in the universe of whom that can be said, and it is said of the Son of God.

parallels.desc: he knew what was in man

verseByVerse.quote: The woman said to him, "Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet. Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman said to him: sir, I perceive that you are a prophet. Our fathers worshipped on this mountain, but you say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship.

Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet. Only a prophet could know such things. Her understanding is growing: from a Jew (v. 9), to sir (v. 11), to a prophet, and soon to the Christ (v. 29).

Our fathers worshiped on this mountain. This mountain is Mount Gerizim, which rose directly above the well; she could have pointed at it as she spoke. Its history is layered. It is where Israel was told to stand to pronounce the blessings when they entered the land (Deuteronomy 11:29; 27:12), and the Samaritans’ whole case rested on that; their own copy of the law of Moses even named Gerizim as the place for the altar.
