On a Tuesday. If you have come to Christ, the Father drew you. Thank him. And when you share the gospel, pray: only the Father can draw. Before your next conversation about Christ, ask the Father by name to draw that person.

For worship. No one ever wandered into the kingdom by accident or fought his way in by strength. Every believer was drawn, hauled up out of the deep like a net full of fish by the Father’s mighty and gentle hand. And the hand that drew will raise. Bless the Father who draws, the Son who receives, and the Spirit who makes the unwilling glad to come. To God alone be the glory for every soul that comes to Christ.

parallels.desc: I will draw all people to myself

verseByVerse.quote: "It is written in the Prophets, 'And they will all be taught by God.' Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me — not that anyone has seen the Father except he who is from God; he has seen the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is written in the Prophets, ‘And they will all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me — not that anyone has seen the Father except he who is from God; he has seen the Father.

It is written in the Prophets. The quotation is from Isaiah 54:13, a promise about the restored people of God in the new covenant age (compare Jeremiah 31:33–34). It sits in a chapter about a barren woman told to enlarge her tent because she is going to need the room.

And they will all be taught by God. “All” here means all God’s people, all the children of the new Jerusalem: in the new age, God himself teaches every one of them, not just prophets and priests. It is a promise in which instruction stops being only something passed down through an institution and becomes something God does in every member of his people.

Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me. This explains what drawing is. The Father draws by teaching: he opens the mind and heart to hear and learn. And everyone who learns comes. Not some; everyone. Drawing is not force but inward teaching, which always succeeds. It is the same as the new birth (3:3–8) and the opening of Lydia’s heart (Acts 16:14). The gloss makes the drawing warmer without making it weaker. Not a mechanical operation on an inert object, but a person being taught by God, and coming as a result. Heard, learned, comes: nobody arrives at Christ without being taught, and nobody so taught fails to arrive.

Not that anyone has seen the Father except he who is from God. Jesus guards against a misunderstanding. Being taught by the Father doesn’t mean having visions of God. Only the Son has seen the Father (1:18). The Father teaches by pointing to the Son.

He has seen the Father. This is the authority of Jesus’ teaching: he speaks what he has seen.

How does God teach me today? Through his word, by his Spirit. He does not normally speak in private voices or visions, and verse 46 warns against expecting to see the Father directly. He teaches as the Scriptures are read and preached, the Spirit opening your mind to understand and your heart to love what you hear (Luke 24:45; 1 Corinthians 2:12). So the way to be taught by God is to put yourself under his word, with prayer, and in the fellowship of his church. Every true insight into Christ you have ever had was a lesson from the Father.

In a sentence. The prophets promised that all God’s people would be taught by God, and everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to Jesus, the only one who has seen the Father.

On a Tuesday. Before you read your Bible today, pray: Father, teach me. Then read expecting to be taught, and stay with the passage until you have seen something of Christ in it.

For worship. The Father has taught you to come to the Son. Every true believer is a pupil of God. The Lord of heaven is not too great to sit beside the least of his children and teach them, and his lessons always end at the feet of his Son. Bless the Father who teaches, and the Son who alone has seen him and makes him known.

parallels.desc: all your children shall be taught by the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes has eternal life. I am the bread of life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes has eternal life. I am the bread of life.

Truly, truly, I say to you. The solemn formula marks a summary of everything so far. The doubled amen is peculiar to this Gospel; elsewhere Jesus says amen once. The word normally goes at the end of someone else’s statement: so be it, that is reliable. He puts it at the front of his own, which is almost without parallel: a man endorsing his own words in advance, on his own authority, with the formula ordinarily used to endorse the words of God. And he does it here to introduce the simplest sentence in the chapter.

Whoever believes has eternal life. Simple and clear. Not whoever believes and does, but whoever believes. And has, now. Eternal life is the gift of God received by faith alone. Notice what the sentence leaves out. Nothing about how much is believed, or how well, or for how long, or with what feelings. No mention of understanding, which is significant in a chapter where nobody understands anything.

I am the bread of life. The great “I am” saying is repeated (v. 35). Everything in the discourse turns on this. Repetition on that scale in a short speech is not accident; it is a preacher who has been interrupted, argued with and grumbled at, going back to the point.

I worry whether I am really one of the elect. What should I do? Stop auditing the secret counsel of God and look at the promise in front of you. There is a way of hearing the strong doctrine of the previous verses, the drawing, the giving, the Father’s will, and then trying to inspect oneself for evidence of a decision made before the world began. That way lies misery, and it is not what those verses are for. The instruction never changes and it is not complicated: whoever believes has eternal life. If you are trusting Christ, however weakly, the promise is yours. Assurance grows as you look at him, not at yourself (Westminster 18.2).

In a sentence. Jesus solemnly declared that whoever believes has eternal life, for he is the bread of life.

On a Tuesday. If you believe, you have eternal life today. Live from that, not towards it. Do one thing today that you would do only if you were sure you were safe in Christ: forgive freely, give generously, speak boldly.

For worship. Truly, truly: the Son of God puts his own seal on the simplest sentence in the Bible, so that the weakest believer may rest on it. Whoever believes has. Not will have if; has. Bless the Lord whose promise is as solid as his throne, and whose gift of life is in the hands of every one who trusts him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die.

Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died. The crowd had held up the manna as the great sign (v. 31). Jesus now points out its limit. It kept people alive for a day. It did not save them from death. The whole generation that ate it died in the wilderness, many in unbelief (Numbers 14:29; 1 Corinthians 10:5). It is one of the coldest sentences in the Gospels and it is aimed straight at the argument they opened with. They had produced the manna as the gold standard. He takes the whole of it and adds: and they died. The bread fell six mornings a week for four decades, and the generation that ate it was buried in the sand between Egypt and the land, which is the part of the story they were not quoting.

The best of our arrangements. So the argument turns round. The manna is not the standard Jesus has to match. It shows that a provision of that kind, however miraculous, does not solve the real problem. It kept alive people who were going to die anyway. And that is a fair description of everything else, said without cynicism. Medicine, food, safety, all the ordinary mercies, are real, and every one of them extends a life rather than saves it. The best possible outcome of all our arrangements is a longer wait.

This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die. Jesus is greater than the manna. The one who feeds on him will not die: not that he will escape the death of the body, but that death will not be the end (11:25–26). Eternal death is what is overcome. Not eat and live longer, not eat and die comfortably: not die.

But Christians still die. What does not die mean? It means that the death that is final, separation from God for ever, will never touch you. Your body will die, unless Christ returns first, and this Gospel will soon show Jesus weeping at a friend’s tomb (11:35). But for the believer death is no longer the end of the sentence. At death the soul goes immediately to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23; Westminster 32.1), and at the last day the body will be raised. The manna could not stop a single funeral. This bread does not stop them either. It stops them being the last word.

In a sentence. Their fathers ate the manna and still died, but Jesus is the bread from heaven, so that whoever eats it will not die.

On a Tuesday. Think of the good things you are depending on to make life secure: health, savings, plans. Thank God for them. Then remind yourself that they can only lengthen the wait, and put your hope on the bread that defeats death.

For worship. Moses’ bread fed bodies that died; Christ feeds souls that live for ever. He is the Lord of life who went down into death himself and came out again, so that those who feed on him might pass through death into life. Bless the living bread, over whom death has no dominion, and in whom his people cannot finally die.

parallels.desc: your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.

I am the living bread that came down from heaven. Living bread: bread that is alive, and gives life. A new form of the claim.

If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. Eating is a picture of believing (compare v. 35 with v. 47). As food becomes part of you and keeps you alive, so receiving Christ by faith unites you to him and gives you life.

And the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh. Here the discourse turns. “I will give”: future, looking to the cross. “For” (hyper) means on behalf of, in place of, the word of sacrifice (10:11, 15; 11:51–52). “My flesh”: his real human body (1:14), given up in death. The bread is not just Jesus’ teaching or his life, but his death. To feed on Christ is to trust in his sacrifice.

The bread is a dying man. This is the sentence the whole discourse has been walking toward, and it lands with a change of tense. Everything so far has been present: I am the bread, whoever comes, whoever believes. Now: the bread that I will give. Something has not happened yet. Up to here a hearer might have taken the bread as his teaching, his presence or his company. He now names it, and it is his body, and it is going to be handed over. The preposition is the one Caiaphas will use without knowing what he says, when he observes that it is better for one man to die for the people (11:50). So the bread is not a metaphor for spiritual sustenance in general. It is a specific man, on a specific afternoon, dying in the place of others, and the reason anyone can be fed by him at all is that he was broken first. That is why the crowd cannot follow it. They came for bread and are told the bread will be given in death.

Nothing compelled it. He had made loaves out of nothing the previous afternoon and could have gone on making them for forty years, as the manna had come, and kept a nation alive and been crowned for it. He declined the crown, walked away up a hill in the dark, and came back to say that what he intended to give was his flesh.

For the life of the world. “The world” in John is humanity in its rebellion against God, Gentiles as well as Jews. Christ’s death is not for Israel alone but for people of every nation (11:51–52).

Where Christians differ: does this mean Christ died for everyone alike? Some take “for the life of the world” to mean that Christ died equally for every human being. Verdict: in John, Christ lays down his life “for the sheep” (10:11, 15), for those the Father has given him (17:9, 19). “The world” here stresses the extent of his people, from every nation, and the greatness of the gift, not that every individual is saved. His death actually gives life, and it gives it to everyone who feeds on him. This is definite atonement: the death that truly secures life for all who are his.

Can I tell anyone that Christ died for sinners like them? Yes. The death of Christ is of infinite worth, sufficient for the whole world, and the gospel offers it freely to everyone without exception: whoever eats of this bread will live for ever. You may say to any person, Christ died for sinners, and if you come to him, you will find that he died for you, and his death will not fail you. Definite atonement does not narrow the offer; it guarantees that the cross actually saves, rather than merely making salvation possible.

In a sentence. Jesus is the living bread from heaven, and whoever eats it will live for ever, and the bread he will give for the life of the world is his flesh, given in death.

On a Tuesday. The bread of life was broken on the cross. Every time you trust Christ’s death for you, you are feeding on him. When guilt rises today, do not argue with it from your record; answer it from his cross.

For worship. The bread of God is not something he carries. It is what he is, and it had to be broken before anyone could eat. The Son gave his flesh, freely, for the life of the world, and from that broken body life flows to every nation and every age. Bless the Lamb who was slain, whose death is our life, and whose broken body is the bread of heaven.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews then disputed among themselves, saying, "How can this man give us his flesh to eat?" So Jesus said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jews then disputed among themselves, saying, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you.”

The Jews then disputed among themselves. “Disputed” (machomai) means fought, quarrelled. The grumbling has become open argument. The room has split, and they are shouting at each other about him.

How can this man give us his flesh to eat? They take him literally and crudely, as Nicodemus took the new birth (3:4) and the woman took living water (4:11). The misunderstanding is part of John’s method: it leads to deeper teaching.

Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood. Jesus doesn’t soften it. He sharpens it. Now he adds the blood. Setting and background: drinking blood was strictly forbidden in the law (Genesis 9:4; Leviticus 17:10–14), because the life is in the blood. To a Jewish ear these words were shocking. Flesh and blood separated speak of a violent death: the body broken and the blood poured out. Jesus is speaking of his death as a sacrifice. To eat his flesh and drink his blood is to receive his death as your life, to take it into yourself by faith, to depend on it entirely.

How appalling this sounded. Familiarity has taken the edge off it, and without the edge the crowd’s reaction is unintelligible. The prohibition on blood was absolute: whoever eats any blood, God would set his face against him and cut him off from his people (Leviticus 17:10). The blood was the life, and the life belonged to God; it was poured out at the altar and never consumed. A Jew did not eat meat until the blood had been drained, and observant Jews still do not. So what he has said is not merely strange. It names the one thing their law forbade on pain of being cut off, and he says it in a synagogue, and then says it again. And he does not de-escalate. Their question was a fair one, and a teacher who wanted the room back would have answered it. He answers by raising the stakes: not only is it possible, it is necessary.

You have no life in you. There is no other way to life. Without union with Christ crucified, there is only death.

What it does not mean. It does not mean literal eating of Jesus’ physical body. The crowd thought that, and Jesus corrects it in v. 63: the flesh is no help at all; his words are spirit. Nor does it mean that everyone who takes the Lord’s Supper has eternal life, or that no one who has not taken it can be saved. The thief on the cross never took it, and was with Christ that day.

Where Christians differ: John 6 and the Lord’s Supper. Roman Catholics read these verses as teaching transubstantiation, the bread and wine becoming Christ’s actual body and blood; Lutherans see Christ’s body present in, with and under the elements; some see here only a symbol of faith. Verdict: the Supper had not yet been instituted, and Jesus speaks to the crowd of something they must do now, on pain of having no life. Feeding on Christ is believing in him (vv. 35, 40, 47). John 6 is about faith, not first about the sacrament. Yet the same feeding is what happens at the Supper: there, as Calvin taught, believers by the Spirit truly feed on Christ’s body and blood, not by a change in the bread, but by being lifted up in faith to the living Christ, who nourishes them with himself. The Supper is a visible, sealing form of what John 6 describes.

Why does Jesus use such shocking language? Because nothing less would describe what he offers. He is speaking of a union with a dying man so complete that the nearest picture is taking him into yourself and living on him. The picture offends precisely because the reality is so total. Faith is not admiring Christ from a distance or agreeing with his teaching; it is depending on his death as your only life, as completely as your body depends on food. Eleven verses later he will tell his disciples that his words are spirit and life. He is not being obscure for effect. He is saying the only thing that is true.

In a sentence. When the Jews argued about how he could give his flesh to eat, Jesus said that unless they eat the flesh and drink the blood of the Son of Man, they have no life in them.

On a Tuesday. There is no life apart from Christ crucified. Ask yourself honestly what you are living on: your own goodness, your church record, your feelings? Bring all of it to the cross today and say: Lord, your death is my only life.

For worship. There is no life in us apart from Christ crucified. Feed on him by faith, daily, and at his table. His body was broken and his blood poured out, so that sinners condemned to death might take his life into themselves and live. Bless the Lamb of God, whose blood is the life of the world, and who gives himself wholly to those who trust him.
verseByVerse.note: Drinking blood was forbidden by the law, which made these words shocking.

parallels.desc: the life is in the blood

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.

Whoever feeds on my flesh. The verb changes here from the usual word for eat (esthiō, phagein) to trōgō, to chew or munch. Some take it as a deliberately vivid, even crude word, insisting on the reality of the feeding. Others note it simply serves as the present tense of eating in later Greek. Either way, the present tense matters: it is the ongoing feeding of a life of faith, not a single act.

And drinks my blood has eternal life. The positive promise of v. 53: has eternal life now.

And I will raise him up on the last day. And resurrection to come. Compare v. 40: whoever looks on the Son and believes has eternal life and will be raised. The parallel shows what feeding means: believing. This is the last appearance of the refrain, four times in this chapter, attached in turn to the Father’s will, to the one who looks, to the one who is drawn, and now to the one who feeds. However the promise is approached, it ends in the same sentence: a preacher hammering one nail.

Does the realism of this language support the Roman Catholic view? The reading deserves to be stated at its strongest. Rome points out that the crowd plainly took Jesus literally, and that instead of correcting them he pressed harder, moving to the more vivid word feeds on; that he says his flesh is true food and his blood true drink; and that when disciples walked away he did not call them back to say he had meant a figure. That is a serious argument and it deserves a serious answer, which the passage itself supplies nine verses later. When his own disciples say the saying is hard, Jesus tells them what it was: it is the Spirit who gives life, the flesh is no help at all; the words he has spoken are spirit and life (v. 63). That is the clarification, given exactly where a reader would want it, and it points away from physical eating. The parallel he offers is that whoever feeds on him abides in him, and abiding is John’s word for a relationship held by faith, not by digestion. And Jesus is speaking a year before the Last Supper, to a crowd who had no sacrament to think of. Whatever this chapter describes, it is how a person receives a crucified Saviour, which is by believing in him, as he said outright in verse 35.

Then is the Lord’s Supper only a memorial? No. None of this makes the Supper a bare reminder or an optional extra. The Reformed churches have taught that Christ is truly given to his people at his table and truly received, really and spiritually, by faith, through the Spirit, so that the feeding is no mere metaphor even though his flesh is not chewed (1689 London Baptist Confession 30.7; Westminster 29.7). The disagreement with Rome is not about whether Christ gives himself to us there. It is about how, and about whether the once-for-all sacrifice can be offered again. It cannot (Hebrews 10:10–14). So come to the table expecting to meet him: not in the bread, but by the Spirit, through faith, the risen Christ feeding you with himself.

In a sentence. Whoever feeds on Jesus’ flesh and drinks his blood has eternal life, and he will raise him up on the last day.

On a Tuesday. Faith is not a one-time meal. Keep feeding on Christ in his word, in prayer, at his table. Next time you come to the Lord’s Supper, prepare for it the day before: confess your sins, give thanks for the cross, and come hungry.

For worship. He gives himself to be fed on, not once but continually, by every believer in every generation, and he never runs out. The bread of heaven is inexhaustible because the one who is the bread is infinite. Bless the Lord who invites us to keep coming, who meets us at his table, and who will raise up on the last day every one who has fed on him.

parallels.desc: a participation in the blood of Christ

verseByVerse.quote: "For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink. Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink. Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.

For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink. “True” (alēthēs): real, genuine. Ordinary food is a shadow; Christ is the reality. He satisfies what bread only points to. It is the same idea as the true light (1:9) and the true bread (v. 32): not genuine as opposed to fake, but the real thing of which every other example is a copy. Every meal anyone has ever eaten was an approximation of this.

Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. “Abides” (menō), remains, dwells: one of John’s great words (15:4–10; 1 John 2:24, 27). Feeding leads to union. As food becomes part of the body, the believer is joined to Christ, and Christ lives in the believer. This mutual indwelling is the heart of salvation: union with Christ.

Both ways. The word has run through this Gospel since chapter 1: the Spirit came down on Jesus and remained (1:32); the first disciples asked where he was staying and then stayed (1:38–39); it will carry the whole of chapter 15. But this is the first time the abiding runs both ways: in me, and I in him. That is a strange thing to claim. Ordinary eating goes one direction; the bread goes into the man and is changed into him. Here what is taken in also takes in. The one fed ends up inside the food. That is the answer to anyone who reads the eating language as a transaction, as if Christ were a commodity to be consumed for benefit. The whole vocabulary has been building toward a relationship, not a supply. Not a substance taken, but two persons who come to be in each other.

What does union with Christ mean in everyday life? It means that everything Christ is and has done is yours, and that your life is now bound up with his. His death counts as your death to sin, his righteousness is credited to you, his Spirit lives in you, and his resurrection guarantees yours (Romans 6:4–11; Galatians 2:20). So you are never alone, never facing temptation in your own strength, never praying to a distant God. When you work, suffer, love or die, you do it in him. Learn to say, with Paul, it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me.

In a sentence. Jesus’ flesh is real food and his blood real drink, and whoever feeds on them lives in him, and he in them.

On a Tuesday. Before the hardest thing you face today, stop and say: I am in Christ, and Christ is in me. Then do it as one who is not alone.

For worship. You are in Christ, and Christ is in you. This is your life. The Son of God has not merely saved us from a distance; he has taken us into himself and come to dwell in us. As the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, so by grace we are drawn into that fellowship. Bless the Lord who abides in his people, and whose people abide in him for ever.

parallels.desc: abide in me

verseByVerse.quote: "As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever feeds on me, he also will live because of me. This is the bread that came down from heaven, not like the bread the fathers ate, and died. Whoever feeds on this bread will live forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever feeds on me, he also will live because of me. This is the bread that came down from heaven, not like the bread the fathers ate, and died. Whoever feeds on this bread will live forever.

As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father. The Son’s life comes from the Father (5:26). The Father is the living God, the fountain of life. He is described by the one adjective that matters here: the living one, the source, who has never had life handed to him.

So whoever feeds on me, he also will live because of me. And as the Son lives from the Father, so the believer lives from the Son. Life flows from the Father, through the Son, to the believer. “Feeds on me”: now not flesh and blood but simply “me.” The point is the person of Christ, received. Three links, and the preposition is the same in the last two. The believer lives because of Christ as Christ lives because of the Father. That is a startling comparison, and it is Jesus who makes it. The relation between a Christian and Christ is described in the same grammar as the relation within the Godhead: not the same in kind, since one is eternal and the other is a gift to a creature, but running along the same line out of the same source.

This is the bread that came down from heaven, not like the bread the fathers ate, and died. The discourse ends where it began, with the manna (vv. 31–32). The contrast is complete. The manna came from heaven, but it did not come from the Father’s own life; it was a substance, and substances sustain and then stop. What is offered here is not a better grade of provision. It is a place in a chain that begins in the life of God and has no end.

Whoever feeds on this bread will live forever. The final word of the sermon: life for ever.

Hard to want. He has now said it four ways in twenty verses: the bread of life, the living bread, the true food, and now the chain of living. The disciples will say in a moment that this is a hard saying, and they are right, though not for the reason they think. It is not hard to follow. It is hard to want.

Does live forever just mean existing for ever? No. Everyone will exist for ever, the lost as well as the saved (5:29). Eternal life is not mere endless existence but a quality of life: knowing the Father and the Son (17:3), sharing in the very life of God, with joy, holiness and love that never fade. It begins now, when you first believe, and it will be complete in the resurrection, in a new creation without sin or death. That is the life that flows from the Father through the Son into all who feed on him.

In a sentence. As the Son lives because of the Father, so whoever feeds on the Son will live because of him; unlike the manna, which could not keep the fathers from death, this bread gives life for ever.

On a Tuesday. Your life depends on Christ as completely as his depends on the Father. Draw from him today. At the end of the day, ask: what did I draw from him today, and what did I try to draw from somewhere else?

For worship. The living Father, the fountain of all life, has life in himself; he has given the Son to have life in himself; and the Son gives that life to all who feed on him. Life flows down from the heart of God into the hearts of sinners and will never run dry. Blessed be the living Father, the life-giving Son, and the Spirit who unites us to him, now and for ever.

parallels.desc: Christ who lives in me

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said these things in the synagogue, as he taught at Capernaum. When many of his disciples heard it, they said, "This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said these things in the synagogue, as he taught at Capernaum. When many of his disciples heard it, they said, “This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?”

Jesus said these things in the synagogue, as he taught at Capernaum. Setting and background. The whole discourse was given in the synagogue at Capernaum, Jesus’ base in Galilee. The remains of a later white limestone synagogue stand there, built on the dark basalt foundations of an earlier one, probably the one Jesus taught in. Luke tells us who paid for a synagogue there: a Roman centurion built it for the town (Luke 7:5). So the room where the crowd finally turned away may well have been a room a Gentile soldier had given them, a short walk from Peter’s house. Not a hillside with a crowd, but the building where the community met to hear the Scriptures read.

When many of his disciples heard it. Not the Twelve, but a wider circle of followers. Being called a disciple did not mean being a true believer (v. 64). Note who is speaking now: not the Jews, who have grumbled since verse 41, but many of his disciples, people who had attached themselves to him, travelled with him, called him teacher. The crowd’s objection was hostility; this is desertion forming in the ranks.

This is a hard saying. “Hard” (sklēros) means harsh, offensive, unacceptable. It was not hard to understand; it was hard to accept. A crucified Messiah, a salvation received by depending wholly on him, and a God who must draw: these were offensive. The word is used of a stiff wind, a harsh master, a cruel word. They are not saying they cannot follow the argument. They are saying they cannot stomach it.

Who can listen to it? “Listen” here means accept, obey. They will not take it. Not who can understand it, but who can go on sitting here while this is said. They are already halfway out of the building.

Two kinds of objection. The distinction matters, because two kinds of objection to Christianity are constantly mistaken for each other. There is genuine intellectual difficulty, and it deserves patient work. And there is the objection that has nothing to do with understanding, where the thing is understood perfectly well and found intolerable. This is the second kind, and Jesus treats it as such: his reply says nothing to clarify the content.

What should I do with a teaching of Jesus I find hard to accept? First, make sure it is what he actually teaches, read in its context, and not a distortion. Then ask honestly whether your difficulty is that you do not understand it, or that you do not like it. If the first, study and ask for help. If the second, bring the struggle to Christ himself, as you would to a friend whose judgement you trust more than your own. Many believers have found that the sayings they once resisted became the ones they love most. Faith does not mean pretending something is easy; it means trusting the one who said it.

In a sentence. Jesus taught this in the synagogue at Capernaum, and many of his disciples said it was a hard saying that no one could accept.

On a Tuesday. Some of what Jesus says will offend you. The question is not whether it is hard, but whether it is true. Name one teaching of Christ you are tempted to quietly ignore, and read what he actually says about it this week.

For worship. Christ does not flatter. He tells the truth in the synagogue and lets the truth do its work, even when it empties the room. His words are hard because they are real, and they are real because he is the truth. Bless the Lord who will not trim his gospel to keep a crowd, and whose hard sayings are the only words of life.
verseByVerse.note: The remains of a later synagogue at Capernaum stand on the foundations of an earlier one, perhaps the one where Jesus taught.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling about this, said to them, "Do you take offense at this? Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling about this, said to them, “Do you take offense at this? Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?”

Knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling about this. Jesus knows what is in people (2:24–25). The disciples are now grumbling like the crowd (v. 41). Nobody reported it. It is the same knowledge that read the woman at the well and saw Nathanael under the fig tree, now turned on his own followers in the moment they are quietly deciding to leave. He watched them go before they went.

Do you take offense at this? “Offense” (skandalizō): to trip, to stumble. The cross is the great stumbling block (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before? The sentence is left unfinished in Greek. Two readings are possible. It could mean: if this offends you, how much more will his ascent, the full revelation of his heavenly origin, overwhelm you? Or: when you see him ascend, you will understand that he truly came from heaven, and that his words about his flesh were not about literal eating. In John, his going up includes the cross, resurrection and ascension together (3:13–14; 12:32–34). Either way, the ascension proves his claim that he came down from heaven (vv. 38, 42), and it shows that his flesh would not stay on earth to be literally eaten.

Both readings hold. On the first, everything from here to the end of the book gets steeper, and faith that cannot take this saying will not survive the next. On the second, the ascension is a clue offered in mercy: the body that ascends is not a body that gets eaten. And either way, the phrase where he was before is the hinge. It is the very thing the objectors in verse 42 denied. They said they knew his father and mother and so he could not have come down. He answers by referring, without argument, to the place he came from and is going back to.

Why does the ascension matter to me? Because the one who ascended is now reigning, praying and preparing. He sits at the Father’s right hand as King over all things for the good of his church (Ephesians 1:20–23). He always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). He has sent the Spirit (16:7). He is preparing a place for you, and will come again (14:2–3). The ascension means you have a friend at the very centre of all power, wearing your nature, and your life is hidden with him there (Colossians 3:1–3).

In a sentence. Knowing that his disciples were grumbling, Jesus asked whether they were offended, and what they would say if they saw the Son of Man ascending to where he was before.

On a Tuesday. When something about Jesus offends or confuses you, lift your eyes to where he is now. Pray today as someone whose Lord is reigning at the Father’s right hand.

For worship. The one who came down has gone up. Our Saviour reigns in heaven, where he was before. He descended to the lowest place and ascended far above all heavens, that he might fill all things. Bless the ascended Lord, crowned with glory and honour, who has taken our humanity into heaven and will bring us there with him.

verseByVerse.quote: "It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. But there are some of you who do not believe." (For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. But there are some of you who do not believe. (For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him.)

It is the Spirit who gives life. Life comes from the Holy Spirit, as in the new birth (3:5–8). The Spirit is the one who makes the words of Jesus effective. This is the key to the chapter, and it should be read slowly, because it is where Jesus tells his own disciples what the previous twenty verses were about.

The flesh is no help at all. “Flesh” here means human nature on its own, apart from the Spirit, not Jesus’ own flesh given for the world (v. 51), which is the source of life. Merely human understanding, human effort, or literal physical eating, accomplishes nothing for salvation. This shuts out a crudely physical reading of the discourse. Notice the word he chooses. He has just spent ten verses telling them to eat his flesh, and now he says flesh is no help at all. That is not a contradiction; it is a signal, placed exactly where a hearer needs it. The category they have been reasoning in, the physical, the literal, the butcher’s shop, is the wrong category, and no amount of it will produce what he offers.

The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. Jesus’ teaching carries the Spirit and gives life. We feed on Christ by receiving his words in faith. Not describe spirit and life: are. The saying they have just called intolerable is itself the thing that carries the life, so the way to eat him is to receive what he has said. That is why the eating is believing. It is not a convenience imposed on a difficult text; it is the explanation the speaker gives when his own followers ask, before anyone had a doctrine to defend.

But there are some of you who do not believe. Among his disciples are unbelievers. Said not to the crowd or the authorities but to the people standing closest, some of whom he is telling to their faces that they do not believe.

For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him. John’s comment. Jesus was not taken by surprise, not even by Judas. “From the beginning” probably means from the start of his ministry, or of their following. He chose the Twelve knowing what Judas would do (v. 70; 13:18). It is the first mention of the betrayal in this Gospel. Every time Judas was sent out, every meal he shared, every miracle he watched, even the night his feet were washed, all of it happened with this known.

Did Jesus’ knowing make Judas betray him? No. Foreknowledge is not the same as compulsion. John does not say Judas was made to do it; he says Jesus knew. God’s eternal purpose does include even the sins of men, so that the betrayal fulfilled Scripture (Acts 2:23), yet God is not the author of sin, and Judas acted freely and wickedly, and was fully responsible (Westminster 3.1; 5.4). And the terrible thing about this sentence is not what it does to Judas’s freedom but what it shows of Christ’s patience. He kept a man beside him for years, giving him everything he gave the others, knowing.

In a sentence. Jesus said it is the Spirit who gives life, not the flesh, and his words are spirit and life, but some of them did not believe, for he knew from the beginning who did not believe and who would betray him.

On a Tuesday. Read Christ’s words and ask the Spirit to make them life to you. Without the Spirit, even the Bible is only ink. Before you open Scripture today, pray in one sentence: Holy Spirit, make these words life to me.

For worship. The Spirit gives life, and the words of Jesus are spirit and life. Through those words, by that Spirit, the dead are raised and the hungry fed. Bless the Lord whose words are not ink but breath, and the Spirit who carries the life of Christ into every heart that receives them.
verseByVerse.note: “Flesh” here means human nature on its own, apart from the Spirit.

parallels.desc: the Spirit gives life

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said, “This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father.”

This is why I told you. The unbelief of some disciples is the explanation of v. 44. He is quoting himself. The doctrine is restated at the very moment it is being demonstrated.

No one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father. “Granted” (dedomenon), given as a gift. Coming to Christ, faith itself, is a gift of God (Ephesians 2:8; Philippians 1:29). Three times in this chapter Jesus says it: the Father gives (v. 37), the Father draws (v. 44), the Father grants (v. 65). Unbelief is not God’s failure but human refusal; faith is not human achievement but God’s gift. The wording has shifted slightly: drawing stressed the power required; granting stresses that it was a present.

No room for pride. That is the effect of the verse on those who stay. Whatever separates them from those leaving, it is not insight, loyalty or a better grasp of the argument: it was granted them. The only people in the building entitled to feel any pride are told, before the doors have swung shut, that they have nothing to be proud of.

The comfort in it. If staying were a matter of resolve, every Christian would be one bad season away from the door, and most of us know our own resolve well enough to find that terrifying. This verse takes the whole question off that ground. The eleven did not out-endure the others. They were given something, and the giving did not depend on their performance that evening or any evening afterward, which is fortunate, since within a year every one of them would run away and one would deny knowing him. They came back. That is the part the doctrine explains and self-confidence cannot.

Are those to whom coming is not granted still responsible? Yes. The inability is not like a prison door shut on someone trying to get out; it is a will that does not want to come (5:40). No one is turned away who comes, and no one stays away against his will. God’s gift is mercy, owed to no one; its absence is justice, not cruelty.

In a sentence. Jesus said that this was why no one can come to him unless the Father grants it.

On a Tuesday. If you are a believer, write down one sentence thanking the Father for granting you faith, and let it humble you toward someone you find it hard to be patient with. You did not get here by being better than them.

For worship. Your faith is the Father’s gift. Give him the glory for it. Every believer will say on the last day, not I chose well, but he chose me; not I held on, but I was held. Bless the giving God, who grants what he commands, and to whom belongs all the praise for every soul that comes to his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him. So Jesus said to the twelve, "Do you want to go away as well?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him. So Jesus said to the twelve, “Do you want to go away as well?”

After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him. The turning point of Jesus’ Galilean ministry. The day began with five thousand fed and a crowd wanting to make him king (v. 15). It ends with many walking away. “Turned back” literally means went away to the things behind, back to their old life. They had followed Jesus for bread and a political Messiah, not for himself. This is not true believers falling away, but false disciples being revealed (v. 64; 1 John 2:19).

And nothing happened. That is the thing to sit with. There was no scandal, no defeat, no failure of nerve, no miracle that went wrong. He did not stop healing or start behaving badly. He preached a sermon, and the sermon emptied the room. This is what John meant at 2:24, when Jesus did not entrust himself to those who believed because of signs; it is what the Galilean welcome of 4:45 was always going to come to; it is the end of the while in which they were willing to rejoice in the Baptist’s light (5:35). Every one of those was a warning, and this is the event.

No longer walked with him. Not a theological formula but a physical description: they stopped travelling in the same direction. Discipleship in the Gospels is largely a matter of where a person’s feet are, and falling away looks less like a decision than like a road no longer taken.

So Jesus said to the twelve. The first mention of “the twelve” in John.

Do you want to go away as well? The Greek form expects the answer no. Jesus doesn’t beg them to stay or soften his teaching. He tests them, and invites a confession. He does not chase the crowd or send anyone after them. He turns to the twelve, the last people he has, and offers them the door. It is a real question, asked by a man who has just watched a room empty and has nothing left to hold anyone with except himself.

Were these disciples true believers who lost their salvation? Some read them so. But John has already shown that following and believing in a shallow way is not the same as being born again (2:23–25), and Jesus says plainly that some of them did not believe (v. 64). The more likely reading is that they had followed without being given saving faith. As John writes later, they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19).

What if someone I love has walked away from Christ? Then this chapter is for you. It happened to Jesus, in his own town, in numbers, on the strength of his own preaching, and it was not evidence that anything had gone wrong in him. It is not necessarily evidence that you failed either. Keep loving them, keep the door open, and keep praying: some who seem to have walked away are wandering believers whom the Shepherd will bring back, like Peter. And the Father who draws can still draw. Leave the final judgement with God, who knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19).

In a sentence. Many of his disciples turned back and stopped following him, so Jesus asked the Twelve whether they wanted to go away too.

On a Tuesday. Popularity is no measure of truth. Jesus let the crowds go rather than change his message. Do not follow a Christ made smaller to keep the crowd.

For worship. He let the crowd go rather than change his message, because the message was himself and he would not be less than he is. He stood in an emptying synagogue and did not flinch, and the same faithfulness took him to a hill outside Jerusalem where every friend fled. Bless the unchanging Christ, who will not be made small to be made popular, and who keeps every one the Father gives him even when the many walk away.

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter answered him, "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.”

Simon Peter answered him. Peter speaks for the Twelve, as he does in the other Gospels (Matthew 16:16).

Lord, to whom shall we go? One of the great confessions of faith. Peter doesn’t claim to understand everything Jesus has said. But he knows there is no alternative. There is no one else to go to. His answer is not a compliment, and not a declaration of loyalty. It is a question, and the question is the point. Nothing suggests the twelve understood the discourse any better than the people walking out; they had heard the same sermon. What Peter says is that there is nowhere else: having been where they have been, the alternatives have stopped being alternatives.

Stronger than enthusiasm. That is a stronger position than excitement, and it needs saying because Christians often measure their faith by how they feel about it, and conclude that a faith held in bewilderment is a poor one. It is not. There is a holding on that survives everything precisely because it no longer depends on full comprehension: not I understand and therefore I stay, but I have nowhere else to take this, and the words that give life are here.

You have the words of eternal life. Peter has heard v. 63: Jesus’ words are spirit and life. He has believed it. Only Jesus has words that give eternal life. And it is not resignation. It is a positive claim and a large one. He has just heard the words called a hard saying by men leaving over it, and he calls the same words life. The difference between Peter and the departing disciples is not that Peter found the saying easier. It is what he concluded about the speaker.

What should I do when I have doubts? Do what Peter did: take them to Jesus, not away from him. Doubt is not the same as unbelief; it is often faith struggling. Be honest with God about your questions (the psalms are full of honest complaint), and ask, where else would I go? Every alternative, unbelief, other religions, self-made spirituality, has its own hard sayings and offers no words of eternal life. Stay close to his word and his people, talk to a mature Christian, and keep coming. Many of the strongest believers have walked through seasons when all they could say was Peter’s question.

In a sentence. Peter answered that there was no one else to go to, because Jesus has the words of eternal life.

On a Tuesday. Think of the doctrine you find hardest, the one it would be a relief to find untrue, and ask what your reason is for staying with it. If the honest answer is that it has been explained to your satisfaction, that is a good reason and will hold as long as the explanation does. Peter’s reason will hold longer, because it rests on the person, not the explanation.

For worship. When you don’t understand, and when others walk away, say with Peter: Lord, to whom shall we go? There is no one else. No philosopher, no prophet, no saint, no human wisdom has the words of eternal life. Christ alone speaks words that raise the dead and feed the soul for ever. Bless the Lord who is our only refuge, and whose words are life.

parallels.desc: all the words of this Life

verseByVerse.quote: "and we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God." Jesus answered them, "Did I not choose you, the twelve? And yet one of you is a devil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God.” Jesus answered them, “Did I not choose you, the twelve? And yet one of you is a devil.”

And we have believed, and have come to know. Both verbs are in the perfect tense: we have come to believe and still do; we have come to know and still know. Faith and knowledge go together. Peter speaks of a settled conviction. And the order is the one this Gospel keeps insisting on: believing first, knowing second. We instinctively reverse it, find out and then commit. But the servants filled the jars before they saw the wine; the official walked home before he had news; and these men believed and then, over time, came to know.

That you are the Holy One of God. “The Holy One of God” is a title used by a demon in Mark 1:24. It marks Jesus as set apart, belonging to God in a unique way, the one consecrated and sent by the Father (10:36). Later manuscripts read “the Christ, the Son of the living God,” borrowed from Matthew 16:16. Textual note: the earliest and best manuscripts read “the Holy One of God,” and the ESV rightly follows them. And the demon’s cry was in a synagogue in this same town of Capernaum. The demon got there first. Peter now says as a confession of faith, after everyone else has left, what the demons had been saying under duress: a reminder that the content of a confession is not the whole of it. The words can be perfectly orthodox and mean two different things depending on who says them and why.

Did I not choose you, the twelve? Jesus’ reply both encourages and warns. He chose them, not they him (15:16). Peter has just said the finest thing anyone says in the chapter, on behalf of all of them, at the lowest point of the ministry so far, and the reply must have been very hard to hear. He will not let the confession stand as a headcount. Eleven of them meant it. He does not correct the substance of what Peter said; he corrects the assumed arithmetic behind the we.

And yet one of you is a devil. “Devil” (diabolos): one who acts for the devil, an adversary. Not that Judas was a demon, but that he was the devil’s tool (13:2, 27). The choice of Judas was a choice to be an apostle, not the electing love that saves (17:12). Even among the twelve there was a traitor. Peter’s confession is true, but it is not the whole story of the Twelve. It is the strongest thing Jesus ever says about one of his own, said of a man who at that moment had done nothing publicly wrong and was standing among the others, having also just stayed.

Can a church contain people who are not truly Christians? Yes. The visible church, those who profess faith and gather for worship, has always included some who are not truly born again, as the Twelve included Judas (Matthew 13:24–30). Only God sees the heart perfectly. That is why churches must preach the gospel to their own members as well as to outsiders, practise loving discipline, and why every believer should examine himself (2 Corinthians 13:5). But it is not a reason for suspicion of everyone. Love believes all things, and we leave the final sorting to Christ.

In a sentence. Peter confessed that they had believed and knew Jesus to be the Holy One of God, and Jesus answered that he had chosen the Twelve, yet one of them was a devil.

On a Tuesday. Hold your confession firmly, and examine yourself humbly. Judas walked beside Jesus for three years.

For worship. He is the Holy One of God, set apart by the Father, without sin, consecrated for us. Demons tremble at his name, and his people bow before it in love. And this Holy One chose twelve weak men, one of them a traitor, and still gave himself for sinners. Bless the Holy One of God, whose holiness does not keep him from us but brought him to us.

parallels.desc: Peter’s confession

verseByVerse.quote: He spoke of Judas the son of Simon Iscariot, for he, one of the twelve, was going to betray him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He spoke of Judas the son of Simon Iscariot, for he, one of the twelve, was going to betray him.

He spoke of Judas the son of Simon Iscariot. “Iscariot” is often taken to mean man of Kerioth, a town in Judea (Joshua 15:25). If so, Judas was the only Judean among the Twelve, the rest being Galileans. John supplies the name, and it is worth noticing when. Not at the time; Jesus said only one of you, and nothing suggests anybody in the room worked out who was meant. At the last supper they will still be asking. John names him here, decades later, for readers who know how it ends.

For he, one of the twelve, was going to betray him. “One of the twelve”: the tragedy is in the words. The betrayer was an insider. Jesus knew, and kept him close, and washed his feet (13:5, 26). Judas’ betrayal fulfilled Scripture (13:18; Psalm 41:9), yet he was fully responsible for it (Mark 14:21). God’s sovereignty and human guilt stand together here too.

Judas stayed. That leaves the reader in a position nobody in the story occupied: watching Judas stay. The crowd leaves, the wider circle leaves, and Judas stays. He heard the hard saying and did not walk out. He stood there when Peter said, to whom shall we go?, and by every visible measure he was one who held on. He remained among the twelve for about another year, was trusted with the money, watched the raising of Lazarus, and had his feet washed by the man he sold. That is more frightening than the mass defection. Those who left at least made their position plain. What the verse says without softening is that nearness guarantees nothing. Three years at close quarters with the Son of God, inside the smallest circle, did not produce faith in one man of twelve. Nothing outward can. The chapter has told us what does: no one can come unless it is granted him by the Father.

Could I be a Judas without knowing it? If you are asking the question in fear, almost certainly not. Consider what the Gospel shows of Judas: he is never once recorded as troubled about his own state. Anxiety about your own heart, sorrow over sin, longing to love Christ more: these are not the marks being described. The mark of Judas is a man entirely at ease while he loves something more than Christ (12:6). So examine yourself honestly, confess what you find, and then look away from yourself to the Saviour who never casts out anyone who comes. Fear that drives you to Christ is grace, not a sign of reprobation.

In a sentence. Jesus was speaking of Judas son of Simon Iscariot, who, though one of the Twelve, was going to betray him.

On a Tuesday. Privilege is not the same as grace. If you have grown up in church, served for years, or know the Bible well, thank God for it, and then make sure you are resting on Christ himself and not on your nearness to his things.

For worship. Jesus loved and kept close the very man who would betray him. Such patience should melt us. He washed the feet of Judas and gave him the morsel at the table, and he went to the cross for sinners as unworthy as any of the twelve. The chapter ends where it began, with bread. Five thousand ate it and were hungry again the next morning. One of the twelve ate at the same table as the one who made it, and starved. But all who come to the living bread are fed for ever. Bless the Bread of Life, broken for us, who never casts out anyone who comes.
verseByVerse.note: “Iscariot” is often taken to mean “man of Kerioth,” a town in Judea, but that is uncertain.

6.title: The Bread of Life
6.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Jesus went away to the other side of the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias.<sup>2</sup>And a large crowd was following him, because they saw the signs that he was doing on the sick.<sup>3</sup>Jesus went up on the mountain, and there he sat down with his disciples.<sup>4</sup>Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand.<sup>5</sup>Lifting up his eyes, then, and seeing that a large crowd was coming toward him, Jesus said to Philip, “Where are we to buy bread, so that these people may eat?”<sup>6</sup>He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do.<sup>7</sup>Philip answered him, “Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for each of them to get a little.”<sup>8</sup>One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him,<sup>9</sup>“There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are they for so many?”<sup>10</sup>Jesus said, “Have the people sit down.” Now there was much grass in the place. So the men sat down, about five thousand in number.<sup>11</sup>Jesus then took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated. So also the fish, as much as they wanted.<sup>12</sup>And when they had eaten their fill, he told his disciples, “Gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost.”<sup>13</sup>So they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves left by those who had eaten.<sup>14</sup>When the people saw the sign that he had done, they said, “This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world!”<sup>15</sup>Perceiving then that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself.<sup>16</sup>When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea,<sup>17</sup>got into a boat, and started across the sea to Capernaum. It was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them.<sup>18</sup>The sea became rough because a strong wind was blowing.<sup>19</sup>When they had rowed about three or four miles, they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were frightened.<sup>20</sup>But he said to them, “It is I; do not be afraid.”<sup>21</sup>Then they were glad to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going.<sup>22</sup>On the next day the crowd that remained on the other side of the sea saw that there had been only one boat there, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples had gone away alone.<sup>23</sup>Other boats from Tiberias came near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks.<sup>24</sup>So when the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they themselves got into the boats and went to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.<sup>25</sup>When they found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him, “Rabbi, when did you come here?”<sup>26</sup>Jesus answered them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, you are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves.<sup>27</sup>Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. For on him God the Father has set his seal.”<sup>28</sup>Then they said to him, “What must we do, to be doing the works of God?”<sup>29</sup>Jesus answered them, “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.”<sup>30</sup>So they said to him, “Then what sign do you do, that we may see and believe you? What work do you perform?<sup>31</sup>Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness; as it is written, ’He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’”<sup>32</sup>Jesus then said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven.<sup>33</sup>For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.”<sup>34</sup>They said to him, “Sir, give us this bread always.”<sup>35</sup>Jesus said to them, “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst.<sup>36</sup>But I said to you that you have seen me and yet do not believe.<sup>37</sup>All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out.<sup>38</sup>For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me.<sup>39</sup>And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day.<sup>40</sup>For this is the will of my Father, that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.”<sup>41</sup>So the Jews grumbled about him, because he said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven.”<sup>42</sup>They said, “Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How does he now say, ’I have come down from heaven’?”<sup>43</sup>Jesus answered them, “Do not grumble among yourselves.<sup>44</sup>No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And I will raise him up on the last day.<sup>45</sup>It is written in the Prophets, ’And they will all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me—<sup>46</sup>not that anyone has seen the Father except he who is from God; he has seen the Father.<sup>47</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes has eternal life.<sup>48</sup>I am the bread of life.<sup>49</sup>Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died.<sup>50</sup>This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die.<sup>51</sup>I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.”<sup>52</sup>The Jews then disputed among themselves, saying, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?”<sup>53</sup>So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you.<sup>54</sup>Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.<sup>55</sup>For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink.<sup>56</sup>Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.<sup>57</sup>As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever feeds on me, he also will live because of me.<sup>58</sup>This is the bread that came down from heaven, not like the bread the fathers ate, and died. Whoever feeds on this bread will live forever.”<sup>59</sup>Jesus said these things in the synagogue, as he taught at Capernaum.<sup>60</sup>When many of his disciples heard it, they said, “This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?”<sup>61</sup>But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling about this, said to them, “Do you take offense at this?<sup>62</sup>Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?<sup>63</sup>It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.<sup>64</sup>But there are some of you who do not believe.” (For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him.)<sup>65</sup>And he said, “This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father.”<sup>66</sup>After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him.<sup>67</sup>So Jesus said to the twelve, “Do you want to go away as well?”<sup>68</sup>Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life,<sup>69</sup>and we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God.”<sup>70</sup>Jesus answered them, “Did I not choose you, the twelve? And yet one of you is a devil.”<sup>71</sup>He spoke of Judas the son of Simon Iscariot, for he, one of the twelve, was going to betray him.
6.overview:
The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle, apart from the resurrection, recorded in all four Gospels. John sets it near Passover and tells it so that it opens into one of Jesus’ longest discourses. On a hillside by the Sea of Galilee Jesus feeds a vast crowd from a boy’s five barley loaves and two fish, and twelve baskets of leftovers are gathered. The crowd hails him as the Prophet like Moses and tries to force him to be their king, so he withdraws. That night, as his disciples row against a storm, he comes to them walking on the water and says, “It is I; do not be afraid,” words that echo the divine name.

Next day, in the synagogue at Capernaum, the crowd that ate the bread wants more. Jesus tells them to work for food that lasts, and that the work God requires is to believe in the one he has sent. They ask for a sign like the manna; he replies, “I am the bread of life.” All the Father gives him will come to him, and he will lose none of them but raise them up on the last day; no one can come unless the Father draws him. Then he says that the bread he will give is his flesh for the life of the world, and that unless they eat his flesh and drink his blood they have no life. Many disciples find this too hard and leave. When Jesus asks the Twelve whether they will go too, Peter answers for them all: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.” Yet even among the Twelve is one who will betray him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With his life in danger in Judea, Jesus stays in Galilee until the Feast of Booths. His unbelieving brothers press him to go and make himself known; he answers that his time is not yet, and goes up privately later. In Jerusalem the crowds argue about him in hushed tones. Midway through the feast he teaches in the temple, and the leaders marvel at his learning. He says his teaching is from God, recognisable to anyone who wants to do God’s will; their anger at his Sabbath healing is inconsistent, since they circumcise on the Sabbath. People debate whether he could be the Messiah, since they think they know his origins. Jesus declares that he comes from the true God, whom they do not know. Attempts to arrest him fail, for his hour has not come, though many believe. When officers are sent, he speaks of going where they cannot follow. On the great last day he invites the thirsty to come to him and drink, promising rivers of living water, meaning the Spirit, to be given after his glorification. The crowd divides over whether he is the Prophet or the Christ, or merely a Galilean. The officers return saying no one has ever spoken like him. The Pharisees scorn them and the crowd, and when Nicodemus pleads for a fair hearing, they mock him as a Galilean.
verseByVerse.theology: The controversy in John 7 turns on the question of Jesus's origins and authority. Where is he from? Did he come from God or from himself? The crowd is divided: some say he is a good man; others say he leads the people astray. Jesus's teaching in the temple provokes astonishment: 'How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied?' His answer is theological: his teaching is not his own but the Father's, and the one who seeks to do God's will will recognize its divine origin. The authority question and the origin question are ultimately the same question: who sent him?
verseByVerse.examples: The Feast of Tabernacles is the most eschatological of the Jewish festivals — it looks forward to the final harvest, the ultimate ingathering. Jesus's claim at the climax of the feast ('out of his heart will flow rivers of living water') is the claim to be the fulfillment of Israel's end-times hope. The officers who were sent to arrest Jesus and returned saying 'no one ever spoke like this man' (v. 46) give one of the most powerful testimonies to the authority of Jesus's teaching in the entire Gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus went about in Galilee. He would not go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him. Now the Jews' Feast of Booths was at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this Jesus went about in Galilee. He would not go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him. Now the Jews’ Feast of Booths was at hand.

Meaning first. John 7 and 8 take place at one feast in Jerusalem, and they are full of conflict. The question running through both chapters is: who is Jesus, and where does he come from? The people are divided, the authorities want him dead, and Jesus makes some of his greatest claims, all set against the background of the feast. Watch the setting, because John has chosen it with care: a week in which the whole nation camped out in shelters of branches to remember the years when God lived among them in a tent, poured out water at the altar to remember the rock in the desert, and lit great lamps in the temple court. Into the middle of that week walks the one in whom God has pitched his tent among us (1:14), and he stands up to say that the water and the light were about him.

After this Jesus went about in Galilee. “After this” covers about six months: from Passover (6:4), in spring, to the Feast of Booths in autumn. “Went about” (periepatei, walked about) describes his travelling ministry. John passes over half a year in four words. The hillside crowd of chapter 6 has melted away, many disciples have stopped walking with him (6:66), and the Twelve have stayed only because there is nowhere else to go. He spends the summer walking the roads of the north, teaching and healing, and John does not record a word of it. What John wants us to see is the next confrontation.

He would not go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him. Since the Sabbath healing in Jerusalem (5:18), the authorities had wanted him dead. Jesus is not afraid, but his hour has not yet come (v. 30), and he will not die before the time the Father has set. Notice how flatly John says it, as an established fact needing no explanation. The decision was taken in chapter 5, and everything in this chapter happens with that sentence standing over it. And notice the kind of man who stays away. He is not running from death; in the spring he will walk into Jerusalem in the open, knowing exactly what waits for him there. He is refusing to die at a time of other people’s choosing. The Son of God is not pushed about by threats. He moves when the Father says, and his moves are never reactions. They are always the next step in a plan made before the world began.

Now the Jews’ Feast of Booths was at hand. The Feast of Booths, or Tabernacles (skēnopēgia, pitching of tents), was the third of the great pilgrim festivals, along with Passover and Pentecost (Deuteronomy 16:16). It came in September or October, at the end of the harvest, and lasted seven days, with an eighth day of solemn assembly (Leviticus 23:33–43). The people lived in shelters made of branches, to remember Israel’s wilderness years when God lived among them in a tent. Families built them in courtyards and on flat roofs and slept in them for the week: a nation camping out in its own capital to remember when it had nothing and God had provided everything. It was the most joyful feast of the year; the rabbis said that whoever had not seen the rejoicing of this feast had never seen rejoicing in his life.

The water and the light. By Jesus’ day two ceremonies had been added. Every morning a priest carried water from the Pool of Siloam in a golden pitcher, brought it up through the Water Gate, and poured it out at the altar, praying for rain, while the people sang the Hallel psalms and Isaiah’s words about drawing water with joy from the wells of salvation (Isaiah 12:3). And at night great lamps were lit in the Court of the Women, lighting up all Jerusalem; the sources say there was not a courtyard in the city that did not glow with their light. Jesus will say “come to me and drink” (v. 37) and “I am the light of the world” (8:12) against this background. He is not choosing images at random. He is standing in front of the ceremony and saying that it was about him. And the prophecy read at this feast was Zechariah 14, which promises that living waters will flow out from Jerusalem and that the LORD will be king over all the earth. That passage was in the air all week.

Was Jesus wrong to avoid danger? Should he not have trusted the Father? No. Trusting God has never meant walking carelessly into harm. Jesus refused to throw himself from the temple to prove that God would catch him (Matthew 4:5–7), and here he refuses to throw himself into the hands of men who had already decided to kill him. Paul did the same when he was let down over the wall of Damascus in a basket (Acts 9:25). The question is not whether we take sensible steps to stay safe, but why. Fear says, I must save my life at any cost. Faith says, my life is in the Father’s hands, so I will neither waste it nor cling to it. When the hour came, the same Jesus who avoided Judea set his face to go to Jerusalem, and nothing could turn him back.

In a sentence. Jesus stayed in Galilee rather than Judea, because the authorities wanted to kill him, as the Feast of Booths drew near.

On a Tuesday. Jesus was not reckless with his life, and not afraid either. He lived by the Father’s timing. So may we. That is a steadier way to live than either of the usual alternatives. Most of us swing between anxious caution, avoiding every risk because we secretly think everything depends on us, and careless bravado, which calls itself faith but is really impatience. The man who knows his times are in God’s hand (Psalm 31:15) can be careful without being frightened, and bold without being foolish. Think of the decision you are facing this week, and ask which voice is driving it: fear, impatience, or the quiet question, Father, what is your will here?

For worship. Every year Israel slept under branches to remember that God had once camped among them in the desert. They kept that feast for more than a thousand years, and in the year John describes, the God they were remembering was walking the roads of Galilee in a body, deciding when to go up to his own festival. The tent they commemorated had become flesh. He who had led them by cloud and fire now led himself by his Father’s word, unhurried and unafraid, towards the feast, and beyond it towards the cross where the true tabernacle would be torn down and raised again in three days.
verseByVerse.note: The Feast of Booths (Tabernacles) was the joyful autumn harvest festival. For a week people lived in shelters made of branches, remembering Israel’s years in the wilderness.

parallels.desc: the Feast of Booths

verseByVerse.quote: So his brothers said to him, "Leave here and go to Judea, that your disciples also may see the works you are doing. For no one works in secret if he seeks to be known openly. If you do these things, show yourself to the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So his brothers said to him, “Leave here and go to Judea, that your disciples also may see the works you are doing. For no one works in secret if he seeks to be known openly. If you do these things, show yourself to the world.”

So his brothers said to him. His brothers were James, Joses, Judas and Simon (Mark 6:3), the children of Joseph and Mary born after Jesus; Mark mentions sisters as well.
