Every person there had spent a lifetime discovering that things run out, and they were keeping a feast in booths of branches to remember a generation who had learned it in a desert.

Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, “Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.” “Heart” is literally “belly” (koilia), the innermost being. No single Old Testament verse says exactly this; Jesus is summing up a theme: Isaiah 58:11 (a spring whose waters do not fail), Ezekiel 47 (the river from the temple), Zechariah 14:8, and the rock in the wilderness. He is not misquoting; he is doing what the New Testament often does, gathering a theme rather than citing a line. The rock struck in the wilderness poured out water for a whole nation (Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11). Isaiah promised water on the thirsty ground (Isaiah 44:3). Ezekiel saw the river from under the temple threshold, deepening as it ran, ankle-deep, knee-deep, waist-deep, until it was a river no one could cross, and everything it touched lived. He is telling a crowd at that feast that the whole river of promise they had been singing about has arrived, and is standing in front of them.

Rivers. And the picture is not a modest one. Not a cup, not a well, not enough to get by on. Rivers: plural, moving, more than any single person could ever use. He is thirty-odd years old, has no house, is under an arrest warrant, and will be dead by spring. And he stands up in the middle of the greatest festival of his people, at the exact moment the water ceremony ends, and offers to be the river.

Whose heart? The Greek can be punctuated two ways. Most take it as the believer’s heart: the one who drinks becomes a source of blessing to others (4:14). Others punctuate: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me, and let him drink who believes in me. As Scripture says, out of his heart...” so that the rivers flow from Christ’s heart. Both are true: the water flows from Christ (19:34 shows water flowing from his side), and through the believer to others. The ESV’s reading is natural and most likely. The second reading has real attractions: it fits a ceremony in which water flows from the temple, and Jesus is the new temple (2:19–21). But the difference is smaller than it first appears, since John explains in the next verse that he is speaking of the Spirit, and the Spirit comes from Christ to the believer and then out through him. The spring is Christ either way; the question is only how far downstream the sentence is looking.

I do not feel thirsty for God. Is this invitation for me? Thirst does not always feel like longing for God. Often it feels like restlessness, boredom, the sense that nothing quite satisfies, or the dull ache after the thing you hoped would fill you has not. Augustine said our hearts are restless until they rest in God, and most restlessness is that thirst in disguise. If you have ever wanted more than this life gives, the invitation is for you. And if you feel nothing at all, come anyway, and ask him to make you thirsty. The invitation is to anyone.

So how do I actually come and drink? To come and drink is to believe: to trust Jesus himself, and to keep trusting him, for what only he can give. In practice it means turning to him in prayer, plainly, as someone who needs him; listening to him in his word, where he speaks; and receiving him in the means he has given, the preaching of the gospel, the fellowship of his people and the Lord’s Supper. Drinking is not a single gulp at conversion. It is a daily return to the spring. When you are dry, do not first try harder. Go back to him and drink again.

In a sentence. On the great last day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out for anyone who is thirsty to come to him and drink, for from the heart of the one who believes in him, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow.

On a Tuesday. Notice where you go when you are dry: the screen, the fridge, the shop, the bottle, the approval of others. None of them is evil in itself, and none of them is the river. This week, when you feel that thirst, stop and pray a single sentence: Lord Jesus, I am thirsty; give me yourself. Then, as he fills you, let it flow on: the word of encouragement, the act of kindness, the gospel shared. Rivers are for giving away.

For worship. Are you thirsty? Come to Christ and drink. And let the river flow on through you to others. The rock was struck in the wilderness and water gushed out for a rebellious people. The true Rock was struck on a hill outside Jerusalem, and from his pierced side came blood and water. Out of the one who had no house and no possessions has poured a river that has been flowing for two thousand years, through every nation, and has never run low. To anyone at all, standing anywhere since, the offer is the same, shouted over the noise of a dispersing crowd: if anyone thirsts, let him come.
verseByVerse.note: Later Jewish writings describe water being carried from the pool of Siloam and poured out at the altar each day of the feast. No single verse says these exact words; Jesus draws on several prophecies. The ESV notes a different punctuation that makes Jesus himself the source of the water.

parallels.desc: come to the waters
water flowing from the temple
living waters from Jerusalem

verseByVerse.quote: Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive, for as yet the Spirit had not been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive, for as yet the Spirit had not been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.

Now this he said about the Spirit. John explains. The living water is the Holy Spirit. The Old Testament often pictures the Spirit as water poured out (Isaiah 44:3; Ezekiel 36:25–27; Joel 2:28). John stops the story to tell the reader what that meant, and that is unusual; he does it only a handful of times in the whole Gospel, when a sentence would otherwise be misread. The rivers are the Spirit. Not an experience, not an influence, not a quality of life, but a person. And John writes as a man on the other side of Pentecost, describing something that had since happened to him and to everyone reading.

Whom those who believed in him were to receive. Every believer receives the Spirit (Romans 8:9; Galatians 3:2). Not some special class.

For as yet the Spirit had not been given. Literally “for the Spirit was not yet.” Of course the Spirit existed and was active in the Old Testament (Psalm 51:11) and in Jesus’ ministry (1:32). The meaning is that the Spirit had not yet been given in the new covenant way, poured out on all God’s people to dwell in them for ever (14:16–17). The bluntness of the phrase shows how enormous the change was in the mind of a man who lived through it. Before Pentecost the Spirit came upon prophets, kings and craftsmen for particular tasks. After it he made his home in fishermen, slaves, widows and children, all who believe.

Because Jesus was not yet glorified. In John, Jesus is glorified in his death, resurrection and ascension (12:23; 13:31; 17:1). The Spirit could not come until Jesus had finished his work and returned to the Father (16:7). The cross opened the way; the exalted Christ poured out the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2:33). That binds the river to the cross. The river could not flow until the rock had been struck. That is not decoration; it is the argument of the chapter, and it is why the invitation of verse 37 was made by a man six months from dying. Every experience of the Spirit since is a gift from the glorified Son, the one through whom the absent Lord is made present.

Where Christians differ: receiving the Spirit. Pentecostal and charismatic teaching often holds that the baptism of the Spirit is a second experience after conversion, marked by speaking in tongues. Verdict: this verse says all who believe receive the Spirit. Every Christian has the Spirit from the moment of faith (1 Corinthians 12:13). There may be many fresh fillings and deeper experiences of the Spirit, but no second class of Christians. The sign gifts of the apostolic age, such as tongues and prophecy, served to confirm the founding of the church and have ceased, while the Spirit himself remains with every believer for ever.

How do I know I have the Spirit? Not first by a feeling, but by what the Spirit does. He brings you to confess that Jesus is Lord and to mean it (1 Corinthians 12:3). He makes Christ precious to you (16:14). He teaches you to call God Father and to trust him as his child (Romans 8:15–16). He makes you hate sin and fight it, and he grows his fruit in you, slowly: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness (Galatians 5:22–23). If you trust Christ, the Spirit lives in you, whether or not you have had any dramatic experience. Weak faith is still Spirit-given faith.

What does it mean to be filled with the Spirit? It means to be more and more under his influence, as a sail is filled by the wind. Paul commands it as a continuing thing, be filled (Ephesians 5:18), and he shows its marks in the next verses: worship, thankfulness and humble service in home and church. It is not a second level of Christian, and it is not measured by how dramatic your experiences are. You seek it by keeping in step with him: reading the word he inspired, praying, confessing sin quickly, obeying what he shows you, and asking. Jesus promised that the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13).

In a sentence. Jesus was speaking about the Spirit whom believers would receive, for the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.

On a Tuesday. If you believe in Christ, the Spirit lives in you. You are not waiting for him; ask him to fill you and flow through you. Before the hard conversation, the temptation you know is coming, or the task that is beyond you, pray simply: Holy Spirit, you live in me; help me now. Then go and do the next thing, trusting that he is not absent.

For worship. The river could not flow until the rock was struck, and the rock was struck for us. Jesus went to the cross, rose, and ascended, and from the Father’s right hand he poured out the Spirit on all his people. God does not merely visit us now, as he once filled the tabernacle and the temple. He lives in us. The Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation and raised Jesus from the dead has made his home in ordinary believers, and he will never leave.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these words, some of the people said, "This really is the Prophet." Others said, "This is the Christ." But some said, "Is the Christ to come from Galilee?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they heard these words, some of the people said, “This really is the Prophet.” Others said, “This is the Christ.” But some said, “Is the Christ to come from Galilee?”

This really is the Prophet. “The Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised (Deuteronomy 18:15–18; compare 1:21; 6:14). Moses gave water from the rock; Jesus offers living water. Some Jews thought of the Prophet as a figure distinct from the Messiah. In fact Jesus is both (Acts 3:22). It is the same identification the crowd made on the hillside in chapter 6, just before they tried to crown him.

Others said, “This is the Christ.” The Messiah. Three verdicts in two verses, and the crowd is now split three ways rather than two. That is what happens when a claim gets large enough that indifference stops being possible.

But some said, “Is the Christ to come from Galilee?” The Greek expects the answer no. They are sure Galilee is the wrong place. And what is remarkable is what John does not do with it. He knows the answer. He is writing after Matthew and Luke have set down the Bethlehem birth in detail, and he could end the objection with one sentence: as a matter of fact, he was born there. He does not. He records the objection, lets it stand, and moves on. He expects his readers to know already, and he is more interested in the pattern than in the correction. All through this Gospel people reject Jesus on grounds that are factually wrong and would have collapsed under one honest question, and nobody asks it. The information was available in Jerusalem that week. Not one person in the courtyard thought to check.

Why did people expect different figures: a prophet, a Christ? Because the Old Testament promises came in many strands, and few saw how they fitted together. Some looked for the prophet like Moses; some for a king of David’s line; some for a priestly figure; some for all of them, arriving separately. Jesus is all of them in one person: the Prophet who speaks God’s word, the Priest who offers himself, the King who reigns. The Reformers spoke of his threefold office for this reason. The categories built to receive him turned out to be too small one by one, and too confusing all together, until he came and filled them all.

In a sentence. When the people heard this, some said he was the Prophet, others the Christ, but others objected that the Christ would not come from Galilee.

On a Tuesday. If you have an objection to Christ, ask it honestly and then look for the answer. The crowd’s objection would have collapsed with a single question to Jesus’ mother. Many objections are like that. Read the Gospel the objection is about, ask a Christian you trust, and let the facts have their say.

For worship. Jesus is the Prophet who speaks God’s words, and the Christ who reigns. All their guesses meet in him. Every hope Israel had, every figure the prophets sketched, every longing the feast expressed, was waiting for one face to fill it. He is the Word the Prophet spoke, the King David foreshadowed, and the water Moses struck from the rock. There is nothing to look for beyond him.
verseByVerse.note: “The Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised.

verseByVerse.quote: "Has not the Scripture said that the Christ comes from the offspring of David, and comes from Bethlehem, the village where David was?" So there was a division among the people over him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Has not the Scripture said that the Christ comes from the offspring of David, and comes from Bethlehem, the village where David was? So there was a division among the people over him.

Has not the Scripture said that the Christ comes from the offspring of David. They were right that the Messiah would be a son of David (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5).

And comes from Bethlehem, the village where David was? And right that he would come from Bethlehem (Micah 5:2; compare Matthew 2:5–6). These are not men twisting the text. They know it well, they are using it correctly, and they reach a false conclusion, because they have a fact wrong and have not thought to test it.

The irony. They did not know that Jesus had been born in Bethlehem, and was descended from David. John doesn’t stop to correct them. He expects his readers to know the story (Matthew 1–2; Luke 2), and to see the irony: they reject him for not meeting the very prophecies he fulfils. And it is a more uncomfortable example than the usual villains. It is possible to be a careful reader of Scripture, to quote it accurately, to apply it validly, and still to end up on the wrong side of God: not through bad interpretation but through an unexamined assumption smuggled in underneath it. The assumption here was, he is from Galilee, and it was never checked because it did not feel like an assumption. It felt like common knowledge.

So there was a division among the people over him. “Division” (schisma): Jesus divides people (9:16; 10:19). No one can stay neutral about him. He came, in the words of the prologue, to his own (1:11). The result is not a nation gathered but a nation torn, and the tear runs through crowds, through the council, and in this chapter through his own family. Jesus said himself that he had not come to bring peace but a sword, and that a man’s enemies would be those of his own household (Matthew 10:34–36). The division is not the goal and it is not the good. It is what happens when a claim this large meets people who are free to refuse it, and the alternative, a Christ small enough that nobody need decide about him, was never on offer.

What if following Christ is dividing my family? It hurts, and Jesus does not pretend otherwise. He knew it from the inside: his own brothers did not believe. First, make sure that the division is over Christ, not over your harshness, pride or a quarrel dressed up as faith. Then stay loving, patient and honest; do not withdraw, retaliate or preach at every meal. Honour your parents and keep your promises where you can do so without denying him (Ephesians 6:2). Pray for them by name. And take comfort that the division need not be the last word: the brothers who stood outside in John 7 were praying with the disciples in Acts 1.

In a sentence. Some argued that Scripture said the Christ would come from David’s line and from Bethlehem, and the people were divided over him.

On a Tuesday. Get the facts before dismissing Jesus. Many objections dissolve when you know the whole story. And examine your own assumptions. Pick one thing you are sure the Bible says, and check it this week: find the verse, read it in context, and see whether it says what you thought.

For worship. The one they said could not be the Christ was born in the very town they named, of the very line they demanded. God kept his word to David to the letter, in a stable, while the scholars of Jerusalem went on arguing. He does not need our recognition to be faithful. He keeps every promise, whether anyone notices or not, and the division over his Son is the sign that the Son has come.
verseByVerse.note: They did not know that Jesus had been born in Bethlehem.

parallels.desc: from Bethlehem shall come a ruler

verseByVerse.quote: Some of them wanted to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of them wanted to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him.

Some of them wanted to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him. Again, as in v. 30. Something held them back. John has told us what: his hour had not yet come. God restrains the hands of the wicked until his purpose is fulfilled. Twice in fourteen verses John writes almost the same sentence (vv. 30, 44), and at verse 45 the officers come back empty-handed too. Three attempts, three failures, and John gives the reason only once, expecting the reader to carry it to the others.

What providence looks like from inside. What is striking is how little there is to see. No lightning, no escape, no crowd parting. Some men in a courtyard felt like seizing a teacher and somehow did not. If any of them had been asked afterwards, they would probably have said the moment passed, or it was not the place, or someone else should have moved first. That is what most providence looks like from inside: not an intervention that anyone notices, but the ordinary reasons why a thing did not happen. And the ordinary reasons are the means God uses, not an alternative to him. Notice too that this time it is not the authorities but individuals in the crowd, acting on impulse, with no warrant and no orders. The restraint worked at the level of a private intention: the impulse rose in a man’s mind and did not become an action, and he would have had no idea that anything had stopped it.

If God restrains evil, why does he not restrain all of it? Scripture does not give us the whole answer, but it gives us enough to trust him. God restrains a great deal of evil we never see, and he permits some evil for purposes we cannot yet see, never approving it, and always turning it to good for those who love him (Genesis 50:20; Romans 8:28). The clearest example is this very story. God held back these hands in the autumn, and in the spring he let wicked hands crucify his Son, because through that greatest evil he was accomplishing the greatest good. If he can do that with the cross, he can be trusted with what he permits in your life.

In a sentence. Some wanted to arrest him, but no one laid a hand on him.

On a Tuesday. It is not only the great events that are governed. So is the thing somebody almost did to you last year and did not. Thank God tonight for one harm you were spared, and then sleep, because the one who keeps you neither slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:4).

For worship. The same God who held back their hands holds your life. No one can touch it apart from his will. He rules not only kings and councils but the half-formed impulse in a stranger’s mind. And the hands he restrained in the temple, he later allowed to bind his Son, because he so loved the world. Nothing is outside his rule: not one sparrow, not one hair, and not one hour of your life.

verseByVerse.quote: The officers then came to the chief priests and Pharisees, who said to them, "Why did you not bring him?" The officers answered, "No one ever spoke like this man!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officers then came to the chief priests and Pharisees, who said to them, “Why did you not bring him?” The officers answered, “No one ever spoke like this man!”

The officers then came to the chief priests and Pharisees. The temple police sent in v. 32 return empty-handed, perhaps several days later. Which means they had been in and around those courts for days: long enough, as it turns out, to hear the invitation of verse 37.

Why did you not bring him? The leaders are angry.

No one ever spoke like this man! An extraordinary admission from men trained to obey orders. They were sent to arrest him, and were arrested by his words. They had heard many teachers in the temple, but never anyone like this (Matthew 7:28–29). And the answer they give is not an excuse. An excuse would have been easy: the crowd was too thick, he slipped away, there would have been a riot. Any of these would have been believed. What they say instead is a sentence of open admiration, delivered to the men who had ordered the arrest, with no attempt to protect themselves. They do not claim to have understood him. They make no confession of faith, and there is no record that any of them became a disciple. They simply could not do it, could not pretend otherwise, and stood before the council and said why.

The truest sentence in the chapter. Consider how exposed that is. These were employees, in a hierarchy, reporting a failure to powerful men in no mood for it, and the next verse shows the contempt they got. The most honest testimony in the chapter comes from men with everything to lose by giving it, who were not believers, and who had been sent to put him in chains. They are never mentioned again. No name is preserved. They walk into the chapter as instruments of an arrest, say the truest sentence in it, are sneered at, and disappear. That is its own small comfort for anyone who has said the right thing once, at cost, and seen nothing come of it. It went into the record. John was still writing it down decades later, and the men who said it had no idea it would outlast the council that mocked them.

What was it about how he spoke? It was not technique. Other teachers quoted authorities; he spoke with his own authority (Matthew 7:29). Other teachers explained God; he spoke as one who had come from him, and his words were spirit and life (6:63). He spoke with perfect truth and perfect love at once, which no one else has managed. He knew what was in a man (2:25), so his words went straight to the heart. And he spoke the Father’s own words (v. 16). When you read the Gospels and find a saying of his lodging in you and refusing to leave, you are feeling what the officers felt.

In a sentence. When the officers came back without Jesus, they explained that no one had ever spoken like him.

On a Tuesday. Read his words slowly this week. Choose one saying from this chapter, if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink, and carry it with you through the day. And if you have ever said the right thing about Christ and seen nothing come of it, take heart from these nameless men. God keeps the record.

For worship. No one ever spoke like this man. Let his words grip you as they gripped the officers. The voice that said let there be light spoke in the temple courts in the accent of Galilee, and hardened men could not lay a hand on him. One day that same voice will call the dead from their graves (5:28–29). Until then, he speaks through his word, and the sheep still hear his voice.

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees answered them, "Have you also been deceived? Have any of the authorities or the Pharisees believed in him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees answered them, “Have you also been deceived? Have any of the authorities or the Pharisees believed in him?”

Have you also been deceived? “Deceived” (planaō): led astray, the same word as v. 12. This is not a request for reasons. It is a warning shot, and its purpose is to make the officers feel foolish, not to answer what they said. Nobody engages with no one ever spoke like this man at all.

Have any of the authorities or the Pharisees believed in him? The argument from authority: none of the experts believe, so it must be false. A familiar argument to this day. The irony: one of them is about to speak up (v. 50), and later Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the council, will be revealed as a secret disciple (19:38), and many priests will believe (Acts 6:7). It is the oldest move there is. The claim is not that Jesus is wrong. It is that no one who matters thinks he is right. And it is aimed at policemen, who are being asked whether they propose to set their judgment against that of the learned. It is designed to remind them of their place, and it works: nothing more is heard from the officers. Meanwhile Nicodemus is sitting in that chamber while the question is put as though it answered itself, and both he and Joseph will carry the body of Jesus the following spring.

Consensus is evidence about people. Consensus is not nothing, and a wise reader does not despise it; the church has generally been right to be suspicious of the man who alone sees the truth. But consensus is evidence about people, not about the matter, and its worth depends entirely on whether the people are free to say what they think. In this room they were not, and the proof is that the one sympathiser present could manage only a question about procedure.

Should I ignore scholars and experts when they reject Christianity? No. Listen to them, learn from them, and take their arguments seriously; many scholars are believers, and honest scholarship has served the church well. But notice what kind of claim is being made. A sentence that begins, most educated people do not believe, is a statement about people, not an argument about the evidence. Ask what the actual reasons are, and weigh them. Remember too that every generation has its consensus, and the consensus of one century is often the embarrassment of the next. The question is not who believes, but whether it is true. Look at Christ yourself, and read the evidence for the resurrection with your own eyes.

In a sentence. The Pharisees asked if the officers had been deceived too, since none of the authorities or Pharisees had believed in him.

On a Tuesday. Truth is not decided by what the experts or the majority think. Look at Christ for yourself. And be careful of using the same move on others: dismissing a fellow believer’s point because of who they are rather than what they have said.

For worship. Not many wise according to worldly standards, not many powerful, not many of noble birth were called (1 Corinthians 1:26). God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise, so that no one may boast before him. The rulers asked, scornfully, whether any of them believed. Within months, a ruler would be carrying the King’s body to the tomb, and within weeks of that, priests would be bowing the knee. Christ needs no committee’s approval. He is Lord whether the experts agree or not, and he humbles the proud and gathers the humble.

parallels.desc: many even of the authorities believed

verseByVerse.quote: "But this crowd that does not know the law is accursed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But this crowd that does not know the law is accursed.

This crowd that does not know the law. Religious leaders despised ordinary people who did not know the details of the law and its oral traditions. They called them the “people of the land” (am ha’aretz), and some rabbinic sayings warn against eating with them or marrying their daughters. The phrase began as an ordinary description of the rural population and hardened, in the mouths of the learned, into something like a caste: people who could not be relied on to tithe properly or keep the purity rules, whose food you could not safely eat and whose testimony you would not readily take.

Is accursed. The law did pronounce a curse on those who did not keep it (Deuteronomy 27:26). They apply it to the crowd. The irony again: the very leaders who know the law are breaking it, as Nicodemus will point out in the next verse. And it was Christ who would bear the curse of the law for his people (Galatians 3:13). So this is not simply an insult thrown in temper. It is the class judgment of the educated on the uneducated, delivered as a theological verdict.

The people who got closest. And it is aimed at the people who had got closest to the truth in this chapter. The crowd is confused, divided and working from bad information. They are also the ones asking whether this might be the Christ, and the officers who could not lay a hand on him were drawn from exactly that class. It is the pattern the whole Gospel reports. A Samaritan woman with a difficult history hears the plainest statement of his identity in the book (4:26). Fishermen stay when the theologians leave. A blind beggar in chapter 9 will out-argue the council. And the men who know most about God’s law say, in the same breath, that nobody who matters believes in him and everybody else is cursed.

Does this mean knowledge is dangerous and I should not study? No. Knowledge of God’s word is a great gift, and Scripture urges us to grow in it (2 Peter 3:18). The problem in this verse is not knowledge but pride: knowledge without love puffs up (1 Corinthians 8:1). The test is what your learning does to the way you see other believers. If it makes you more patient, more humble and more delighted when an untrained Christian sees something true, it is doing its proper work. If it makes you contemptuous, it has become the thing in this verse. Study hard, and stay low.

In a sentence. The Pharisees dismissed the crowd that believed in Jesus as ignorant of the law and therefore cursed.

On a Tuesday. Beware of religious pride that looks down on the ordinary believer. Jesus welcomed the people the experts despised. Notice what happens in you when someone with no training says something about God that is clumsily put and substantially right. If the first response is to correct the form, that instinct is the one in this verse. Learning is a gift. It becomes deadly at the moment it starts producing contempt.

For worship. The rulers called the crowd accursed. Christ became a curse for them, and for us, hanging on a tree, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the people of the land and the Gentiles alike (Galatians 3:13–14). He did not curse the ignorant. He taught them, healed them and died for them. The despised people of the land turned out to be the people of his heart.
verseByVerse.note: Religious leaders despised ordinary people who did not know the finer points of the law.

parallels.desc: cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law

verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus, who had gone to him before, and who was one of them, said to them, "Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing and learning what he does?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus, who had gone to him before, and who was one of them, said to them, “Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing and learning what he does?”

Nicodemus, who had gone to him before. Nicodemus was a member of the council, the man who came to Jesus by night (3:1–2). We see him growing: first by night, now a cautious word in council, and finally openly at the burial (19:39). John reminds the reader who this is, and it is a kind reminder, because the man has not been mentioned for four chapters. He came at night, asked how a man could be born when he is old, and was told about the wind that blows where it wishes.

And who was one of them. The answer to their question (v. 48): one of the Pharisees and rulers is at least open to Jesus.

Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing and learning what he does? He doesn’t defend Jesus outright, but appeals to justice. The law required a fair hearing (Deuteronomy 1:16–17; 17:4). The men who boast of knowing the law are condemning a man without trial. Nicodemus exposes them with their own law. It is easy to be disappointed in that, so be accurate about the risk. He has just heard the room agree that no authority believes in Jesus and that anyone who does is deceived. Speaking at all marks him as a possible sympathiser, and the sneering reply he gets shows he was heard exactly that way. It names the price of going further. And on the merits he is entirely right. It is the only legally correct sentence spoken in the chamber, and it comes from the one man there who has actually met him.

The shape of his story. Three appearances: by night with a question (3:1–2); here, with a cautious objection about procedure; and finally at the cross, in daylight, in public, carrying about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes to bury a condemned man (19:39), a quantity fit for a king, at the moment when being associated with him could not possibly have looked worse. The journey took perhaps two years, and at this point in it he could manage no more than a question. Nobody in that room would have picked him out as a future disciple. Grace was not in a hurry, and it did not let go.

Is it all right to be a secret or cautious believer? A cautious beginning is not the same as settled secrecy. Nicodemus’ first steps were small, and Jesus did not despise them; many true believers begin quietly. But John does not leave him there, and neither should we stay there. Jesus warns that whoever is ashamed of him, he will be ashamed of (Mark 8:38), and John says sadly of some rulers that they believed but did not confess him, because they loved human praise (12:42–43). If you are a quiet believer, ask what the next honest step is: telling one friend, joining a church, being baptised. Faith that is real grows towards the light.

In a sentence. Nicodemus, one of the rulers who had come to Jesus before, asked whether their law condemned a man without first hearing him and finding out what he had done.

On a Tuesday. Faith sometimes grows slowly. Nicodemus said little here, but he said something. Speak up for justice, even if it’s only one sentence. In the meeting where someone is being talked about unfairly, the one sentence may be simply: should we not hear his side first? It costs something to say it. Say it.

For worship. The Lord who met Nicodemus by night did not give up on him. He bore with his caution, his questions and his slowness, and drew him step by step until he stood at the foot of the cross in daylight. He is the same with us. He does not break the bruised reed or quench the smouldering wick (Isaiah 42:3). Whoever he begins with, he finishes with.
verseByVerse.note: Nicodemus was a member of the council.

parallels.desc: inquire diligently

verseByVerse.quote: They replied, "Are you from Galilee too? Search and see that no prophet arises from Galilee." They went each to his own house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They replied, “Are you from Galilee too? Search and see that no prophet arises from Galilee.” They went each to his own house.

Are you from Galilee too? They don’t answer his point. They mock him: are you one of these northern peasants too? Nicodemus asked a question about legal procedure. Nobody answers it. This is not a rebuttal but a way of putting a man in a category so that nothing he says needs weighing.

Search and see that no prophet arises from Galilee. “Search” means search the Scriptures. They were wrong: the prophet Jonah came from Gath-hepher in Galilee (2 Kings 14:25), and Isaiah had promised that a great light would shine in Galilee of the nations (Isaiah 9:1–2; Matthew 4:15–16). In their anger they forget their own Scriptures. Gath-hepher is only a few miles from Nazareth. These are men whose profession is the Scriptures, telling a colleague to go and search the very texts they have just misreported. It is the closing irony of a chapter full of them. The crowd was dismissed as ignorant of the law in verse 49. The men who said it get a fact about the prophets wrong in verse 52, and they get it wrong because they are angry, and they never notice.

Textual note. One early papyrus reads “the Prophet” here, meaning the prophet like Moses would not arise from Galilee, which would make their claim less obviously false. The ESV follows the majority of manuscripts.

They went each to his own house. The council breaks up without decision. This sentence (v. 53) begins the passage about the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11), which the ESV places in brackets. The earliest and most reliable manuscripts do not contain it, and some place it elsewhere (after Luke 21:38, for example). Its style is unlike John’s. It is very likely a true story about Jesus preserved in the church, but not originally part of John’s Gospel. The ESV keeps it with a note, and we comment on it in chapter 8 with that caution.

The flattest sentence in the chapter. No verdict, no arrest, no resolution. A council that had met to deal with him breaks up in the evening having achieved nothing at all, while the man they were discussing, as the bracketed story goes on to say, went out to the Mount of Olives. They went each to his own house. He had no house to go to. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58).

Why does my Bible put brackets here, in the middle of a scene? Because the passage that begins with this sentence and runs to 8:11 is the one the brackets surround, and it opens at the last verse of a chapter. That is why the bracket in your Bible seems to start in an odd place. The brackets are not a sign that the translators are hiding anything; they are telling you honestly what the manuscripts show. The story itself, and how to read it with that caution, is handled at the start of chapter 8.

In a sentence. The rulers mocked Nicodemus as a Galilean and claimed no prophet came from Galilee, and then they all went home.

On a Tuesday. When you notice yourself answering a point by attacking the person who made it, stop. Ask whether what they said is true. Anger makes clever people careless with facts, and it made these scholars forget their own Bibles. If you are angry about a disagreement, wait until you are calm before you answer.

For worship. The light has dawned in Galilee of the Gentiles, whatever the rulers said. Christ came from where God promised, and comes to all who are humble enough to receive him. The council went home to their houses and their certainties. The Son of God went out to the hillside with nowhere to lay his head, and he did it gladly, for them and for us. The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light, and it came from the very place the scholars said nothing good could come from.
verseByVerse.note: They were wrong: the prophet Jonah came from Gath-hepher in Galilee. The ESV notes that the earliest manuscripts do not include 7:53–8:11 and brackets the passage.

parallels.desc: Jonah son of Amittai, of Gath-hepher
Galilee of the nations

7.title: Rivers of Living Water
7.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Jesus went about in Galilee. He would not go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him.<sup>2</sup>Now the Jews’ Feast of Booths was at hand.<sup>3</sup>So his brothers said to him, “Leave here and go to Judea, that your disciples also may see the works you are doing.<sup>4</sup>For no one works in secret if he seeks to be known openly. If you do these things, show yourself to the world.”<sup>5</sup>For not even his brothers believed in him.<sup>6</sup>Jesus said to them, “My time has not yet come, but your time is always here.<sup>7</sup>The world cannot hate you, but it hates me because I testify about it that its works are evil.<sup>8</sup>You go up to the feast. I am not going up to this feast, for my time has not yet fully come.”<sup>9</sup>After saying this, he remained in Galilee.<sup>10</sup>But after his brothers had gone up to the feast, then he also went up, not publicly but in private.<sup>11</sup>The Jews were looking for him at the feast, and saying, “Where is he?”<sup>12</sup>And there was much muttering about him among the people. While some said, “He is a good man,” others said, “No, he is leading the people astray.”<sup>13</sup>Yet for fear of the Jews no one spoke openly of him.<sup>14</sup>About the middle of the feast Jesus went up into the temple and began teaching.<sup>15</sup>The Jews therefore marveled, saying, “How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied?”<sup>16</sup>So Jesus answered them, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me.<sup>17</sup>If anyone’s will is to do God’s will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my own authority.<sup>18</sup>The one who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory; but the one who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and in him there is no falsehood.<sup>19</sup>Has not Moses given you the law? Yet none of you keeps the law. Why do you seek to kill me?”<sup>20</sup>The crowd answered, “You have a demon! Who is seeking to kill you?”<sup>21</sup>Jesus answered them, “I did one work, and you all marvel at it.<sup>22</sup>Moses gave you circumcision (not that it is from Moses, but from the fathers), and you circumcise a man on the Sabbath.<sup>23</sup>If on the Sabbath a man receives circumcision, so that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because on the Sabbath I made a man’s whole body well?<sup>24</sup>Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment.”<sup>25</sup>Some of the people of Jerusalem therefore said, “Is not this the man whom they seek to kill?<sup>26</sup>And here he is, speaking openly, and they say nothing to him! Can it be that the authorities really know that this is the Christ?<sup>27</sup>But we know where this man comes from, and when the Christ appears, no one will know where he comes from.”<sup>28</sup>So Jesus proclaimed, as he taught in the temple, “You know me, and you know where I come from. But I have not come of my own accord. He who sent me is true, and him you do not know.<sup>29</sup>I know him, for I come from him, and he sent me.”<sup>30</sup>So they were seeking to arrest him, but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come.<sup>31</sup>Yet many of the people believed in him. They said, “When the Christ appears, will he do more signs than this man has done?”<sup>32</sup>The Pharisees heard the crowd muttering these things about him, and the chief priests and Pharisees sent officers to arrest him.<sup>33</sup>Jesus then said, “I will be with you a little longer, and then I am going to him who sent me.<sup>34</sup>You will seek me and you will not find me. Where I am you cannot come.”<sup>35</sup>The Jews said to one another, “Where does this man intend to go that we will not find him? Does he intend to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks and teach the Greeks?<sup>36</sup>What does he mean by saying, ’You will seek me and you will not find me,’ and, ’Where I am you cannot come’?”<sup>37</sup>On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.<sup>38</sup>Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, ’Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.’”<sup>39</sup>Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive, for as yet the Spirit had not been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.<sup>40</sup>When they heard these words, some of the people said, “This really is the Prophet.”<sup>41</sup>Others said, “This is the Christ.” But some said, “Is the Christ to come from Galilee?<sup>42</sup>Has not the Scripture said that the Christ comes from the offspring of David, and comes from Bethlehem, the village where David was?”<sup>43</sup>So there was a division among the people over him.<sup>44</sup>Some of them wanted to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him.<sup>45</sup>The officers then came to the chief priests and Pharisees, who said to them, “Why did you not bring him?”<sup>46</sup>The officers answered, “No one ever spoke like this man!”<sup>47</sup>The Pharisees answered them, “Have you also been deceived?<sup>48</sup>Have any of the authorities or the Pharisees believed in him?<sup>49</sup>But this crowd that does not know the law is accursed.”<sup>50</sup>Nicodemus, who had gone to him before, and who was one of them, said to them,<sup>51</sup>“Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing and learning what he does?”<sup>52</sup>They replied, “Are you from Galilee too? Search and see that no prophet arises from Galilee.”<sup>53</sup>[[They went each to his own house,
7.overview:
Six months after the feeding of the five thousand, the Feast of Booths (Tabernacles) arrives: the joyful autumn festival when Israel lived in shelters of branches to remember the wilderness, and prayed for rain. Jesus’ unbelieving brothers urge him to go to Jerusalem and show himself; he refuses to move on their timetable, then goes up privately. Halfway through the feast he teaches openly in the temple, and the chapter becomes a swirl of opinions: he is a good man; he deceives the people; he has a demon; he is the Prophet; he is the Christ; he cannot be, because the Christ comes from Bethlehem. Jesus answers that his teaching comes from God, that anyone willing to do God’s will can recognise it, and that their anger at his Sabbath healing is hypocrisy, since they circumcise on the Sabbath. The authorities send officers to arrest him.

On the last and greatest day of the feast, when water from the Pool of Siloam was poured out at the altar, Jesus stands and cries out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink,” and promises rivers of living water flowing from within. John explains that he meant the Spirit, who would be given once Jesus was glorified. The officers return without him, saying, “No one ever spoke like this man!” The Pharisees scorn them and the ignorant crowd, until Nicodemus, one of their own, asks whether the law condemns a man without a hearing, and is mocked for it. The chapter shows a people divided by Jesus, as every generation has been.

8.title: The Light of the World

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–30 — Light in the Darkness: The Second I AM
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus spends the night on the Mount of Olives and returns to the temple at dawn, where crowds gather and he sits to teach. The scribes and Pharisees bring a woman caught in adultery, stand her before everyone, and ask him whether she should be stoned as Moses commanded, hoping to trap him. Jesus bends down and writes on the ground with his finger. When they keep pressing, he straightens up and tells whoever among them is without sin to throw the first stone, then stoops and writes again. One by one, the oldest first, they leave, until only Jesus and the woman remain. He asks where her accusers are: has no one condemned her? No one, she says. Neither does he; she may go, and must leave her sin behind. Then Jesus declares that he is the light of the world: his followers will not walk in darkness but have the light of life. The Pharisees object that his self-testimony is invalid. He replies that his testimony is true because he knows where he came from and where he is going, and the Father who sent him also testifies; they do not know the Father, because they do not know him. He says this in the treasury, and no one seizes him, for his hour has not come. He warns that he is going away, and they will die in their sin, unable to follow; unless they believe that he is who he claims, they will die in their sins. When they have lifted up the Son of Man, they will realise who he is and that he speaks as the Father taught him, the Father who is always with him because he always pleases him. Many believe.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter is saturated with the language of witness and judgment (a courtroom), light and darkness (the ceremonial torch-lighting of Tabernacles still in view), and the 'I AM' sayings that claim identity with the God who spoke to Moses. Jesus simultaneously judges (he is the one who judges truly, v. 16) and refuses to judge (he did not come to condemn, v. 15). This paradox is resolved in the cross: all judgment was poured out on him so that those who come to him face no condemnation.
verseByVerse.examples: The woman caught in adultery: the accusers depart one by one, beginning with the oldest (the most self-aware of their own sin). Only two are left: the woman and the one who could have condemned her. She goes free not because the law is set aside but because Jesus will shortly bear its full penalty. Every Christian stands where she stood: condemned by the law, set free by the one who alone can say 'neither do I condemn you,' because he bore the condemnation himself.

verseByVerse.quote: but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. Early in the morning he came again to the temple. All the people came to him, and he sat down and taught them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. Early in the morning he came again to the temple. All the people came to him, and he sat down and taught them.

Meaning first. John 8 continues the confrontation at the Feast of Booths, in the temple courts, and it climbs higher than anything Jesus has yet said. It opens with the bracketed story of a woman caught in adultery, whom Jesus neither condemns nor excuses. Then John’s own narrative resumes with the second great I am: I am the light of the world, spoken beside the lamps of the feast. The argument that follows is about witness, about where Jesus comes from and where he is going, about true freedom and true parentage, and about who a person’s father really is. Three times Jesus uses the bare words I am, the name God gave himself at the burning bush, and the third time, when he says that before Abraham was, I am, his hearers pick up stones. The chapter begins with a sinner who deserved stoning and was spared, and ends with the sinless one who deserved nothing of the kind and was nearly stoned himself. That exchange is the whole gospel in miniature.

A textual note first. The story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11) is printed in brackets in the ESV. The earliest and best Greek manuscripts do not have it; the early church fathers who commented on John verse by verse pass straight from 7:52 to 8:12; and where the story does appear in later manuscripts, it wanders: after 7:36, after 7:44, at the end of John, or after Luke 21:38. Its vocabulary and style are more like Luke’s than John’s. Most scholars, including conservative evangelical ones, conclude that it was not part of John’s original Gospel. Yet many also believe it records a true event from Jesus’ life, preserved in the church’s memory and later written into the Gospels. It fits everything we know of Jesus. Because Scripture is God’s word as originally given, the church should not build doctrine on this passage alone; but what it shows of Jesus is taught elsewhere in Scripture too.

How could such a thing happen? A reader who has been told a passage may not be original usually wants to know. The evidence is not evenly balanced. The great fourth-century manuscripts do not have these verses, and neither does the earliest papyrus of John. Where later manuscripts do carry the passage, they cannot agree where to put it, and a floating passage is a strong sign of one that was added rather than removed. Many of the manuscripts that include it also mark it with the little symbols scribes used for doubtful material. They knew. And yet almost nobody thinks the story was invented. It was known very early in the Latin-speaking churches, and Jerome says he found it in many manuscripts. Augustine suggested that some men of little faith had removed it, fearing it would give their wives licence. Whether or not that is the reason, it is the kind of story that would be uncomfortable to keep and impossible to make up. It is very probably a true memory of Jesus that circulated on its own and was written into John’s Gospel at a point where it fitted.

Should I be shaken by the brackets in my Bible? No. The brackets are the church showing its working, in public, about twelve verses out of some eight thousand in the New Testament. Nothing in them is a hidden embarrassment; it is printed in your Bible with an honest note precisely so that you can see it. And nothing is lost either way. The passage teaches nothing that the rest of Scripture does not teach plainly: the same Lord who says neither do I condemn you here says it in substance on every page of the Gospels, and calls sinners to leave their sin everywhere. So it may be read, treasured and preached as a faithful record of Jesus, with the caution that no doctrine should rest on it alone.

But Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. Jesus spent nights on the Mount of Olives during his time in Jerusalem (Luke 21:37), across the Kidron Valley east of the city, perhaps with friends in Bethany on its far slope. The council had just gone each to his own house (7:53). He went out into the open air. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head, and he spent the night under the olive trees on the hillside where, months later, he would pray in agony and be arrested.

Early in the morning he came again to the temple. At dawn he is back in the temple courts. The men who wanted him dead would find him in the most public place in Jerusalem at first light.

All the people came to him. While the leaders plot, ordinary people come. Those without standing flock to the one who has all authority, and the temple, which had become a place of politics, becomes again at daybreak a house of teaching.

And he sat down and taught them. Sitting was the posture of a teacher. It is the posture of authority: the rabbi seated, the people gathered round. He is not a guest in the temple. He is its Lord, teaching in his Father’s house.

In a sentence. Jesus spent the night on the Mount of Olives and came back to the temple at dawn, where all the people gathered and he sat down to teach them.

On a Tuesday. Jesus began the day early with God’s people and God’s word. A good pattern for ours. Before the phone, the news and the inbox, give the first part of the day to listening to him: a passage read slowly, a prayer offered honestly. It does not need to be long. It needs to be first.

For worship. The Lord of the temple slept on a hillside and rose before the sun to teach in his Father’s house. He who made the stars did not have a roof of his own in his own capital. He gave up comfort so that the people of the land could hear the word of life at dawn, and he still gathers ordinary people to himself, sits down among them, and teaches them by his word.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus spent nights on the Mount of Olives during his time in Jerusalem. Teachers sat to teach.

verseByVerse.quote: The scribes and the Pharisees brought a woman who had been caught in adultery, and placing her in the midst they said to him, "Teacher, this woman has been caught in the act of adultery."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scribes and the Pharisees brought a woman who had been caught in adultery, and placing her in the midst they said to him, “Teacher, this woman has been caught in the act of adultery.”

The scribes and the Pharisees. The scribes were the experts in the law; John never uses the word elsewhere, another sign of the passage’s different origin. It is common in the other Gospels.

Brought a woman who had been caught in adultery. Caught in the act. Where is the man? Adultery is not committed alone. The law required both to die (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22). His absence suggests the whole thing was a set-up. He was there; they saw him; and he is not standing in the temple courts. The men who open their mouths with Moses commanded us have already broken the commandment they are citing, in the very act of citing it, by leaving half the guilty party at home. That single missing man tells you what this really is. They are not defending the law; they are using it, and they have chosen the defendant who is easier to drag and cheaper to spend. It is also, in the oldest and most familiar way, a woman made to carry in public a shame that a man is quietly allowed to walk away from.

And placing her in the midst. They humiliate her publicly, standing her in front of the crowd. She is a pawn in their game. In the middle, in a ring of men, in the temple courts at dawn, with the crowd of verse 2 already gathered to hear him teach. She is not brought to a court. She is brought to a lesson, and made the visual aid. And this is the human condition before the court of divine justice: no cover, no defence, fully seen.

Teacher, this woman has been caught in the act of adultery. The charge is stated. There is no doubt of her guilt. And the word they open with is Teacher, the title of respect, spoken in front of his hearers by men who have arranged the one situation in which they think any answer he gives will destroy him.

Why does Jesus never mention the missing man? He does not need to. Everyone present could count. By refusing to play the part they had written for him, he declines to complete a sentence that was never being passed honestly, and he refuses to let the law of God be used as a stone in somebody else’s fight. The missing man stands as a silent witness against the accusers. And it is a warning for every age: when a community is fierce about one person’s sin and silent about another’s, according to who is more convenient to blame, it is not defending holiness. It is using it.

In a sentence. The scribes and Pharisees brought a woman caught in adultery, stood her before everyone, and told Jesus she had been caught in the act.

On a Tuesday. Never use another person’s sin to score a point. They did not care about her, or about holiness, only about trapping Jesus. Watch for the moment in a conversation when someone else’s failure becomes useful to you: to win an argument, to look better, to settle a score. Put it down. And if you are ever in a position to deal with someone’s sin, in a family, a church or a workplace, ask whether everyone involved is being treated by the same measure.

For worship. Here is a woman with no advocate, dragged into the light by men who despised her. And the one she is brought to is the only one in the courtyard who will treat her as a person. Christ is the friend of the friendless, the defender of those who have no defence. When we are exposed and have nothing to plead, he does not join the accusers. He stands between us and them.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now in the Law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. So what do you say?" This they said to test him, that they might have some charge to bring against him. Jesus bent down and wrote with his finger on the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now in the Law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. So what do you say? This they said to test him, that they might have some charge to bring against him. Jesus bent down and wrote with his finger on the ground.

Now in the Law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. The law required both the man and the woman caught in adultery to be put to death (Leviticus 20:10). Stoning was specified for a betrothed woman (Deuteronomy 22:23–24). They quote half the law. They may be right about her circumstances, or they may be rounding the law up to its harshest form. Either way, men this careless about the letter are not the guardians of it they claim to be.

So what do you say? The trap. If Jesus says, “Let her go,” he contradicts Moses and loses his standing as a teacher of the law. If he says, “Stone her,” he loses his reputation as the friend of sinners, and he defies Rome, which did not allow the Jews to carry out death sentences (18:31). Either way, they have a charge.

This they said to test him, that they might have some charge to bring against him. The narrator makes their motive clear. The woman is not a person to them but a prop. They have used her sin as a tool in their game, which is the deepest kind of exploitation.

Jesus bent down and wrote with his finger on the ground. What did he write? We are not told, and guesses abound: the sins of the accusers; the words of the law requiring both parties; Jeremiah 17:13, where those who turn away from the Lord are written in the earth. Some note that the law was written by the finger of God (Exodus 31:18). Perhaps the point is simply that he refuses to be rushed into their trap. The Bible doesn’t tell us, so we should not build on a guess.

The one guess worth knowing. One suggestion is worth more than the others, because it depends on where this scene sits rather than on imagination. Jeremiah says that those who turn away from the LORD shall be written in the earth, for they have forsaken the LORD, the fountain of living water (Jeremiah 17:13). The fountain of living water is the very thing Jesus had stood up and shouted about on the last day of the feast (7:37–38). If that is what his finger traced in the dust, the accusers were watching their own verdict being written while they waited for his. It cannot be proved and should not be preached as certain. It is worth knowing because it fits the week.

The posture. What can be said with confidence is the posture. He is asked to pronounce a death sentence, and his first act is to go down: to stoop into the dirt of the courtyard while a woman stands in the middle of a circle of men. Whatever he wrote, he had put himself lower than everyone present, including her. The one who is asked to condemn stoops first before he speaks.

In a sentence. They reminded Jesus that Moses had commanded such women to be stoned and asked what he said, to trap him, but he bent down and wrote on the ground.

On a Tuesday. When you are pushed for an instant answer by someone who has already decided what they want you to say, you are allowed to pause. Silence is sometimes the wisest reply. Stoop before you speak: pray, think, and let the heat go out of the moment.

For worship. Jesus is never trapped. He answers in his own time and his own way. The finger that wrote in the dust is the finger of the one who wrote the law on tablets of stone, and who now stooped to write in the dirt beside a sinner. He who gave the law came down to the ground to fulfil it, and in the end he would be lifted up from the ground to bear its curse.
verseByVerse.note: The law required both the man and the woman caught in adultery to be put to death; the man is missing. Rome did not allow the Jewish authorities to carry out executions, so the question was a trap either way.

parallels.desc: both of them shall die

verseByVerse.quote: And as they continued to ask him, he stood up and said to them, "Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her." And once more he bent down and wrote on the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as they continued to ask him, he stood up and said to them, “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her.” And once more he bent down and wrote on the ground.

As they continued to ask him. They press him.

Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her. Under the law the witnesses were to throw the first stones (Deuteronomy 17:7). They had to be honest witnesses, and not guilty of the same thing. Jesus does not deny the law, or say the sin doesn’t matter. He turns the light on the accusers. Are they fit to carry out God’s judgment? “Without sin” (anamartētos) probably means without sin of this kind, or more broadly, without guilt. Every one of them has sinned. And notice what he does not do. He does not deny the law, dispute the facts, or make a speech about mercy. He affirms the sentence and hands them the stones, and simply attaches the condition the law already contained. It is the most conservative possible answer, and it empties the courtyard. In a group that had arrived with a woman and without the man, it would have landed like a hand on the shoulder.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that no one may ever judge wrongdoing or that sin should never be punished. Scripture gives authority to courts and to the church to judge (Romans 13:1–4; 1 Corinthians 5:12–13). Jesus is exposing hypocrites who used the law as a weapon, not abolishing justice. He himself commanded right judgment only days before (7:24). What he condemns here is a corrupt prosecution: the man absent, the woman used as bait, and accusers with no clean hands.

And once more he bent down and wrote on the ground. He leaves them with their consciences. He does not stand there watching them decide. Having said the one sentence, he goes back to the ground and gives them what mattered most: the freedom to leave without being stared at. The genius of grace is that it does not humiliate even the accusers; it invites them to look at themselves.

So does a church or a court have to be sinless to deal with sin? No. If that were the rule, no human court could ever sit and no church could ever discipline anyone, and Scripture commands both. Judges and elders act as servants of God’s justice, not as people claiming to be better than the accused (Romans 13:4; Galatians 6:1). What this verse demands is honesty: that those who judge are not guilty of the same thing, are not using the process for their own ends, and come to it knowing their own need of mercy. A pastor confronting a sin, a parent correcting a child, a court sentencing a crime, can all do right, provided they do it with clean hands and a humble heart.

In a sentence. When they kept asking, Jesus stood and said the one without sin should throw the first stone, and then bent down again to write.

On a Tuesday. Before you pick up a stone, look at your own heart. Think of the last time you were quite certain somebody else was in the wrong. Would your certainty have survived being asked, in front of witnesses, whether you were clear of the same thing? Most of our indignation depends on the question not being put. Put it to yourself before you speak.

For worship. There was one man in that courtyard who was without sin, and he did not throw a stone. He who alone had the right to condemn chose to stoop in the dust instead. The holiness that could have crushed her became the shelter she stood under. That is the wonder of our Lord: perfectly holy, and perfectly merciful, at the same time and in the same act.
verseByVerse.note: Under the law the witnesses were to throw the first stones.

parallels.desc: the hand of the witnesses first against him

verseByVerse.quote: But when they heard it, they went away one by one, beginning with the older ones, and Jesus was left alone with the woman standing before him. Jesus stood up and said to her, "Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you?" She said, "No one, Lord." And Jesus said, "Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when they heard it, they went away one by one, beginning with the older ones, and Jesus was left alone with the woman standing before him. Jesus stood up and said to her, “Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you?” She said, “No one, Lord.” And Jesus said, “Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.”

They went away one by one, beginning with the older ones. The oldest have the longest memories of their own sins, or simply the wisdom to know they are guilty. No dramatic confrontation; just the quiet withdrawal of men whose consciences have been touched. Stones are put down, one by one, and footsteps go out of the courtyard.

And Jesus was left alone with the woman. Augustine’s famous phrase: two were left, misery and mercy. The only one without sin, the only one with the right to throw the stone, remains.

Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you? “Woman” is a respectful address (2:4). The question is gentle, almost wondering. The trap has collapsed, and what remains is a woman, a silence, and mercy.

Neither do I condemn you. Jesus, who is without sin, does not condemn her. Not because her sin doesn’t matter, but because he came not to condemn the world but to save it (3:17). And how can the holy one release the guilty? Because he himself would bear her condemnation on the cross (Romans 8:1–3). This is not leniency. He does not say the charge was false, or exaggerated, or that the law was harsh. The whole weight of the sentence rests on who is saying it. Everyone else had merely lost the right to throw; he had the right and declined to use it. Mercy from a man who cannot punish is worth nothing. This is mercy from the bench. And it costs. Within months the man who said neither do I condemn you was under condemnation himself, outside the city, with the sentence being carried out on him. She walked out of that courtyard alive because somebody else did not.

Go, and from now on sin no more. Grace and holiness together. He does not say, “Your sin is fine.” He calls it sin, and tells her to leave it. Forgiveness comes first, then the new life. Jesus does not say, “Sin no more, and then I won’t condemn you.” He says, “I don’t condemn you; now go and sin no more.” Grace is the root of obedience, not its reward. Note the order, because it is the whole gospel in one sentence and it is nearly always reversed in practice. The acquittal comes first and is unconditional. The change of life is what follows an acquittal, not what purchases one. And grace does not leave people where it finds them. The instruction is real, and it is addressed to a real situation she has to go home to.

Was she forgiven if she had not repented? The story does not tell us what was in her heart, and we should not invent it. What it shows is the order of grace: Jesus speaks mercy and then calls for a changed life, and that call is itself a call to repent. Elsewhere Scripture is plain that forgiveness is received through repentance and faith (Luke 24:47; Acts 3:19). The point here is not that repentance is unnecessary, but that it is not the price. No one earns the verdict by changing first. We come to Christ as we are, receive his mercy, and his mercy sends us out to live differently.

What if I keep falling into the same sin after being forgiven? Then come back, as often as you need to. Go and sin no more is a real command, and Christ means it to be obeyed. But it is the command of the one who has already said, I do not condemn you, and that verdict is not withdrawn when you stumble (1 John 1:9–2:1). Fight the sin, seriously: cut off what feeds it, tell a trusted believer, ask for help. And when you fall, do not hide from him, which is what shame always urges. Run to him. The freedom to obey grows out of being forgiven; it never grows out of the fear that he might stop forgiving you.

In a sentence. The accusers left one by one, and when Jesus was alone with the woman, he asked who condemned her, and said that neither did he, and that she should go and sin no more.

On a Tuesday. Ask which order your own conscience is working in. If you are trying to earn a verdict you have already been given, you are reading the sentence backwards. The woman in this story could have told you that the freedom to go and sin no more was a consequence of being let go, and would have been impossible before it. Take the old guilt that still comes back at you, bring it to Christ again today, and hear his verdict. Then go and live as someone set free.

For worship. No condemnation, and a new life. That is what Christ gives every sinner who comes to him. Misery and mercy stood face to face in that courtyard, and mercy spoke first. The only one with the right to throw the stone took the stones himself, and the judge became the one judged in her place. There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1), and the voice that sent her home still says to every forgiven sinner: neither do I condemn you; go.

parallels.desc: no condemnation

verseByVerse.quote: Again Jesus spoke to them, saying, "I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life." So the Pharisees said to him, "You are bearing witness about yourself; your testimony is not true." Jesus answered, "Even if I do bear witness about myself, my testimony is true, for I know where I came from and where I am going, but you do not know where I come from or where I am going.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again Jesus spoke to them, saying, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.” So the Pharisees said to him, “You are bearing witness about yourself; your testimony is not true.” Jesus answered, “Even if I do bear witness about myself, my testimony is true, for I know where I came from and where I am going, but you do not know where I come from or where I am going.

Again Jesus spoke to them. John’s original narrative picks up from 7:52: still the Feast of Booths, still in the temple.

I am the light of the world. The second great “I am” saying (after 6:35). At the Feast of Booths great lamps were lit in the temple courts, so bright, the rabbis said, that every courtyard in Jerusalem was lit up. They recalled the pillar of fire that led Israel through the wilderness (Exodus 13:21). Against this background Jesus says: I am the true light. Not just for Israel, but for the world (1:4–9; Isaiah 42:6; 49:6). Light in Scripture means God’s presence, truth, holiness, salvation (Psalm 27:1).

Beside the cold lamps. The setting has to be recovered, or the claim loses most of its force. John tells us where he was standing eight verses later: in the treasury (v. 20), in the Court of the Women, which is where the great lampstands of the feast had been lit every night. The sources describe four enormous golden lampstands, so tall that young priests climbed ladders with jars of oil to fill them, with wicks made from the worn-out linen garments of the priests. When they burned, men danced with torches and sang through the night. Now the feast is over. The lamps are out and cold. And a man stands in that court, beside the extinguished stands, and says, I am the light of the world. It is the same move he made with the water. He waits until the ceremony has finished, and then says that the thing it pointed at is standing in front of them, and does not go out.

Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness. As Israel followed the pillar of fire. Darkness in John means sin, ignorance and death (1:5; 3:19; 12:35). And the promise is not first illumination but company. The verb is about walking, not seeing. He does not promise to explain everything; he promises not to leave anyone in the dark while they are following him. Israel did not get a map in the wilderness. They got a pillar of fire that moved, and they followed it one night at a time.

But will have the light of life. The light that gives life, and is life. In him was life, and the life was the light of men (1:4).

You are bearing witness about yourself; your testimony is not true. They object on legal grounds: self-testimony was not accepted. Jesus himself had granted the principle (5:31). The objection is not stupid. Their rule is a good one: a man’s word about himself is not evidence. And readers notice the apparent clash with chapter 5. It deserves an answer rather than a shrug.

Even if I do bear witness about myself, my testimony is true. But the principle is meant for ordinary witnesses. Jesus is unique. He alone knows the truth about himself. And he is not withdrawing what he said in chapter 5 but denying that he is alone, which is exactly what he says next: it is not I alone who judge, but I and the Father (v. 16).

For I know where I came from and where I am going. He knows his origin, the Father, and his destiny, return to the Father. They don’t. No human can verify his testimony from outside; only God can, and he does (v. 18). An ordinary witness to his own identity is limited and interested. He is claiming to be neither.

What does it mean in practice to follow the light? It means trusting Jesus and going where he leads, one step at a time, by his word. It does not mean you will always see far ahead, or understand why things happen. It means you will not be left in the darkness of sin, confusion about God, or hopelessness about death. Practically: read his words and do what they say; when you face a choice, ask what honours him and obeys him; when you sin, bring it into the light quickly rather than hiding it (1 John 1:7). Following the light is less like being given a floodlight and more like being given a lamp for your feet (Psalm 119:105).

In a sentence. Jesus said he is the light of the world and his followers will have the light of life, and when the Pharisees objected that his testimony about himself was not valid, he said it was, since he alone knew where he came from and where he was going.

On a Tuesday. Follow the light. Wherever Christ leads, you will not be in darkness. Name the area of your life that feels darkest at the moment: a decision, a grief, a secret. Bring it to him in prayer today, and take one step of obedience in it, however small. The light comes to the one who follows.

For worship. The lamps of the feast burned for a week and went out. The light of the world has never gone out. He was the light of the pillar of fire, the glory over the tabernacle, the radiance that filled Solomon’s temple, and now he stood in the temple in a body, beside the cold lamps, offering himself to everyone. The darkness tried to put him out on a cross and could not; the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it (1:5). One day the city of God will need no sun or lamp, for the Lamb is its lamp (Revelation 21:23).
verseByVerse.note: At the Feast of Booths great lamps were lit in the temple courts. This is the second of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

parallels.desc: a pillar of fire to give them light
a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: "You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one. Yet even if I do judge, my judgment is true, for it is not I alone who judge, but I and the Father who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one. Yet even if I do judge, my judgment is true, for it is not I alone who judge, but I and the Father who sent me.

You judge according to the flesh. By human standards, by appearances (7:24), from a merely human point of view. It is a charge of shallowness before it is a charge of malice. They have looked at a Galilean with no credentials and drawn the obvious conclusion, and the obvious conclusion was wrong.
