But you have not known him. I know him. If I were to say that I do not know him, I would be a liar like you. But I do know him and I keep his word. Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day. He saw it and was glad.

But you have not known him. I know him. They call him their God, but don’t know him. Jesus does, perfectly.

If I were to say that I do not know him, I would be a liar like you. False modesty would be a lie.

But I do know him and I keep his word. Jesus keeps the Father’s word, as he calls us to keep his (v. 51).

Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day. “My day”: the time of Messiah’s coming. Abraham received the promise that in his offspring all nations would be blessed (Genesis 12:3; 22:18). He looked forward to it with joy. Hebrews 11:13 says the patriarchs saw the promises and greeted them from afar. Some rabbis taught that God showed Abraham the future ages (from Genesis 15). Two verbs, and they are not the same. He rejoiced in the anticipation, and then he saw it, and the seeing made him glad. Whatever this is, it is not a vague hope about the future. Something was shown to him, and he looked at it.

He saw it and was glad. How? By faith, through the promise. Perhaps especially at Mount Moriah, when God provided the ram in Isaac’s place (Genesis 22:8, 13–14), a picture of the Father giving his Son. Abraham, whom they claim, rejoiced in the one they reject.

On the mountain of the LORD. That mountain is the strongest candidate. Abraham walks up it with his son, the wood on the boy’s back, and the boy asks the question, where is the lamb? And the father says that God will provide the lamb. At the top, with the knife raised, a ram is caught in a thicket, and Abraham names the place, the LORD will provide, and the narrator adds a strange note: as it is said to this day, on the mount of the LORD it shall be provided (Genesis 22:14). A father, an only son, a sacrifice, a substitute supplied at the last moment, on a hill, and a name for the place that points forward rather than back. And Moriah is where the temple was later built (2 Chronicles 3:1). Abraham gave a prophetic name to the very ridge these men were standing on as they argued.

What did believers before Christ actually believe? Not something else. Not a different religion of law-keeping later replaced by grace. The same Christ, seen at a distance, through promise and shadow. These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar (Hebrews 11:13). Old Testament believers were saved exactly as we are: by grace, through faith in God’s promise of a Saviour, whose work they saw dimly and we see plainly (Romans 4:3, 23–25). Abraham is here described as a man who looked down the centuries and was glad about a particular day. There has only ever been one way of salvation, and one Saviour.

In a sentence. Jesus said that they did not know God but he did and kept his word, and that Abraham rejoiced at the thought of seeing his day, and saw it and was glad.

On a Tuesday. Abraham rejoiced to see Christ’s day from far off. We see it plainly. How much more should we rejoice. He had almost nothing to go on: no Gospel, no creed, no resurrection to look back on; a promise, a son given back to him from under a raised knife, and a ram in a bush. And it was enough to make him glad. Count what you have been given to see, and let it make you glad today.

For worship. Abraham climbed a mountain with his only son and came down with him alive, because God provided a substitute. Two thousand years later, on that same ridge, God did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all. There was no ram in the thicket for Jesus. He was the Lamb. And Abraham, who saw that day from far off, was glad. How much more should we be, who stand on this side of it and know that the LORD has provided.

parallels.desc: having seen them and greeted them from afar

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews said to him, "You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?" Jesus said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the Jews said to him, “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am.”

You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham? They twist his words: he said Abraham saw his day, they ask whether he has seen Abraham. Fifty was a round number for the end of a man’s working life (Numbers 4:3); Jesus was in his early thirties (Luke 3:23). Abraham had lived some two thousand years earlier. They have reversed what he said, which is what people do when they are no longer really listening. And there is dismissiveness in it: you are not even at the end of a working life, and you are talking about the patriarchs.

Before Abraham was, I am. The climax of the chapter, and one of the greatest statements in the Bible. Notice the two verbs. “Was” (genesthai) means came into being: Abraham was born, had a beginning. “I am” (egō eimi) is present tense, timeless. Jesus doesn’t say “before Abraham was, I was,” which would mean only that he existed earlier. He says “I am,” claiming eternal, uncreated existence. “I am” without anything added echoes the name God gave himself at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14) and the “I am he” of Isaiah (Isaiah 43:10–13). Jesus is claiming to be the eternal God.

The grammar broken on purpose. Everything in the chapter has been built to hold this sentence. The grammar is broken on purpose, and the breakage is the meaning. The first verb is an ordinary past, which is what happens to creatures: they begin. The second refuses the past tense altogether. I was would have claimed enormous age and nothing more, and it is what any careful writer would have put. I am. Two claims are packed into two words. The first is that he has no beginning: everything true of Abraham’s kind of existence, which started, is not true of his. The second is the Name. He has been laying it down all chapter, at verse 24 and verse 28, with nothing after it. Here he sets it beside Abraham, and the crowd finally understands.

Where Christians differ: what does “I am” mean here? Some, especially Jehovah’s Witnesses, translate “before Abraham was, I have been,” to make it a claim only to pre-existence, not deity. Verdict: the Greek present tense, set against the past tense of Abraham’s coming to be, marks a contrast between created and eternal being. And the hearers’ reaction settles it: they pick up stones, the penalty for blasphemy (v. 59; 10:33). They understood that he was claiming to be God.

His enemies are the best witnesses. That reaction disposes of every reading that makes this a modest claim by a good teacher. Nobody picks up a stone because a man has claimed to be wise, or sent, or even a prophet. The penalty for blasphemy was stoning (Leviticus 24:16), and they went straight for it, in the temple, without discussion. His enemies are among the best witnesses in the New Testament to what he was claiming, because they had no motive to exaggerate it and every motive to wish he had not said it.

If Jesus is eternal, how could he be born, grow and die? Because the eternal Son took a true human nature without ceasing to be God. As God he has no beginning; as man he was conceived in Mary’s womb, grew, learned, hungered, wept and died. One person, two natures, without mixture and without division. The Word who is from eternity became flesh (1:14). So when we say that Jesus was born at Bethlehem, we mean that the eternal I AM entered time as a baby. He did not stop being who he always was; he added to himself what we are, so that he could save us.

In a sentence. When they asked whether he, not yet fifty, had seen Abraham, Jesus solemnly declared that before Abraham came into being, he eternally is.

On a Tuesday. The one who says I am has no yesterday that has slipped away from him and no tomorrow he is anxious about. Bring him the regret from your past and the fear about your future. He was there before both, and he is there now.

For worship. Before Abraham, before the world, Christ is. The eternal God came near enough to be stoned. Worship him. Before the mountains were brought forth, from everlasting to everlasting, he is God (Psalm 90:2). He spoke to Moses from the fire, and he stood in the temple in a body that would bleed. The I AM, without beginning, consented to have a birthday, a hometown and a grave, so that creatures who began could live with him for ever.
verseByVerse.note: “I am” without anything added echoes the name God gave himself at the burning bush.

parallels.desc: “I AM WHO I AM”
from everlasting to everlasting

verseByVerse.quote: So they picked up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they picked up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.

So they picked up stones to throw at him. Stoning was the penalty for blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16). The temple was being rebuilt in this period, and stones would have been lying around in the courts. They are about to lynch him. The same people who had “believed” (v. 31) now want to kill him. That is what shallow faith becomes when confronted with the full truth of Jesus. Herod’s rebuilding had been going on for forty-six years (2:20) and would not be finished for decades. So the men who had come to worship picked up the building material of the house of God to kill the one it was built for.

But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple. How? Perhaps simply slipping away in the crowd; perhaps by a miraculous hiding. In any case, his hour had not come. There may be a deeper sign: the glory of God leaving the temple, as in Ezekiel 10, as the one in whom God dwells walks out of the house that has rejected him. John describes no miracle, no lightning, no rebuke. He says only that he hid himself and left, in the middle of a crowd. It is the same restraint that ran through chapter 7. And consider who leaves. The Word who made the stone walks out of the temple, through a crowd holding pieces of it. The building went on standing for about forty more years, and then the Romans burned it to the ground, and it has never been rebuilt. The glory had already gone out of the door, and nobody in the courtyard noticed.

Two stonings that did not happen. Chapter 8 began with a woman who deserved to be stoned and was not, and it ends with a man who deserved nothing of the kind and very nearly was. That is the exchange the whole book is about, acted out twice in one feast. The stones aimed at him would wait until the hour came, and then nails would do what stones could not, and the guilty would go free because the innocent was condemned.

Can people who once seemed to believe turn so completely against Christ? Sadly, yes, and the New Testament warns of it (Hebrews 6:4–6; 1 John 2:19). Those who were truly born of God are kept by him, but there is a kind of interest in Jesus that never reached the heart, and when his full claims are pressed, it can turn into hostility. That is why Jesus tested these hearers so hard. It should not make true believers anxious, because the very fact that you are troubled by the possibility shows a heart that wants Christ. But it should make all of us honest: not resting in a past moment of interest, but abiding in his word, which is the mark of the real thing (v. 31).

In a sentence. They picked up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and left the temple.

On a Tuesday. The same Jesus who walked out of their temple is willing to dwell in the humblest heart that receives him. Don’t drive him away. When his word presses on something in your life that you would rather keep, that is the moment the stones come out. Put them down. Let him stay.

For worship. They picked up stones against the I AM, and he walked out through the middle of them, because his hour had not yet come. When it came, he did not hide. He gave himself up to be lifted on a cross, and there the stones of our sin fell on him. The temple they defended has gone. The true temple, his body, was torn down and raised in three days, and now he builds a living temple out of people who once picked up stones against him. Glory to the eternal I AM, who walked out of their house so that he could make his home in ours.
verseByVerse.note: Stoning was the penalty for blasphemy.

8.overview:
The chapter opens with the story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11), which the earliest manuscripts of John do not contain; it appears in later manuscripts in various places, sometimes after Luke 21:38. Most scholars, conservative ones included, conclude that it was not part of John’s original Gospel but preserves a genuine memory of Jesus. Its message is unforgettable: the accusers, convicted by Jesus’ words, leave one by one; Jesus does not condemn the woman, and tells her to go and sin no more.

The rest of the chapter continues Jesus’ teaching at the Feast of Booths, where great lamps lit the temple courts. “I am the light of the world,” he says. The Pharisees challenge his self-testimony; he answers that the Father testifies with him, and that unless they believe that “I am he” they will die in their sins; when they have lifted up the Son of Man they will know. To Jews who had believed him he promises that if they abide in his word, the truth will set them free, which offends them as Abraham’s descendants who have never been slaves. Jesus answers that everyone who commits sin is a slave, and that their murderous intent shows that their true father is not Abraham, nor God, but the devil, the father of lies. The argument climaxes in the most explicit claim to deity in the Gospels: “Before Abraham was, I am.” They take up stones, and Jesus leaves the temple. Because the chapter has been used to fuel hatred of Jews, it must be read with care: Jesus speaks as a Jew to particular opponents who were seeking to kill him, and his words warn every religious person, not one people.

9.title: The Man Born Blind

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–41 — Sight and Blindness: The Light of the World at Work
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus sees a man blind from birth, and the disciples ask whose sin caused it. Jesus answers that it is not a matter of blame: it happened so that God’s work could be shown. As the world’s light, he spreads mud made with saliva on the man’s eyes and sends him to wash in Siloam, and the man returns seeing. Neighbours dispute whether he is the same beggar. Because it is the Sabbath, the Pharisees question him; some say a Sabbath-breaker cannot be from God, others that a sinner could not do such signs. The man calls Jesus a prophet. His frightened parents, fearing expulsion from the synagogue, confirm only that he is their son and was born blind. Pressed again to condemn Jesus, the man says he knows only that he was blind and now sees, and teasingly asks if they want to become disciples. They abuse him as a follower of Jesus, while they follow Moses. He argues that God would not answer a sinner, and no one has ever opened eyes born blind, so Jesus must be from God. They expel him. Jesus seeks him out and reveals himself as the Son of Man, and the man believes and worships. Jesus says he came so that the blind might see and those who think they see might become blind; the Pharisees who claim sight remain guilty.
verseByVerse.theology: Physical sight and spiritual sight run in parallel throughout the chapter. The man born blind is a picture of humanity in its natural state — unable to see the Light from birth, requiring an external, sovereign act to receive vision. The Pharisees, who see perfectly with physical eyes, are spiritually blind precisely because they are confident they see (v. 41). This is the paradox of total depravity and spiritual pride: the one who knows he cannot see is the one who can be given sight; the one who insists he sees will remain blind. Spiritual humility is the precondition of illumination.
verseByVerse.examples: The progression of the healed man's confession is a model of growing faith: 'the man called Jesus' (v. 11), 'a prophet' (v. 17), 'from God' (v. 33), 'Lord, I believe' and worship (v. 38). Every encounter with Jesus under pressure produces clearer confession. The Pharisees' investigation — a hostile inquisition — inadvertently drives the man deeper into faith. Opposition to the gospel, when it cannot overcome the testimony of experience, ends by casting out the witness (v. 34) — and Jesus finds the cast-out (v. 35).

verseByVerse.quote: As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. And his disciples asked him, "Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. And his disciples asked him, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?”

Meaning first. John 9 is the sixth sign in John’s Gospel, and it acts out what Jesus has just said: I am the light of the world (8:12; 9:5). A man born blind receives his sight and, step by step, comes to see who Jesus is, while the religious leaders, who claim to see, become more and more blind. It is a picture of salvation: we are all born blind, and only Christ can open our eyes. Watch the man’s words about Jesus grow as the chapter goes on: the man called Jesus, a prophet, from God, and at last Lord, as he falls down and worships. Watch the leaders’ words shrink: we know, we know, and finally we see, which is the one claim that keeps them blind. And watch who does the seeking. The chapter opens with Jesus seeing a man who did not know he was there, and closes with Jesus finding the same man after everyone else has thrown him out.

As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. Jesus sees him first. The man doesn’t ask for anything. Grace takes the initiative. “Blind from birth”: the only healing in the Gospels of someone born with a condition. Medically hopeless, and a picture of the human condition: spiritually blind from birth (2 Corinthians 4:4). And notice where Jesus is. The chapter break hides it, but the previous sentence in the Gospel is that Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple (8:59), with stones in the air behind him. He has just escaped a lynching, and what he does on the way out is stop for a beggar. Nobody asked him to. The man does not call out; he does not know anyone is there. In a chapter that will be entirely about seeing, the first act of seeing is done by Jesus.

Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind? Many assumed that disability was punishment for a particular sin. If born blind, either his parents had sinned (Exodus 20:5 was misapplied), or he had sinned in the womb, which some rabbis thought possible (citing Jacob and Esau struggling, Genesis 25:22). Job’s friends made the same mistake. The disciples were not inventing the theology; they were working with the material they had, and it is the material most people still work with. When something terrible happens, the mind goes looking for the cause in the sufferer: what did they do, what did I do, what am I being punished for?

A man turned into a case. And notice what the question does to the man. He is standing there. They discuss him in front of him, as a theological problem, using him as the exhibit, which is presumably what had happened to him all his life. Nobody in the verse speaks to him. That is the other reason people still ask the question. Once suffering has a cause, it can be filed; and once it is filed, nothing more is required of the person looking at it. The disciples want an explanation, and an explanation would have let them walk on. What Jesus does instead is refuse the question, and then kneel in the road.

Is my suffering a punishment for my sins? Not in the way the disciples meant. All suffering exists because we live in a fallen world, and sometimes a particular sin does bring painful consequences: drunkenness ruins a liver, lies ruin a friendship. But Scripture refuses to let us read every illness, disability or loss as God’s verdict on someone’s private sin (Luke 13:1–5; Job 42:7). If you are a Christian, your punishment was borne by Christ; there is now no condemnation (Romans 8:1). Your Father may discipline you in love (Hebrews 12:6), but discipline is the training of a child, not the sentence of a judge. So when trouble comes, do not torment yourself trying to find the sin that caused it. Bring it to God, ask him what he wants to do in it, and trust him.

In a sentence. Jesus saw a man blind from birth, and his disciples asked whose sin had caused it, his own or his parents’.

On a Tuesday. When you see someone suffering, don’t ask first whose fault it is. Ask what God might do. And ask what you might do. Think of the person you know who is disabled, chronically ill or simply struggling, and who is more often talked about than talked to. Go and speak to them this week, as a person, not a case.

For worship. The Lord of glory, with stones still in the air behind him, stopped for a blind beggar who had not asked him for anything. He saw him before the man knew anyone was there. That is how grace always begins: not with our seeking, but with his seeing. Before we ever looked for him, he had already looked on us and loved us.
verseByVerse.note: Many assumed that disability was punishment for a particular sin, even a parent’s.

parallels.desc: the son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him. We must work the works of him who sent me while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered, “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him. We must work the works of him who sent me while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work.”

It was not that this man sinned, or his parents. Jesus rejects the simple link between a particular sin and a particular suffering. All suffering exists because of the fall (Romans 8:20–22), and some suffering is a direct result of a particular sin (5:14; 1 Corinthians 11:30). But not all. Here there is no such link.

But that the works of God might be displayed in him. Jesus moves from cause to purpose. The question is not “why” but “what for.” God had a purpose in this man’s blindness: to show his works through Christ. This does not make the suffering less real, but it gives it meaning.

Did God blind a baby to set up a miracle? A parent will read this verse differently from a commentator, and the question has to be met. Put like that it sounds intolerable, and no one should pretend otherwise. Two things need saying. First, the verse says less than the objection assumes. It does not say God caused the blindness in order to show off. It says the works of God will be displayed in this man, and the display, when it comes, is that Jesus gives him his sight, then goes looking for him after he has been thrown out, and gives him himself. Whatever the years cost, the man ends the chapter seeing, worshipping, and known to the Son of God, which is more than the men who questioned him ever got. Second, some readers punctuate the Greek differently, so that the purpose clause begins the next sentence: neither this man nor his parents sinned; but that the works of God might be displayed in him, we must work the works of him who sent me. On that reading Jesus is not giving a reason for the blindness at all, but turning from cause to calling. The ESV’s reading is the more natural Greek, and it means that God had a purpose in this man’s blindness from the start. But on either reading the comfort stands: God does not waste the suffering of those he loves.

We must work the works of him who sent me while it is day. “We”: Jesus includes his disciples in the mission. “Must” (dei): divine necessity. “While it is day”: while the opportunity lasts. The question the disciples asked was about the past, and it had no useful answer. The question Jesus answers is what God intends to do about it, and to that there is an answer, and it walked up the road towards a blind beggar.

Night is coming, when no one can work. For Jesus, the night is his death. For us, it is our death or his return. The time to work is now. Urgency here is not anxiety but faithfulness. The servant who knows the time is short does not coast, and does not panic either. He does today’s work.

How can I believe my suffering has a purpose when I cannot see it? You may not see it yet, and you may not see all of it in this life. This man was blind for many years before anyone explained anything, and the explanation, when it came, was not a theory but a person. What Scripture promises is not that every sorrow will make sense to us now, but that God works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), and that our light and momentary affliction is preparing an eternal weight of glory (2 Corinthians 4:17). Hold on to what you know of his character, revealed in Christ, while you wait for what you cannot yet see of his purpose. And look for the works of God in small things now: comfort given, faith deepened, others helped through what you have suffered (2 Corinthians 1:3–4).

In a sentence. Jesus said the blindness was not caused by the man’s or his parents’ sin, but happened so that God’s works might be shown in him, and that they must do God’s work while it was still day.

On a Tuesday. Stop asking only why, and start asking what for. Take the hardest thing in your life right now and pray: Father, display your works in this. Then do the work in front of you today, because the day does not last for ever.

For worship. God can display his works through your weakness. Don’t waste your sorrows; and don’t waste the day. The Father who sent his Son into a dark world did not leave the blind man in the dark, and he will not leave you there. The night came for Jesus at the cross, and through it he brought the morning that will never end. Every sorrow carried by his people is held in the hands that were pierced for them, and none of it will be wasted.

verseByVerse.quote: "As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world." Having said these things, he spit on the ground and made mud with the saliva. Then he anointed the man's eyes with the mud
verseByVerse.commentary:
As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world. Having said these things, he spit on the ground and made mud with the saliva. Then he anointed the man’s eyes with the mud

As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world. The same claim as 8:12, now about to be shown in action. The light of the world gives light to a man who has never seen it. And there is a qualification here that was not in the earlier saying: as long as I am in the world. He is measuring the daylight, as in verse 4. What he does not say is that the world goes dark afterwards. He had already told his disciples that they are the light of the world (Matthew 5:14). The light does not go out. It is handed on to those who carry his light.

He spit on the ground and made mud with the saliva. Saliva was widely believed to have healing power, and Jesus used it elsewhere (Mark 7:33; 8:23). But there may be more. Some see an echo of creation: God formed man from the dust of the ground (Genesis 2:7); now the Creator uses the earth to make new eyes. Kneading mud was also one of the kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath by the rabbis’ rules (v. 14). This man’s eyes had never worked from the beginning; there was nothing to repair. So the hands that once made dust into a man make dust into eyes, and it is a piece of creation rather than a piece of medicine.

Then he anointed the man’s eyes with the mud. “Anointed” (epechrisen, smeared on). Why use mud at all? Jesus could heal by a word. Perhaps to involve the man’s faith, sending him to wash; perhaps as a deliberate challenge to the Sabbath traditions. He healed by a word constantly, even from miles away (4:50). Here he spits on the ground, works the dirt into paste with his fingers, and smears it on a blind man’s face.

The undignified way. Mud is undignified. The man cannot see; he can only feel a stranger’s fingers putting wet earth on his face, and hear an instruction. Whatever he expected of the day, it was not this. And there is something here for anyone whose experience of God’s work in them has felt less like a miracle than like being handled: the process was messy, and he had no idea what was happening while it was going on.

Does God still heal today? Yes, God can and does heal, in answer to prayer and through the ordinary means of doctors and medicine, which are also his gifts (James 5:14–16). He is the same Lord. But the sign-miracles of Jesus and his apostles were given to confirm who he was and to launch the church, and Scripture does not promise that every believer who prays in faith will be healed now. Paul left Trophimus ill (2 Timothy 4:20) and lived with his own thorn (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). So pray boldly for healing, use every good means, and trust God with the answer. The final healing of every believer is certain, at the resurrection, when he will make all things new.

In a sentence. Jesus said that while he was in the world he was its light, and spat on the ground, made mud, and put it on the man’s eyes.

On a Tuesday. If God’s work in you feels messy and slow, you are in good company. Trust his hands even when you cannot see what he is doing. And let your light shine where you are this week: the light was handed on to you.

For worship. The one who formed Adam from the dust stooped to the dust to give a blind man eyes. Our Creator is our Healer. The hands that shaped the first man knelt in the dirt of a Jerusalem street, and the God who said let there be light made light enter eyes that had never known it. He is still the Maker, and he still makes all things new.
verseByVerse.note: Saliva was widely believed to have healing power. Kneading mud counted as work on the Sabbath under the traditions.

parallels.desc: the LORD God formed the man of dust

verseByVerse.quote: and said to him, "Go, wash in the pool of Siloam" (which means Sent). So he went and washed and came back seeing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and said to him, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam” (which means Sent). So he went and washed and came back seeing.

Go, wash in the pool of Siloam. The pool of Siloam lay at the south end of the city, fed by Hezekiah’s tunnel, cut through solid rock to bring water from the Gihon spring inside the walls (2 Kings 20:20). Its remains were uncovered in 2004: a large stepped pool. It was the source of the water carried to the altar at the Feast of Booths (7:37). Like Naaman told to wash in the Jordan (2 Kings 5:10), the man must obey. Isaiah speaks of the waters of Shiloah that go softly, and sets them against the great river of empire (Isaiah 8:6): the small, quiet, sufficient supply. And it was from this pool that the golden pitcher had been filled every morning of the feast, a few days earlier. Now Jesus sends a blind man to the very pool the whole city had been drawing from all week, and the water they had been pouring out at the altar opens a man’s eyes.

Which means Sent. John points out the meaning of the name (from the Hebrew shalach, to send). Jesus is the one sent by the Father, a theme all through the Gospel (v. 4). The man washes in “Sent” and is healed by the Sent One. John does not explain place names this way often. He does it here because the word is the Gospel’s own word for Jesus, who speaks of himself as sent dozens of times, and has just done so three verses earlier. A man is sent by the Sent One to a pool called Sent, and comes back seeing.

So he went and washed and came back seeing. Simple obedience, immediate result. He walked there blind, perhaps half a mile through the city, with mud on his eyes. He came back seeing for the first time in his life. And measure the obedience. He is told to walk across Jerusalem with mud on his face by a voice he does not recognise, having asked for nothing. Siloam is downhill and some distance from the temple; a blind beggar making that journey with a plastered face would have been noticed by everyone he passed. And there was no promise attached: Jesus does not say, and you will see. He said, go and wash.

Does God heal through my obedience, or is it all grace? It is all grace, and grace works through obedience. The man did not heal himself by walking to Siloam; the power was entirely Christ’s. But Christ chose to give his gift through the man’s act of trusting obedience. That is the pattern of the Christian life: God works in you, both to will and to work (Philippians 2:13), and you work out what he works in. The water did not have the power, and the walking did not earn the sight. But a man who refused to go would have stayed blind. So do what Christ says, not to earn his gift, but because the gift comes along the road of trust.

In a sentence. Jesus told him to wash in the pool of Siloam, which means Sent, and he went, washed, and came back able to see.

On a Tuesday. Faith obeys before it sees. Do what Christ says, and the seeing will follow. Think of the last clear instruction you had from Scripture that came without any explanation of what it would accomplish: to forgive, to give, to confess, to rest. Obedience that waits for the mechanism to be explained is not obedience; it is negotiation. This man had mud on his eyes and a direction, and that was enough.

For worship. The Sent One sent a blind man to a pool called Sent, and the water of the feast became the water of new sight. The Father sent the Son into the world, not to condemn it, but that through him we might see. He is the true Siloam, the spring that flows softly and never fails, and whoever washes in him comes back seeing.
verseByVerse.note: The pool of Siloam lay at the south end of the city, fed by Hezekiah’s tunnel.

parallels.desc: Hezekiah brought water into the city
the waters of Shiloah

verseByVerse.quote: The neighbors and those who had seen him before as a beggar were saying, "Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?" Some said, "It is he." Others said, "No, but he is like him." He kept saying, "I am the man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The neighbors and those who had seen him before as a beggar were saying, “Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?” Some said, “It is he.” Others said, “No, but he is like him.” He kept saying, “I am the man.”

Is this not the man who used to sit and beg? A blind man had few options but begging. His neighbours knew him only as the blind beggar. That is how they had him filed. Not by name: John never gives us his name in the whole chapter, and neither do his neighbours. He was his condition.

Some said, “It is he.” Others said, “No, but he is like him.” The change is so great they hardly recognise him. A man who now sees moves, looks, and carries himself differently. Their confusion is not stupidity. They had known this man as a fixed feature of the street, in his place every day for years. What stands in front of them now looks like him and does not behave like him: upright, moving freely, meeting their eyes. People are recognised as much by their bearing as by their faces.

He kept saying, “I am the man.” The phrase is egō eimi, “I am,” used here in its ordinary sense: it’s me. The man begins his testimony. He has to keep saying it, because they will not have it. The first thing he does with a voice that anyone is finally listening to is insist that he is the same person.

The same man, made new. That matters for understanding the miracle, and for understanding conversion. It did not make him somebody else. The change is total, and the man is continuous. The neighbours were looking for a different man. What God does is give the same man his eyes. And notice the pattern this first questioning sets. The evidence is not in dispute: everyone agrees a man who was blind can now see. What is in dispute is whether that can be allowed to mean anything. And the first move, made here by neighbours with nothing at stake, is to question who the witness is. It will be repeated in verse 18 by professionals.

If I am a new creation, why do I still feel so much like my old self? Because God remakes you without replacing you. You are still you: your history, your personality, your memories. What has changed is your standing with God, the life of the Spirit in you, and the direction you are now facing (2 Corinthians 5:17). The old habits and feelings do not all vanish at once; the new nature grows over a lifetime, often slowly (Romans 12:2). Like this man, you may find that others notice the change before you do. Do not measure your new birth by how new you feel this morning. Measure it by Christ, who has made you his, and keep walking in the light.

In a sentence. His neighbours argued over whether he was the beggar they knew, while he kept insisting that he was.

On a Tuesday. When Christ changes someone, people notice. Is the change in you noticeable? And when you meet someone who claims Christ has changed them, do not be the neighbour who insists it cannot be the same person. Rejoice with them.

For worship. Christ did not throw away the beggar and make a new man in his place. He took the same man, with the same name nobody used, and gave him eyes. He does not discard us. He redeems us, and makes us new from the inside, and one day the change will be so complete that we will hardly recognise ourselves, and still we will be his.

parallels.desc: they recognized him as the one who sat begging

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Then how were your eyes opened?" He answered, "The man called Jesus made mud and anointed my eyes and said to me, 'Go to Siloam and wash.' So I went and washed and received my sight."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they said to him, “Then how were your eyes opened?” He answered, “The man called Jesus made mud and anointed my eyes and said to me, ‘Go to Siloam and wash.’ So I went and washed and received my sight.”

Then how were your eyes opened? The question “how” runs through the chapter (vv. 15, 19, 26).

The man called Jesus. Notice the growth in the man’s understanding through the chapter: “the man called Jesus” (v. 11), “a prophet” (v. 17), one “from God” (v. 33), “the Son of Man,” “Lord,” worshipped (vv. 35–38). As his physical sight is given in a moment, his spiritual sight grows step by step. Here he has only the name. He has never seen Jesus’ face, he does not know where he went, and he reports the name the way you would report a stranger’s.

So I went and washed and received my sight. He tells it simply, without embellishment. The testimony does exactly three things. It says what was done to him, who did it, and what happened. No interpretation, no theology, no claim about who Jesus is. He does not know yet. And the versions get shorter rather than longer. Here it is a full sentence with the name and the instruction. To the Pharisees it will be a dozen words (v. 15). Under real pressure it will shrink to its core (v. 25). A story that is being invented grows in the telling. This one contracts.

The beggar who told it flat. And notice what he does not say. He does not add that he had been blind from birth, or that he had begged at that spot for years, or that nobody had ever helped before. He has no interest in the pathos of his own case, which is remarkable in a man whose living had depended on it. Beggars survive by their story. This one, given an audience for the first time in his life, tells it plainly.

I do not have a dramatic testimony. Do I have anything to say? Yes. Your testimony is not the story of how bad you were, or how sudden your conversion was. It is what Jesus has done for you, and that is never small. This man’s first testimony was three plain sentences, and it set off an investigation that ran the length of a chapter and defeated the best-trained men in Jerusalem. If you were raised in a Christian home and cannot remember not believing, your testimony is that God kept you and opened your eyes early. Say it in your own words: what Christ is to you, what he has forgiven, what he has changed, why you trust him. That is enough.

In a sentence. When they asked how his eyes were opened, he told them simply what the man called Jesus had done.

On a Tuesday. Your testimony doesn’t need to be clever. Just tell what Jesus did. Write it down this week in five sentences or fewer, so that when someone asks, you are ready.

For worship. The man called Jesus: that was all he knew, and it was enough to begin. By the end of the chapter he would be on his face before him. Christ is patient with small beginnings. He gives sight in a moment and understanding over time, and he is pleased with the plainest word spoken about him by anyone whose eyes he has opened.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Where is he?" He said, "I do not know." They brought to the Pharisees the man who had formerly been blind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said to him, “Where is he?” He said, “I do not know.” They brought to the Pharisees the man who had formerly been blind.

Where is he? The question of where Jesus is runs through chapters 7–9.

I do not know. He has never seen Jesus. When he came back seeing, Jesus had gone. It is easy to skip, and it is one of the more remarkable facts in the chapter. He has been healed by someone he has never seen and cannot identify, who gave him an instruction and left. He will not see him until verse 35. So the whole defence he is about to make, against trained interrogators, at the cost of his place in the community, is made on behalf of a man he could not pick out of a crowd. He has no relationship with Jesus yet. He has an event and a name.

They brought to the Pharisees the man who had formerly been blind. Perhaps they want an official ruling, because it was a Sabbath. The neighbours take him to the religious authorities. The referral is not obviously hostile. An unexplained healing was a religious matter, and taking it to the authorities is what a careful neighbourhood would do. What turns a proper enquiry into an interrogation is not the procedure but what the men conducting it stand to lose. And the man goes willingly, with nothing to hide, with the confidence of someone who assumes that people who ask questions want answers. He will learn otherwise within about ten verses, and the learning is what makes him.

What if I believe, but there is still so much about Jesus I do not know? You are where this man was. A great deal of real faith begins with something that happened before there was much understanding to attach it to: a prayer answered, a word that struck home, a sense of being found. The understanding comes later, often through trouble, as it did for him. Do not despise your beginnings, and do not stay in them. Ask to know him better, read his word, and expect to grow. And take comfort: you may not yet know where Jesus is in every situation, but he always knows where you are.

In a sentence. When they asked where Jesus was, the man said he did not know, and they took him to the Pharisees.

On a Tuesday. If you are facing questions about your faith that you cannot answer, do not be ashamed to say, I do not know. Then say what you do know.

For worship. He did not yet know where Jesus was, but Jesus knew where he was, and would find him (v. 35). The Shepherd who knows his sheep by name had his eye on a man who could not have found him. We are not held by the strength of our grip on Christ, but by the strength of his grip on us.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it was a Sabbath day when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes. So the Pharisees again asked him how he had received his sight. And he said to them, "He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and I see."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now it was a Sabbath day when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes. So the Pharisees again asked him how he had received his sight. And he said to them, “He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and I see.”

Now it was a Sabbath day. Now we see the problem. As in 5:9, a Sabbath healing. The rabbis’ rules forbade kneading on the Sabbath, and making mud was a form of kneading. They also debated whether healing was allowed when life was not in danger; some forbade putting saliva on the eyes on the Sabbath. Jesus broke their traditions, not God’s law. John holds this detail back until now, having told the healing without mentioning it. The reader meets the miracle first and the legal problem second, which is the reverse of how the authorities will meet it. The rabbinic tradition listed thirty-nine kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath, and kneading was one of them. And a man blind from birth was in no danger; he could have waited until sundown.

He chose this on purpose. So this is not an accident. He could have spoken a word, as he usually does, and no rule would have been touched. He chose the one method that would cross their Sabbath rules in a way nobody could miss. That tells you what the sign is for. The healing is real, and the man’s eyes matter; but Jesus is also, deliberately, forcing the question of who has authority over the Sabbath, the same question he raised in chapter 5 with a man and his mat. My Father is working until now, and I am working (5:17).

So the Pharisees again asked him how he had received his sight. “Again”: after the neighbours.

He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and I see. Shorter each time he tells it. He is getting impatient. No name, no instruction, no explanation. He is not being evasive. He is being questioned by men whose intentions he cannot read, and the instinct that serves him is to say the thing that cannot be taken apart.

Did Jesus really break the Sabbath? He broke the rules the teachers had added to it, which forbade kneading and healing, not God’s command. The law of Moses never forbade doing good on the Sabbath, and Jesus taught that works of mercy were always lawful (Matthew 12:12). He is Lord of the Sabbath (Mark 2:28). The Pharisees’ premise, that he did not keep the Sabbath, was false.

In a sentence. It was the Sabbath when Jesus made mud and healed him, so the Pharisees asked how he had received his sight, and he told them.

On a Tuesday. Don’t let human rules stand between people and the mercy of God. Ask honestly whether any of the expectations in your church, or in your own heart, are making it harder for hurting people to come to Christ. Keep what God commands. Hold everything else loosely.

For worship. The Lord of the Sabbath made mud on the Sabbath and gave a man eyes on the day of rest. He did not break his Father’s law; he showed what it was for. The God who rested on the seventh day after making the world was at work on this seventh day making a new creation, and he is still at work, until the day when all his people enter his rest.

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the Pharisees said, "This man is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath." But others said, "How can a man who is a sinner do such signs?" And there was a division among them. So they said again to the blind man, "What do you say about him, since he has opened your eyes?" He said, "He is a prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of the Pharisees said, “This man is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath.” But others said, “How can a man who is a sinner do such signs?” And there was a division among them. So they said again to the blind man, “What do you say about him, since he has opened your eyes?” He said, “He is a prophet.”

This man is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath. Their reasoning starts with their rules: anyone who breaks our Sabbath rules cannot be from God. So the miracle must be explained away.

How can a man who is a sinner do such signs? Others start from the miracle: a sinner couldn’t do this. A fair argument. The two positions are the two positions people still take. One party reasons from the rule to the man: he broke the Sabbath, so he is not from God. The other reasons from the works to the man: how could a sinner do this? Both argue honestly from a real premise. The difference is which fact they treat as fixed.

And there was a division among them. “Division” (schisma): Jesus divides even the Pharisees (7:43; 10:19). The crowd tore over him in chapter 7; now the council itself does. And it is a small mercy in the chapter: not everyone in the building was against him. Some of the men whose job was to guard the people from false prophets were following the evidence, and said so out loud. Belonging to an institution that has decided something does not oblige a man to have decided it.

What do you say about him, since he has opened your eyes? They ask the man himself, perhaps hoping he will help their case. A council of trained men, deadlocked, asking the opinion of the exhibit. It is asked dismissively, and it is the question that starts him thinking.

He is a prophet. His second step of understanding. Like Elijah and Elisha, who did miracles, Jesus must be a man sent from God. Nobody taught him that. He has reasoned it out under questioning: the prophets did mighty works, this man opened my eyes, so he stands in that line. His faith is being built by the very process designed to dismantle it.

What if I start from the wrong fixed point? Everyone starts somewhere. These Pharisees had made their own reading of the Sabbath the one thing that could not be questioned, and so they could not see God at work in front of them. Christians can do the same with a tradition, a political view, a favourite teacher or a past experience. The test is whether you will let Scripture and the facts of what Christ has done correct your fixed point, or whether you explain away anything that does not fit. Hold firm to what God has clearly said. Hold everything else humbly, ready to be corrected.

In a sentence. Some Pharisees said Jesus could not be from God because he broke the Sabbath, others asked how a sinner could do such signs, and when they asked the man, he said Jesus was a prophet.

On a Tuesday. When pressure comes, let it drive you deeper into what you know of Christ, not away from it. This man grew more certain with every hostile question. Ask God to use the hard questions people put to you to make your faith clearer.

For worship. Jesus is more than a prophet, but he is not less. Listen to his words. He is the Prophet like Moses, who speaks the very words of God; and he is more than a prophet, for the prophets spoke the word, and he is the Word. A beggar called him a prophet and was right. Heaven calls him Lord, and is right.

parallels.desc: a prophet who gives a sign

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews did not believe that he had been blind and had received his sight, until they called the parents of the man who had received his sight and asked them, "Is this your son, who you say was born blind? How then does he now see?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jews did not believe that he had been blind and had received his sight, until they called the parents of the man who had received his sight and asked them, “Is this your son, who you say was born blind? How then does he now see?”

The Jews did not believe that he had been blind. “The Jews” here means the same Pharisees, the leaders. Unable to deny the healing, they question whether he was ever blind. It is the anatomy of a mind that has decided in advance. They cannot fault the testimony, so they attack the fact. If the miracle can be shown not to have happened, everything else goes away.

Until they called the parents. The parents are the best witnesses. And the summoning is also a tactic. They already have a witness who will not budge; what they want is a witness who will. Parents are the softest point in a family: older, with more to lose, likely to do the arithmetic of consequences that their son has not yet thought to do.

Is this your son, who you say was born blind? How then does he now see? Three questions: is he your son, was he born blind, and how does he see? And the phrasing is a small masterpiece of insinuation. Not, who was born blind, but, who you say was born blind. Before a single answer is given, the family has been put in the position of alleging something. The Pharisees do not say the man is lying. They arrange the sentence so that his blindness becomes a claim rather than a fact, and then investigate the claimants. It is a permanent technique, and it does not even require malice to work.

How should I handle evidence that is inconvenient? Honestly. The tempting move, when a fact threatens something we have decided, is to turn it into somebody’s opinion and then question the person. The honest move is to look at the fact itself. That applies to the evidence for Christ, which deserves to be weighed rather than waved away. It also applies to Christians, when something we do not want to hear comes to light: a hard passage of Scripture, a just complaint against us, a wrong done in our church. Truth is never the enemy of faith. The God of truth is not served by anyone’s refusal to look.

In a sentence. The leaders refused to believe he had been blind until they called his parents and asked whether he was their son, born blind, and how he now saw.

On a Tuesday. Unbelief will often try every explanation except the true one. Watch for it in yourself. When God has plainly done something, in your life or someone else’s, do not reach for the explanation that lets you avoid thanking him.

For worship. Every effort to explain away what Christ had done only made it plainer. The parents were called to disprove the miracle and confirmed it instead. God’s works stand up to every investigation, because they are real. The Light cannot be argued out of the room; it only shows more clearly the more closely it is examined.

verseByVerse.quote: His parents answered, "We know that this is our son and that he was born blind. But how he now sees we do not know, nor do we know who opened his eyes. Ask him; he is of age. He will speak for himself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His parents answered, “We know that this is our son and that he was born blind. But how he now sees we do not know, nor do we know who opened his eyes. Ask him; he is of age. He will speak for himself.”

We know that this is our son and that he was born blind. They answer the first two questions plainly. The miracle is confirmed. Look first at what they actually do. Under direct pressure from the body that could destroy their standing, they confirm the two facts that make the miracle undeniable. The Pharisees’ whole line of attack, that the blindness was invented, dies in their answer.

But how he now sees we do not know, nor do we know who opened his eyes. They avoid the third. They probably did know; their son must have told them. They are afraid.

Ask him; he is of age. A son was regarded as of age at about thirteen, able to give legal testimony. He was an adult. They shift the danger onto their son. They are not lying, and they are not being cruel in any way a court could name. They are simply declining to stand next to their own son at the moment he most needs someone beside him. They had carried him, fed him, and lived for years with the very question the disciples asked about whose fault it was; and when he could finally see, they stepped back.

Be fair to them. The parents are often handled with a contempt that lands on the wrong reader. They were the parents of a blind child in a world with no provision for one. They had raised a boy who would beg for his living, in a society that had already decided someone’s sin was responsible; the disciples’ question in verse 2 is what these two had been hearing about themselves all his life. And now the same authorities were asking them to volunteer for expulsion. So the honest verdict is a divided one. They did not lie, and they did not stand. John records it without a word of comment, which is his way of letting a thing be seen.

I have gone quiet about Christ when I should have spoken. Is that the end of me? No. If you have gone quiet when the subject came up at work, or let a remark pass, or answered a direct question with something technically true and deliberately empty, this is that, and Scripture names it accurately without screaming about it. Notice what does not happen to these two. They are not cursed or written off. Peter would do far worse within months, three times, out loud, and be given breakfast on a beach and a commission (21:15–19). The failure is real, and it need not be final. Confess it to the Lord, ask for courage, and take the next opportunity he gives you.

In a sentence. His parents confirmed he was their son and had been born blind, but said they did not know how he now saw or who healed him, and told them to ask him, since he was of age.

On a Tuesday. Fear can make us abandon the people we love. Pray for courage to stand with those who speak for Christ. Think of the believer near you who is paying a price for faithfulness: the colleague who refused to lie, the student who is mocked, the family member who has been shut out. Stand next to them this week, in some visible way.

For worship. His parents stepped back, and the Lord stepped forward. When father and mother forsake me, the LORD will take me in (Psalm 27:10). The Son of God was abandoned by his friends at the hour he most needed them, and he did not abandon them in return. He restores the fearful, strengthens the weak, and stands beside those whom everyone else has left.
verseByVerse.note: A son was regarded as of age at about thirteen.

verseByVerse.quote: (His parents said these things because they feared the Jews, for the Jews had already agreed that if anyone should confess Jesus to be Christ, he was to be put out of the synagogue. Therefore his parents said, "He is of age; ask him.")
verseByVerse.commentary:
(His parents said these things because they feared the Jews, for the Jews had already agreed that if anyone should confess Jesus to be Christ, he was to be put out of the synagogue. Therefore his parents said, “He is of age; ask him.”)

Because they feared the Jews. The leaders.

For the Jews had already agreed that if anyone should confess Jesus to be Christ, he was to be put out of the synagogue. Being put out of the synagogue (aposynagōgos, 12:42; 16:2) meant exclusion from the community: from worship, from friends, from business, from family life. It was social death. Some scholars argue this reflects a later period, after AD 70, when a curse on heretics was added to the synagogue prayers. But there is no reason why local exclusion could not have happened already in Jesus’ lifetime; Luke 6:22 records Jesus warning of it. The word itself appears in no Greek writing we know of before John, who uses it three times. He seems to have needed a word for something that cut that deep.

What it cost. It has to be measured in the terms of that world, or the parents’ fear looks excessive. The synagogue was not a church one might change. It was the school, the court, the welfare system and the register of who belonged. Exclusion meant that no one would trade with you, marry your children or sit with you; it meant losing the festivals, the whole shape of the year; and in a small community, it meant your neighbours were expected to treat you as absent. So the threat hanging over this family is not embarrassment. It is the removal of every relationship they have, in a society where a person outside the community had no way to live.

Already agreed. And John notes that the decision had already been taken. This is policy, made in advance, before this man’s case came up. The verdict on Jesus was settled and the machinery was waiting; the investigation in this chapter was never really an investigation. Notice too that nobody in the chapter has yet confessed Jesus as the Christ. The man has said a prophet, and will say from God. Yet the policy is applied to him anyway (v. 34). The written ground is narrow and the application is wide, and by the time a man finds out which he is being judged by, he is already outside.

Confess Jesus to be Christ. To confess means to openly declare him as Messiah. Confession of Christ has always been costly.

What if confessing Christ would cost me my family or my job? Then you are in the company of this man, and of believers in many countries today for whom it is exactly that costly. Jesus does not hide the price: whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me (Matthew 10:37). But he also promises that no one who leaves home or family for his sake will fail to receive a hundredfold now, in the family of his church, and eternal life in the age to come (Mark 10:29–30). Count the cost honestly. Seek wisdom about how and when to speak, and the support of other believers. But do not deny him. What you lose for Christ, you never lose for ever.

In a sentence. His parents answered this way because they feared the authorities, who had agreed to expel from the synagogue anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ.

On a Tuesday. Most of us will never be thrown out of anything for Christ. But we are often tempted to keep quiet to avoid a much smaller cost. Pray today for believers who are facing real expulsion for their faith, and ask God to make you braver in the small costs you face.

For worship. Confessing Christ may cost us our place among people, but it gives us a place with him that can never be taken. He himself was cast out: led outside the city, rejected by the leaders of his people, and crucified outside the gate. So let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured (Hebrews 13:12–13). The one who was put out for us has made a home for us that no council can shut.
verseByVerse.note: Being put out of the synagogue meant exclusion from the community’s worship and social life.

parallels.desc: they will put you out of the synagogues

verseByVerse.quote: So for the second time they called the man who had been blind and said to him, "Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner." He answered, "Whether he is a sinner I do not know. One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So for the second time they called the man who had been blind and said to him, “Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner.” He answered, “Whether he is a sinner I do not know. One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see.”

Give glory to God. “Give glory to God” was a solemn call to tell the truth, especially to confess wrongdoing, as Joshua said to Achan (Joshua 7:19). They mean: tell the truth, admit this was a fraud. The irony is that he is giving glory to God, by telling what God did. It is not an invitation to praise but a formula for putting a man on oath. So the second interview opens by treating the healed man as the guilty party.

We know that this man is a sinner. They have settled the matter: a Sabbath-breaker is a sinner. The verdict is announced before the testimony is taken. He is being asked to swear to their conclusion.

Whether he is a sinner I do not know. The man won’t argue theology with them. He will not be drawn onto ground he cannot hold. He is not a theologian and does not pretend to be, and he refuses to give an opinion he does not have, which is itself a kind of integrity, and rarer than it sounds in a man under pressure to say something.

One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see. One of the great testimonies in Scripture. Theological arguments can be debated; experience of Christ’s power cannot be argued away. John Newton echoed it in “Amazing Grace”: I once was blind, but now I see. Every believer can say it. It is the shortest form his story has yet taken, and it is unbreakable, because it does not depend on anything he could be argued out of. They can outrank him, out-argue him and out-quote him. They cannot make him doubt that he was blind yesterday.

Is my experience enough to prove Christianity is true? It is part of your witness, but it is not the whole case, and this man shows why. His experience is where he stands; it is not where he stops. In verse 33 he reasons from Scripture and history to a conclusion about who Jesus is. Experience can be misread, and people of other faiths also report experiences. The Christian faith rests on what God has done in history, above all the death and resurrection of Christ, and on what he has said in Scripture. Your experience of his grace is the personal confirmation of that public truth. So tell what has happened to you, and point beyond yourself to the Christ it all depends on.

In a sentence. When they called him again and told him to give glory to God by admitting Jesus was a sinner, he said he did not know about that, but one thing he knew: he was blind, and now he saw.

On a Tuesday. You don’t need to win every argument. Say what you know: I was blind, now I see. When you are asked a question about your faith that you cannot answer, it is honest and good to say, I do not know. Then add the thing you do know. That is often more persuasive than a clever answer.

For worship. Amazing grace, how sweet the sound. A blind beggar stood in front of the most learned men in Jerusalem and gave glory to God by saying the simplest thing in the world. The Light had shone in his darkness. Every believer since has been able to sing it with him: I once was lost, but now am found; was blind, but now I see.
verseByVerse.note: “Give glory to God” was a solemn call to tell the truth.

parallels.desc: give glory to the LORD and tell me now what you have done

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?" He answered them, "I have told you already, and you would not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become his disciples?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said to him, “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?” He answered them, “I have told you already, and you would not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become his disciples?”

What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes? They go over it again, looking for a contradiction.

I have told you already, and you would not listen. He is growing bolder. He sees that they are not listening. The exasperation is genuine, and it is funny, which the chapter needs by now. He has worked out what the repetition is for. They are not asking because they want the answer; they are asking because they hope the story will come out differently the second time. Anyone who has been cross-examined in bad faith knows the feeling exactly. And notice the word: you would not listen. It is the chapter’s other sense running alongside sight. These men have working eyes and working ears and are getting nothing through either. He is the only person in the room who has had a sense restored, and the only one receiving anything.

Why do you want to hear it again? There is a mischievous edge to it. He knows the answer before he asks.

Do you also want to become his disciples? A daring, ironic question. The Greek form expects the answer no. And “also” implies that he himself is, or is becoming, one. It is sarcasm, and it is also, accidentally, evangelism: the first invitation in the chapter, issued by a beggar to the council’s investigators. Up to now he has been reporting. Here he takes sides. And notice what has produced this. Not a conversation with Jesus, whom he has still never seen. Not teaching. Being pushed. Every question they ask drives him one step further into a position he had not held before, and by the end of the interview he is a disciple of a man he could not recognise.

How can opposition make faith stronger? Because it forces us to decide what we really believe, and to lean on God rather than on comfort. Peter says that trials test faith as fire tests gold (1 Peter 1:6–7), and James that testing produces steadfastness (James 1:2–4). This man had faith the size of a name when the questioning began, and a clear confession when it ended. It is not that hardship automatically strengthens faith; sometimes it shakes it. But God uses it, for those who keep turning to him, to burn away what is false and make the real thing plain. If your faith is under pressure now, do not assume it is failing. It may be growing.

In a sentence. When they asked again what Jesus had done, he said he had told them already, and asked if they too wanted to become his disciples.

On a Tuesday. When people keep pressing you about your faith, it is not always a sign of hostility; sometimes it is the sign of a conscience that will not leave the subject alone. Keep answering, gently. You might find, as this man did, that your own convictions become clearer every time.

For worship. A beggar teaching the theologians. God gives courage and wit to those who stand for Christ (Luke 21:15). He chooses what is weak in the world to shame the strong, so that no one may boast in his presence. The Spirit who gave this man his boldness gives it still to timid believers in hostile rooms, and the gates of hell will not prevail against the church he builds out of people like him.

verseByVerse.quote: And they reviled him, saying, "You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses. We know that God has spoken to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he comes from."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they reviled him, saying, “You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses. We know that God has spoken to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he comes from.”

And they reviled him. “Reviled” (eloidorēsan): abused, insulted. It is what the argument has come to. They began with an investigation, moved to intimidation, and end by shouting at a beggar.

You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses. They set Moses against Jesus. But Moses wrote of Jesus (5:46). To be a true disciple of Moses is to follow Jesus. Their claim is not merely wrong but self-cancelling: a disciple of Moses who meets the one Moses described and refuses him has stopped being a disciple of Moses in the only sense that matters. And notice the pronouns. You are his disciple; we are disciples of Moses. The line has been drawn, and the man has been put on the other side of it before he has finished speaking. The expulsion in verse 34 is not a decision; it is a formality.

We know that God has spoken to Moses. That much was true (Exodus 33:11). And the tense is revealing. Spoken: past, closed, delivered. It is their whole religion in one tense. God said something to somebody a long time ago, and the task now is to guard it. Against which the man in front of them is evidence that God has done something this morning, which is the very thing their theology had no room for.

But as for this man, we do not know where he comes from. The question of his origin again (7:27; 8:14). Earlier they claimed to know where he came from (7:27); now they say they don’t know. Either way, they miss that he came from God. They say it as a disqualification. It is in fact the exact statement of their problem. They stand in front of a man whose eyes were opened by someone whose origin they cannot account for, and they conclude that the origin must be nothing much.

Is the Old Testament still for Christians, or has Jesus replaced Moses? Jesus has not replaced Moses; he has fulfilled him. The whole Old Testament is God’s word and points to Christ (Luke 24:27, 44). Its promises are kept in him, its sacrifices fulfilled in his once-for-all death, its moral law written on our hearts by the Spirit. The Pharisees’ error was not loving Moses too much but reading him without Christ, so that the book meant to lead them to Jesus became a wall against him. Read the Old Testament gladly, as Christian Scripture, and ask in every part how it leads you to the one Moses wrote about.

In a sentence. They insulted him, saying he was Jesus’ disciple, but they were disciples of Moses, to whom God had spoken, while they did not know where Jesus came from.

On a Tuesday. You can’t honour Moses and reject Christ. All of Scripture points to him. And beware of a faith that is all about what God did long ago and has no room for what he is doing now in people’s lives. The God of the Bible is not retired.

For worship. God spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. Then he spoke to us by his Son, the radiance of his glory and the exact imprint of his nature (Hebrews 1:1–3). Moses was faithful in God’s house as a servant; Christ is faithful over it as a Son. The one they did not know where he came from had come from the Father’s side, and Moses himself had longed to see his glory.

verseByVerse.quote: The man answered, "Why, this is an amazing thing! You do not know where he comes from, and yet he opened my eyes. We know that God does not listen to sinners, but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, God listens to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man answered, “Why, this is an amazing thing! You do not know where he comes from, and yet he opened my eyes. We know that God does not listen to sinners, but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, God listens to him.”

Why, this is an amazing thing! The beggar becomes the teacher. He is amazed that the experts don’t see the obvious.

You do not know where he comes from, and yet he opened my eyes. The answer to where he comes from is staring them in the face.

We know that God does not listen to sinners. He turns their “we know” back on them. This was a common Jewish belief, drawn from Scripture: God does not hear the prayers of the wicked who cling to their sin (Psalm 66:18; Proverbs 15:29; Isaiah 1:15). It does not mean God never hears a repentant sinner’s prayer (Luke 18:13–14); it means God does not empower the wicked to work miracles in his name. He is arguing from shared ground, using their own first person plural and quoting their own theology back to them. That is what makes the argument so hard to answer.

A sentence that needs a guard. Lifted out of this courtyard, these words have frightened people badly. Read flatly, as a rule about prayer, they shut the door on every person who most needs it open. And it is worth being clear about what they are. They are the healed man’s words, not a formula handed down from heaven. Scripture reports his reasoning faithfully, and his reasoning serves him well here, but he is a new believer arguing from the common piety of his day. Even the psalm behind it says something narrower: if I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened (Psalm 66:18). The word is cherished. What closes God’s ear is not the presence of sin in a person but his fondness for it: the man who hugs his sin and demands God’s help at the same time.

But if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, God listens to him. So, he concludes, Jesus must be a godly man whom God hears.

I am a sinner. Will God listen to my prayers? Yes. The plainest answer is a story Jesus told. A tax collector stood far off, would not lift his eyes, beat his breast and prayed for mercy as a sinner, and Jesus said that man went home justified (Luke 18:13–14). God listened to a sinner, at the very moment he called himself one. If you have been afraid that your sin has stopped God’s ears, notice which way the fear runs. The person whose sin has closed God’s ear is not troubled about it. The trouble you feel is not evidence that he has stopped listening. It is very often the first evidence that he has already begun to work. Come to him through Christ, honestly, and he will hear you.

In a sentence. The man said it was amazing that they did not know where Jesus came from, though he had opened his eyes, since God does not listen to sinners but to those who worship him and do his will.

On a Tuesday. Is there a sin you are holding on to while asking God for help? Let it go, and pray. And if you are a sinner who wants to be rid of your sin, do not let anyone tell you God will not hear you. He hears the cry of the humble.

For worship. God gives wisdom to the simple (Psalm 19:7). Ask him for it. The Lord who hid these things from the wise and revealed them to little children gave a beggar the clearest reasoning in the room. And he gives more than wisdom: he gives a hearing to every sinner who comes to him through his Son, because the Son is the one sinless man whom God always hears, and he lives to intercede for us.

parallels.desc: if I had cherished iniquity, the Lord would not have listened

verseByVerse.quote: "Never since the world began has it been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Never since the world began has it been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.

Never since the world began has it been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind. There is no record in the Old Testament of anyone healing a person born blind. The Old Testament reserves the opening of blind eyes to God himself (Psalm 146:8; Exodus 4:11), and promises it as a sign of the messianic age (Isaiah 29:18; 35:5; 42:7). This miracle is unique, a sign that God himself is at work, that the Messiah has come. He is right, and it is worth checking how right. The Old Testament has spectacular healings: Elijah and Elisha each raised a dead child, and Naaman’s leprosy went. But no one anywhere in Scripture before this opens the eyes of someone blind from birth. So his argument is not enthusiasm; it is an accurate survey of the record, from a man who had evidently listened to a great deal of Scripture read aloud in the synagogue he was about to be thrown out of.

If this man were not from God, he could do nothing. His third step: Jesus is from God. The very question they cannot answer, the beggar answers. And notice the restraint of the sentence. He does not say that Jesus is the Messiah, which he has no way yet of knowing. He states the least the evidence will bear, and it is enough to end the argument, which is why they stop arguing and start shouting. He has brought in nothing new. He has taken their own premises and walked them to a conclusion they will not accept, which leaves them nothing to attack except him.

How should I think about the evidence for Christ? Like this man: clearly, honestly, and from the facts. Christianity does not ask you to switch off your mind. The signs were written so that you may believe (20:30–31), and the resurrection was a public event witnessed by many (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Weigh the evidence: the Old Testament promises, the life and claims of Jesus, the empty tomb, the transformation of the disciples. Evidence alone does not save; the Spirit must open the heart. But God uses evidence, and a mind that reasons honestly from what Christ has done will find that it points to God.

In a sentence. The man said that no one had ever opened the eyes of a man born blind, so if Jesus were not from God, he could do nothing.

On a Tuesday. Reason clearly from what Christ has done. The evidence points to God. If someone you know dismisses Christianity without looking at it, ask them gently whether they have ever read one Gospel through. Offer to read it with them.

For worship. Never since the world began. What no prophet had done, Christ did, because the prophets were servants and he is the Lord who opens the eyes of the blind (Psalm 146:8).
