Isaiah’s promise came true in a Jerusalem street: the eyes of the blind shall be opened. The age to come had broken into this one, and the God who made the eye had come to give it sight.

parallels.desc: the eyes of the blind shall be opened

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "You were born in utter sin, and would you teach us?" And they cast him out. Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and having found him he said, "Do you believe in the Son of Man?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They answered him, “You were born in utter sin, and would you teach us?” And they cast him out. Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and having found him he said, “Do you believe in the Son of Man?”

You were born in utter sin. They go back to the disciples’ mistaken assumption (v. 2): your blindness proves you were born in sin. In admitting he was born blind, they finally admit the miracle. And yet the irony is that it is true of all of us: we are all born in sin (Psalm 51:5). They, too. What the disciples raised as a theological puzzle, these men use as a weapon. And they say it having just been given, by this same man, the best reasoning anyone offers in the chapter.

And would you teach us? Pride: a beggar can’t teach scholars. The whole thing is in a few words. Not, you are wrong; they never manage that. But, who do you think you are? Argument defeated, rank asserted.

And they cast him out. Out of the room, and probably out of the synagogue (v. 22). He has lost everything for confessing Jesus. His community, his standing, his family’s standing, and every relationship outside his own house. He is a man with new eyes and nothing else.

Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and having found him. Jesus seeks him out. Rejected by the religious leaders, he is found by the Good Shepherd, who will speak in the next chapter of leading his sheep out (10:3–4). Jesus never casts out (6:37). Those cast out for his sake, he gathers in. Everything is in the two verbs. Heard: Jesus was not there, and it reached him. Having found him: the word implies looking. He went out into a crowded city and found one man who had just lost everything for defending him. Consider what the man had at that moment. He had no idea what Jesus looked like. He could not have gone looking if he had wanted to. Every road from where he stood was closed. And while he was standing in the street with nowhere to go, he was already being looked for. Sought before he knew there was anyone to seek him; sought again the moment he had nothing left.

Do you believe in the Son of Man? “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself. From Daniel 7:13–14, the heavenly figure who receives an everlasting kingdom. Jesus is asking a man who has just been stripped of his standing in Israel whether he will believe in the one to whom every kingdom is finally given.

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “Son of God.” The earliest and best manuscripts read “Son of Man,” and a scribe is more likely to have changed it to the more familiar confession than the other way round. The meaning is not changed: in John the Son of Man is the one who comes from heaven (3:13).

I have been rejected by a church or by Christians. Has Christ rejected me? No. Sometimes believers are put out unjustly, as this man was, and Christ sees it and comes looking for them. If you have been wronged by a church, bring it to him; he is the Good Shepherd, and he has not cast you out. At the same time, be honest: sometimes church discipline is a loving and right response to unrepented sin (Matthew 18:15–17), meant to bring a person home, not to destroy them. Whatever has happened, do not let the failures of Christians keep you from Christ, and do not give up on his people. Seek a faithful church where you can be known and cared for.

In a sentence. They mocked him as born in sin and threw him out, but Jesus heard and found him, and asked whether he believed in the Son of Man.

On a Tuesday. Who has been pushed out of the circles you move in: the family, the friendship group, the church? Christ went looking for the cast-out man. Go and look for them.

For worship. When others cast you out for Christ, Christ comes to find you. The one who saw the man first, when he was blind and begging and unaware anyone was there, came back and found him again the moment the world had finished with him. That is the whole Gospel in one man’s afternoon. The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost, and he has never stopped looking for those that everyone else has thrown away.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself.

parallels.desc: brought forth in iniquity

verseByVerse.quote: He answered, "And who is he, sir, that I may believe in him?" Jesus said to him, "You have seen him, and it is he who is speaking to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He answered, “And who is he, sir, that I may believe in him?” Jesus said to him, “You have seen him, and it is he who is speaking to you.”

And who is he, sir, that I may believe in him? “Sir” (kyrie) can mean sir or Lord. He is ready to believe; he only needs to know who. It is the most attractive sentence in the chapter. Note the order: he commits before he knows the answer. He does not say, tell me who he is and I will consider it. He says he is ready to believe and needs only the name. And he is speaking to a stranger; he still does not know who is talking to him, because he has never seen the face.

You have seen him. A beautiful line. The first person this man has ever seen with his eyes may be Jesus. And now he sees him truly. He can say you have seen him only because of what happened at the pool. Any other person Jesus revealed himself to could have seen him at any time. This man could not have, until Siloam. The eyes he is using to look at Jesus were made by the man he is looking at, out of dirt.

And it is he who is speaking to you. As Jesus revealed himself to the Samaritan woman (4:26). Twice in this Gospel Jesus states his identity outright, without being pressed, and both times it is to someone with no standing at all: a Samaritan woman at noon, and an excommunicated beggar in a street. He has spent two chapters declining to give a plain answer to the men who run the temple.

How does Jesus reveal himself to people today? Through his word, by his Spirit. He no longer stands in the street to be seen with physical eyes; he speaks in Scripture, in the preaching of the gospel, and the Spirit opens hearts to see him there (Romans 10:17; 2 Corinthians 4:6). That is not second best. Jesus said that those who have not seen and yet believe are blessed (20:29). If you want to know him, go where he speaks: read a Gospel, sit under faithful preaching, and ask him to show himself to you. Like this man, you may find he has been speaking to you all along.

In a sentence. The man asked who the Son of Man was so that he could believe in him, and Jesus said he had seen him, and it was he who was speaking.

On a Tuesday. Christ reveals himself to those who want to believe. Ask him to show himself to you. Pray this man’s prayer in your own words: Lord, who are you, that I may believe in you more?

For worship. You have seen him, and it is he who is speaking to you. The Lord who made the man’s eyes let them rest first on his own face. He reveals himself not to the proud but to the humble, not to those who claim to see but to those who know they need sight. And one day every believer will see him face to face, and the first sight will be the Lord who sought us.

parallels.desc: I who speak to you am he

verseByVerse.quote: He said, "Lord, I believe," and he worshiped him. Jesus said, "For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said, “Lord, I believe,” and he worshiped him. Jesus said, “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”

Lord, I believe. Now “Lord” (kyrie) in its full sense. The final step: from “the man called Jesus,” to “a prophet,” to “from God,” to “Lord.” The word he used for sir two verses ago now means what it means.

And he worshiped him. “Worshiped” (prosekynēsen): bowed down before him. In John this word is used only of worshipping God (4:20–24; 12:20). Jesus accepts it. Angels and apostles refused worship (Acts 10:25–26; Revelation 19:10). Jesus receives it, because he is God. That is the last step of the chapter, and it is not a title but an action. He began with the man called Jesus, moved to a prophet, then from God, and ends on his face.

Textual note. A few early manuscripts lack “He said, ‘Lord, I believe,’ and he worshiped him. Jesus said.” Most scholars think the words are original: they are found in the great majority of manuscripts, including very early ones, and the omission may be accidental.

For judgment I came into this world. Jesus did not come to condemn (3:17), but his coming brings a separation, a verdict. His light shows who is who. Set against 3:17, it looks like a contradiction, and it is not. The resolution is in the chapter just told. Jesus came to give sight, and the giving of sight is itself a sorting: the man who knew he was blind can see, and the men who were certain they could see have spent forty verses proving they cannot. Nobody was condemned by a new verdict. They were exposed by a light, which is what light does.

That those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind. Those who know they are blind receive sight. Those who think they see are confirmed in their blindness. The proud are blinded, the humble enlightened (Isaiah 6:9–10; Matthew 11:25; Luke 1:51–53).

Is it right to worship Jesus? Yes, and this verse is one of the plainest reasons. Scripture forbids worshipping anyone but God (Exodus 20:3–5; Matthew 4:10), and when Cornelius bowed before Peter, or John before an angel, they were told at once to stand up. Jesus never says that. He receives this man’s worship, and Thomas’ confession, my Lord and my God (20:28), because he is God the Son. The Father wills that all should honour the Son just as they honour the Father (5:23). So Christians rightly pray to Jesus, sing to him and bow before him, together with the Father and the Spirit, one God.

In a sentence. The man said, “Lord, I believe,” and worshipped Jesus, and Jesus said he came for judgment, so that the blind would see and those who think they see would become blind.

On a Tuesday. Let your faith end where this man’s did: on your knees. Belief that never becomes worship has not yet seen Jesus clearly. Take a few minutes today simply to adore him: not to ask for anything, but to tell him who he is.

For worship. Bow before Christ as this man did. He is worthy of the worship due to God alone. Angels refuse it; apostles refuse it; Jesus receives it, because every knee in heaven and on earth will bow to him. A beggar in a Jerusalem street was the first in this Gospel to fall down before him, and he will not be the last. Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honour and glory and blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the Pharisees near him heard these things, and said to him, "Are we also blind?" Jesus said to them, "If you were blind, you would have no guilt; but now that you say, 'We see,' your guilt remains."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of the Pharisees near him heard these things, and said to him, “Are we also blind?” Jesus said to them, “If you were blind, you would have no guilt; but now that you say, ‘We see,’ your guilt remains.”

Are we also blind? The Greek form expects the answer no. Surely not us? They are not asking; they are inviting a denial, and they ask because they have understood him perfectly well.

If you were blind, you would have no guilt. If they knew themselves to be blind, and came to him for sight, their sin would be forgiven. Or: if they truly had no opportunity to see, they would be less guilty. That is the mercy in the sentence, and it is real. But no one in that crowd is in that position, and the answer sounds like a reprieve for a moment before it turns.

But now that you say, “We see,” your guilt remains. “Remains” (menei): stays, abides. The most dangerous condition is not blindness but the proud claim to see. The one who thinks he needs no light will never come to the light. Their claim to see is what keeps them in their sin. Compare Revelation 3:17. The whole weight falls on the claim rather than the condition. A man who knows he cannot see will ask for help. A man who is sure he can see will not, and there is nothing further to be done for him while he goes on saying it. And the last word of the chapter is remains, the same word this Gospel uses for abiding, turned the wrong way round. Some things stay because they have been given. This stays because it has been chosen.

Two kinds of blind men. That is the chapter in one line. One of them said, I do not know, twice (vv. 12, 25), and ended on his face worshipping. The others said, we know (vv. 24, 29), and we see (v. 41), and ended holding a verdict and nothing else. They were not defeated by an argument they could not answer. They were defeated by where it came from, and they would rather be blind than be taught by a beggar.

How do I know whether I am one of those who think they see? Ask whether you are still teachable. The Pharisees could not be taught by anyone below them. Ask when you last changed your mind about something because Scripture corrected you, or when you last let a doctrine you hold be questioned by someone with less standing than you. Ask whether you pray for light, or assume you already have it. This test is meant to catch the confident, not to crush the anxious. If you are worried that you might be blind, and want Christ to open your eyes, that very worry shows you are not where these men were. The humble cry, Lord, that I may see, is the cry he always answers.

In a sentence. When some Pharisees asked whether they were blind too, Jesus said that if they were blind they would have no guilt, but because they claimed to see, their guilt remained.

On a Tuesday. The first step to sight is admitting you are blind. Pray, “Lord, open my eyes.” Take the thing you are most sure you understand about God, and ask him this week to show you more of it than you have yet seen.

For worship. The Light of the world gives sight to the blind who know they are blind. He opened the eyes of a beggar and left the self-assured in their darkness, not because he was unwilling to give them light, but because they would not receive it. We were all born blind. If we now see, it is because he stooped to the dust and touched us. Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18), and above all, the wonder of your Son.

parallels.desc: a guide to the blind

9.text: <sup>1</sup>As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth.<sup>2</sup>And his disciples asked him, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?”<sup>3</sup>Jesus answered, “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him.<sup>4</sup>We must work the works of him who sent me while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work.<sup>5</sup>As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.”<sup>6</sup>Having said these things, he spit on the ground and made mud with the saliva. Then he anointed the man’s eyes with the mud<sup>7</sup>and said to him, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam” (which means Sent). So he went and washed and came back seeing.<sup>8</sup>The neighbors and those who had seen him before as a beggar were saying, “Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?”<sup>9</sup>Some said, “It is he.” Others said, “No, but he is like him.” He kept saying, “I am the man.”<sup>10</sup>So they said to him, “Then how were your eyes opened?”<sup>11</sup>He answered, “The man called Jesus made mud and anointed my eyes and said to me, ’Go to Siloam and wash.’ So I went and washed and received my sight.”<sup>12</sup>They said to him, “Where is he?” He said, “I do not know.”<sup>13</sup>They brought to the Pharisees the man who had formerly been blind.<sup>14</sup>Now it was a Sabbath day when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes.<sup>15</sup>So the Pharisees again asked him how he had received his sight. And he said to them, “He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and I see.”<sup>16</sup>Some of the Pharisees said, “This man is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath.” But others said, “How can a man who is a sinner do such signs?” And there was a division among them.<sup>17</sup>So they said again to the blind man, “What do you say about him, since he has opened your eyes?” He said, “He is a prophet.”<sup>18</sup>The Jews did not believe that he had been blind and had received his sight, until they called the parents of the man who had received his sight<sup>19</sup>and asked them, “Is this your son, who you say was born blind? How then does he now see?”<sup>20</sup>His parents answered, “We know that this is our son and that he was born blind.<sup>21</sup>But how he now sees we do not know, nor do we know who opened his eyes. Ask him; he is of age. He will speak for himself.”<sup>22</sup>(His parents said these things because they feared the Jews, for the Jews had already agreed that if anyone should confess Jesus to be Christ, he was to be put out of the synagogue.<sup>23</sup>Therefore his parents said, “He is of age; ask him.”)<sup>24</sup>So for the second time they called the man who had been blind and said to him, “Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner.”<sup>25</sup>He answered, “Whether he is a sinner I do not know. One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see.”<sup>26</sup>They said to him, “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?”<sup>27</sup>He answered them, “I have told you already, and you would not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become his disciples?”<sup>28</sup>And they reviled him, saying, “You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses.<sup>29</sup>We know that God has spoken to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he comes from.”<sup>30</sup>The man answered, “Why, this is an amazing thing! You do not know where he comes from, and yet he opened my eyes.<sup>31</sup>We know that God does not listen to sinners, but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, God listens to him.<sup>32</sup>Never since the world began has it been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind.<sup>33</sup>If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.”<sup>34</sup>They answered him, “You were born in utter sin, and would you teach us?” And they cast him out.<sup>35</sup>Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and having found him he said, “Do you believe in the Son of Man?”<sup>36</sup>He answered, “And who is he, sir, that I may believe in him?”<sup>37</sup>Jesus said to him, “You have seen him, and it is he who is speaking to you.”<sup>38</sup>He said, “Lord, I believe,” and he worshiped him.<sup>39</sup>Jesus said, “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”<sup>40</sup>Some of the Pharisees near him heard these things, and said to him, “Are we also blind?”<sup>41</sup>Jesus said to them, “If you were blind, you would have no guilt; but now that you say, ’We see,’ your guilt remains.
9.overview:
Jesus has just called himself the light of the world (8:12); now he gives sight to a man blind from birth, the sixth sign in John. The disciples ask whose sin caused the blindness; Jesus answers that it happened so that God’s works might be displayed in him. He makes mud with saliva, spreads it on the man’s eyes and sends him to wash in the pool of Siloam, “Sent”, and the man comes back seeing. Then follows one of the most dramatic and humorous scenes in the Gospels, a series of interrogations. The neighbours cannot agree it is the same man. The Pharisees are split, because the healing happened on a Sabbath. The parents, afraid of being expelled from the synagogue, refuse to say more than that he is their son and was born blind. Questioned again, the man refuses to call Jesus a sinner: “One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see.” When he asks, with an edge, whether they want to become disciples too, they insult him and throw him out.

Meanwhile his understanding of Jesus grows: “the man called Jesus”, then “a prophet”, then a man “from God”, and finally, when Jesus finds him after his expulsion, “Lord, I believe”, as he worships him. The Pharisees go the other way, from confident sight to blindness. Jesus says he came so that the blind may see and those who see may become blind; because they claim to see, their guilt remains. The chapter is a parable of conversion and of religious self-deception.

10.title: The Good Shepherd

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — The Good Shepherd Lays Down His Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus contrasts the true shepherd with thieves who climb into the sheepfold another way. The shepherd comes through the gate; the sheep recognise his voice as he calls each by name and leads them out, but they run from strangers. When his hearers miss the meaning, Jesus says plainly that he is the door: whoever enters through him will be saved and find pasture. Thieves come to steal and destroy; he came to give life to the full. He is the good shepherd, who gives his life for the sheep, unlike the hired hand who abandons them to the wolf. He knows his sheep and they know him, as he and the Father know each other. He has other sheep outside this fold, whom he will gather into one flock under one shepherd. The Father loves him because he lays down his life freely, with authority to take it up again. Some in the crowd say he is mad and possessed; others reply that no demon could open blind eyes.
verseByVerse.theology: The shepherd imagery draws on the entire Old Testament tradition: God as shepherd (Ps. 23; Ezek. 34), the coming Davidic shepherd-king (Ezek. 34:23-24; Jer. 23:4), and the contrast between true and false shepherds throughout the prophets. Jesus claims all of these simultaneously: he is the door (the only legitimate access to God), the good shepherd (who gives rather than takes), and the one who lays down his life voluntarily (the self-giving that no hired hand would perform). The death is central: the shepherd metaphor cannot be understood apart from the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: The sheep hear his voice: the recognition of Christ by the elect is not achievement but gift. The sheep do not learn to recognize the shepherd's voice; they already know it because they are his sheep. This is Calvinist soteriology rendered in pastoral imagery: election precedes hearing, calling brings the elect home, and not one of the Father's sheep is lost. The Pharisees cannot hear because they are not sheep (v. 26); the church hears because she has been given ears by the Shepherd himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, he who does not enter the sheepfold by the door but climbs in by another way, that man is a thief and a robber. But he who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, truly, I say to you, he who does not enter the sheepfold by the door but climbs in by another way, that man is a thief and a robber. But he who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep.

Meaning first. John 10 follows straight on from chapter 9, with no break. The Pharisees have just thrown out a sheep of God’s flock, the healed man, and Jesus has found him. Now Jesus tells them who the true shepherd is. Behind the whole chapter lies Ezekiel 34, where God condemns the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves and not the flock, and promises: I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep, and I will set over them one shepherd, my servant David. Jesus says: I am that shepherd.

Truly, truly, I say to you. The solemn opening.

He who does not enter the sheepfold by the door but climbs in by another way. Setting and background. A sheepfold was a walled enclosure where several flocks might be kept overnight, often a courtyard by a house or a stone pen in the open country, with a single doorway guarded by a gatekeeper. Anyone who climbed the wall instead of using the door was obviously up to no good.

That man is a thief and a robber. “Thief” (kleptēs) works by stealth; “robber” (lēstēs) by violence. The word for robber is used of Barabbas (18:40) and of rebels. Jesus has in mind false leaders of God’s people, including the Pharisees who have just cast out the man born blind.

But he who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep. The true shepherd comes openly, by the proper way, with the right to be there.

In a sentence. Jesus said that anyone who climbs into the sheepfold another way is a thief and a robber, but the one who comes in by the door is the shepherd.

On a Tuesday. Ask of any spiritual leader: did he come by the door, through Christ and his word, or climb in another way?
verseByVerse.note: A sheepfold was a walled enclosure where several flocks might be kept overnight, with a single doorway.

parallels.desc: the false shepherds of Israel

verseByVerse.quote: "To him the gatekeeper opens. The sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out. When he has brought out all his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To him the gatekeeper opens. The sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out. When he has brought out all his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice.

To him the gatekeeper opens. The gatekeeper knows the true shepherd. Don’t press the detail; it is part of the picture.

The sheep hear his voice. The sheep recognise him.

And he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out. Key words. Setting and background. Shepherds in the East led their flocks rather than drove them, and often had names for their sheep. When several flocks shared a fold, each shepherd called his own, and they came out to him. “His own” (ta idia): Jesus knows his own people personally, by name (Isaiah 43:1). “Leads them out” (exagei): the word used of God leading Israel out of Egypt. He has just led the man born blind out of the synagogue.

When he has brought out all his own. All of them, not one left behind.

He goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice. He leads from the front, and they follow because they know him.

In a sentence. The gatekeeper opens to the shepherd, his sheep hear his voice, he calls them by name and leads them out, walking ahead of them, and they follow because they know his voice.

For worship. The Shepherd knows your name. He goes before you into every day. Follow him.
verseByVerse.note: Shepherds in the East led their flocks rather than drove them, and named their sheep; the sheep knew their shepherd’s call.

parallels.desc: who shall go out before them and bring them in

verseByVerse.quote: "A stranger they will not follow, but they will flee from him, for they do not know the voice of strangers." This figure of speech Jesus used with them, but they did not understand what he was saying to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A stranger they will not follow, but they will flee from him, for they do not know the voice of strangers. This figure of speech Jesus used with them, but they did not understand what he was saying to them.

A stranger they will not follow, but they will flee from him. True sheep won’t follow false shepherds. The healed man would not follow the Pharisees. There is a spiritual instinct in God’s people that recognises the voice of Christ and turns from other voices. This is a comfort, not a reason for carelessness: we are still warned to test the spirits (1 John 4:1).

This figure of speech Jesus used with them. “Figure of speech” (paroimia): a proverb, an illustration with a hidden meaning. Not quite a parable in the other Gospels’ sense.

But they did not understand what he was saying to them. The Pharisees miss it again, proving they are not his sheep.

In a sentence. Jesus said his sheep will not follow a stranger but will run from him, but the Pharisees did not understand this illustration.

On a Tuesday. Learn Christ’s voice in Scripture so well that you can tell at once when another voice is speaking.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus again said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, I am the door of the sheep. All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Jesus again said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, I am the door of the sheep. All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them.”

I am the door of the sheep. Key words. This is the third of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John (after the bread, 6:35, and the light, 8:12). The picture shifts. Now Jesus is not the shepherd who enters by the door, but the door itself. Some shepherds slept across the entrance of the fold, so that nothing could come in or out except over them: the shepherd was the door. There is only one way into God’s flock, and he is it (14:6).

All who came before me are thieves and robbers. Not the prophets, who pointed to him, but those who claimed to be saviours or leaders apart from him: false messiahs, rebel leaders, and the corrupt religious authorities. They came for themselves.

But the sheep did not listen to them. God’s true people were not taken in.

In a sentence. Jesus said he is the door of the sheep, and all who came before claiming that role were thieves and robbers, but the true sheep did not listen to them.

For worship. Christ is the door. There is no other way in, and through him, the way is open to anyone.
verseByVerse.note: This is the third of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture. The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture. The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly.

If anyone enters by me, he will be saved. Open to anyone, but only by him.

And will go in and out and find pasture. “Go in and out” is a Hebrew expression for living in safety and freedom, the ordinary life of a protected people (Numbers 27:17; Deuteronomy 28:6; Psalm 121:8). Salvation is not a cage, but a safe home and a full life.

The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. False shepherds take; they use the flock for themselves.

I came that they may have life and have it abundantly. Key words. “Abundantly” (perisson): more than enough, overflowing. Jesus gives not just survival but the fullness of eternal life, knowing God (17:3).

What it does not mean. Abundant life is not a promise of health, wealth and comfort, as prosperity teachers claim. The same Shepherd will speak in the next verse of laying down his life. Abundant life is life with God, rich in him, whatever our circumstances (Philippians 4:11–13).

In a sentence. Jesus said he is the door, and anyone who enters by him will be saved and find pasture; the thief comes to steal, kill and destroy, but he came to give life in abundance.

On a Tuesday. Abundant life is not a fuller diary or a fuller bank account. It is Christ. Drink deeply of him today.
verseByVerse.note: “Go in and out” is a Hebrew expression for living in safety.

parallels.desc: this is the gate of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. He who is a hired hand and not a shepherd, who does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches them and scatters them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. He who is a hired hand and not a shepherd, who does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches them and scatters them.

I am the good shepherd. Key words. The fourth “I am” saying. “Good” (kalos): not only morally good, but noble, beautiful, the model shepherd. In the Old Testament, God is the shepherd of Israel (Psalm 23:1; 80:1; Isaiah 40:11). He promised to shepherd his people himself (Ezekiel 34:11–16), and to set over them one shepherd, David (Ezekiel 34:23). Jesus is both: God himself and David’s son.

The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. Setting and background. Shepherds risked their lives against wild animals and thieves, as David fought lions and bears (1 Samuel 17:34–35). But a shepherd who died left the sheep defenceless. This shepherd’s death is the very thing that saves the sheep. “For” (hyper): on behalf of, in the place of. This is substitution: he dies so that they live.

He who is a hired hand and not a shepherd, who does not own the sheep. A hired hand works for wages. When danger comes, he runs. The sheep aren’t his.

The wolf snatches them and scatters them. The wolf stands for anything that attacks God’s people: false teachers (Acts 20:29), persecutors, the devil himself.

In a sentence. Jesus said he is the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, unlike the hired hand who does not own them and runs from the wolf, leaving them to be scattered.

For worship. The Lord is my shepherd, and he laid down his life for me.
verseByVerse.note: Shepherds risked their lives against wild animals and thieves.

parallels.desc: David rescues a lamb from a lion

verseByVerse.quote: "He flees because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep. I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He flees because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep. I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me.

He flees because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep. The root of his failure: he doesn’t care. A warning for every pastor (1 Peter 5:2–4).

I am the good shepherd. Said again, for emphasis.

I know my own and my own know me. Key words. “Know” (ginōskō) means more than information. It is the knowledge of love and relationship, as in Amos 3:2, where God says Israel alone he has known. Jesus knows his own personally, and has always known them (2 Timothy 2:19). And they know him. A two-way relationship of love.

In a sentence. The hired hand runs because he doesn’t care for the sheep, but Jesus, the good shepherd, knows his own and they know him.

On a Tuesday. You are known by Christ, not as a number but as his own. Get to know him better in return.

parallels.desc: woe to my worthless shepherd
the Lord knows those who are his

verseByVerse.quote: "just as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep. And I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice. So there will be one flock, one shepherd."
verseByVerse.commentary:
just as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep. And I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice. So there will be one flock, one shepherd.

Just as the Father knows me and I know the Father. The knowledge between Christ and his sheep is modelled on the knowledge between the Father and the Son. Astonishing intimacy.

And I lay down my life for the sheep. Key words. Said for the third time (vv. 11, 15, 17). The death of Christ is for “the sheep,” those he knows as his own.

Where Christians differ: for whom did Christ die? Many Christians believe Christ died equally for every person, making salvation possible for all, effective for those who believe. Verdict: here Jesus says he lays down his life for the sheep, and in v. 26 he tells some of his hearers that they are not his sheep. His death has a particular purpose: to save those the Father has given him (6:37–39; 17:9). This is definite atonement. It does not limit the offer of the gospel, which goes to all, nor the sufficiency of his death, which is infinite. It means that the cross actually saves those it was meant to save; it does not merely make salvation possible.

And I have other sheep that are not of this fold. The “other sheep” are Gentiles who would believe. “This fold” is Israel. Before they have heard of him, they are already his sheep, because the Father has given them to him (Acts 18:10).

I must bring them also. “Must” (dei): it is certain, it is the Father’s plan.

And they will listen to my voice. Not “might” but “will.” His voice will reach them through the gospel, and they will respond (Acts 13:48).

So there will be one flock, one shepherd. Jews and Gentiles together, one people of God (Ephesians 2:14–16). One flock, not many folds: the unity of the church is grounded in one shepherd.

In a sentence. Jesus said he knows his sheep as the Father knows him, and he lays down his life for them, and he has other sheep outside Israel whom he must bring, who will listen to his voice, so that there will be one flock and one shepherd.

For worship. If you are a Gentile believer, you were one of the other sheep. He brought you in. Give him thanks.
verseByVerse.note: The “other sheep” are Gentiles who would believe.

parallels.desc: I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David

verseByVerse.quote: "For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life that I may take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. This charge I have received from my Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life that I may take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. This charge I have received from my Father.

For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life. The Father has always loved the Son (17:24). But he especially delights in the Son’s obedience to death.

That I may take it up again. His death is not the end. He lays down his life with the purpose of taking it up again in the resurrection.

No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. Key words. Jesus’ death was voluntary. Not the Jews, not Pilate, not the soldiers, took his life. He gave it. At the arrest the soldiers fell back at his word (18:6). On the cross he gave up his spirit (19:30).

I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. “Authority” (exousia): right and power. Who but God has authority over his own death and resurrection? Elsewhere Scripture says the Father raised him (Acts 2:24), and the Spirit (Romans 8:11). The Trinity acts together.

This charge I have received from my Father. His death and resurrection are the Father’s command, freely obeyed.

In a sentence. The Father loves the Son because he lays down his life to take it up again; no one takes it from him, but he lays it down freely, with authority to lay it down and take it up again, as the Father commanded.

For worship. No one took his life. He gave it, for you.

verseByVerse.quote: There was again a division among the Jews because of these words. Many of them said, "He has a demon, and is insane; why listen to him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was again a division among the Jews because of these words. Many of them said, “He has a demon, and is insane; why listen to him?”

There was again a division among the Jews. As in 7:43 and 9:16.

He has a demon, and is insane; why listen to him? The charge of madness again (7:20; 8:48). A man who says he will lay down his life and take it up again sounds mad, unless he is God.

In a sentence. His words divided the Jews again, and many said he had a demon and was mad, so why listen.

On a Tuesday. Jesus leaves no middle ground. Either he is mad, or he is Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: Others said, "These are not the words of one who is oppressed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Others said, “These are not the words of one who is oppressed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?”

These are not the words of one who is oppressed by a demon. Others see that his words are too wise, too good, for madness.

Can a demon open the eyes of the blind? They point back to chapter 9. The work of opening blind eyes is God’s work (Psalm 146:8).

In a sentence. Others said these were not the words of a demon-possessed man, for no demon could open the eyes of the blind.

For worship. His words and his works together testify: this is the Son of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–42 — I and the Father Are One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the winter Feast of Dedication, the leaders corner Jesus in Solomon’s Colonnade and demand that he say plainly whether he is the Christ. He replies that his works already testify, but they do not believe because they are not his sheep. His sheep hear his voice and follow; he gives them eternal life, and neither he nor the Father will let anyone snatch them away. He and the Father are one. They reach for stones, accusing him of making himself God. He answers from the psalm in which God’s word calls human judges “gods”: since Scripture cannot be overturned, how can they call it blasphemy when the one the Father consecrated and sent calls himself God’s Son? At least they should believe his works, and see that the Father is in him and he in the Father. Escaping arrest, he withdraws beyond the Jordan, where many believe in him, saying that everything John said about him has proved true.
verseByVerse.theology: The climactic declaration — I and the Father are one — is the theological summit of the Good Shepherd discourse and of John's presentation of Jesus' identity in the public ministry. The unity is not merely unity of purpose (though it includes that) but ontological unity — the unity of shared divine nature that the Jews correctly understand as a claim to deity (v. 33). Jesus defends the claim not by retreating from it but by appealing to the greater logic: if Scripture can call judges 'gods,' how much more can the one the Father consecrated and sent be called the Son of God? The defense is not a reduction of the claim but an escalation of it.
verseByVerse.examples: Beyond the Jordan, many believe on the basis of John's testimony confirmed by Jesus' works. This is the pattern of fruitful ministry: the faithful witness of the forerunner, confirmed by the reality of the one the forerunner announced, produces lasting faith. The chapter ends not in Jerusalem with hostility but in the wilderness with harvest — a reminder that the gospel often bears its richest fruit outside the centers of established religion.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem. It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in the colonnade of Solomon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that time the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem. It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in the colonnade of Solomon.

The Feast of Dedication. Setting and background. The Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) celebrated the re-dedication of the temple in 164 BC by Judas Maccabeus, after the Syrian king Antiochus IV Epiphanes had defiled it by setting up an altar to Zeus and sacrificing pigs on it. It lasted eight days, in December, with lamps lit in homes. It celebrated the deliverance of Israel by a liberator and the cleansing of God’s house. Two months have passed since the Feast of Booths.

It was winter. Perhaps also a hint at the spiritual coldness of his hearers.

In the colonnade of Solomon. A covered walkway along the east side of the temple courts, sheltered from the winter wind. The early church later met there (Acts 3:11; 5:12).

Why it matters. At a feast celebrating a temple consecrated again, Jesus will speak of himself as the one the Father consecrated (v. 36), the true temple (2:21). At a feast remembering a political deliverer, the crowd wants to know if he is the Christ.

In a sentence. It was winter and the Feast of Dedication, and Jesus was walking in Solomon’s colonnade in the temple.

On a Tuesday. Christ walked in the temple at Hanukkah as its true Lord. He is the light that no darkness extinguishes.
verseByVerse.note: The Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) celebrated the re-dedication of the temple in 164 BC, after Antiochus IV had defiled it. It fell in December. Solomon’s colonnade ran along the east side of the temple courts.

parallels.desc: Solomon’s Portico

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews gathered around him and said to him, "How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly." Jesus answered them, "I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father's name bear witness about me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the Jews gathered around him and said to him, “How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.” Jesus answered them, “I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name bear witness about me.”

So the Jews gathered around him. “Gathered around” (ekyklōsan): surrounded, hemmed in. A menacing picture.

How long will you keep us in suspense? Literally “How long will you take away our life?” an idiom for keeping someone hanging.

If you are the Christ, tell us plainly. They want a political statement they can either rally to or report to the Romans. Jesus avoided the title Messiah in public because of its political meaning (6:15).

I told you, and you do not believe. He has told them, in all his claims (5:17–47; 8:58). The problem is not clarity but unbelief.

The works that I do in my Father’s name bear witness about me. His miracles speak plainly enough.

In a sentence. The Jews surrounded Jesus and demanded he tell them plainly if he was the Christ, and he answered that he had told them, but they did not believe, and his works bore witness to him.

On a Tuesday. If you’re waiting for more evidence before you trust Christ, ask whether the problem is the evidence or your heart.

verseByVerse.quote: "but you do not believe because you are not among my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
but you do not believe because you are not among my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.

But you do not believe because you are not among my sheep. Key words. Notice the order. Jesus does not say, “You are not my sheep because you do not believe,” but “you do not believe because you are not my sheep.” Being his sheep comes first; believing follows. Who his sheep are is settled by the Father’s gift (v. 29; 6:37). This is election. It doesn’t remove their guilt: they don’t believe because they will not (5:40). But it explains why some believe and others don’t.

My sheep hear my voice. The marks of a true sheep: they hear, they are known, they follow.

And I know them. He knows them as his own (v. 14).

And they follow me. Faith shows itself in following.

In a sentence. Jesus said they did not believe because they were not his sheep, for his sheep hear his voice, are known by him, and follow him.

For worship. If you hear his voice and follow, you are his sheep. And you are his because the Father gave you to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father's hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand.

I give them eternal life. Eternal life is a gift, not a reward.

And they will never perish. Key words. “Never” (ou mē … eis ton aiōna): the strongest possible denial, not ever, to eternity. Eternal life that could end would not be eternal.

And no one will snatch them out of my hand. “Snatch” (harpazō): the word used of the wolf in v. 12. No wolf, no thief, no devil, no persecutor, can take them.

My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all. The sheep are the Father’s gift to the Son. The Father is greater than every enemy.

No one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand. Two hands hold the sheep: the Son’s and the Father’s. Double security.

Where Christians differ: can a believer be lost? Some argue that while no one else can snatch the sheep, a sheep may choose to leave. Verdict: “no one” includes the sheep themselves, and Jesus says plainly that his sheep will never perish. The sheep are kept not by their own grip on Christ but by his grip on them (Romans 8:38–39; Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). This is the perseverance of the saints. Those who fall away for good show that they were never his sheep (1 John 2:19). True sheep may stray and stumble, but the Shepherd brings them back.

In a sentence. Jesus gives his sheep eternal life, and they will never perish, for no one can snatch them out of his hand, or out of the hand of the Father, who gave them to him and is greater than all.

On a Tuesday. When you doubt whether you will make it, look at the hands that hold you. Rest in his grip, not yours.

parallels.desc: there is none that can deliver out of my hand

verseByVerse.quote: "I and the Father are one." The Jews picked up stones again to stone him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I and the Father are one. The Jews picked up stones again to stone him.

I and the Father are one. Key words. “One” is neuter in Greek (hen): one in nature and purpose, not one person. If Jesus had said “one person” (heis), it would mean the Father and the Son are the same person, the old heresy of modalism. He does not say that: “I and the Father” are two persons; “are” is plural. But they are one thing, one in being. In context, he has just said that no one can snatch the sheep from his hand or the Father’s: the hand of the Son and the hand of the Father do the same work with the same power, because the Son and the Father are one. This is the doctrine of the Trinity in a sentence: distinct persons, one God.

The Jews picked up stones again to stone him. As in 8:59. They understood exactly what he meant (v. 33).

Where Christians differ. Some say this means only unity of will and purpose, as believers are to be one (17:22). Verdict: it includes unity of purpose, but cannot stop there. The hearers took it as a claim to be God, and Jesus did not correct them; instead he went on to say the Father is in him and he in the Father (v. 38). Believers share a unity of love; the Son shares the Father’s very being (1:1; 5:18).

In a sentence. Jesus said he and the Father are one, and the Jews picked up stones again to stone him.

For worship. The Son is one with the Father. To see him is to see God, and to be held by him is to be held by God.
verseByVerse.note: “One” is neuter in Greek — one in nature and purpose, not one person.

parallels.desc: the LORD is one

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "I have shown you many good works from the Father; for which of them are you going to stone me?" The Jews answered him, "It is not for a good work that we are going to stone you but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered them, “I have shown you many good works from the Father; for which of them are you going to stone me?” The Jews answered him, “It is not for a good work that we are going to stone you but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God.”

I have shown you many good works from the Father; for which of them are you going to stone me? A calm, ironic question with stones raised above him. “Good” (kala): noble, beautiful works, like the good shepherd.

It is not for a good work that we are going to stone you but for blasphemy. Stoning was the penalty for blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16).

Because you, being a man, make yourself God. Key words. The charge is clear. They understood his words as a claim to deity. Their mistake was not in understanding him, but in thinking he was “making himself” God. The truth is the opposite: he was God, making himself man (1:14; Philippians 2:6–7).

In a sentence. Jesus asked which of his good works they were stoning him for, and they answered that it was for blasphemy, because, being a man, he made himself God.

For worship. He did not make himself God; he is God, who made himself man for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Is it not written in your Law, 'I said, you are gods'? If he called them gods to whom the word of God came — and Scripture cannot be broken —"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered them, “Is it not written in your Law, ‘I said, you are gods’? If he called them gods to whom the word of God came — and Scripture cannot be broken —

Is it not written in your Law, “I said, you are gods”? Setting and background. “Law” here means the whole Old Testament. The quotation is from Psalm 82:6. The psalm calls Israel’s judges “gods” because they represented God’s justice, exercising his authority among his people (compare Exodus 21:6; 22:8–9, where judges are called elohim). God then rebukes them for judging unjustly, and says they will die like men.

If he called them gods to whom the word of God came. The argument goes from lesser to greater. If Scripture can call mere human judges “gods,” because they received God’s word and acted for him, how can it be blasphemy for the one whom the Father consecrated and sent to call himself the Son of God?

And Scripture cannot be broken. Key words. “Broken” (lythēnai): annulled, set aside, emptied of its authority. A remarkable statement of Jesus’ view of Scripture. Even a single word in an obscure psalm carries God’s authority and cannot be set aside. This is the foundation of the doctrine of the inerrancy and authority of Scripture: Jesus himself held it.

What it does not mean. Jesus is not saying he is a god only in the sense the judges were. He is arguing from their own Scripture that his claim cannot be dismissed as blasphemy on principle. And then he goes further than the judges ever could: the Father is in me and I in the Father (v. 38). Nor does Psalm 82 teach that believers become gods, as some teach.

In a sentence. Jesus answered that their Scripture called those who received God’s word “gods,” and Scripture cannot be set aside.

On a Tuesday. Treat every word of Scripture as Jesus did: it cannot be broken.
verseByVerse.note: The psalm calls Israel’s judges “gods” because they represented God’s authority. “Your Law” here means the Scriptures as a whole.

parallels.desc: “I said, ‘You are gods’”

verseByVerse.quote: "do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, 'You are blaspheming,' because I said, 'I am the Son of God'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, ‘You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?

Him whom the Father consecrated. Key words. “Consecrated” (hēgiasen): set apart as holy, sanctified. At the Feast of Dedication, which celebrated the consecration of the altar and the temple, Jesus says he is the one whom the Father consecrated. He is the true temple, the holy place where God dwells (2:19–21).

And sent into the world. Consecrated before he was sent: he existed with the Father before coming.

You are blaspheming, because I said, “I am the Son of God”? If the judges could be called gods, how much more he, uniquely set apart and sent, can be called the Son of God.

In a sentence. Jesus asked how they could accuse of blasphemy the one whom the Father had set apart and sent into the world, because he said he was the Son of God.

For worship. Christ is the holy one, consecrated by the Father and sent for us. In him, God dwells among us.

parallels.desc: before you were born I consecrated you

verseByVerse.quote: "If I am not doing the works of my Father, then do not believe me; but if I do them, even though you do not believe me, believe the works, that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I am not doing the works of my Father, then do not believe me; but if I do them, even though you do not believe me, believe the works, that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.

If I am not doing the works of my Father, then do not believe me. Jesus invites testing. He doesn’t ask for blind faith.

But if I do them, even though you do not believe me, believe the works. If his words are too much for them, let them start with his works. The works are evidence (14:11).

That you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father. Key words. Mutual indwelling. This goes beyond Psalm 82’s judges. No human judge could say this. The Father and the Son dwell in each other: the theologians call it perichōrēsis. It is the deepest statement of their oneness (14:10–11; 17:21).

In a sentence. Jesus said that if he was not doing his Father’s works they should not believe him, but if he was, they should believe the works, so that they would know the Father is in him and he in the Father.

On a Tuesday. Faith is not blind. Look at what Jesus did, and let it lead you to who he is.

verseByVerse.quote: Again they sought to arrest him, but he escaped from their hands. He went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had been baptizing at first, and there he remained.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again they sought to arrest him, but he escaped from their hands. He went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had been baptizing at first, and there he remained.

Again they sought to arrest him, but he escaped from their hands. His hour has not yet come. No one can snatch the sheep out of his hand (v. 28); and no one can seize him out of the Father’s plan.

He went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had been baptizing at first. “Across the Jordan” is Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John first baptised (1:28). The ministry comes full circle. Jesus withdraws there until he goes to Bethany near Jerusalem for Lazarus (11:7), and then to the cross.

And there he remained. A time of withdrawal, about three months before the final Passover.

In a sentence. They tried again to arrest him, but he escaped and went back across the Jordan to the place where John first baptised, and stayed there.

For worship. Jesus withdraws and returns at the Father’s time. His life is ordered by love, not fear.
verseByVerse.note: “Across the Jordan” is Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John had baptized.

verseByVerse.quote: And many came to him. And they said, "John did no sign, but everything that John said about this man was true." And many believed in him there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And many came to him. And they said, “John did no sign, but everything that John said about this man was true.” And many believed in him there.

And many came to him. A contrast with Jerusalem. Away from the leaders, people come.

John did no sign. John the Baptist worked no miracles. His greatness was in his witness.

But everything that John said about this man was true. A beautiful epitaph for John. He pointed to Jesus, and everything he said proved true: the Lamb of God (1:29), the one who would baptise with the Spirit (1:33), the Son of God (1:34). The greatest thing that can be said of any servant of Christ: what he said about Jesus was true.

And many believed in him there. Faith flourishes where John’s witness had prepared the ground. The chapter, full of rejection, ends with many believing.

In a sentence. Many came to Jesus across the Jordan, saying that though John did no sign, everything he said about Jesus was true, and many believed in him there.

On a Tuesday. You may never work a miracle. But you can tell the truth about Jesus. Let that be your life’s witness.

The sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.<sup>4</sup>When he has brought out all his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice.<sup>5</sup>A stranger they will not follow, but they will flee from him, for they do not know the voice of strangers.”<sup>6</sup>This figure of speech Jesus used with them, but they did not understand what he was saying to them.<sup>7</sup>So Jesus again said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, I am the door of the sheep.<sup>8</sup>All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them.<sup>9</sup>I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture.<sup>10</sup>The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly.<sup>11</sup>I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.<sup>12</sup>He who is a hired hand and not a shepherd, who does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches them and scatters them.<sup>13</sup>He flees because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep.<sup>14</sup>I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me,<sup>15</sup>just as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep.<sup>16</sup>And I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice. So there will be one flock, one shepherd.<sup>17</sup>For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life that I may take it up again.<sup>18</sup>No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. This charge I have received from my Father.”<sup>19</sup>There was again a division among the Jews because of these words.<sup>20</sup>Many of them said, “He has a demon, and is insane; why listen to him?”<sup>21</sup>Others said, “These are not the words of one who is oppressed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?”<sup>22</sup>At that time the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem. It was winter,<sup>23</sup>and Jesus was walking in the temple, in the colonnade of Solomon.<sup>24</sup>So the Jews gathered around him and said to him, “How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.”<sup>25</sup>Jesus answered them, “I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name bear witness about me,<sup>26</sup>but you do not believe because you are not among my sheep.<sup>27</sup>My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.<sup>28</sup>I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.<sup>29</sup>My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand.<sup>30</sup>I and the Father are one.”<sup>31</sup>The Jews picked up stones again to stone him.<sup>32</sup>Jesus answered them, “I have shown you many good works from the Father; for which of them are you going to stone me?”<sup>33</sup>The Jews answered him, “It is not for a good work that we are going to stone you but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God.”<sup>34</sup>Jesus answered them, “Is it not written in your Law, ’I said, you are gods’?<sup>35</sup>If he called them gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be broken—<sup>36</sup>do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, ’You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ’I am the Son of God’?<sup>37</sup>If I am not doing the works of my Father, then do not believe me;<sup>38</sup>but if I do them, even though you do not believe me, believe the works, that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.”<sup>39</sup>Again they sought to arrest him, but he escaped from their hands.<sup>40</sup>He went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had been baptizing at first, and there he remained.<sup>41</sup>And many came to him. And they said, “John did no sign, but everything that John said about this man was true.”<sup>42</sup>And many believed in him there.
10.overview:
Chapter 10 follows straight on from the healing of the blind man, whom the Pharisees had thrown out and Jesus had found. Against those false shepherds Jesus describes himself in two pictures from village life. He is the door of the sheepfold: those who enter through him are saved, and find pasture and abundant life. And he is the good shepherd, who knows his sheep by name, leads them out, and lays down his life for them, unlike hired hands who run from the wolf. The background is Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel’s selfish shepherds and promises to shepherd his flock himself through his servant David. Jesus has other sheep, not of this fold, whom he must also bring, so that there will be one flock and one shepherd. He lays down his life of his own accord and has authority to take it up again.

Two months later, at the winter Feast of Dedication, which celebrated the cleansing of the temple by the Maccabees, the leaders surround Jesus in Solomon’s Colonnade and demand that he tell them plainly whether he is the Messiah. He answers that his works testify, but they do not believe because they are not his sheep. His sheep hear his voice and follow him; he gives them eternal life, they will never perish, and no one can snatch them from his hand or from the Father’s. “I and the Father are one.” They take up stones for blasphemy. Jesus answers from Psalm 82, where human judges are called “gods”, arguing that Scripture cannot be broken and that the one the Father consecrated and sent is rightly called the Son of God. Escaping, he withdraws across the Jordan, where many believe in him.

11.title: The Resurrection and the Life

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–44 — Lazarus Raised: The Sign That Decides
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Lazarus of Bethany falls ill, his sisters Martha and Mary send word to Jesus, whom they know loves him. Jesus says this sickness will end in God’s glory, not death, and deliberately waits two more days before returning to Judea despite the danger. He tells the disciples that Lazarus has fallen asleep and he will wake him; when they misunderstand, he tells them plainly that Lazarus has died, and Thomas resolves that they will go and die with him. Lazarus has been entombed four days when they arrive. Martha meets Jesus, grieving that he came too late yet trusting him still. He promises that her brother will rise and declares that he himself is the resurrection and the life; she confesses him as the Christ, the Son of God. Mary comes and falls weeping at his feet, and Jesus, deeply stirred and troubled, weeps with them. At the tomb he orders the stone moved despite Martha’s fear of the stench, prays aloud to the Father so that the crowd may believe, and calls Lazarus out. The dead man emerges, still wrapped, and Jesus tells them to free him.
verseByVerse.theology: The miracle is a preview of Jesus' own resurrection and, through his, the resurrection of all who are in him. I am the resurrection and the life (v. 25) is not merely a claim about what Jesus can do but about what he is: the source and substance of resurrection-life, the one in whom the age-to-come has already broken into the present. Those who believe in him will never die — not because they avoid physical death but because they have already passed from death to life (5:24). Lazarus' resurrection is the bodily demonstration of what Jesus gives spiritually to every believer.
verseByVerse.examples: The weeping of Jesus (vv. 33-35) is one of the most theologically dense moments in the gospel: the one who knows he is about to raise Lazarus weeps with those who grieve. His tears are not ignorance of the outcome but solidarity with human grief, genuine compassion that does not remove itself from suffering even when it is about to overcome suffering. This is the incarnation at its most moving: God in the flesh does not observe human sorrow from a distance; he enters it, feels it, and weeps in it — before he conquers it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha. It was Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was ill.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha. It was Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was ill.

Meaning first. The raising of Lazarus is the seventh and greatest sign in John’s Gospel. It shows that Jesus is the resurrection and the life, with power over death itself. It is also the turning point that leads to the cross: because of it the council decides Jesus must die (v. 53). The giver of life will lose his life for giving it.

Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany. “Lazarus” is a short form of Eleazar, meaning “God helps.” Setting and background: Bethany was a village on the Mount of Olives, about two miles east of Jerusalem (v. 18), on the road to Jericho. Not the same as Bethany beyond the Jordan (1:28; 10:40), where Jesus was staying.

The village of Mary and her sister Martha. The sisters appear in Luke 10:38–42: Martha busy serving, Mary sitting at Jesus’ feet.

It was Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair. John looks ahead to 12:1–8. He assumes his readers know the story, which was told wherever the gospel was preached (Mark 14:9). This is not the sinful woman of Luke 7:36–50, which was an earlier and different anointing in Galilee.

In a sentence. Lazarus of Bethany, brother of Mary and Martha, was ill; this was the Mary who later anointed the Lord’s feet.

On a Tuesday. Jesus had friends, a home where he was welcome. Make your home a place where Christ is welcome.
verseByVerse.note: Bethany was a village on the Mount of Olives, about two miles east of Jerusalem. John mentions Mary’s anointing ahead of time; it comes in chapter 12.

parallels.desc: Martha and Mary

verseByVerse.quote: So the sisters sent to him, saying, "Lord, he whom you love is ill." But when Jesus heard it he said, "This illness does not lead to death. It is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the sisters sent to him, saying, “Lord, he whom you love is ill.” But when Jesus heard it he said, “This illness does not lead to death. It is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.”

Lord, he whom you love is ill. A model prayer. They don’t tell Jesus what to do. They simply tell him the need and appeal to his love. “Love” here is phileō, the love of friendship.

This illness does not lead to death. Not that Lazarus will not die, but that death will not be the end of the story. Its final outcome is not death but resurrection.

It is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it. Key words. As with the man born blind (9:3), the purpose is God’s glory. And the glory of God is the glory of the Son. There is a double meaning: the Son will be glorified by the miracle, and also by the death it will bring him to (v. 53; 12:23). In John, Jesus is glorified on the cross.

In a sentence. The sisters sent word that the one Jesus loved was ill, and Jesus said the illness would not end in death but was for God’s glory, so that the Son of God might be glorified.

For worship. Bring your needs to Jesus simply: Lord, the one you love is ill. Trust his love to do what is best.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was.

Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. Key words. “Loved” here is agapaō, the deep, committed love. John is careful to say it before he tells us of the delay.

So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer. “So” is the surprise. Because he loved them, he stayed away. His delay was not indifference but love. He meant to give them something far greater than a healing: a resurrection, and a deeper knowledge of who he is.

Was Lazarus already dead? Probably, by the time the message arrived. The journey from Bethany beyond the Jordan took a day; Jesus stayed two; and a day to return makes four (v. 17). Lazarus may have died soon after the messengers left. Jesus’ delay did not cause his death, but it ensured no one could doubt that he was truly dead.

In a sentence. Jesus loved Martha, Mary and Lazarus, so when he heard Lazarus was ill, he stayed where he was two more days.

On a Tuesday. When God delays, it is not because he doesn’t love you. It may be because he loves you too much to give you less than his best.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after this he said to the disciples, "Let us go to Judea again." The disciples said to him, "Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then after this he said to the disciples, “Let us go to Judea again.” The disciples said to him, “Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?”

Let us go to Judea again. Not just Bethany, but Judea, the place of danger.

Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you. At the Feast of Dedication (10:31, 39), a few weeks earlier.

And are you going there again? The disciples are afraid for him, and for themselves.

In a sentence. Jesus told the disciples they were going back to Judea, and they protested that the Jews had just tried to stone him there.

For worship. Jesus walked toward danger to give life to his friend. He walked toward the cross to give life to us.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered, “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.”

Are there not twelve hours in the day? Setting and background. The daylight hours were counted as twelve, from sunrise to sunset, whatever the season. The day has a fixed length, set by God. Jesus’ “day” is the appointed time of his ministry, and it cannot be cut short until it is finished (9:4).

If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. On the plain level: you can walk safely by daylight. On the deeper level: the one who walks in God’s will, in the light of Christ, walks safely.

But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him. The one without the light stumbles (12:35). Jesus is safe, because he walks in his Father’s will. His enemies cannot touch him till his hour.

In a sentence. Jesus answered that the day has twelve hours, and whoever walks in daylight does not stumble, but whoever walks at night stumbles, for the light is not in him.

On a Tuesday. Walk in the light of God’s will, and you are safe, wherever it takes you.
verseByVerse.note: The daylight hours were counted as twelve, from sunrise to sunset.

verseByVerse.quote: After saying these things, he said to them, "Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him." The disciples said to him, "Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After saying these things, he said to them, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him.” The disciples said to him, “Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover.”

Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep. Key words. “Our friend”: Lazarus is the friend of the disciples too. Sleep was a common picture of death for believers (Matthew 9:24; Acts 7:60; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14). For the believer, death is like sleep: it is not the end, and there will be an awakening. The word “cemetery” comes from the Greek word for a sleeping place.

But I go to awaken him. As easily as we wake someone from sleep, Jesus will wake Lazarus from death.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the soul sleeps unconscious between death and resurrection, as some teach. Sleep describes the body’s rest and the certainty of waking. The believer’s spirit goes at once to be with Christ (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8).

Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover. They take it literally: sleep is a good sign in illness.

In a sentence. Jesus said their friend Lazarus had fallen asleep and he was going to wake him, and the disciples said that if he was asleep, he would get better.

For worship. For those who belong to Christ, death is sleep, and he will wake us.
verseByVerse.note: Sleep was a common picture of death for believers.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep. Then Jesus told them plainly, "Lazarus has died,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep. Then Jesus told them plainly, “Lazarus has died,

Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep. Another of John’s misunderstandings.

Then Jesus told them plainly, “Lazarus has died.” Jesus knows without being told. The plain statement is stark.

In a sentence. Jesus had meant Lazarus’s death, though they thought he meant ordinary sleep, so he told them plainly that Lazarus had died.

On a Tuesday. Jesus does not avoid the hard word “died.” Neither should we. But we can say it with hope.

verseByVerse.quote: "and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him." So Thomas, called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, "Let us also go, that we may die with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.” So Thomas, called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, “Let us also go, that we may die with him.”

For your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. A surprising gladness. If he had been there, he would have healed Lazarus. Because he was not, the disciples will see something greater, and their faith will be deepened. Faith grows, and the disciples already believed (2:11), but they need more.

But let us go to him. To him, though dead.

So Thomas, called the Twin. Thomas’s name means “twin” in Aramaic; Didymus is the Greek equivalent. We don’t know who his twin was.

Let us also go, that we may die with him. “Him” probably means Jesus. Thomas is a pessimist, expecting the worst, but loyal and courageous. Better known for his doubts (20:24–25), he shows here that he would rather die with Jesus than live without him.
