In a sentence. Jesus said that for their sake he was glad he had not been there, so that they would believe, and Thomas told the others that they should go too, to die with him.

On a Tuesday. Courage doesn’t always feel cheerful. Thomas expected the worst and went anyway. Follow Christ even when you fear what it will cost.
verseByVerse.note: Thomas’s name means “twin” in Aramaic; Didymus is the Greek equivalent.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus came, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days. Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when Jesus came, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days. Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles off.

He found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days. Setting and background. In that climate, burial took place on the day of death. After four days there could be no doubt that he was dead. There was a Jewish belief that the soul lingered near the body for three days, hoping to return, and then departed when decay set in. Whether or not John’s readers knew that, the point is the same: Lazarus was beyond any hope of revival.

Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles off. Literally about fifteen stadia, almost three kilometres. Close enough for mourners to come from the city, and for the news to reach the authorities.

In a sentence. When Jesus arrived, Lazarus had been in the tomb four days, in Bethany, about two miles from Jerusalem.

For worship. No situation is too dead for Christ. Four days is not too late for him.
verseByVerse.note: After four days there could be no doubt that he was dead. The ESV notes that the distance is literally fifteen stadia.

verseByVerse.quote: and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother. So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary remained seated in the house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother. So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary remained seated in the house.

Many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them. Setting and background. Mourning for a close relative lasted seven days, with friends and neighbours coming to sit with the family, weep, and bring food. Hired mourners and flute players often added to the lament (Matthew 9:23). The many mourners suggest the family was well known. “The Jews” here is neutral: friends from Jerusalem.

So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him. Martha, the active one, goes out.

But Mary remained seated in the house. Mourners sat on the ground. Mary, perhaps more crushed, stays. The sisters are true to their characters in Luke 10.

In a sentence. Many had come to comfort the sisters, and when Martha heard Jesus was coming she went to meet him, while Mary stayed in the house.

On a Tuesday. Go and sit with those who grieve. Presence matters more than words.
verseByVerse.note: Mourning for a close relative lasted seven days, with friends coming to console the family.

verseByVerse.quote: Martha said to Jesus, "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you.”

Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. Grief, and perhaps a note of complaint. She believes he could have healed him. Mary will say the same words (v. 32): the sisters must have said them to each other many times over four days.

But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you. Faith in the middle of grief. She does not quite dare to ask for resurrection (v. 39 shows she didn’t expect it), but she trusts that Jesus’ prayers are heard. Her faith is real, but not yet complete: she thinks of Jesus as one who asks God, not yet as the one who is himself the life.

In a sentence. Martha told Jesus that if he had been there her brother would not have died, but that even now God would give him whatever he asked.

For worship. You can bring your honest grief and your questions to Jesus, and still say: even now I know.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Your brother will rise again." Martha said to him, "I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to her, “Your brother will rise again.” Martha said to him, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day.”

Your brother will rise again. Jesus’ words are deliberately open. They could mean now, or at the end.

I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day. Setting and background. Pharisees and most Jews believed in a resurrection at the end of the age, based on Daniel 12:2 and Isaiah 26:19. The Sadducees denied it (Mark 12:18; Acts 23:8). Martha holds the orthodox hope. But it seems far off and little comfort now. She has the doctrine, and Jesus is about to show her it is a person.

In a sentence. Jesus told Martha her brother would rise again, and she answered that she knew he would rise in the resurrection on the last day.

On a Tuesday. Doctrine is precious, but it is not the end. The resurrection is not only a future event; it is a living person, and he stands next to you.
verseByVerse.note: Pharisees and most Jews believed in a resurrection at the end of the age.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?”

I am the resurrection and the life. Key words. This is the fifth of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John. Martha spoke of the resurrection as an event on the last day; Jesus says it is a person, and he is here now. He doesn’t just bring resurrection; he is it. The power that will raise the dead at the end is present in him.

Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live. “The resurrection”: believers who die physically will live, raised by him (5:28–29).

And everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. “The life”: believers who are alive now have a life that death cannot end. “Never die” means never die the true death, separation from God (8:51). Physical death becomes a doorway.

Do you believe this? The question to Martha, and to every reader. Not “do you believe in a resurrection?” but “do you believe this, about me?”

In a sentence. Jesus told Martha that he is the resurrection and the life, so that whoever believes in him will live though he dies, and whoever lives and believes in him will never die, and asked whether she believed it.

For worship. Christ is the resurrection and the life. Answer his question at every graveside: Yes, Lord, I believe.
verseByVerse.note: This is the fifth of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

verseByVerse.quote: She said to him, "Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world." When she had said this, she went and called her sister Mary, saying in private, "The Teacher is here and is calling for you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
She said to him, “Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world.” When she had said this, she went and called her sister Mary, saying in private, “The Teacher is here and is calling for you.”

Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world. Key words. One of the great confessions in John, as great as Peter’s (6:69; Matthew 16:16). “Believe” is perfect tense: I have come to believe and I still believe. Three titles: the Christ, the Messiah; the Son of God; the one coming into the world, the long-awaited one. It is almost exactly the confession John wants all his readers to make (20:31).

She went and called her sister Mary, saying in private. Privately, perhaps to avoid alerting the mourners, some of whom may have been hostile to Jesus.

The Teacher is here and is calling for you. He calls each one personally.

In a sentence. Martha confessed that she believed Jesus was the Christ, the Son of God, who was coming into the world, and then went and quietly told Mary that the Teacher was calling for her.

For worship. The Teacher is here, and he is calling for you. Go to him.

verseByVerse.quote: And when she heard it, she rose quickly and went to him. Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when she heard it, she rose quickly and went to him. Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him.

She rose quickly and went to him. At his call, she goes at once.

Now Jesus had not yet come into the village. He waits outside, perhaps to meet the sisters away from the crowd, or near the tomb, which would be outside the village.

In a sentence. When Mary heard, she got up quickly and went to Jesus, who was still outside the village where Martha had met him.

On a Tuesday. When Christ calls, go quickly.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Jews who were with her in the house, consoling her, saw Mary rise quickly and go out, they followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there. Now when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet, saying to him, "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Jews who were with her in the house, consoling her, saw Mary rise quickly and go out, they followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there. Now when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet, saying to him, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”

They followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there. So the mourners become witnesses of the miracle. God’s providence gathers the crowd.

She fell at his feet. Mary is always at Jesus’ feet: listening (Luke 10:39), grieving here, worshipping (12:3).

Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. The same words as Martha. But Mary says no more. She has no confession yet, only tears.

In a sentence. The mourners followed Mary, thinking she was going to the tomb, and when she reached Jesus she fell at his feet and said that if he had been there, her brother would not have died.

For worship. When you have no words, fall at his feet. He understands tears.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled. And he said, "Where have you laid him?" They said to him, "Lord, come and see."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled. And he said, “Where have you laid him?” They said to him, “Lord, come and see.”

When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping. “Weeping” (klaiō): loud wailing, the public lament of mourning.

He was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled. Key words. The words behind “deeply moved” (embrimaomai) carry a sense of anger or indignation. The word is used of a horse snorting, and elsewhere of a stern rebuke (Mark 1:43; 14:5). Jesus is angry. At what? Not at Mary, but at death itself, the enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26), at the devil who brought it, at the ruin sin has caused in God’s world. “Greatly troubled” (etaraxen heauton): literally he troubled himself, a deep inner agitation. As he faces his friend’s grave, he faces the power he came to destroy.

Where have you laid him? He goes to the grave.

Lord, come and see. The same words Jesus used to the first disciples (1:39), and Philip to Nathanael (1:46).

In a sentence. When Jesus saw Mary and the mourners weeping, he was moved with indignation and deeply troubled, and asked where they had laid him, and they told him to come and see.

For worship. Jesus is angry at death. He does not call it natural or good. He came to destroy it.
verseByVerse.note: The words behind “deeply moved” carry a sense of anger or indignation — at death itself and the grief it brings.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus wept. So the Jews said, "See how he loved him!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus wept. So the Jews said, “See how he loved him!”

Jesus wept. Key words. This is the shortest verse in the English Bible, and one of the deepest. The word changes: not the loud wailing of the mourners (klaiō), but dakryō, to shed tears, quiet weeping. Why does Jesus weep, when he knows he is about to raise Lazarus? Because he truly loves, and truly grieves with those who grieve (Romans 12:15). Because death is a real evil. Because he is truly man. The God who will wipe every tear from our eyes (Revelation 21:4) first shed tears himself. Here is the full humanity of the Son of God: in the same chapter, he weeps like a man and raises the dead like God.

See how he loved him! Some of the mourners see his love truly.

In a sentence. Jesus wept, and the mourners said, “See how he loved him!”

On a Tuesday. Christians grieve, but not as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Tears are not unbelief. Jesus wept.
verseByVerse.note: This is the shortest verse in the English Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: But some of them said, "Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man also have kept this man from dying?" Then Jesus, deeply moved again, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But some of them said, “Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man also have kept this man from dying?” Then Jesus, deeply moved again, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.

Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man also have kept this man from dying? Others are cynical. They point to the healing in chapter 9, a few miles away, and taunt: if he could do that, why didn’t he do this?

Then Jesus, deeply moved again, came to the tomb. The same word of indignation (v. 33). Perhaps at their unbelief too.

It was a cave, and a stone lay against it. Setting and background. Tombs were caves or rock chambers, with a large stone across the entrance to keep out animals and robbers. Some were cut horizontally into a hillside, others with steps leading down. The stone was usually a heavy disc or a block. The body was laid on a shelf inside.

In a sentence. Some mocked that the man who healed the blind could have kept Lazarus from dying, and Jesus, deeply moved again, came to the tomb, a cave with a stone across it.

For worship. Jesus walked to the cave of death and stood at its door. One day he will stand at yours, and call.
verseByVerse.note: Tombs were caves or rock chambers, with a large stone across the entrance.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said, "Take away the stone." Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, "Lord, by this time there will be an odor, for he has been dead four days." Jesus said to her, "Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, “Lord, by this time there will be an odor, for he has been dead four days.” Jesus said to her, “Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?”

Take away the stone. Jesus could move it with a word. He tells them to do it. God often uses human obedience in his works.

Lord, by this time there will be an odor, for he has been dead four days. Martha the practical one. Bodies were not embalmed; after four days decay was well under way. Spices were used, but did not stop it. Her faith of v. 27 is real, but she can’t imagine what Jesus will do.

Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God? He reminds her of v. 4 and v. 25–26. Believe, and you will see. Faith comes before sight.

In a sentence. Jesus told them to take away the stone, and when Martha objected that after four days there would be a smell, he reminded her that if she believed she would see God’s glory.

On a Tuesday. What stone is Christ telling you to move? Obey, even when it seems pointless, and you will see the glory of God.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were not embalmed; after four days decay was well under way.

verseByVerse.quote: So they took away the stone. And Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, "Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me, but I said this on account of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they took away the stone. And Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, “Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me, but I said this on account of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me.”

And Jesus lifted up his eyes. Jews commonly prayed looking upward (17:1; Psalm 123:1).

Father, I thank you that you have heard me. He gives thanks before the miracle, as though it were already done. He had already prayed, perhaps when he first heard of Lazarus’s illness.

I knew that you always hear me. The Son is in perfect communion with the Father.

But I said this on account of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me. He prays aloud so that the crowd will understand that the miracle comes from the Father, and that the Father sent him. It is not magic, nor a power of his own apart from the Father.

In a sentence. When the stone was removed, Jesus looked up and thanked the Father for hearing him, saying he knew the Father always hears him, but said it aloud so that the people would believe the Father had sent him.

For worship. Thank God before you see the answer. Faith gives thanks in advance.
verseByVerse.note: Jews commonly prayed looking upward.

verseByVerse.quote: When he had said these things, he cried out with a loud voice, "Lazarus, come out." The man who had died came out, his hands and feet bound with linen strips, and his face wrapped with a cloth. Jesus said to them, "Unbind him, and let him go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he had said these things, he cried out with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out.” The man who had died came out, his hands and feet bound with linen strips, and his face wrapped with a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Unbind him, and let him go.”

He cried out with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out.” Key words. A loud voice, so that all could hear. A command, not a prayer. Augustine said that if Jesus had not named Lazarus, all the dead would have come out. It anticipates the last day: an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out (5:28–29).

The man who had died came out. The simplest description of the greatest miracle. The man is still described as “the one who had died.”

His hands and feet bound with linen strips, and his face wrapped with a cloth. Setting and background. Bodies were wrapped in strips of linen, with a separate cloth for the face, and spices between the strips. Compare Jesus’ own grave clothes, left neatly behind (20:6–7). Lazarus comes out still wrapped; Jesus will rise leaving his behind. Lazarus will die again; Jesus will never die again (Romans 6:9). This is a resuscitation, a return to mortal life; Jesus’ resurrection will be the first of the new creation.

Unbind him, and let him go. Again, others help. John does not draw a lesson from this, but we may fairly apply it: Christ alone gives life, and his people help the newly living out of their grave clothes.

A picture of salvation. We were dead in sins (Ephesians 2:1–5). We could not respond, any more than Lazarus could. Christ called, and his voice gave life. This is regeneration, God’s effectual call: the dead hear and live (5:25).

In a sentence. Jesus cried out with a loud voice for Lazarus to come out, and the dead man came out, bound in grave clothes, and Jesus told them to unbind him and let him go.

For worship. The voice that called Lazarus called you from spiritual death. One day it will call your body from the grave.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were wrapped in strips of linen, with a separate cloth over the face.

parallels.desc: all who are in the tombs will hear his voice

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 45–57 — The Decision to Kill Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Many who saw the miracle believe in Jesus, but some report it to the Pharisees. The chief priests and Pharisees convene the council in alarm: if this man keeps doing signs, everyone will follow him and the Romans will destroy their temple and nation. Caiaphas, high priest that year, tells them they understand nothing: better that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish. John explains that he was unwittingly prophesying that Jesus would die for the nation, and also to gather God’s scattered children into one. From then on they plot his death, so Jesus withdraws from public view to Ephraim, near the desert, with his disciples. As Passover approaches and pilgrims arrive early to purify themselves, people look for Jesus in the temple, wondering if he will come, while the authorities order anyone who knows his whereabouts to report it so they can arrest him.
verseByVerse.theology: Caiaphas' political calculation — sacrifice one man to save the nation — is simultaneously cynical expediency and unconscious prophecy. John explicitly identifies it as prophecy (v. 51): the high priest, by virtue of his office, spoke better than he knew. The death he plots as preservation of institutional power is the death that will actually accomplish the salvation of God's people — and not only of the Jewish nation, but of the scattered children of God throughout the world (v. 52). The cross is always more than its perpetrators intend and exactly what God intends.
verseByVerse.examples: The decision of the Sanhedrin is the human side of the decree that was made in eternity: Christ was the Lamb slain before the foundation of the world (Rev. 13:8). Human hatred and divine love converge on the same event. The leaders plot what God has purposed; the victim goes willingly to what they intend as murder and he intends as sacrifice. The sovereign grace that works through human wickedness without being compromised by it is most visible at Calvary.

verseByVerse.quote: Many of the Jews therefore, who had come with Mary and had seen what he did, believed in him, but some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many of the Jews therefore, who had come with Mary and had seen what he did, believed in him, but some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.

Many of the Jews therefore, who had come with Mary and had seen what he did, believed in him. The sign leads to faith, as it was meant to (20:31).

But some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done. Others saw the same miracle and went to report it. The same sight produces faith in some and hostility in others. Abraham said it in the parable: if they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31). A different Lazarus, but the point stands.

In a sentence. Many who had seen what Jesus did believed in him, but some went and reported it to the Pharisees.

On a Tuesday. Miracles don’t create faith by themselves. Pray for the Spirit to open hearts as you tell what Christ has done.

verseByVerse.quote: So the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered the council and said, "What are we to do? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered the council and said, “What are we to do? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.”

The chief priests and the Pharisees gathered the council. The council (synedrion), the Sanhedrin: the supreme Jewish court of seventy-one members, led by the high priest.

For this man performs many signs. They don’t deny the miracles. They can’t.

If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him. Their fear is popularity.

And the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation. Setting and background. “Our place” means the temple, and perhaps their own positions. The leaders feared a messianic uprising would bring Roman reprisals. The Romans allowed Jewish self-rule as long as there was order. A popular messianic movement could end it. The irony: they killed Jesus to save the temple and the nation, and in AD 70 the Romans came and destroyed both.

In a sentence. The chief priests and Pharisees called the council, worried that if Jesus kept doing signs everyone would believe, and the Romans would destroy the temple and the nation.

On a Tuesday. Fear for your position can make you oppose God. Hold your place loosely.
verseByVerse.note: “Our place” means the temple. The leaders feared a messianic movement would bring Roman retaliation — as happened in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, "You know nothing at all. Nor do you understand that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, “You know nothing at all. Nor do you understand that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish.”

Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. Setting and background. Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36, an unusually long term, kept in office by the Romans. “That year” means that fateful year, the year Jesus died. His father-in-law Annas had been high priest before him and was still powerful (18:13). An ossuary (bone box) inscribed with the name of Joseph son of Caiaphas was found in Jerusalem in 1990.

You know nothing at all. Rude and arrogant, in the Sadducee style.

It is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish. Political calculation: sacrifice one to save many. Cold, cynical, and unjust. He means: kill Jesus before the Romans kill us all.

In a sentence. Caiaphas, the high priest that year, told the council they knew nothing, and that it was better for one man to die for the people than for the whole nation to perish.

For worship. A wicked man spoke the gospel without knowing it: one man died for the people.
verseByVerse.note: Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36; “that year” means that fateful year.

verseByVerse.quote: He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad.

He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied. Key words. God spoke through Caiaphas without his knowing it, as he spoke through Balaam (Numbers 23–24). The high priest was traditionally linked with God’s guidance (the Urim and Thummim, Exodus 28:30). God can speak even through wicked men, and overrule their evil for good (Genesis 50:20; Acts 4:27–28).

That Jesus would die for the nation. “For” (hyper): on behalf of, in place of. Caiaphas meant a political substitute. God meant a saving substitute. Penal substitution: one dies in the place of the many.

And not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad. John adds the wider meaning. “The children of God scattered abroad” are the elect among the Gentiles, the “other sheep” of 10:16. They are already called children of God before they are gathered, because God has chosen them. Christ’s death gathers them into one people. His death is not a general provision, but a purposeful gathering of God’s children.

In a sentence. Caiaphas did not speak on his own, but as high priest he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not only for it, but to gather into one the scattered children of God.

For worship. Christ died to gather God’s scattered children into one family. If you are in Christ, you were one of them.

parallels.desc: I will gather yet others

verseByVerse.quote: So from that day on they made plans to put him to death. Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and there he stayed with the disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So from that day on they made plans to put him to death. Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and there he stayed with the disciples.

So from that day on they made plans to put him to death. The official decision. The giving of life to Lazarus seals Jesus’ death.

Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews. His hour is close, but not yet.

To a town called Ephraim. Setting and background. The town of Ephraim was probably north-east of Jerusalem, on the edge of the wilderness, perhaps modern et-Taiyibeh, about fifteen miles away (2 Chronicles 13:19).

And there he stayed with the disciples. A quiet time with his disciples before the end.

In a sentence. From that day the leaders plotted to kill Jesus, so he no longer moved openly among them but went to Ephraim near the wilderness and stayed there with his disciples.

On a Tuesday. Jesus took time away with his disciples before the storm. Make room for quiet with him before hard seasons.
verseByVerse.note: The town of Ephraim was probably north-east of Jerusalem, on the edge of the wilderness.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand, and many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves. They were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, "What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand, and many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves. They were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, “What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all?”

Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand. The third Passover in John (2:13; 6:4), the one at which Jesus will die as the true Passover Lamb (1:29; 19:36).

Many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves. Setting and background. Pilgrims came early to undergo purification rites so they would be ritually clean to eat the Passover (Numbers 9:6–12; 2 Chronicles 30:17–18). Some rites took a week. The irony: they purify themselves for a feast at which they will kill the Lamb who alone can make them clean.

What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all? The Greek expects that he won’t. Surely he won’t dare?

In a sentence. As Passover approached, many came early to Jerusalem to purify themselves, and they looked for Jesus in the temple, wondering whether he would come to the feast at all.

For worship. He did come. The Lamb came to the feast to be sacrificed for us.
verseByVerse.note: Pilgrims came early to undergo purification rites so they would be ritually clean for the feast.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he should let them know, so that they might arrest him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he should let them know, so that they might arrest him.

Had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he should let them know. Jesus is now a wanted man. Anyone who knows must inform. This sets the scene for Judas (12:4; 18:2–3).

So that they might arrest him. The net is closing. But the one they plan to arrest is the one who has authority to lay down his life (10:18).

In a sentence. The chief priests and Pharisees had ordered that anyone who knew where Jesus was should report it, so that they could arrest him.

On a Tuesday. When the world seems to close in, remember that the Lord of your life is not at the mercy of his enemies.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha.<sup>2</sup>It was Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was ill.<sup>3</sup>So the sisters sent to him, saying, “Lord, he whom you love is ill.”<sup>4</sup>But when Jesus heard it he said, “This illness does not lead to death. It is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.”<sup>5</sup>Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.<sup>6</sup>So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was.<sup>7</sup>Then after this he said to the disciples, “Let us go to Judea again.”<sup>8</sup>The disciples said to him, “Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?”<sup>9</sup>Jesus answered, “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world.<sup>10</sup>But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.”<sup>11</sup>After saying these things, he said to them, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him.”<sup>12</sup>The disciples said to him, “Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover.”<sup>13</sup>Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep.<sup>14</sup>Then Jesus told them plainly, “Lazarus has died,<sup>15</sup>and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.”<sup>16</sup>So Thomas, called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, “Let us also go, that we may die with him.”<sup>17</sup>Now when Jesus came, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days.<sup>18</sup>Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles off,<sup>19</sup>and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother.<sup>20</sup>So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary remained seated in the house.<sup>21</sup>Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.<sup>22</sup>But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you.”<sup>23</sup>Jesus said to her, “Your brother will rise again.”<sup>24</sup>Martha said to him, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day.”<sup>25</sup>Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live,<sup>26</sup>and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?”<sup>27</sup>She said to him, “Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world.”<sup>28</sup>When she had said this, she went and called her sister Mary, saying in private, “The Teacher is here and is calling for you.”<sup>29</sup>And when she heard it, she rose quickly and went to him.<sup>30</sup>Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him.<sup>31</sup>When the Jews who were with her in the house, consoling her, saw Mary rise quickly and go out, they followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there.<sup>32</sup>Now when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet, saying to him, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”<sup>33</sup>When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled.<sup>34</sup>And he said, “Where have you laid him?” They said to him, “Lord, come and see.”<sup>35</sup>Jesus wept.<sup>36</sup>So the Jews said, “See how he loved him!”<sup>37</sup>But some of them said, “Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man also have kept this man from dying?”<sup>38</sup>Then Jesus, deeply moved again, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.<sup>39</sup>Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, “Lord, by this time there will be an odor, for he has been dead four days.”<sup>40</sup>Jesus said to her, “Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?”<sup>41</sup>So they took away the stone. And Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, “Father, I thank you that you have heard me.<sup>42</sup>I knew that you always hear me, but I said this on account of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me.”<sup>43</sup>When he had said these things, he cried out with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out.”<sup>44</sup>The man who had died came out, his hands and feet bound with linen strips, and his face wrapped with a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Unbind him, and let him go.”<sup>45</sup>Many of the Jews therefore, who had come with Mary and had seen what he did, believed in him,<sup>46</sup>but some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.<sup>47</sup>So the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered the council and said, “What are we to do? For this man performs many signs.<sup>48</sup>If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.”<sup>49</sup>But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, “You know nothing at all.<sup>50</sup>Nor do you understand that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish.”<sup>51</sup>He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation,<sup>52</sup>and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad.<sup>53</sup>So from that day on they made plans to put him to death.<sup>54</sup>Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and there he stayed with the disciples.<sup>55</sup>Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand, and many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves.<sup>56</sup>They were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, “What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all?”<sup>57</sup>Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he should let them know, so that they might arrest him.
11.overview:
The raising of Lazarus is the seventh and greatest sign in John, and the event that leads directly to the cross. Lazarus of Bethany, brother of Martha and Mary, falls ill, and the sisters send word to Jesus: “Lord, he whom you love is ill.” Because he loves them, Jesus waits two more days, then returns to Judea despite the danger, telling the disciples that Lazarus has fallen asleep and he is going to wake him. Thomas gloomily urges the others to go and die with him. By the time they arrive, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. Martha meets Jesus with grief and faith mixed; he tells her, “I am the resurrection and the life,” and she confesses him the Christ, the Son of God. Mary falls at his feet weeping, and Jesus, deeply moved and troubled, weeps too. At the tomb he orders the stone removed, prays aloud to his Father, and cries, “Lazarus, come out.” The dead man walks out still bound in grave-clothes.

Many believe, but some report to the Pharisees, and the Sanhedrin meets in alarm: if Jesus goes on like this, the Romans will destroy the temple and the nation. The high priest Caiaphas declares that it is better for one man to die for the people than for the whole nation to perish. John comments that, without knowing it, he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and to gather into one the scattered children of God. From that day they plan to kill him. Jesus withdraws to Ephraim, and as Passover approaches the crowds wonder whether he will dare to come to the feast. The one who gives life will give his own life, so that the dead may live.

12.title: The Hour Has Come

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–19 — The Anointing and the Entry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six days before Passover, at a dinner in Jesus’ honour in Bethany, with Martha serving and Lazarus at table, Mary anoints Jesus’ feet with a pound of expensive nard and wipes them with her hair, filling the house with fragrance. Judas, the future betrayer and a thief who pilfers from the common purse, protests that it could have been sold for the poor. Jesus defends her: she has kept it for his burial, and they will always have the poor, but not always him. Crowds come to see Jesus and the risen Lazarus, and the chief priests resolve to kill Lazarus too. Next day festival crowds carry palm branches out to meet Jesus, hailing him as the blessed King of Israel, and he rides in on a young donkey as the prophet foretold, though the disciples grasp this only later. Witnesses of Lazarus’s raising spread the news, drawing more people, and the Pharisees despair that the whole world is following him.
verseByVerse.theology: Mary's extravagance is the gospel's aesthetic: 'she has done a beautiful thing' (Matt. 26:10). The ointment worth a year's wages poured out on Jesus is the only appropriate response to the one who will pour out his life for the world. Judas' objection — it should have been sold and given to the poor — sounds pious but is calculated. He uses the language of charity to mask the language of control. The contrast between Mary's love and Judas' calculation is the contrast between authentic discipleship and the discipleship that has never really left the world's economy.
verseByVerse.examples: The triumphal entry is at once a royal procession and a misunderstood one. The crowd hails Jesus as king; they are right about the title and wrong about what it means. They expect a Davidic warrior-king who will restore national sovereignty; Jesus enters on a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9, the prophecy of the humble king of peace. The disciples do not understand this until after the resurrection (v. 16) — another instance of John's pattern where events are incomprehensible until the Spirit illuminates them in the light of the cross and resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: Six days before the Passover, Jesus therefore came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead. So they gave a dinner for him there. Martha served, and Lazarus was one of those reclining with him at table.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six days before the Passover, Jesus therefore came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead. So they gave a dinner for him there. Martha served, and Lazarus was one of those reclining with him at table.

Meaning first. John 12 closes the first half of the Gospel, the “Book of Signs.” Jesus is anointed for burial, enters Jerusalem as king, announces that his hour has come, and makes a last appeal to the crowd. The chapter ends with John’s explanation of Israel’s unbelief and Jesus’ final public words. From chapter 13 on, Jesus speaks only to his disciples, and then goes to the cross.

Six days before the Passover. Probably the Saturday evening before Passover week, after the Sabbath ended. Time is now counted in days.

Jesus therefore came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead. John reminds us of the miracle that has put Jesus under sentence of death.

So they gave a dinner for him there. Mark and Matthew place it in the house of Simon the leper (Mark 14:3), perhaps a friend of the family.

Martha served, and Lazarus was one of those reclining with him at table. Martha still serving (Luke 10:40), now without complaint. Lazarus, once dead, now eating: proof that he is truly alive. Diners reclined on couches around a low table, leaning on the left elbow, with feet stretched out behind.

In a sentence. Six days before Passover Jesus came to Bethany, where they gave a dinner for him, with Martha serving and Lazarus at the table.

On a Tuesday. Jesus spent his last week among friends at a table. Fellowship is not a waste of time. It is a gift.

verseByVerse.quote: Mary therefore took a pound of expensive ointment made from pure nard, and anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume. But Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples (he who was about to betray him), said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary therefore took a pound of expensive ointment made from pure nard, and anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume. But Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples (he who was about to betray him), said,

Mary therefore took a pound of expensive ointment made from pure nard. Setting and background. The ESV notes that the pound was a Roman pound, about 11½ ounces or 327 grams. Nard was an aromatic oil from a plant grown in the Himalayas, imported from India. It was very costly. “Pure” (pistikēs) may mean genuine, unadulterated. This may have been a family treasure, perhaps her dowry.

And anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair. Mark and Matthew say she poured it on his head (Mark 14:3); John on his feet. She probably did both: the amount was large. Anointing the head honoured a king; anointing the feet was the act of the humblest servant. And a respectable woman did not let down her hair in public. Mary forgets her dignity in her devotion.

The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume. An eyewitness detail. Some see a picture: her devotion fills the house, and the story fills the world (Mark 14:9).

But Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples (he who was about to betray him), said. The contrast is deliberate: Mary gives everything; Judas will sell Jesus for silver.

In a sentence. Mary anointed Jesus’ feet with a pound of costly nard and wiped them with her hair, filling the house with fragrance, but Judas, who would betray him, objected.

For worship. Nothing is too costly to pour out for Christ. What would your extravagant love look like?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the pound was a Roman pound, about 11½ ounces. Nard was a costly perfume imported from India. A respectable woman did not normally let down her hair in public.

parallels.desc: a different woman in Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: "Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?" He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?” He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it.

Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor? The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; three hundred was nearly a year’s pay for a labourer. The objection sounds pious. Mark says some of the disciples joined in (Mark 14:4); Judas started it.

He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief. John knows what was in his heart.

And having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it. “Moneybag” (glōssokomon): the common purse of Jesus and the disciples, from which the poor were helped (13:29). Judas was the treasurer, and he stole from it. Love of money opened the door to his betrayal (Matthew 26:14–15; 1 Timothy 6:10).

In a sentence. Judas asked why the ointment was not sold for a year’s wages and given to the poor, not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief who stole from the common purse.

On a Tuesday. Beware of criticising others’ devotion with pious words. And beware the love of money: it made a thief of an apostle.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; three hundred denarii was about a year’s wages.

parallels.desc: Judas had the moneybag

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said, "Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial. For the poor you always have with you, but you do not always have me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said, “Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial. For the poor you always have with you, but you do not always have me.”

Leave her alone. Jesus defends her.

So that she may keep it for the day of my burial. Bodies were anointed with spices for burial. The Greek is difficult: perhaps she had kept it for this moment, or this is an anticipation of his burial. Either way, Jesus sees her act as preparing his body for death. Did Mary understand that he would die? Perhaps more than the disciples did. She, who sat at his feet, may have heard what they missed.

For the poor you always have with you. An echo of Deuteronomy 15:11, which goes on: therefore open wide your hand to the poor. Jesus is not dismissing the poor. There will always be time to help them, and his people must (Galatians 2:10).

But you do not always have me. This was a unique moment. In a few days he would be gone. Devotion to Christ himself comes first; care for the poor flows from it.

In a sentence. Jesus told Judas to leave her alone, for she was keeping it for his burial, and they would always have the poor, but not always him.

For worship. Worship and mercy are not rivals. But worship comes first, and the love that pours itself out on Christ will pour itself out on the poor.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were anointed with spices for burial.

parallels.desc: there will never cease to be poor in the land

verseByVerse.quote: When the large crowd of the Jews learned that Jesus was there, they came, not only on account of him but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead. So the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well, because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the large crowd of the Jews learned that Jesus was there, they came, not only on account of him but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead. So the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well, because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.

Not only on account of him but also to see Lazarus. Lazarus has become a living proof, a walking sign.

So the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well. The depth of their hardness. The chief priests were Sadducees, who denied the resurrection (Acts 23:8). A resurrected man was an embarrassment. Rather than believe the evidence, they plot to destroy it.

Because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus. “Going away”: leaving the authorities’ side.

In a sentence. Crowds came to see Jesus and Lazarus, so the chief priests planned to kill Lazarus too, since because of him many were leaving and believing in Jesus.

On a Tuesday. A changed life is the most powerful testimony. It may also be the most opposed.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day the large crowd that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem. So they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, crying out, "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!" And Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, just as it is written,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day the large crowd that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem. So they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, crying out, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!” And Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, just as it is written,

The next day. Palm Sunday.

They took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him. Setting and background. Palm branches had become a symbol of national victory and celebration, ever since the Maccabees cleansed the temple and the people carried palms (1 Maccabees 13:51; 2 Maccabees 10:7). The palm appeared on Jewish coins of the revolt. Going out to meet him (hypantēsis) was how cities greeted a visiting king or conqueror.

Hosanna! Hebrew for Save us now! (Psalm 118:25). By this time it had become a shout of praise, like “hurrah,” but its meaning is a prayer for salvation.

Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. From Psalm 118:26, one of the Hallel psalms sung at Passover and the Feast of Booths, a pilgrim psalm of welcome.

Even the King of Israel! The crowd adds this title. They are hailing a national liberator, like the Maccabees. Jesus is king, but not the kind they expect (6:15; 18:36).

And Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it. The other Gospels give the details of how he found it (Mark 11:1–7). Jesus acts deliberately.

In a sentence. The next day, hearing Jesus was coming, the crowd went out with palm branches shouting Hosanna and hailing him as the King of Israel, and Jesus found a young donkey and rode on it, as Scripture says.

For worship. Hosanna: save us now. Make that cry your praise and your prayer.
verseByVerse.note: Palm branches had become a symbol of national victory and celebration. “Hosanna” means “save, we pray.”

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD
branches of palm trees at the Feast of Booths

verseByVerse.quote: "Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey's colt!" His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him and had been done to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey’s colt!” His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him and had been done to him.

Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey’s colt! From Zechariah 9:9, combined perhaps with Isaiah 40:9 or Zephaniah 3:16 (“fear not”). “Daughter of Zion” is Jerusalem. Setting and background. A king riding a donkey came in peace, not on a warhorse. Zechariah goes on to say that this king will cut off the chariot and the war horse and speak peace to the nations (Zechariah 9:10). Jesus corrects the crowd’s hopes by his choice of mount. He is king, but humble, bringing peace, not a sword.

His disciples did not understand these things at first. An honest admission. They only understood later.

But when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered. After the resurrection and ascension, and with the Spirit’s help (14:26), they understood the Scriptures (2:22). The whole Old Testament became clear in the light of Christ (Luke 24:27, 45).

In a sentence. As Zechariah foretold, Zion’s king came humbly on a donkey’s colt, and the disciples did not understand this until Jesus was glorified, when they remembered what had been written and done.

On a Tuesday. Some things in your life you will only understand later. Trust Christ now; the meaning will come.
verseByVerse.note: A king riding a donkey came in peace, not on a warhorse.

parallels.desc: your king, mounted on a donkey
fear not, O Zion

verseByVerse.quote: The crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to bear witness. The reason why the crowd went to meet him was that they heard he had done this sign.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to bear witness. The reason why the crowd went to meet him was that they heard he had done this sign.

Continued to bear witness. The eyewitnesses of Lazarus’s raising keep telling.

The reason why the crowd went to meet him was that they heard he had done this sign. John connects the triumphal entry directly to Lazarus. Two crowds: one from Bethany, telling what they saw, and one from Jerusalem, coming out to see.

In a sentence. Those who had seen Lazarus raised kept testifying, and that was why the crowd came out to meet Jesus.

For worship. Keep telling what you have seen Christ do. Your witness draws others to him.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Pharisees said to one another, "You see that you are gaining nothing. Look, the world has gone after him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the Pharisees said to one another, “You see that you are gaining nothing. Look, the world has gone after him.”

You see that you are gaining nothing. Frustration.

Look, the world has gone after him. An exaggeration, but a prophetic one. Just after this, Greeks come asking for Jesus (v. 20): the world, indeed. Like Caiaphas, the Pharisees speak more truly than they know.

In a sentence. The Pharisees told one another they were getting nowhere, for the whole world had gone after Jesus.

On a Tuesday. The world has gone after him, from every nation. You are part of that crowd.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–50 — The Hour Has Come: Lifting Up the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some Greeks who have come to worship at the feast ask Philip to let them see Jesus. When Philip and Andrew tell him, Jesus declares that the hour for the Son of Man’s glory has come. A grain of wheat stays alone unless it falls into the ground and dies; then it yields a great harvest. Whoever clings to life loses it, and whoever lets go of it in this world keeps it for eternity. His servants must follow him, and the Father will honour them. His soul is troubled, yet he will not ask to be spared this hour, for it is why he came; he prays that the Father will glorify his name. A voice from heaven replies that it has and will again. Some hear thunder, others an angel. Jesus says the voice was for them: now this world is judged, its ruler is driven out, and when he is lifted up he will draw everyone to himself, meaning the death he would die. The crowd asks how the Messiah, who remains for ever, can be lifted up, and who this Son of Man is. Jesus urges them to walk in the light while they have it and become children of light, then hides from them. Despite all his signs they do not believe, fulfilling Isaiah’s words about unbelief and hardened hearts; Isaiah said this because he saw Jesus’ glory. Even many leaders believe but keep quiet for fear of expulsion, preferring human praise to God’s. Jesus cries out that to believe in him is to believe in the one who sent him; he came as light so that believers need not stay in darkness. He does not judge those who reject his words now, for he came to save; but his word will judge them on the last day, for he speaks what the Father commanded, and the Father’s command is eternal life.
verseByVerse.theology: The hour is the theological center of John's gospel — referenced as 'not yet come' repeatedly throughout the narrative (2:4; 7:30; 8:20), now announced as arrived (v. 23). The hour is the cross-resurrection-ascension event, the moment when the Son of Man is simultaneously lifted up in humiliation and glorified in triumph. The cross is not the Father's defeat but his decisive victory; it is not the Son's shame but his glory. This is the theology that has to be maintained against every attempt to split the crucifixion from the resurrection: both are the one event called 'the hour.'
verseByVerse.examples: Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. This is the law of the kingdom: life through death, fruitfulness through sacrifice. Jesus applies it first to himself and then to his disciples. The disciple who 'hates his life in this world' — who does not cling to temporal existence at the cost of eternal loyalty — will find life preserved in ways that the self-preserver never can. The call to follow him is a call to follow him even into death.

verseByVerse.quote: Now among those who went up to worship at the feast were some Greeks. So these came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and asked him, "Sir, we wish to see Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now among those who went up to worship at the feast were some Greeks. So these came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and asked him, “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.”

Now among those who went up to worship at the feast were some Greeks. These Greeks were probably Gentiles who worshipped the God of Israel, “God-fearers” (Acts 10:2; 17:4), who came to the feasts and worshipped in the Court of the Gentiles, but were not full converts. Their coming fulfils the Pharisees’ complaint: the world goes after him.

So these came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee. Philip has a Greek name, and Bethsaida was near Gentile areas. Perhaps they thought he would understand them.

Sir, we wish to see Jesus. Key words. A request repeated on pulpits around the world. “See” means meet, come to know. The Gentiles are asking for Jesus. It is the sign that his hour has come.

In a sentence. Some Greeks who had come to worship at the feast came to Philip from Bethsaida and asked to see Jesus.

For worship. Sir, we wish to see Jesus. Let that be the cry of every person who comes to church, and the aim of every preacher.
verseByVerse.note: These Greeks were probably Gentiles who worshipped the God of Israel, like the centurion Cornelius. Philip had a Greek name.

parallels.desc: other sheep

verseByVerse.quote: Philip went and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus. And Jesus answered them, "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip went and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus. And Jesus answered them, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.”

Philip went and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus. Andrew, who brought Peter (1:41) and the boy with the loaves (6:8), brings people to Jesus again.

The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. Key words. Jesus’ “hour” in John is the time of his death and glorification. Until now it had “not yet come” (2:4; 7:30; 8:20). Now, when the Gentiles come, it has. Why? Because the Gentiles can only truly “see” him through his death, when he is lifted up and draws all people (v. 32). “Glorified” in John means the cross, resurrection and return to the Father, seen as one. The cross is not a defeat followed by glory; the cross is itself the glory.

In a sentence. Philip and Andrew told Jesus, and he answered that the hour had come for the Son of Man to be glorified.

For worship. The hour of his glory was the hour of his death. See the glory of God in the cross.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus’ “hour” in John is the time of his death and glorification.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life.

Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone. Key words. A picture from farming. A seed kept in the barn stays a single seed. Planted in the ground, it “dies,” and from it a plant grows with many seeds. Jesus’ death is like that. If he did not die, he would remain alone. Through his death comes a great harvest of people from every nation, including the Greeks who have just asked to see him.

But if it dies, it bears much fruit. The cross is the way to fruitfulness. Life comes out of death.

Whoever loves his life loses it. The principle applies to his followers too (Mark 8:35). “Life” here is psychē, the self, one’s earthly life. Clinging to your life, living for yourself, is the way to lose everything.

And whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life. “Hates” is a Hebrew way of saying “loves less,” prefers something else (Luke 14:26). Not self-loathing, but putting Christ above self. Those who give up their lives for him find true life.

In a sentence. Jesus said a grain of wheat remains alone unless it falls into the earth and dies, but if it dies it bears much fruit; whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates it in this world will keep it for eternal life.

On a Tuesday. What are you clinging to? Plant it, let it die for Christ’s sake, and see what fruit he brings.

verseByVerse.quote: "If anyone serves me, he must follow me; and where I am, there will my servant be also. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him. Now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? 'Father, save me from this hour'? But for this purpose I have come to this hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone serves me, he must follow me; and where I am, there will my servant be also. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him. Now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? ‘Father, save me from this hour’? But for this purpose I have come to this hour.

If anyone serves me, he must follow me. Serving Christ means following him, even on the road of the grain of wheat.

And where I am, there will my servant be also. Where he goes, through death to glory, his servants go too (14:3; 17:24).

If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him. The Father honours those who serve his Son. Not human glory, but the Father’s approval.

Now is my soul troubled. Key words. “Troubled” (tetaraktai): agitated, shaken. This is John’s version of Gethsemane (Mark 14:34). Jesus is truly human and feels the horror of what lies ahead: not just physical death, but bearing the wrath of God against sin.

And what shall I say? “Father, save me from this hour”? He considers the prayer, and rejects it.

But for this purpose I have come to this hour. He came for this. The whole of his life led to this hour.

In a sentence. Jesus said that his servant must follow him, and will be where he is and be honoured by the Father; and then said his soul was troubled, but he would not ask to be saved from this hour, for this was why he had come.

For worship. He was troubled, and still he went to the cross for us. His resolve is our salvation.

parallels.desc: Gethsemane

verseByVerse.quote: "Father, glorify your name." Then a voice came from heaven: "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again." The crowd that stood there and heard it said that it had thundered. Others said, "An angel has spoken to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Father, glorify your name.” Then a voice came from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.” The crowd that stood there and heard it said that it had thundered. Others said, “An angel has spoken to him.”

Father, glorify your name. Key words. This is his prayer instead: not “save me,” but “glorify your name.” Like “your will be done” in Gethsemane. The glory of God matters more to Jesus than his own escape from suffering.

Then a voice came from heaven. The third time in the Gospels that the Father speaks from heaven (at the baptism, Mark 1:11; at the transfiguration, Mark 9:7). The only one John records.

I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again. He has glorified it in Jesus’ life and signs; he will glorify it again in Jesus’ death and resurrection.

The crowd that stood there and heard it said that it had thundered. Others said, “An angel has spoken to him.” Some heard only noise; others knew it was speech, but not whose. Compare Paul’s companions on the Damascus road (Acts 9:7; 22:9). In the Old Testament, God’s voice is likened to thunder (Psalm 29:3; Exodus 19:19).

In a sentence. Jesus prayed for the Father to glorify his name, and a voice from heaven said he had glorified it and would glorify it again, which some of the crowd took for thunder and others for an angel.

On a Tuesday. When you’re troubled, pray as Jesus did: Father, glorify your name. It is a prayer God always answers.

parallels.desc: the Father’s voice at the baptism and transfiguration

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "This voice has come for your sake, not mine. Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered, “This voice has come for your sake, not mine. Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out.”

This voice has come for your sake, not mine. Jesus didn’t need it; he knew the Father’s will. It was for the crowd, to confirm him.

Now is the judgment of this world. Key words. At the cross, the world is judged. Its verdict on Jesus is overturned by God, and the world’s sin is exposed and condemned.

Now will the ruler of this world be cast out. “The ruler of this world” is Satan (14:30; 16:11; 2 Corinthians 4:4). At the cross, he is cast out, dethroned. How? By the cross, Christ removed the ground of Satan’s accusation, our sin (Colossians 2:14–15; Hebrews 2:14–15; Revelation 12:9–11). Satan still works, but he is a defeated enemy.

Where Christians differ: the binding of Satan. Premillennial Christians often teach that Satan will be bound only in a future thousand-year reign after Christ’s return. Verdict: Jesus says Satan is cast out “now,” at the cross. Revelation 20’s binding of Satan describes this present age, in which he can no longer deceive the nations or stop the gospel going to them (Matthew 12:29). This is the amillennial view: the thousand years are the gospel age between Christ’s first and second comings.

In a sentence. Jesus said the voice came for their sake, and now was the judgment of the world and the casting out of its ruler.

For worship. At the cross, the devil was cast out. You serve a conquering King.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself." He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die.

And I, when I am lifted up from the earth. Key words. In John, “lifted up” means both the cross and his exaltation (3:14; 8:28). He will be lifted up on the cross, and that lifting up will be his exaltation.

Will draw all people to myself. “Draw” (helkō): the same verb as 6:44, an effective pulling. “All people”: in context, the Greeks have just asked to see him. Through the cross, Jesus will draw people from every nation, not only Jews. This is the answer to their request.

He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die. Crucifixion: lifted up from the earth on a cross.

Where Christians differ: does Christ draw every person? Some take “all people” to mean every individual, drawn with a resistible grace. Verdict: in 6:44 the one who is drawn is raised up on the last day. If every person were drawn in that sense, every person would be saved, which Scripture denies. Here, “all people” means all kinds of people, Gentiles as well as Jews, as the context of the Greeks shows (compare 11:52). The cross draws, effectively, people from every nation.

In a sentence. Jesus said that when he is lifted up from the earth he will draw all people to himself, which showed the kind of death he would die.

For worship. Christ lifted up still draws people from every nation. Lift him up in your preaching and your life.
verseByVerse.note: In John, “lifted up” means both the cross and his exaltation.

parallels.desc: he shall be high and lifted up

verseByVerse.quote: So the crowd answered him, "We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. How can you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?" So Jesus said to them, "The light is among you for a little while longer. Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you. The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the crowd answered him, “We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. How can you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?” So Jesus said to them, “The light is among you for a little while longer. Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you. The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going.”

We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. “The Law” here is the Old Testament. They may be thinking of Psalm 89:36–37, Psalm 110:4, Isaiah 9:7 or Daniel 7:14: the Messiah’s kingdom is everlasting. True, but they couldn’t imagine that he would reach it through death.

How can you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? They understand “lifted up” as death. A dying Messiah made no sense to them (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Who is this Son of Man? They don’t know who he is talking about.

The light is among you for a little while longer. Jesus doesn’t argue. He warns. The time is short.

Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you. “Overtake” (katalabē): the same word as 1:5, where the darkness has not overcome the light. Now the darkness will overtake those who refuse the light.

The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going. Life without Christ is aimless.

In a sentence. The crowd objected that the Christ would remain for ever, so how could the Son of Man be lifted up, and who was he? Jesus warned them that the light was with them only a little longer, and they should walk in it before darkness overtook them.

On a Tuesday. The light won’t always be offered. If you haven’t come to Christ, come now.

parallels.desc: his offspring shall endure forever

verseByVerse.quote: "While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light." When Jesus had said these things, he departed and hid himself from them. Though he had done so many signs before them, they still did not believe in him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light.” When Jesus had said these things, he departed and hid himself from them. Though he had done so many signs before them, they still did not believe in him,

While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light. “Sons of light”: a Hebrew way of saying people who belong to the light, share its character (Luke 16:8; Ephesians 5:8; 1 Thessalonians 5:5). Believing makes you a child of the light.

When Jesus had said these things, he departed and hid himself from them. His last public appeal. The light withdraws.

Though he had done so many signs before them, they still did not believe in him. Key words. John now explains the great mystery of the Gospel: why did Israel, God’s own people, reject their Messiah? The signs were many and clear. The problem was not lack of evidence.

In a sentence. Jesus urged them to believe in the light while they had it, then withdrew and hid himself, and though he had done so many signs, they still did not believe.

For worship. If you believe, you are a child of light. Live as one.

parallels.desc: walk as children of light

verseByVerse.quote: so that the word spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: "Lord, who has believed what he heard from us, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" Therefore they could not believe. For again Isaiah said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
so that the word spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: “Lord, who has believed what he heard from us, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” Therefore they could not believe. For again Isaiah said,

So that the word spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled. Their unbelief was foretold. It did not take God by surprise; it was part of his plan.

Lord, who has believed what he heard from us, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? From Isaiah 53:1, at the start of the great Suffering Servant passage. The prophet asks who has believed the message about the Servant who would be despised and rejected, wounded for our transgressions. Few believed. “The arm of the Lord” is God’s power in salvation, revealed in Christ’s signs and in his cross.

Therefore they could not believe. Key words. Not merely “did not” but “could not.” Their unbelief has become an inability. Why? The next quotation explains.

In a sentence. Their unbelief fulfilled Isaiah’s words asking who had believed the message and to whom the Lord’s arm had been revealed, and so they could not believe, because Isaiah also said...

For worship. The arm of the Lord was revealed in the crucified Servant. If you believe, it was revealed to you. What grace.

parallels.desc: who has believed what he has heard from us?

verseByVerse.quote: "He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I would heal them." Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I would heal them.” Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him.

He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart. From Isaiah 6:10, quoted freely. When Isaiah was called, God told him his preaching would harden Israel. This passage is quoted in all four Gospels and in Acts (Mark 4:12; Acts 28:26–27) to explain Israel’s unbelief.

Lest they see with their eyes, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I would heal them. Hardening is God’s judgment on persistent unbelief. They first refused to believe (v. 37); then God gave them over to their refusal (Romans 1:24; 2 Thessalonians 2:11). God’s sovereignty and human responsibility stand together. They would not; therefore they could not.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is the author of sin or that they were innocent victims. They had seen and rejected the light (v. 37). Nor does it mean all Israel is hardened for ever: Paul says a partial hardening has come upon Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in (Romans 11:25), and many Jews have believed and will believe.

Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him. Key words. Isaiah saw the Lord’s glory in the temple, high and lifted up, the seraphim crying “Holy, holy, holy” (Isaiah 6:1–5). John says that glory was Christ’s. The Lord whom Isaiah saw on the throne was the Son.
