One of the clearest statements in the New Testament that Jesus is the Lord of the Old Testament, Yahweh himself.

In a sentence. Isaiah said God had blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts so that they would not see, understand, turn and be healed, and he said this because he saw Christ’s glory and spoke of him.

For worship. The Lord high and lifted up whom Isaiah saw is Jesus. Holy, holy, holy is he.
verseByVerse.note: Isaiah saw the Lord’s glory in the temple; John says that glory was Christ’s.

parallels.desc: make the heart of this people dull
I saw the Lord, high and lifted up

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, many even of the authorities believed in him, but for fear of the Pharisees they did not confess it, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue; for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nevertheless, many even of the authorities believed in him, but for fear of the Pharisees they did not confess it, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue; for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God.

Nevertheless, many even of the authorities believed in him. Not all rejected him. Some of the rulers believed. Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were among these secret believers (19:38–39).

But for fear of the Pharisees they did not confess it. Belief without confession. They were afraid.

So that they would not be put out of the synagogue. The same threat as 9:22.

For they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God. Key words. “Glory” (doxa) here means honour, approval. A play on Isaiah’s glory in v. 41: Isaiah saw the glory of God; they preferred human glory. The root of their silence was not fear alone but love of human approval (5:44). Is this saving faith? Jesus said that whoever is ashamed of him, he will be ashamed of (Mark 8:38), and that confession with the mouth goes with true belief (Romans 10:9–10). Their faith is at best weak and immature, at worst not real. Joseph and Nicodemus later came out into the open.

In a sentence. Even so, many of the rulers believed, but for fear of the Pharisees they kept quiet so as not to be expelled from the synagogue, because they loved human praise more than God’s.

On a Tuesday. Whose approval do you crave most? Choose the glory that comes from God.
verseByVerse.note: Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were among these secret believers.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus cried out and said, "Whoever believes in me, believes not in me but in him who sent me. And whoever sees me sees him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus cried out and said, “Whoever believes in me, believes not in me but in him who sent me. And whoever sees me sees him who sent me.”

And Jesus cried out and said. These final verses (vv. 44–50) are a summary of Jesus’ public teaching, perhaps spoken earlier, placed here as his last word to the world.

Whoever believes in me, believes not in me but in him who sent me. Not that faith in Jesus is wrong, but that it doesn’t stop with him: it reaches the Father. To trust Jesus is to trust God.

And whoever sees me sees him who sent me. Key words. Jesus is the perfect revelation of the Father (1:18; 14:9). There is no hidden God behind Jesus who is different from him.

In a sentence. Jesus cried out that whoever believes in him believes in the one who sent him, and whoever sees him sees the one who sent him.

For worship. When you look at Jesus, you see God. There is no other face of God than his.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have come into the world as light, so that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness. If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have come into the world as light, so that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness. If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world.

I have come into the world as light. The theme of 1:4–9 and 8:12.

So that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness. “Remain” implies that everyone starts in darkness. Faith brings us out.

If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him. Not now, at his first coming.

For I did not come to judge the world but to save the world. The purpose of his first coming was salvation (3:17). Judgment will come at his second coming (5:22, 27).

In a sentence. Jesus said he came as light so that believers would not remain in darkness, and he did not judge those who heard and did not keep his words, for he came not to judge but to save the world.

On a Tuesday. Christ came to save you, not to condemn you. Come into his light.

verseByVerse.quote: "The one who rejects me and does not receive my words has a judge; the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day. For I have not spoken on my own authority, but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment — what to say and what to speak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who rejects me and does not receive my words has a judge; the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day. For I have not spoken on my own authority, but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment — what to say and what to speak.

The one who rejects me and does not receive my words has a judge. Rejection has consequences. There is a judge.

The word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day. Key words. His words themselves will be the evidence. Those who heard and rejected them will be judged by them. To hear the gospel is a great privilege and a great responsibility (Matthew 11:20–24; Hebrews 2:1–3).

For I have not spoken on my own authority, but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment. His words are the Father’s words, which is why rejecting them is so serious.

In a sentence. Jesus said that whoever rejects him and his words has a judge, for his word will judge him on the last day, since he did not speak on his own but as the Father commanded.

For worship. The words that save us now will judge the world on the last day. Receive them gladly.

parallels.desc: I will put my words in his mouth

verseByVerse.quote: "And I know that his commandment is eternal life. What I say, therefore, I say as the Father has told me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I know that his commandment is eternal life. What I say, therefore, I say as the Father has told me.

And I know that his commandment is eternal life. The Father’s command to the Son, and through the Son to the world, leads to eternal life. The message Jesus brings is life-giving.

What I say, therefore, I say as the Father has told me. Jesus’ last public words in John: complete obedience to the Father. From here, he turns to his own (13:1).

In a sentence. Jesus said he knew the Father’s command is eternal life, and so he speaks just as the Father has told him.

On a Tuesday. Christ’s words are eternal life. Read them today as if your life depended on them, for it does.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>Six days before the Passover, Jesus therefore came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead.<sup>2</sup>So they gave a dinner for him there. Martha served, and Lazarus was one of those reclining with him at table.<sup>3</sup>Mary therefore took a pound of expensive ointment made from pure nard, and anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.<sup>4</sup>But Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples (he who was about to betray him), said,<sup>5</sup>“Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?”<sup>6</sup>He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it.<sup>7</sup>Jesus said, “Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial.<sup>8</sup>For the poor you always have with you, but you do not always have me.”<sup>9</sup>When the large crowd of the Jews learned that Jesus was there, they came, not only on account of him but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead.<sup>10</sup>So the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well,<sup>11</sup>because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.<sup>12</sup>The next day the large crowd that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem.<sup>13</sup>So they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, crying out, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!”<sup>14</sup>And Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, just as it is written,<sup>15</sup>“Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey’s colt!”<sup>16</sup>His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him and had been done to him.<sup>17</sup>The crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to bear witness.<sup>18</sup>The reason why the crowd went to meet him was that they heard he had done this sign.<sup>19</sup>So the Pharisees said to one another, “You see that you are gaining nothing. Look, the world has gone after him.”<sup>20</sup>Now among those who went up to worship at the feast were some Greeks.<sup>21</sup>So these came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and asked him, “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.”<sup>22</sup>Philip went and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus.<sup>23</sup>And Jesus answered them, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.<sup>24</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.<sup>25</sup>Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life.<sup>26</sup>If anyone serves me, he must follow me; and where I am, there will my servant be also. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him.<sup>27</sup>“Now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? ’Father, save me from this hour’? But for this purpose I have come to this hour.<sup>28</sup>Father, glorify your name.“ Then a voice came from heaven: ”I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.”<sup>29</sup>The crowd that stood there and heard it said that it had thundered. Others said, “An angel has spoken to him.”<sup>30</sup>Jesus answered, “This voice has come for your sake, not mine.<sup>31</sup>Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out.<sup>32</sup>And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”<sup>33</sup>He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die.<sup>34</sup>So the crowd answered him, “We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. How can you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?”<sup>35</sup>So Jesus said to them, “The light is among you for a little while longer. Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you. The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going.<sup>36</sup>While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light.” When Jesus had said these things, he departed and hid himself from them.<sup>37</sup>Though he had done so many signs before them, they still did not believe in him,<sup>38</sup>so that the word spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: “Lord, who has believed what he heard from us, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?”<sup>39</sup>Therefore they could not believe. For again Isaiah said,<sup>40</sup>“He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I would heal them.”<sup>41</sup>Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him.<sup>42</sup>Nevertheless, many even of the authorities believed in him, but for fear of the Pharisees they did not confess it, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue;<sup>43</sup>for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God.<sup>44</sup>And Jesus cried out and said, “Whoever believes in me, believes not in me but in him who sent me.<sup>45</sup>And whoever sees me sees him who sent me.<sup>46</sup>I have come into the world as light, so that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness.<sup>47</sup>If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world.<sup>48</sup>The one who rejects me and does not receive my words has a judge; the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day.<sup>49</sup>For I have not spoken on my own authority, but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment—what to say and what to speak.<sup>50</sup>And I know that his commandment is eternal life. What I say, therefore, I say as the Father has told me.”
12.overview:
Chapter 12 closes the first half of John’s Gospel, the “book of signs”, and opens the way to the cross. Six days before Passover, at a dinner in Bethany with Lazarus at the table, Mary pours a pound of costly nard on Jesus’ feet and wipes them with her hair. Judas, a thief, complains about the waste; Jesus defends her: she has kept it for the day of his burial. The next day crowds wave palm branches and hail Jesus as the King of Israel as he rides into Jerusalem on a young donkey, fulfilling Zechariah. The Pharisees despair: “the world has gone after him.”

Then some Greeks ask to see Jesus, and he announces that the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. Like a grain of wheat he must fall into the ground and die to bear much fruit; whoever loves his life will lose it. His soul is troubled, but he will not ask to be saved from this hour; instead he prays, “Father, glorify your name,” and a voice from heaven answers. Lifted up from the earth, he will draw all people to himself, and the ruler of this world will be cast out. John then sums up Jesus’ public ministry: despite all his signs, most did not believe, fulfilling Isaiah’s words about blinded eyes and hardened hearts; even among the leaders some believed secretly but would not confess him, loving human glory more than God’s. Jesus’ final public appeal follows: he has come as light into the world, and his word will judge those who reject it on the last day.

13.title: The Foot Washing and the New Commandment

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Foot Washing: Love to the End
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Just before Passover, knowing his hour has come to return to the Father, Jesus shows the full extent of his love for his own. At supper, with Judas already moved by the devil to betray him, Jesus, conscious of his authority and his origin and destiny in God, lays aside his outer clothes, ties a towel around himself and washes the disciples’ feet. Peter protests and is told he will understand later; when he refuses, Jesus warns that without this washing Peter has no share in him. Peter then asks for a complete wash, but Jesus says the one already bathed needs only his feet cleaned; they are clean, except one. Back at table, Jesus explains that as their Lord and Teacher he has given them an example: they must wash each other’s feet, for no servant outranks his master, and blessing lies in doing it. He knows whom he chose, yet Scripture foretold that a companion at his table would turn against him. He tells them in advance so that they will believe. To receive his messengers is to receive him and the Father who sent him.
verseByVerse.theology: The foot washing is simultaneously a moral example (do as I have done) and a picture of the cleansing only Christ gives (you need to have your feet washed to have a part in me). Peter's characteristic resistance — then misunderstanding, then over-correction — clarifies both aspects: the washing Jesus gives is not merely a lesson in humility but the cleansing that makes fellowship with him possible. The once-washed disciple needs only the cleaning of feet — the ongoing renewal of those already justified, not re-justification. This is the distinction between initial cleansing (bath) and ongoing renewal (feet-washing): the one already clean needs only this.
verseByVerse.examples: You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am (v. 13). The authority of the foot-washing is its own argument. Jesus does not wash feet because he has forgotten who he is; he washes feet because he knows exactly who he is (v. 3-4). The servant heart flows from the secure identity: those who are anxious about their position never serve freely; those who know their position in Christ serve without self-protection. Genuine servanthood is not self-abasement but the overflow of a heart that has been secured by the Father's love.

verseByVerse.quote: Now before the Feast of the Passover, when Jesus knew that his hour had come to depart out of this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. During supper, when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon's son, to betray him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now before the Feast of the Passover, when Jesus knew that his hour had come to depart out of this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. During supper, when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him,

Meaning first. The second half of John’s Gospel begins here. Setting and background: John’s account of the last evening fills five chapters (13–17), far more than the other Gospels. Jesus washes his disciples’ feet, exposes the betrayer, gives the new commandment, and then teaches them about his going, the Spirit, and the life of union with him, before praying for them. John doesn’t describe the institution of the Lord’s Supper, which the other Gospels and Paul had already recorded (1 Corinthians 11:23–26). He gives us what they left out.

Now before the Feast of the Passover. The setting is Thursday evening.

When Jesus knew that his hour had come to depart out of this world to the Father. His death is a “departure” (metabē, a passing over) to the Father. Fitting at Passover.

Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. Key words. “His own”: those the Father gave him (10:3–4; 17:6). “To the end” (eis telos) means both to the very last moment of his life and to the uttermost, completely. His love would not stop, and it held nothing back. Everything in chapters 13–17 is an expression of this love, and so is the cross.

When the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him. Love and treachery side by side. The devil had planted the idea; Judas had welcomed it. Jesus will wash the feet of the man who has already decided to betray him.

In a sentence. Before Passover, knowing his hour had come to go to the Father, Jesus loved his own to the end, and during supper, when the devil had already put it into Judas’s heart to betray him...

For worship. He loved his own to the end. If you are his, his love for you will never run out.
verseByVerse.note: John’s account of the last evening fills five chapters (13–17). “Simon’s son” is a different Simon from Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going back to God, rose from supper. He laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going back to God, rose from supper. He laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist.

Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands. Key words. The hands into which the Father had given all authority (3:35) are the hands that will wash feet. Jesus doesn’t stoop because he has forgotten who he is. He stoops because he knows exactly who he is. True greatness serves.

And that he had come from God and was going back to God. Secure in his origin and destiny, he is free to serve.

Rose from supper. In the middle of the meal.

He laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist. Setting and background. Washing guests’ feet was the job of the lowest household slave. Even Jewish slaves were often not required to do it. Roads were dusty, and people wore sandals, so feet were filthy. No disciple had done it; Luke tells us they were arguing about who was the greatest (Luke 22:24). “Laid aside” (tithēsin) is the same verb used of the shepherd laying down his life (10:11, 17), and “resumed” in v. 12 is the verb of taking it up again. The footwashing is a picture of the incarnation and the cross: he laid aside his glory, took the form of a servant, and humbled himself to death (Philippians 2:6–8).

In a sentence. Knowing that the Father had given him all things, and that he had come from God and was returning to God, Jesus got up from supper, took off his outer garments, and tied a towel around his waist.

On a Tuesday. You will never be too important for the towel. The one with all things in his hands picked it up.
verseByVerse.note: Washing guests’ feet was the job of the lowest household slave; roads were dusty and people wore sandals.

parallels.desc: I am among you as the one who serves

verseByVerse.quote: Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples' feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him. He came to Simon Peter, who said to him, "Lord, do you wash my feet?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him. He came to Simon Peter, who said to him, “Lord, do you wash my feet?”

Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet. The details are slow and deliberate, as if an eyewitness remembered every movement. The Lord of glory kneeling at each pair of feet, including Judas’s.

He came to Simon Peter. Perhaps not first.

Lord, do you wash my feet? In Greek the words “you” and “my” stand side by side for emphasis: You, my feet? Peter is shocked. It seems all wrong for the Lord to do this.

In a sentence. Jesus poured water into a basin and began washing and drying the disciples’ feet, and when he came to Peter, Peter asked whether he, the Lord, would wash his feet.

For worship. The Lord kneels before sinners to wash them. Stand amazed with Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "What I am doing you do not understand now, but afterward you will understand." Peter said to him, "You shall never wash my feet." Jesus answered him, "If I do not wash you, you have no share with me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered him, “What I am doing you do not understand now, but afterward you will understand.” Peter said to him, “You shall never wash my feet.” Jesus answered him, “If I do not wash you, you have no share with me.”

What I am doing you do not understand now, but afterward you will understand. After the cross and resurrection, by the Spirit, he would understand that this washing pointed to Jesus’ death for him (12:16).

You shall never wash my feet. “Never” (ou mē … eis ton aiōna): the strongest denial, not ever. Peter’s pride dressed up as humility. He would rather serve than be served. But refusing grace is not humility.

If I do not wash you, you have no share with me. Key words. “Share” (meros): part, portion, inheritance. The washing now clearly means more than feet. Unless Christ cleanses us from sin, we have no part in him or his kingdom. Salvation begins with letting Christ do for us what we cannot do for ourselves.

In a sentence. Jesus told Peter he would understand later, and when Peter refused to let him wash his feet, Jesus said that unless he washed him, Peter would have no share with him.

On a Tuesday. Let Christ serve you. The hardest humility is accepting grace you cannot repay.

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter said to him, "Lord, not my feet only but also my hands and my head!" Jesus said to him, "The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean. And you are clean, but not every one of you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, not my feet only but also my hands and my head!” Jesus said to him, “The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean. And you are clean, but not every one of you.”

Lord, not my feet only but also my hands and my head! Peter swings to the other extreme. If washing means belonging to Jesus, then wash all of me! Impulsive, but full of love.

The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean. Key words. Setting and background. Guests bathed before a banquet and needed only their feet washed on arrival, since the roads dirtied them. Two words: “bathed” (louō), a full bath, and “wash” (niptō), washing part of the body. The spiritual meaning: the one who has been cleansed by Christ once for all, in justification and regeneration (Titus 3:5), does not need to be saved again. But he does need daily cleansing from the sins that soil his walk (1 John 1:7–9). Justification happens once; confession and forgiveness go on.

And you are clean, but not every one of you. The disciples are clean, cleansed by his word (15:3). But not all.

In a sentence. Peter asked Jesus to wash his hands and head too, but Jesus said that one who has bathed needs only his feet washed, being completely clean, and they were clean, though not all of them.

For worship. If you are in Christ, you are completely clean. Bring him the dust of today, and he will wash it.
verseByVerse.note: Guests bathed before a banquet and needed only their feet washed on arrival.

parallels.desc: you are already clean

verseByVerse.quote: For he knew who was to betray him; that was why he said, "Not all of you are clean." When he had washed their feet and put on his outer garments and resumed his place, he said to them, "Do you understand what I have done to you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he knew who was to betray him; that was why he said, “Not all of you are clean.” When he had washed their feet and put on his outer garments and resumed his place, he said to them, “Do you understand what I have done to you?”

For he knew who was to betray him. Judas had his feet washed, but was not clean. Outward contact with Jesus does not make a person clean. Only faith does.

When he had washed their feet and put on his outer garments and resumed his place. “Put on” (elaben): the verb of taking up his life again (10:17–18). After the cross, the resurrection, and return to his place at the Father’s side.

Do you understand what I have done to you? Now he explains a second meaning: an example.

In a sentence. Because Jesus knew who would betray him, he said not all were clean; and after washing their feet and returning to his place, he asked if they understood what he had done.

On a Tuesday. Being near Jesus is not the same as belonging to him. Judas sat at the table and was washed, and was lost.

verseByVerse.quote: "You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am. If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am. If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.

You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am. Jesus doesn’t deny his authority. His service doesn’t lessen it; it shows what kind of Lord he is.

If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. Key words. The argument goes from greater to lesser. If the Lord serves, how much more should the servants. “Ought” (opheilete): you owe it, you are obligated.

Where Christians differ: is footwashing an ordinance? Some churches practise footwashing as a regular ordinance alongside baptism and the Lord’s Supper. Verdict: Jesus calls it an example (v. 15), not a sacrament. The apostles never practised or commanded it as a church rite; in 1 Timothy 5:10 it appears as an act of humble hospitality. The command is to do the humble, menial, loving service that meets real needs, whatever form that takes today. A literal footwashing can be a moving act, but the point is the lowly love behind it.

In a sentence. Jesus said that they were right to call him Teacher and Lord, and if he, their Lord and Teacher, had washed their feet, they should wash one another’s feet.

On a Tuesday. What is the lowest, dirtiest job no one wants to do in your home, church, or workplace? That is your towel today.

verseByVerse.quote: "For I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you. Truly, truly, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you. Truly, truly, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him.

For I have given you an example. “Example” (hypodeigma): a pattern, a model to copy (1 Peter 2:21).

That you also should do just as I have done to you. Not just similar things, but in the same spirit.

A servant is not greater than his master. If the master isn’t too proud to wash feet, the servant cannot be.

Nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him. “Messenger” (apostolos): the word apostle. The apostles are sent ones, and they must not think themselves above the one who sent them.

In a sentence. Jesus said he had given them an example to follow, for a servant is not greater than his master, nor a messenger than the one who sent him.

For worship. Christ is our pattern as well as our Saviour. Follow him in lowly love.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them. I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But the Scripture will be fulfilled, 'He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them. I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But the Scripture will be fulfilled, ‘He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me.’

If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them. Key words. Knowing is not enough. The blessing is in doing (James 1:22–25).

I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen. Jesus chose the Twelve, including Judas (6:70). But here “whom I have chosen” probably means chosen for salvation: he knows his own, and he knows Judas is not among them.

He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me. From Psalm 41:9, where David laments a close friend’s betrayal, probably Ahithophel (2 Samuel 15–17), who later hanged himself, as Judas would. Setting and background. Lifting the heel against someone is a picture of treachery: like a horse kicking, or showing someone the sole of one’s foot, a deep insult in the East. To eat someone’s bread was to bind yourself in friendship. Judas would betray the friend who had just fed him and washed his feet.

In a sentence. Jesus said they would be blessed if they did what they knew, but he was not speaking of all of them, for he knew whom he had chosen, and Scripture would be fulfilled that one who ate his bread would turn against him.

On a Tuesday. Knowing about service is easy. Doing it is the blessing. Do one hidden act of service today.
verseByVerse.note: Lifting the heel against someone is a picture of treachery.

parallels.desc: my close friend, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me

verseByVerse.quote: "I am telling you this now, before it takes place, that when it does take place you may believe that I am he. Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever receives the one I send receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am telling you this now, before it takes place, that when it does take place you may believe that I am he. Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever receives the one I send receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me.

I am telling you this now, before it takes place. Jesus foretells the betrayal, so that it won’t shake their faith.

That when it does take place you may believe that I am he. Again “I am” (egō eimi). The God of Isaiah declares the end from the beginning (Isaiah 46:10; 48:5). Only God knows the future. Jesus’ prediction proves that he is the I AM. Isaiah 43:10 is closely echoed: “that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he.”

Whoever receives the one I send receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me. Even after Judas’s betrayal, the apostles’ mission stands. Their authority comes from Christ, and Christ’s from the Father. To receive the apostles’ message is to receive Christ, and to receive God (Matthew 10:40).

In a sentence. Jesus told them this before it happened so that when it did they would believe that he is the I AM, and that whoever receives those he sends receives him and the Father who sent him.

For worship. Nothing takes Christ by surprise, not even betrayal. Rest in his foreknowledge.

parallels.desc: that you may know and believe that I am he

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–38 — The Betrayer Exposed and the New Commandment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Troubled in spirit, Jesus announces that one of them will betray him, and the bewildered disciples look at one another. At Peter’s signal, the disciple Jesus loves, reclining beside him, asks who it is. Jesus answers that it is the one to whom he gives the dipped morsel, and he hands it to Judas. Satan enters Judas, and Jesus tells him to act quickly; the others assume he is being sent on an errand with the common purse. Judas goes out into the night. Then Jesus says that the Son of Man is now glorified, and God in him. He will soon leave them, and they cannot follow yet. He gives them a new command, to love one another as he has loved them, the mark by which all will recognise his disciples. When Peter insists he will follow even to death, Jesus predicts that before the rooster crows Peter will disown him three times.
verseByVerse.theology: Love one another as I have loved you is the social ethics of the atonement made into community commandment. The 'as I have loved you' is the measure and the model: not abstract love or sentiment, but the costly, self-giving, foot-washing, cross-bearing love that Jesus has just demonstrated and is about to complete. This is a new commandment not because love was absent from the Mosaic law (Lev. 19:18) but because the standard is new: as I have loved you is qualitatively greater than 'as yourself.' The measure of Christian community love is the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: The prediction of Peter's denial is embedded within Peter's most confident declaration. He will not only follow Jesus but lay down his life for him. Jesus accepts neither the protest nor the probability: Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you — the triple denial will come before morning. Jesus does not shame Peter but tells the truth that Peter needs to hear: his fidelity rests on a foundation Peter has not yet tested. The testing will come, the failure will happen, and the restoration that follows (ch. 21) will be built on a more honest foundation than confidence ever was.

verseByVerse.quote: After saying these things, Jesus was troubled in his spirit, and testified, "Truly, truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me." The disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After saying these things, Jesus was troubled in his spirit, and testified, “Truly, truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me.” The disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke.

Jesus was troubled in his spirit. The same word as at Lazarus’s tomb (11:33) and in 12:27. Betrayal by a friend cut deep.

And testified. A solemn declaration.

One of you will betray me. “One of you”: one of the Twelve.

The disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke. No one suspected Judas. He had hidden his heart perfectly. The others asked, “Is it I?” (Mark 14:19). A healthy self-suspicion.

In a sentence. Deeply troubled, Jesus solemnly declared that one of them would betray him, and the disciples looked at one another, not knowing whom he meant.

On a Tuesday. Judas seemed no different from the others. Examine your own heart before you suspect others’.

verseByVerse.quote: One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining at table at Jesus' side, so Simon Peter motioned to him to ask Jesus of whom he was speaking.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining at table at Jesus’ side, so Simon Peter motioned to him to ask Jesus of whom he was speaking.

One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved. Key words. The first appearance of “the disciple whom Jesus loved” (19:26; 20:2; 21:7, 20). The Gospel’s author (21:24), almost certainly John, son of Zebedee, who never names himself. He describes himself not by his love for Jesus but by Jesus’ love for him. Not that Jesus didn’t love the others, but John marvels that he was loved.

Was reclining at table at Jesus’ side. Setting and background. Guests reclined on couches, leaning on the left elbow; the one on the host’s right had his head near the host’s chest. Literally “in Jesus’ bosom,” as the Son is in the Father’s bosom (1:18).

So Simon Peter motioned to him to ask Jesus of whom he was speaking. Peter was further away and couldn’t ask quietly.

In a sentence. The disciple Jesus loved was reclining next to him, so Peter signalled to him to ask Jesus who he meant.

For worship. Think of yourself as John did: the one whom Jesus loves. It is true of every believer.
verseByVerse.note: Guests reclined on couches, leaning on the left elbow; the one on the host’s right lay with his head near the host’s chest. The disciple “whom Jesus loved” is traditionally identified as John, the Gospel’s author.

verseByVerse.quote: So that disciple, leaning back against Jesus, said to him, "Lord, who is it?" Jesus answered, "It is he to whom I will give this morsel of bread when I have dipped it." So when he had dipped the morsel, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So that disciple, leaning back against Jesus, said to him, “Lord, who is it?” Jesus answered, “It is he to whom I will give this morsel of bread when I have dipped it.” So when he had dipped the morsel, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.

Leaning back against Jesus. He leans back to whisper.

It is he to whom I will give this morsel of bread when I have dipped it. Setting and background. Handing a guest a dipped morsel was a mark of honour, a special gesture of friendship from the host. Bread was dipped into a common dish, perhaps of bitter herbs or sauce. Judas may have been reclining at Jesus’ left, the place of honour.

So when he had dipped the morsel, he gave it to Judas. A final offer of love. Even now, Jesus reaches out to him. Only John knew the meaning of the gesture.

In a sentence. The disciple leaned back and asked Jesus who it was, and Jesus said it was the one to whom he would give the dipped morsel, and gave it to Judas son of Simon Iscariot.

On a Tuesday. Jesus honoured his betrayer to the end. Love your enemies, and keep offering kindness to those who wrong you.
verseByVerse.note: Handing a guest a dipped morsel was a mark of honour.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after he had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him. Jesus said to him, "What you are going to do, do quickly." Now no one at the table knew why he said this to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then after he had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him. Jesus said to him, “What you are going to do, do quickly.” Now no one at the table knew why he said this to him.

Then after he had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him. Key words. The devil had put the thought into his heart (v. 2). Now, as Judas takes the gift of love and rejects it, Satan takes full control (Luke 22:3). Refused love hardens. Judas is not a puppet; he chose, and his choice gave Satan entry.

What you are going to do, do quickly. Jesus is in control. He sets the timing of his own betrayal.

Now no one at the table knew why he said this to him. Even John didn’t yet put it together.

In a sentence. When Judas took the morsel, Satan entered him, and Jesus told him to do quickly what he was going to do, though no one at the table understood why.

For worship. Even the hour of betrayal was under Christ’s command. Nothing in your life is out of his hands.

verseByVerse.quote: Some thought that, because Judas had the moneybag, Jesus was telling him, "Buy what we need for the feast," or that he should give something to the poor. So, after receiving the morsel of bread, he immediately went out. And it was night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some thought that, because Judas had the moneybag, Jesus was telling him, “Buy what we need for the feast,” or that he should give something to the poor. So, after receiving the morsel of bread, he immediately went out. And it was night.

Some thought that, because Judas had the moneybag. He was the treasurer (12:6).

Buy what we need for the feast. For the rest of the Passover week, perhaps.

Or that he should give something to the poor. Giving to the poor at Passover was a custom. Jesus’ group gave regularly.

So, after receiving the morsel of bread, he immediately went out. He leaves the light.

And it was night. Key words. Four words, full of meaning. Literally night: it was dark outside. But spiritually, Judas walked out of the presence of the light of the world into the darkness (3:19; 11:10; 12:35). He went out into night, and night went into him.

In a sentence. Some thought Jesus was telling Judas, the treasurer, to buy supplies or give to the poor, but he took the bread, went out at once, and it was night.

On a Tuesday. To leave Christ is to walk into the night. Stay near the light.
verseByVerse.note: Giving to the poor at Passover was a custom.

parallels.desc: send portions to anyone who has nothing ready
the power of darkness

verseByVerse.quote: When he had gone out, Jesus said, "Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him. If God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and glorify him at once."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he had gone out, Jesus said, “Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him. If God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and glorify him at once.”

When he had gone out. The betrayer gone, the events are set in motion.

Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him. Key words. “Glorified” five times in two verses. With Judas gone, the cross is certain, and Jesus speaks of it as already done. The cross is the glory of the Son: there his love, obedience and holiness shine most brightly. And it is the glory of the Father: there God’s justice and mercy are both displayed (Romans 3:25–26).

If God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and glorify him at once. The Father will respond by glorifying the Son in his own presence: the resurrection and ascension. “At once”: very soon.

In a sentence. When Judas had gone, Jesus said the Son of Man was now glorified, and God was glorified in him, and God would glorify him in himself, at once.

For worship. Look at the cross and see the glory of God. Nowhere does it shine more brightly.

verseByVerse.quote: "Little children, yet a little while I am with you. You will seek me, and just as I said to the Jews, so now I also say to you, 'Where I am going you cannot come.' A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Little children, yet a little while I am with you. You will seek me, and just as I said to the Jews, so now I also say to you, ‘Where I am going you cannot come.’ A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another.

Little children. “Little children” (teknia): a tender word, used only here in John’s Gospel, and often in 1 John. Like a father about to leave his children.

Yet a little while I am with you. A few hours.

Where I am going you cannot come. As he told the Jews (7:34; 8:21). But for the disciples there is a difference: not yet (v. 36).

A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Key words. Setting and background. Love of neighbour was old (Leviticus 19:18). What is new? The new standard is “as I have loved you”: the love that washes feet and lays down its life. And the new community: a family of disciples bound to one another in Christ. And the new covenant, of which this is the law (Jeremiah 31:33). The Latin for “commandment,” mandatum, gives us “Maundy Thursday.”

Just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another. His love is both the pattern and the power for ours (1 John 4:19).

In a sentence. Jesus told his little children he would be with them only a little longer, and they could not come where he was going, and gave them a new commandment, to love one another as he had loved them.

On a Tuesday. Measure your love for other Christians against his love for you. Then ask him for more.
verseByVerse.note: Love of neighbour was old; the new standard is “as I have loved you.”

verseByVerse.quote: "By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another." Simon Peter said to him, "Lord, where are you going?" Jesus answered him, "Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward."
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another. Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus answered him, “Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward.”

By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another. Key words. The mark of a Christian community before the watching world is not first its doctrine, buildings or programmes, but its love. The second-century writer Tertullian reported that pagans said of Christians, “See how they love one another.” This is the church’s great apologetic.

Lord, where are you going? Peter skips over the commandment to ask about Jesus’ departure.

Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward. Peter will follow later: in death, as a martyr (21:18–19), and into glory.

In a sentence. Jesus said all people would know they were his disciples by their love for one another, and when Peter asked where he was going, said Peter could not follow now, but would later.

For worship. Let the world see Christ in your love for his people.

parallels.desc: the death by which Peter would glorify God

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said to him, "Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you." Jesus answered, "Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you, the rooster will not crow till you have denied me three times."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter said to him, “Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.” Jesus answered, “Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you, the rooster will not crow till you have denied me three times.”

Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you. Peter means it. He will draw a sword in the garden (18:10). But he doesn’t know his own weakness.

Will you lay down your life for me? Gently, Jesus echoes his words. The irony: Peter says he will lay down his life for Jesus; in fact, Jesus will lay down his life for Peter (10:11).

The rooster will not crow till you have denied me three times. Before dawn. Roosters crowed in the early morning; the Romans called the watch from midnight to three “cockcrow.” Peter’s denials follow in 18:15–27. And yet Jesus doesn’t give up on him. He prays for him (Luke 22:32) and restores him with three questions (21:15–17).

In a sentence. Peter asked why he couldn’t follow now and promised to die for Jesus, and Jesus asked if he really would, and said that before the rooster crowed Peter would deny him three times.

On a Tuesday. Don’t trust your own strength. Trust the one who laid down his life for you, and who keeps you even when you fail.

He laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist.<sup>5</sup>Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.<sup>6</sup>He came to Simon Peter, who said to him, “Lord, do you wash my feet?”<sup>7</sup>Jesus answered him, “What I am doing you do not understand now, but afterward you will understand.”<sup>8</sup>Peter said to him, “You shall never wash my feet.” Jesus answered him, “If I do not wash you, you have no share with me.”<sup>9</sup>Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, not my feet only but also my hands and my head!”<sup>10</sup>Jesus said to him, “The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean. And you are clean, but not every one of you.”<sup>11</sup>For he knew who was to betray him; that was why he said, “Not all of you are clean.”<sup>12</sup>When he had washed their feet and put on his outer garments and resumed his place, he said to them, “Do you understand what I have done to you?<sup>13</sup>You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am.<sup>14</sup>If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.<sup>15</sup>For I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you.<sup>16</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him.<sup>17</sup>If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.<sup>18</sup>I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But the Scripture will be fulfilled, ’He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me.’<sup>19</sup>I am telling you this now, before it takes place, that when it does take place you may believe that I am he.<sup>20</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever receives the one I send receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me.”<sup>21</sup>After saying these things, Jesus was troubled in his spirit, and testified, “Truly, truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me.”<sup>22</sup>The disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke.<sup>23</sup>One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining at table at Jesus’ side,<sup>24</sup>so Simon Peter motioned to him to ask Jesus of whom he was speaking.<sup>25</sup>So that disciple, leaning back against Jesus, said to him, “Lord, who is it?”<sup>26</sup>Jesus answered, “It is he to whom I will give this morsel of bread when I have dipped it.” So when he had dipped the morsel, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.<sup>27</sup>Then after he had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him. Jesus said to him, “What you are going to do, do quickly.”<sup>28</sup>Now no one at the table knew why he said this to him.<sup>29</sup>Some thought that, because Judas had the moneybag, Jesus was telling him, “Buy what we need for the feast,” or that he should give something to the poor.<sup>30</sup>So, after receiving the morsel of bread, he immediately went out. And it was night.<sup>31</sup>When he had gone out, Jesus said, “Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him.<sup>32</sup>If God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and glorify him at once.<sup>33</sup>Little children, yet a little while I am with you. You will seek me, and just as I said to the Jews, so now I also say to you, ’Where I am going you cannot come.’<sup>34</sup>A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another.<sup>35</sup>By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”<sup>36</sup>Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus answered him, “Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward.”<sup>37</sup>Peter said to him, “Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.”<sup>38</sup>Jesus answered, “Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you, the rooster will not crow till you have denied me three times.
13.overview:
With chapter 13 the “book of glory” begins. The public ministry is over; for five chapters Jesus is alone with his disciples on the night before he dies, in what is often called the Upper Room or Farewell Discourse (13–17). John opens it with a sentence that sums up the cross: having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, Jesus rises from supper, ties a towel round his waist and washes his disciples’ feet, the task of a slave. Peter protests, then asks to be washed all over; Jesus explains that one who has bathed needs only his feet washed, and that unless he washes Peter, Peter has no share with him. He tells them he has given them an example: as their Lord and Teacher has served them, they must serve one another.

Then Jesus, troubled, announces that one of them will betray him. At Peter’s prompting the disciple whom Jesus loved asks who it is; Jesus gives a morsel of bread to Judas, Satan enters him, and Judas goes out: “and it was night.” With the betrayer gone, Jesus speaks of his glorification and gives his disciples a new commandment: to love one another as he has loved them, so that all people will know they are his disciples. When Peter vows to lay down his life for him, Jesus foretells that before the rooster crows Peter will deny him three times. The chapter holds together the humility of Christ, the treachery of a friend, the weakness of the boldest disciple, and a love that does not let go.

14.title: I Am the Way, the Truth, and the Life

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Way to the Father
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus calms his troubled disciples: as they trust God, they should trust him. In his Father’s house there is ample room, and he goes to prepare a place and will return to take them to himself. Thomas protests that they do not know the way; Jesus replies that he is the way, the truth and the life, the only route to the Father. To know him is to know the Father. When Philip asks to see the Father, Jesus says that anyone who has seen him has seen the Father, for the Father lives in him and does his works through him. Believers will do the same works and greater, because he is going to the Father, and he will do whatever they ask in his name for the Father’s glory.
verseByVerse.theology: I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me is both comfort and exclusivity. Comfort: there is a way to the Father, it is real, it is accessible, it is Jesus. Exclusivity: this is the only way, and all other paths are paths that do not lead to the Father. The exclusivity is not arrogance; it is the necessary consequence of the incarnation. If God has come in one place, in one person, for one purpose, then there is one way home. The scandal of particularity cannot be removed without removing the gospel itself.
verseByVerse.examples: Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do (v. 13). Prayer in Jesus' name is not a formula attached to the end of requests; it is prayer aligned with his character, his purposes, and his glory. To ask in Jesus' name is to ask as he would ask, for what he would ask for, in the way that honors the Father through the Son. This is why prayer in Jesus' name is effective: it brings human desire into alignment with divine will, and divine will always accomplishes its purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let not your hearts be troubled. Believe in God; believe also in me. In my Father's house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let not your hearts be troubled. Believe in God; believe also in me. In my Father’s house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you?

Meaning first. John 14 is Jesus’ comfort to frightened disciples. He has just told them he is leaving, that one of them will betray him, and that Peter will deny him. Now he tells them why they need not be troubled: he is going to prepare a place for them, he is the way to the Father, he will send the Spirit, and he gives them his peace. It is one of the most loved chapters in the Bible, read at countless funerals.

Let not your hearts be troubled. Key words. “Troubled” (tarassesthō): stirred up, agitated. The same word used of Jesus himself (11:33; 12:27; 13:21). He was troubled so that they need not be. “Hearts” is plural, but “heart” in Greek is singular: the shared heart of the group.

Believe in God; believe also in me. The Greek can be read as commands or statements. Most likely: keep trusting God, and keep trusting me. Jesus puts faith in himself alongside faith in God. No mere man could say this.

In my Father’s house are many rooms. “Rooms” (monai): dwelling places, from the verb “abide” (menō). The old translation “mansions” comes from the Latin mansiones, which simply meant dwellings. The picture is of a great family house with room for all the children. “Many”: there is room enough for all his people.

If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you? The ESV notes an alternative reading of verse 2: “if it were not so, I would have told you; for I go to prepare a place for you.” Either way, the point is that Jesus would never mislead them. He is going ahead to make ready.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples not to be troubled, but to trust God and him, for there are many rooms in his Father’s house, and he is going to prepare a place for them.

For worship. There is a room in the Father’s house with your name on it. Christ has gone to prepare it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes an alternative reading of verse 2: “if it were not so, I would have told you, for I go to prepare a place for you.” Family houses were often extended with rooms as the family grew.

parallels.desc: I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever

verseByVerse.quote: "And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also. And you know the way to where I am going."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also. And you know the way to where I am going.

And if I go and prepare a place for you. How does he prepare it? By his death, resurrection and ascension, he opens the way into the Father’s presence (Hebrews 6:19–20; 9:24). The place is prepared by the cross.

I will come again and will take you to myself. Key words. A clear promise of the second coming. Some also see here his coming to each believer at death, or his coming by the Spirit (v. 18). The primary meaning is his visible return at the end of the age (Acts 1:11; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17).

That where I am you may be also. The heart of heaven is not the place, but the person. To be with Christ is the joy of heaven (17:24; Philippians 1:23).

Where Christians differ: the coming again and the rapture. Dispensationalists see this as a secret “rapture” before a seven-year tribulation, distinct from Christ’s visible return. Verdict: Scripture speaks of one return of Christ, visible, glorious, and final, at which the dead are raised, believers caught up to meet him, and the world judged (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). There is no secret rapture. The Lord comes once, and takes his people to be with him for ever.

And you know the way to where I am going. They know him, and he is the way (v. 6).

In a sentence. Jesus said that if he went to prepare a place for them, he would come again and take them to himself, so that they would be where he is, and they knew the way.

On a Tuesday. Heaven is where Jesus is. The best thing about it is him.

verseByVerse.quote: Thomas said to him, "Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?" Jesus said to him, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thomas said to him, “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?” Jesus said to him, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.”

Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way? Honest Thomas (11:16; 20:25). He doesn’t pretend to understand.

I am the way, and the truth, and the life. Key words. This is the sixth of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John. Not “I show the way,” but “I am the way.” Jesus doesn’t point to a road; he is the road. “The truth”: he is the reality of God revealed (1:14, 17). “The life”: he is the source of eternal life (1:4; 11:25). The way is the main idea; truth and life explain why he is the way: because he is the truth about God and the life of God.

No one comes to the Father except through me. Key words. One of the most exclusive statements in Scripture. There are not many ways to God. There is one, Jesus Christ (Acts 4:12; 1 Timothy 2:5).

Where Christians differ: are there other ways to God? Many today hold that all religions lead to God (pluralism), or that people may be saved through Christ without knowing him, by following the light they have (inclusivism). Verdict: “no one” leaves no exceptions, and Acts 4:12 says there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved. Salvation is through conscious faith in Christ (Romans 10:13–17). This is why the church must send missionaries. It is not arrogance to say this; it is what Jesus himself said. And the way is open to anyone, from any background, who comes through him.

In a sentence. When Thomas said they didn’t know where he was going or the way, Jesus answered that he is the way, the truth and the life, and no one comes to the Father except through him.

For worship. Christ is not one way among many. He is the way, and the door is wide open.
verseByVerse.note: This is the sixth of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

parallels.desc: no other name
the Way

verseByVerse.quote: "If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on you do know him and have seen him." Philip said to him, "Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on you do know him and have seen him. Philip said to him, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.”

If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. To know Jesus is to know the Father (8:19).

From now on you do know him and have seen him. “From now on”: from the coming hour of the cross and resurrection. They have seen the Father in seeing Jesus.

Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us. Philip wants a vision of God, like Moses asking to see God’s glory (Exodus 33:18). He means it sincerely. But he doesn’t realise the Father has been in front of him all along.

In a sentence. Jesus said that if they had known him, they would have known his Father, and from now on they did, and Philip asked him to show them the Father, which would be enough.

On a Tuesday. You don’t need a vision. You have Jesus. To know him is to know God.

parallels.desc: please show me your glory

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. How can you say, 'Show us the Father'? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to him, “Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works.

Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? A gentle rebuke, with a hint of sadness. Three years together.

Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. Key words. One of the greatest claims in Scripture. Jesus is the exact image of the Father (Colossians 1:15; Hebrews 1:3). Not that Jesus is the Father: they are distinct persons. But the Father is fully revealed in the Son. Do you want to know what God is like? Look at Jesus: his compassion, his holiness, his tears at the tomb, his anger at the temple, his hands washing feet, his body on the cross.

Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? Mutual indwelling (10:38).

The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works. His words and works are the Father’s words and works.

In a sentence. Jesus asked Philip whether he still didn’t know him after so long, for whoever has seen him has seen the Father, since he is in the Father and the Father in him, doing his works.

For worship. When you see Jesus, you see God. Look long at him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me, or else believe on account of the works themselves. Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me, or else believe on account of the works themselves. Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father.

Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me. Believe his word.

Or else believe on account of the works themselves. And if not, believe the evidence of his works.

Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do. Believers will continue Jesus’ work.

And greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father. Key words. “Greater works” refers to the worldwide spread of the gospel after Pentecost. Not greater in kind: no one has done anything greater than raising Lazarus. But greater in extent and effect: at Pentecost three thousand were saved in one day, more than in Jesus’ whole earthly ministry; and the gospel went to the nations. And greater because it belongs to the new age: the age of the Spirit, after the cross. Jesus’ going to the Father makes it possible, because he will send the Spirit (16:7).

Where Christians differ: greater works and miracles. Some take this as a promise that every believer can do greater miracles than Jesus. Verdict: no believer has ever done greater miracles than Jesus; the promise must mean something else. The greater works are the saving works of the Spirit through the gospel, bringing people from death to life. Miraculous sign gifts accompanied the apostles to confirm their message (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12), and ceased with the apostolic age. But the greatest work, new birth, goes on wherever the gospel is preached.

In a sentence. Jesus told them to believe him, or at least his works, and said that whoever believes in him will do his works, and greater works, because he is going to the Father.

On a Tuesday. When you share the gospel and someone is born again, that is a greater work than healing a body. Take part in it.
verseByVerse.note: “Greater works” refers to the worldwide spread of the gospel after the Spirit came.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it.

Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do. Key words. Praying “in my name” means praying as his representatives, according to his will and for his glory (1 John 5:14). It is not a magic formula added to the end of a prayer. In the ancient world a person’s name stood for his character and authority. To pray in Jesus’ name is to come to the Father on the basis of who Jesus is and what he has done, and to ask what he would ask.

That the Father may be glorified in the Son. The purpose of prayer: the Father’s glory.

If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it. “Ask me”: prayer to Jesus himself, as well as to the Father. Prayer to Christ is right, because he is God (Acts 7:59).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we can get anything we want by saying “in Jesus’ name.” Prayer in his name is prayer shaped by his will and aimed at the Father’s glory.

In a sentence. Jesus promised that whatever they asked in his name he would do, so that the Father would be glorified in the Son.

For worship. Pray boldly in Jesus’ name. Ask for what will glorify the Father, and he will do it.
verseByVerse.note: Praying “in my name” means praying as his representatives, according to his will.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–31 — The Promise of the Spirit and the Peace of Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love for Jesus shows itself in obeying him. He will ask the Father to give them another Helper, the Spirit of truth, who will stay with them for ever. The world cannot receive him, but they know him, for he lives with them and will be in them. Jesus will not leave them orphaned; he will come to them. Soon the world will not see him, but they will, and because he lives, they will live. Then they will know that he is in the Father, they in him and he in them. Whoever keeps his commands loves him and will be loved by the Father, and Jesus will show himself to them. Judas (not Iscariot) asks why he will reveal himself to them and not the world. Jesus replies that he and the Father will come and make their home with anyone who loves him and keeps his word. The Spirit, sent in his name, will teach them everything and remind them of all he said. He leaves them his peace, unlike the world’s, so they need not be troubled or afraid. If they loved him, they would be glad he is going to the Father, who is greater than he. He tells them now so they will believe when it happens. The ruler of this world is coming, but has no hold on him; he goes to show the world that he loves the Father and does what he commands. Then he tells them to get up and leave.
verseByVerse.theology: The Helper (Parakletos — Advocate, Comforter, Counselor) is described with four characteristics in the farewell discourse: he is the Spirit of truth (14:17), the Holy Spirit who teaches and reminds (14:26), the Spirit who testifies about Jesus (15:26), and the one who convicts the world (16:8). Each characteristic is an aspect of the single mission: to continue and apply what Jesus accomplished. The Spirit does not bring new revelation beyond Jesus but illuminates everything Jesus said and did, making it present and personal to each generation of believers.
verseByVerse.examples: My peace I give to you: not as the world gives. The world's peace is the absence of conflict, the management of anxiety, the temporary resolution of problems. Jesus' peace is an interior stability that coexists with external trouble — the shalom of the covenant, the wholeness that comes from being right with God and secure in his love. Not as the world gives: the two kinds of peace are not on the same spectrum; one is the presence of order, the other is the presence of God. The disciples will need this peace before the night is over.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you love me, you will keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you love me, you will keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever,

If you love me, you will keep my commandments. Key words. Love shows itself in obedience (vv. 21, 23; 1 John 5:3). Not obedience to earn love, but obedience as the fruit of love. “Keep” (tērēsete): guard, treasure, obey.

And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper. Key words. “Helper” (Paraklētos): the ESV notes that “Helper” can also be rendered “Advocate” or “Counselor.” Literally, one called alongside: someone who comes to stand with you, to help, comfort, plead for you, and speak for you. “Another” (allon): another of the same kind. Jesus has been their Helper; the Spirit will be another like him. This shows that the Spirit is a person, not a force: Jesus would not compare himself to a power. Note the Trinity: the Son asks, the Father gives, the Spirit comes.

To be with you forever. Unlike Jesus’ earthly presence, which is about to end, the Spirit will never leave them.

In a sentence. Jesus said that if they loved him they would keep his commandments, and he would ask the Father, who would give them another Helper to be with them for ever.

On a Tuesday. You are never alone. The Helper is beside you, and in you, today and for ever.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Helper” can also be rendered “Advocate” or “Counselor.” “Another” implies one like Jesus himself.

parallels.desc: an advocate with the Father

verseByVerse.quote: "even the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you. I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
even the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you. I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you.

Even the Spirit of truth. He is the Spirit who brings and teaches the truth, Christ (15:26; 16:13).

Whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. The unbelieving world has no capacity to receive him (1 Corinthians 2:14).

You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you. “With you” now, in the person of Jesus and his ministry; “in you” after Pentecost, dwelling within. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “and is in you.” The difference is small; the future reading fits the context of Jesus’ promise better.

I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you. Key words. “Orphans” (orphanous): disciples without their teacher were sometimes called orphans. “I will come to you”: in the resurrection appearances (v. 19), and by the Spirit, who brings Christ’s presence (v. 23). Christ comes to his people in the Spirit.

In a sentence. The Helper is the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, but whom the disciples know, for he is with them and will be in them; Jesus will not leave them orphans but will come to them.

For worship. You are not an orphan. Christ has come to you by his Spirit.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “and is in you.”

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet a little while and the world will see me no more, but you will see me. Because I live, you also will live. In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet a little while and the world will see me no more, but you will see me. Because I live, you also will live. In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you.

Yet a little while and the world will see me no more. After his death, the world will not see him again until he returns.

But you will see me. In the resurrection appearances, and by faith.

Because I live, you also will live. Key words. His resurrection life is the source and guarantee of theirs. “I live” (present tense): he is the living one, even facing death. Our life is bound to his.

In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you. “That day” is the day of resurrection and Pentecost. Three circles of union: the Son in the Father, believers in the Son, the Son in believers. Union with Christ is the heart of the Christian life. We are drawn into the fellowship of the Trinity (17:21–23).

In a sentence. Jesus said that soon the world would not see him, but they would, and because he lives they would live, and on that day they would know that he is in the Father, they in him, and he in them.

On a Tuesday. Because he lives, you will live. Nothing can break that link.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him." Judas (not Iscariot) said to him, "Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him. Judas (not Iscariot) said to him, “Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world?”

Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. Having them (knowing them) and keeping them (doing them).

And he who loves me will be loved by my Father. Not that the Father’s love is earned, but that those who love Christ experience the Father’s love in a special, intimate way.

And I will love him and manifest myself to him. “Manifest” (emphanisō): reveal, make visible. Jesus makes himself known to those who love him.

Judas (not Iscariot). This Judas is Judas the son of James, probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark’s lists (Luke 6:16; Matthew 10:3). John is careful to say he is not the betrayer.

Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world? He expects the Messiah to show himself publicly to the world. Why only to them?

In a sentence. Jesus said that whoever keeps his commandments loves him and will be loved by the Father, and he will reveal himself to him, and Judas (not Iscariot) asked why he would reveal himself to them and not to the world.

For worship. Christ shows himself to those who love him. Love him, and he will make himself more and more real to you.
verseByVerse.note: This Judas is Judas the son of James, probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him. Whoever does not love me does not keep my words. And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father's who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
