Jesus answered him, “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him. Whoever does not love me does not keep my words. And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father’s who sent me.

If anyone loves me, he will keep my word. Jesus answers indirectly. He reveals himself to those who love him and keep his word; the world neither loves nor obeys.

And my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him. Key words. “Home” (monē): the same word as the “rooms” in v. 2. Jesus goes to prepare a dwelling for us in the Father’s house; meanwhile the Father and the Son come to make their dwelling in us. “We”: the Father and Son, by the Spirit. The whole Trinity dwells in the believer. Every believer is a temple of God (1 Corinthians 3:16; 6:19).

Whoever does not love me does not keep my words. The other side.

And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father’s who sent me. To reject Christ’s word is to reject the Father’s.

In a sentence. Jesus answered that whoever loves him keeps his word, and the Father will love him, and they will come and make their home with him; whoever does not love him does not keep his words, which are the Father’s.

On a Tuesday. God makes his home in you. Keep the house ready for such guests.

parallels.desc: my dwelling place shall be with them

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I have spoken to you while I am still with you. But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
These things I have spoken to you while I am still with you. But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you.

These things I have spoken to you while I am still with you. They have heard much they don’t yet understand.

But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name. The Father sends him in the Son’s name: as the Son’s representative, to continue his work.

He will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you. Key words. A promise especially to the apostles. The Spirit would remind them of all Jesus said, and teach them its meaning. This is the basis of the New Testament: the Gospels were written by men whom the Spirit helped to remember (the Spirit’s work of inspiration, 2 Peter 1:21), and the letters by men whom he taught. We have the apostles’ testimony in Scripture because of this promise.

Where Christians differ: the Spirit’s teaching today. Some claim the Spirit gives new revelation today, beyond Scripture. Verdict: the promise is first to the apostles, and was fulfilled in the New Testament, which is complete and sufficient (Jude 3; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). The Spirit still teaches every believer, not by new revelation, but by illuminating the Scripture he inspired. The canon is closed; the Spirit opens our eyes to it.

In a sentence. Jesus said that he had spoken these things while still with them, but the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father would send in his name, would teach them all things and remind them of everything he had said.

For worship. Thank God for the New Testament, the Spirit’s gift through the apostles. Ask him to teach you as you read it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid. You heard me say to you, 'I am going away, and I will come to you.' If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid. You heard me say to you, ‘I am going away, and I will come to you.’ If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I.

Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Key words. Setting and background. “Peace” (shalom) was the everyday greeting and farewell. But Jesus gives far more than a greeting. His peace is wholeness, right relationship with God, the calm that comes from reconciliation (Romans 5:1; Philippians 4:7). It is his last will and testament: what he leaves them.

Not as the world gives do I give to you. The world’s peace is the absence of trouble, and it doesn’t last. Christ’s peace holds in the middle of trouble (16:33).

Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid. The chapter returns to its start (v. 1).

If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father. His going is gain for him: return to glory.

For the Father is greater than I. Key words. “The Father is greater than I.” How can this be, if the Son is equal with God (5:18; 10:30)? Not greater in nature or being, but greater in position: in his incarnation and earthly mission, the Son took the role of a servant, and the Father sent him. Now he returns to the glory he had with the Father (17:5). The Son is equal in essence, but submits in role.

Where Christians differ. Arians in the fourth century, and Jehovah’s Witnesses today, cite this verse to show that the Son is a lesser being. Verdict: the same Gospel calls him God (1:1; 20:28). This verse speaks of his incarnate state, as the one sent; “greater” refers to role and position, not essence. A son can be equal to his father in nature and still honour his father as the head of the house. Athanasius and the Nicene Creed held both truths together.

In a sentence. Jesus gave them his peace, unlike the world’s, telling them not to be troubled or afraid, and that if they loved him they would rejoice that he was going to the Father, who is greater than he.

On a Tuesday. Christ’s peace doesn’t depend on your circumstances. Receive it today, in the middle of whatever troubles you.
verseByVerse.note: “Peace” (shalom) was the everyday greeting and farewell. “The Father is greater” speaks of the Son in his humble human state, not a lesser divine nature.

parallels.desc: the LORD give you peace

verseByVerse.quote: "And now I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe. I will no longer talk much with you, for the ruler of this world is coming. He has no claim on me,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe. I will no longer talk much with you, for the ruler of this world is coming. He has no claim on me,

And now I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe. As in 13:19. His foreknowledge will strengthen their faith.

I will no longer talk much with you, for the ruler of this world is coming. Satan comes through Judas and the soldiers (13:27; 18:3).

He has no claim on me. Key words. Literally “in me he has nothing.” Satan has no hold on Jesus, no foothold of sin, no legal claim. Jesus is sinless. The devil has a claim on every sinner, for the wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23). On Jesus he has none. So Jesus doesn’t die because Satan has power over him, but freely, for love of the Father.

In a sentence. Jesus said he had told them beforehand so that they would believe, and he would not talk much more, for the ruler of this world was coming, but had no claim on him.

For worship. The devil had no claim on Christ. Because Christ is yours, the devil has no claim on you either (Romans 8:33–34).

verseByVerse.quote: "but I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father. Rise, let us go from here."
verseByVerse.commentary:
but I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father. Rise, let us go from here.

But I do as the Father has commanded me. Jesus goes to the cross in obedience to the Father.

So that the world may know that I love the Father. Key words. The only place in the Gospels where Jesus says he loves the Father. The cross is the proof. His obedience unto death shows the world the love of the Son for the Father.

Rise, let us go from here. Some think they left the upper room here, with chapters 15–17 spoken on the way to the garden, perhaps passing the vines on the slopes or the golden vine on the temple gate (15:1). Others think they rose but lingered. Chapter 18:1 says they went out across the Kidron. Either is possible.

In a sentence. Jesus said he would do as the Father commanded, so the world would know he loves the Father, and told them to get up and leave.

On a Tuesday. Love for God shows itself in obedience, even costly obedience. Rise, and go where he sends you.
verseByVerse.note: Some think they left the upper room here, with chapters 15–17 spoken on the way; others that they rose but stayed.

14.text: <sup>1</sup>“Let not your hearts be troubled. Believe in God; believe also in me.<sup>2</sup>In my Father’s house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you?<sup>3</sup>And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also.<sup>4</sup>And you know the way to where I am going.”<sup>5</sup>Thomas said to him, “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?”<sup>6</sup>Jesus said to him, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.<sup>7</sup>If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on you do know him and have seen him.”<sup>8</sup>Philip said to him, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.”<sup>9</sup>Jesus said to him, “Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. How can you say, ’Show us the Father’?<sup>10</sup>Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works.<sup>11</sup>Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me, or else believe on account of the works themselves.<sup>12</sup>“Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father.<sup>13</sup>Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son.<sup>14</sup>If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it.<sup>15</sup>“If you love me, you will keep my commandments.<sup>16</sup>And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever,<sup>17</sup>even the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you.<sup>18</sup>“I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you.<sup>19</sup>Yet a little while and the world will see me no more, but you will see me. Because I live, you also will live.<sup>20</sup>In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you.<sup>21</sup>Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.”<sup>22</sup>Judas (not Iscariot) said to him, “Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world?”<sup>23</sup>Jesus answered him, “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him.<sup>24</sup>Whoever does not love me does not keep my words. And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father’s who sent me.<sup>25</sup>“These things I have spoken to you while I am still with you.<sup>26</sup>But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you.<sup>27</sup>Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid.<sup>28</sup>You heard me say to you, ’I am going away, and I will come to you.’ If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I.<sup>29</sup>And now I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe.<sup>30</sup>I will no longer talk much with you, for the ruler of this world is coming. He has no claim on me,<sup>31</sup>but I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father. Rise, let us go from here.
14.overview:
Jesus has just told his friends that he is leaving, that one of them will betray him and that Peter will deny him. Into their fear he speaks some of the most comforting words in Scripture: “Let not your hearts be troubled.” He is going to prepare a place for them in his Father’s house and will come again to take them to himself. When Thomas asks the way, Jesus answers, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” When Philip asks to see the Father, Jesus replies that whoever has seen him has seen the Father. Those who believe will do greater works, because he is going to the Father, and whatever they ask in his name he will do.

The second half of the chapter introduces the Holy Spirit as “another Helper”, the Spirit of truth, who will be with them for ever and in them. Jesus will not leave them as orphans; he will come to them, and he and the Father will make their home with those who love him and keep his word. The Spirit will teach them all things and remind them of everything Jesus said, the promise that underlies the writing of the New Testament. He leaves them his peace, not as the world gives. The ruler of this world is coming, but has no claim on him; Jesus goes to the cross so that the world may know that he loves the Father. Here the doctrine of the Trinity is not argued but lived: the Father sends, the Son goes and prays, the Spirit comes, and all three make their home with the believer.

15.title: The True Vine

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — Abide in Me: The Vine and the Branches
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus calls himself the true vine, with his Father as the gardener who removes fruitless branches and prunes fruitful ones to make them more productive. The disciples are already made clean by his word. They must stay joined to him, for no branch bears fruit cut off from the vine, and without him they can achieve nothing; branches that do not remain are thrown out to wither and burn. If his words remain in them, their prayers will be answered, and their abundant fruit will glorify the Father and prove them disciples. He has loved them as the Father loves him, and they remain in his love by obeying him, as he obeys the Father, so that his joy may fill them. His command is that they love one another as he has loved them; the highest love gives its life for friends. They are his friends, not mere servants, for he has shared with them all he heard from the Father. He chose them, not they him, and appointed them to bear fruit that lasts.
verseByVerse.theology: I am the true vine: Israel was the vine God planted (Ps. 80:8; Isa. 5:1-7; Jer. 2:21; Ezek. 15; Hos. 10:1). Israel repeatedly failed as the vine. Jesus is the vine Israel was always meant to be — the true Israel, the faithful son, the one who bears fruit that lasts. The disciples are branches in this vine: their fruitfulness is entirely dependent on their connection to Jesus. Apart from me you can do nothing is the Reformed doctrine of total human dependence stated for the community of disciples. The branch does not produce fruit; it bears fruit — the distinction between human effort and Spirit-mediated connection.
verseByVerse.examples: You did not choose me, but I chose you (v. 16): the elective basis of discipleship. The disciples' following of Jesus is traced back to his choosing, not their decision. This does not make the disciples passive; they are appointed to go and bear fruit. But the initiative, the foundation, and the guarantee of fruitfulness reside in the one who chose, not in those who were chosen. Whatever fruit the Christian life produces is the fruit of the Vine, borne through the branches who abide.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit.

Meaning first. John 15 teaches what life in Christ looks like after he has gone. First, the vine and the branches: union with Christ, from which all fruit flows (vv. 1–17). Then the world’s hatred, which his people must expect (vv. 18–27). Abiding in Christ, loving one another, and bearing witness in a hostile world: that is the Christian life.

I am the true vine. Key words. The seventh and last “I am” saying in John. Setting and background. The vine was a familiar picture of Israel, planted by God but often fruitless (Psalm 80:8–16; Isaiah 5:1–7; Jeremiah 2:21; Ezekiel 15; Hosea 10:1). A great golden vine decorated the entrance to the temple. Israel was meant to be God’s fruitful vine, and failed. Jesus is the “true” (alēthinē) vine: the real Israel, the one who bears the fruit Israel didn’t. To belong to God’s people is to be joined to him.

And my Father is the vinedresser. “Vinedresser” (geōrgos): farmer, gardener. The Father tends the vine.

Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away. Who are these fruitless branches “in” the vine? In context, Judas is the clearest example: outwardly attached to Christ, a disciple, but never truly united to him by faith. Some take “takes away” (airei) as “lifts up,” as a vinedresser lifts trailing branches off the ground; but v. 6 makes clear that fruitless branches are removed and burned.

And every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit. “Prunes” (kathairei): cleans, cuts back. A play on words with “clean” in v. 3. Pruning hurts, but it makes a vine more fruitful. The Father uses trials, discipline and his word to cut away what hinders fruit (Hebrews 12:5–11).

In a sentence. Jesus said he is the true vine and his Father the vinedresser, who removes every branch in him that bears no fruit and prunes every fruitful branch so that it bears more.

On a Tuesday. If you are being pruned, it means you are bearing fruit, and the Father wants more. Trust the gardener’s knife.
verseByVerse.note: The vine was a familiar picture of Israel, planted by God but often fruitless; Jesus is the true vine. This is the seventh of his “I am” sayings in John. Vinedressers cut away dead wood and pruned living branches hard.

parallels.desc: a vine brought out of Egypt
the vineyard that yielded wild grapes
discipline yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: "Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me.

Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you. “Clean” (katharoi): the eleven have been cleansed by receiving his word in faith (13:10). Judas has gone.

Abide in me, and I in you. Key words. “Abide” (menō) appears eleven times in vv. 1–10. Remain, stay, live in. It is both a command and a promise. The believer is already in Christ; now he must stay there, living in conscious dependence on him. And Christ lives in him. How do we abide? By keeping his word in us (v. 7), keeping his commandments (v. 10), prayer, and resting in his love (v. 9).

As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you. A branch doesn’t produce fruit by effort. It bears fruit by staying connected to the life of the vine. All fruit comes from the life of Christ flowing through us.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples they were already clean by his word, and must abide in him as he in them, for no branch can bear fruit unless it remains in the vine.

For worship. You don’t have to manufacture fruit. Stay close to Christ, and his life will bear it in you.

parallels.desc: the washing of water with the word

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing. If anyone does not abide in me he is thrown away like a branch and withers; and the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing. If anyone does not abide in me he is thrown away like a branch and withers; and the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned.

I am the vine; you are the branches. Simple and clear.

Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit. “Much fruit”: not a little, but abundant. What is the fruit? Christlike character, the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23); obedience (v. 10); love (v. 12); joy (v. 11); answered prayer (v. 7); and people brought to Christ (4:36; Romans 1:13).

For apart from me you can do nothing. Key words. “Nothing” of spiritual value. A humbling truth. All our gifts, efforts and plans produce nothing that lasts without him. And an encouraging one: with him, everything is possible (Philippians 4:13).

If anyone does not abide in me he is thrown away like a branch and withers. Setting and background. Vine wood is useless for building; pruned branches were burned (Ezekiel 15:2–5). It is good for nothing else.

And the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned. A picture of final judgment (Matthew 13:40–42).

Where Christians differ: can a true believer be cut off? Some take this to teach that genuine Christians can lose their salvation if they stop abiding. Verdict: the branches that are burned are those who “do not abide,” like Judas: outwardly attached, never inwardly united. True abiding is the mark of true disciples (8:31), and Jesus has promised that his sheep will never perish (10:28). The warning is real, and it is one of the means God uses to keep his people abiding. It calls us to examine whether our union with Christ is real, not to fear that the Father will drop his own.

In a sentence. Jesus said he is the vine and they the branches, and whoever abides in him bears much fruit, for without him they can do nothing, but whoever does not abide is thrown away like a branch, withers, and is burned.

On a Tuesday. Start your day with this: apart from him I can do nothing. Then ask him to work through you.
verseByVerse.note: Vine wood is useless for building; pruned branches were burned.

parallels.desc: the wood of the vine

verseByVerse.quote: "If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and so prove to be my disciples."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and so prove to be my disciples.

If you abide in me, and my words abide in you. Key words. Abiding in Christ goes with his words abiding in us. You can’t abide in him while ignoring his word. Scripture filling the mind and heart is how Christ dwells in us (Colossians 3:16).

Ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. The promise has a condition. When Christ’s words fill us, our wishes are shaped by his will. Then we ask what he wants to give.

By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit. The goal of fruit-bearing is the Father’s glory (Matthew 5:16).

And so prove to be my disciples. “Prove to be” (genēsthe): become, show yourselves to be. Fruit is the evidence of discipleship, not its cause.

In a sentence. Jesus said that if they abide in him and his words abide in them, they may ask what they wish and it will be done, for the Father is glorified when they bear much fruit and so show themselves to be his disciples.

For worship. Fill your heart with his words, and your prayers will be shaped by his will. Then ask boldly.

verseByVerse.quote: "As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father's commandments and abide in his love."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love.

As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Key words. The measure of Christ’s love for us is the Father’s love for him: eternal, infinite, perfect. Breathtaking.

Abide in my love. Live in it. Make his love your home. Don’t wander out into doubt or self-reliance.

If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love. Obedience is how we stay in his love, not to earn it but to enjoy it. As a child who disobeys does not stop being loved, but loses the sense of closeness.

Just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love. Jesus is the model. His obedience and the Father’s love went together.

In a sentence. Jesus said that he loves them as the Father loves him, and they should abide in his love by keeping his commandments, as he has kept his Father’s and abides in his love.

On a Tuesday. Christ loves you as the Father loves him. Live there today.

parallels.desc: keep yourselves in the love of God

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full. This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full. This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.

That my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full. Key words. On the night before the cross, Jesus speaks of joy. His joy: the joy of the Son in the Father’s love and in doing his will (Hebrews 12:2). He wants us to share it, and to be full of it. The Christian life is not grim duty. Obedience and joy go together.

This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you. The new commandment of 13:34, repeated.

In a sentence. Jesus said he had told them these things so that his joy would be in them and their joy would be full, and his commandment was that they love one another as he loved them.

For worship. Christ wants your joy to be full. Ask him for his joy today.

verseByVerse.quote: "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. You are my friends if you do what I command you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. You are my friends if you do what I command you.

Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. Key words. The highest human love: to die for someone else. Jesus is about to do it. And Paul goes further: Christ died for us while we were still sinners, his enemies (Romans 5:8, 10). His love is greater than the greatest love.

You are my friends if you do what I command you. Not that obedience makes us his friends, but that it shows we are. Friendship with Christ is shown in doing what he says.

In a sentence. Jesus said there is no greater love than to lay down one’s life for one’s friends, and they are his friends if they do what he commands.

For worship. He laid down his life for his friends, and he calls you his friend. What love.

parallels.desc: he laid down his life for us

verseByVerse.quote: "No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you. You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give it to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you. You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give it to you.

No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing. A slave just obeys orders without explanation.

But I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you. Key words. Abraham and Moses were each called the friend of God (Isaiah 41:8; Exodus 33:11). God shared his plans with them (Genesis 18:17). Now Jesus calls all his disciples friends, because he has shared the Father’s plans. They are still his servants (v. 20; Romans 1:1), but more than servants: trusted friends.

You did not choose me, but I chose you. Key words. In that culture, disciples chose their rabbi. Jesus reverses it. He chose them. Primarily this is about choosing them as apostles (6:70), but it reflects the deeper truth of election to salvation (13:18; 17:6; Ephesians 1:4). Our salvation starts with his choice, not ours. We chose him only because he first chose us.

And appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide. Chosen for a purpose: to go and bear lasting fruit, in lives changed by the gospel.

So that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give it to you. Prayer is connected with fruitful mission.

In a sentence. Jesus said he no longer calls them servants but friends, for he has told them all the Father told him, and they did not choose him but he chose and appointed them to go and bear lasting fruit, so that the Father will give them whatever they ask in his name.

On a Tuesday. You are Christ’s friend, chosen by him. Live today as one entrusted with his purposes.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham and Moses were each called the friend of God.

parallels.desc: Abraham, my friend
as a man speaks to his friend

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I command you, so that you will love one another."
verseByVerse.commentary:
These things I command you, so that you will love one another.

These things I command you, so that you will love one another. The section ends with love. Everything he has commanded, abiding, obeying, bearing fruit, has love as its goal. It is the third time in this chapter (vv. 12, 17) and the theme of the whole discourse. The world will hate them (v. 18); they must love one another.

In a sentence. Jesus said he commanded these things so that they would love one another.

For worship. All Christ’s commands lead to love. Ask yourself today: whom can I love as he loves me?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — The World's Hatred and the Spirit's Witness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If the world hates them, they should remember it hated Jesus first. If they belonged to the world, it would love them, but because he chose them out of it, it hates them. No servant is greater than his master: those who persecuted him will persecute them, and those who kept his word will keep theirs. All this will happen because of his name, for they do not know the one who sent him. Had he not come and spoken, they would not be guilty, but now they have no excuse; to hate him is to hate his Father. Had he not done works no one else did, they would not be guilty, but they have seen and hated both him and the Father, fulfilling the words of their law that they hated him without cause. But when the Helper comes, the Spirit of truth whom Jesus will send from the Father, he will testify about Jesus, and the disciples must testify too, for they have been with him from the start.
verseByVerse.theology: The world's hatred of the church is not an accident to be explained away but a structural feature of the relationship between the kingdom of God and the kingdom of this world. Jesus does not promise that clever strategy or cultural accommodation will eliminate the hatred; he promises that the Spirit will sustain the witnesses through it. The Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father (v. 26) — a phrase that has generated centuries of debate about the procession of the Spirit — testifies about Jesus, and the disciples testify because they have been with Jesus from the beginning.
verseByVerse.examples: If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (v. 20). The disciple is not above the master. This is simultaneously warning and honor: to be persecuted for Christ is to share in Christ's experience, to enter the fellowship of his sufferings. The church that is never persecuted has either been culturally absorbed to the point of invisibility or is living in an extraordinarily tolerant society — possibly both. The cross-bearing disciple should expect the world's hostility as confirmation, not contradiction, of authentic discipleship.

verseByVerse.quote: "If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you. If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you. If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.

If the world hates you. “The world” in John is humanity in rebellion against God. From love (vv. 9–17) to hatred (vv. 18–25): the contrast is deliberate.

Know that it has hated me before it hated you. The world’s hatred is first directed at Christ. Disciples share in what he suffered (1 Peter 4:12–14).

If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own. The world loves its own kind.

But because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you. Key words. Christ’s choice took them out of the world. They now belong to another kingdom (17:14–16). The world senses the difference and resents it.

In a sentence. Jesus said that if the world hates them, it hated him first, and it would love them if they belonged to it, but it hates them because he chose them out of the world.

On a Tuesday. Don’t be surprised when the world resents your faith. It means you belong to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember the word that I said to you: 'A servant is not greater than his master.' If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will also keep yours. But all these things they will do to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember the word that I said to you: ‘A servant is not greater than his master.’ If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will also keep yours. But all these things they will do to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me.

A servant is not greater than his master. He said this in 13:16 about serving; now it applies to suffering.

If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. The church shares her Lord’s experience (Acts 9:4; 2 Timothy 3:12).

If they kept my word, they will also keep yours. And some will receive their message, as some received his.

On account of my name. Because they belong to him.

Because they do not know him who sent me. The root cause: ignorance of the true God (16:3).

In a sentence. Jesus reminded them that a servant is not greater than his master, so if they persecuted him they would persecute them, and those who kept his word would keep theirs, all because of his name, for they do not know the Father.

For worship. To suffer for his name is to be counted with him (Acts 5:41).

verseByVerse.quote: "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have been guilty of sin, but now they have no excuse for their sin. Whoever hates me hates my Father also."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have been guilty of sin, but now they have no excuse for their sin. Whoever hates me hates my Father also.

If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have been guilty of sin. Not that they would be sinless, but that they would not be guilty of this sin, rejecting God’s Son. Privilege increases responsibility (9:41; Luke 12:47–48).

But now they have no excuse for their sin. “Excuse” (prophasin): pretext, cover. They have heard him clearly.

Whoever hates me hates my Father also. There is no loving the Father while hating the Son (5:23; 1 John 2:23).

In a sentence. Jesus said that if he had not come and spoken, they would not have this guilt, but now they have no excuse, for whoever hates him hates the Father too.

On a Tuesday. If you have heard of Christ, you have no excuse. Respond to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin, but now they have seen and hated both me and my Father. But the word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: 'They hated me without a cause.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin, but now they have seen and hated both me and my Father. But the word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: ‘They hated me without a cause.’

If I had not done among them the works that no one else did. His works were unique (9:32).

But now they have seen and hated both me and my Father. Seeing and hating: the clearest evidence of the depth of sin.

The word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: “They hated me without a cause.” “Their Law” here means the Scriptures as a whole, including the Psalms. The words come from Psalm 35:19 and 69:4, laments of David hated by enemies without reason. David’s greater Son suffered the same, perfectly innocent. Psalm 69 is often applied to Jesus (2:17; 19:28–29; Romans 15:3). Even their hatred fulfilled Scripture.

In a sentence. Jesus said that if he had not done unique works among them they would not be guilty, but they had seen and hated both him and his Father, fulfilling the Scripture that they hated him without cause.

For worship. Christ was hated without cause, and loved us without cause. Marvel at his grace.
verseByVerse.note: “Their Law” here means the Scriptures as a whole, including the Psalms.

parallels.desc: those who hate me without cause

verseByVerse.quote: "But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.

But when the Helper comes. The ESV notes that “Helper” can also be rendered “Advocate” or “Counselor.” In a hostile world, the Spirit is our advocate.

Whom I will send to you from the Father. The Son sends the Spirit; in 14:16, 26, the Father sends him. Both send.

The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father. Key words. “Proceeds” (ekporeuetai): goes out from, comes forth. Most take this to describe the Spirit’s mission, his being sent out into the world. Theologians have also seen in it his eternal relationship to the Father.

Where Christians differ: does the Spirit proceed from the Son? The Western church added to the Nicene Creed that the Spirit proceeds from the Father “and the Son” (filioque). The Eastern Orthodox church rejected the addition, and it was a major cause of the split of 1054. Verdict: the Western confession, held by the Reformed churches (Westminster Confession 2.3), is right in substance: the Spirit is the Spirit of the Son as well as of the Father (Galatians 4:6; Romans 8:9), and the Son sends him, as here. Yet the matter is subtle, and should be held humbly, with respect for Eastern brothers and sisters who confess the same Trinity.

He will bear witness about me. The Spirit’s great work is to point to Christ (16:14).

And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning. The Spirit and the apostles bear witness together. The apostles were eyewitnesses from the beginning of his ministry (Acts 1:21–22). Their witness, preserved in Scripture, is the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20). And the Spirit still bears witness through every believer who speaks of Christ.

In a sentence. Jesus said that the Helper, the Spirit of truth, whom he would send from the Father and who comes from the Father, would bear witness about him, and they also would bear witness, having been with him from the beginning.

For worship. When you speak of Christ, you never speak alone. The Spirit bears witness with you.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Helper” can also be rendered “Advocate” or “Counselor.”

parallels.desc: we are witnesses, and so is the Holy Spirit

15.text: <sup>1</sup>“I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser.<sup>2</sup>Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit.<sup>3</sup>Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you.<sup>4</sup>Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me.<sup>5</sup>I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.<sup>6</sup>If anyone does not abide in me, he is thrown away like a branch and withers; and the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned.<sup>7</sup>If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you.<sup>8</sup>By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and so prove to be my disciples.<sup>9</sup>As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love.<sup>10</sup>If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love.<sup>11</sup>These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full.<sup>12</sup>“This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.<sup>13</sup>Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.<sup>14</sup>You are my friends if you do what I command you.<sup>15</sup>No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you.<sup>16</sup>You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give it to you.<sup>17</sup>These things I command you, so that you will love one another.<sup>18</sup>“If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you.<sup>19</sup>If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.<sup>20</sup>Remember the word that I said to you: ’A servant is not greater than his master.’ If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will also keep yours.<sup>21</sup>But all these things they will do to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me.<sup>22</sup>If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have been guilty of sin, but now they have no excuse for their sin.<sup>23</sup>Whoever hates me hates my Father also.<sup>24</sup>If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin, but now they have seen and hated both me and my Father.<sup>25</sup>But the word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: ’They hated me without a cause.’<sup>26</sup>“But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me.<sup>27</sup>And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.
15.overview:
In the Old Testament Israel was God’s vine, planted and tended by him but so often fruitless (Psalm 80:8–16; Isaiah 5:1–7; Jeremiah 2:21). Jesus now says, “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser.” His disciples are the branches. Fruitless branches are removed; fruitful ones are pruned to bear more. The secret of fruitfulness is to abide in him, to remain joined to him by faith, his words living in them, as he lives in them: apart from him they can do nothing. Abiding means remaining in his love by keeping his commandments, the chief of which is to love one another as he has loved them, with the greatest love of all, laying down one’s life for one’s friends. He calls them no longer servants but friends, because he has made known to them all he heard from the Father. They did not choose him; he chose them and appointed them to go and bear lasting fruit.

The second half turns from love within the church to hatred from the world. If the world hates them, it hated him first; a servant is not greater than his master. Their hatred is without excuse, since Jesus spoke and did works no one else did, and it fulfils the psalm, “They hated me without a cause.” Yet the disciples will not be alone: the Helper, the Spirit of truth who comes from the Father, will bear witness about Jesus, and they too will bear witness, because they have been with him from the beginning.

16.title: The Spirit and the Joy of the Disciples

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Spirit Convicts the World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus forewarns the disciples so that persecution will not make them fall: they will be thrown out of synagogues, and their killers will think it service to God, not knowing the Father or the Son. Grief has filled them at the news of his departure, but his going is for their good, since only then will he send the Helper. The Spirit will prove the world wrong about sin, shown in its unbelief; about righteousness, proved by Jesus’ return to the Father; and about judgment, for the world’s ruler is condemned. There is more Jesus could tell them, more than they can now bear, but the Spirit of truth will lead them into all truth, speaking what he hears, revealing what is to come, and glorifying Jesus by making known what belongs to him, which is all that the Father has. Soon they will not see him, and soon after they will see him again.
verseByVerse.theology: The conviction work of the Spirit operates on three fronts: sin (the world's refusal to believe in Jesus), righteousness (the vindication of Jesus in his ascension to the Father), and judgment (the condemnation of the ruler of this world at the cross). This Trinitarian work of conviction is not coercive but illuminating — the Spirit opens eyes to what is actually true about the world's condition, about Jesus' identity, and about the decisive verdict already rendered at Calvary. Evangelism that presents the gospel as optional enhancement rather than rescue from genuine condemnation has not yet let the Spirit do his convicting work.
verseByVerse.examples: He will guide you into all truth (v. 13): the Spirit's hermeneutical function is ongoing, not merely the initial inspiration of the apostolic witness. The community that has the Spirit has access to the interpretive presence of the one who knows the mind of God (1 Cor. 2:10-11). This does not mean every Christian's interpretation is equally valid; it means that the Spirit-guided community reading the Spirit-inspired text under the guidance of the Spirit through his word can arrive at the truth Jesus promised. The church's theology is a work of the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said all these things to you to keep you from falling away. They will put you out of the synagogues. Indeed, the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have said all these things to you to keep you from falling away. They will put you out of the synagogues. Indeed, the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God.

Meaning first. John 16 completes Jesus’ farewell teaching. He warns of persecution, explains why his going is good for them, describes the Spirit’s work in the world and in the church, and promises that their sorrow will turn to joy. It ends with one of the great promises of Scripture: I have overcome the world.

I have said all these things to you to keep you from falling away. Key words. “Falling away” (skandalisthēte): stumbling, being tripped up. Forewarned is forearmed. Persecution will not shake those who expected it. Jesus’ warnings are one of the means by which he keeps his people.

They will put you out of the synagogues. As happened to the man born blind (9:22, 34).

Whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God. “Service” (latreia): worship, religious duty. Paul had been such a man, persecuting believers as a service to God (Acts 26:9–11; Galatians 1:13–14). Religious zeal without the knowledge of God can become murderous. Stephen was the first to die this way (Acts 7:58–60).

In a sentence. Jesus said he told them these things to keep them from stumbling, for they would be expelled from synagogues, and the time was coming when those who killed them would think they were serving God.

On a Tuesday. Don’t be shaken when opposition comes in religious dress. Jesus told us it would.
verseByVerse.note: Paul had been such a man, persecuting believers as a service to God.

parallels.desc: Paul’s zeal as a persecutor

verseByVerse.quote: "And they will do these things because they have not known the Father, nor me. But I have said these things to you, that when their hour comes you may remember that I told them to you. I did not say these things to you from the beginning, because I was with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they will do these things because they have not known the Father, nor me. But I have said these things to you, that when their hour comes you may remember that I told them to you. I did not say these things to you from the beginning, because I was with you.

Because they have not known the Father, nor me. The root of persecution: ignorance of God (15:21).

That when their hour comes you may remember that I told them to you. “Their hour”: the hour of the persecutors. Remembering his words will steady them.

I did not say these things to you from the beginning, because I was with you. While he was with them, the hostility was aimed at him. Now it will turn on them.

In a sentence. Jesus said they would do this because they did not know the Father or him, and he told them so that they would remember when it came, having not said it before because he was with them.

For worship. Christ shielded his disciples while he was with them. He shields us still, by his word and Spirit.

parallels.desc: I had acted ignorantly in unbelief

verseByVerse.quote: "But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, 'Where are you going?' But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’ But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart.

None of you asks me, “Where are you going?” Peter and Thomas had asked (13:36; 14:5), but only about the separation, not about where he was going and why it would be good. They are thinking only of their loss.

Because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart. Grief has crowded out understanding.

In a sentence. Jesus said that he was going to the one who sent him, and none of them asked where, because sorrow had filled their hearts.

On a Tuesday. Sorrow can make us forget to ask what God is doing. Lift your eyes from your loss to his purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: "Nevertheless, I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you. And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nevertheless, I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you. And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment:

It is to your advantage that I go away. Key words. A startling statement. Better for them that Jesus leave? Yes. While on earth, Jesus was in one place at a time. The Spirit is with every believer everywhere, always, and within them. The Spirit applies the finished work of the cross, which had to be completed first.

For if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you. The order of salvation history: the cross, resurrection and ascension first; then Pentecost (7:39; Acts 2:33).

And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment. Key words. “Convict” (elenxei): expose, prove guilty, bring to conviction. The Spirit acts like a prosecutor in a courtroom, proving the world wrong on three counts. The world thinks it has judged Jesus; the Spirit turns the case around.

In a sentence. Jesus said it was good for them that he was going away, for otherwise the Helper would not come, but he would send him, and the Spirit would convict the world about sin, righteousness and judgment.

For worship. You are better off with the Spirit than the disciples were with Jesus in Galilee. Live in that privilege.

parallels.desc: they were cut to the heart

verseByVerse.quote: "concerning sin, because they do not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will see me no longer;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
concerning sin, because they do not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will see me no longer;

Concerning sin, because they do not believe in me. Key words. The world’s great sin is not first its immorality, but unbelief: rejecting Christ (3:18–19). The Spirit shows people that their refusal of Christ is sin, and the root of all their sins. This is how conviction began at Pentecost: “cut to the heart” over the one they crucified (Acts 2:36–37).

Concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father. The world thought Jesus was a sinner, a blasphemer, rightly executed. His return to the Father, in resurrection and ascension, proves that he was righteous (Acts 2:24, 32–36; 1 Timothy 3:16). The Spirit convinces people that Jesus was in the right, and that their own righteousness is worthless. And the righteousness of Christ, now accepted in heaven, is the righteousness God gives to all who believe (Romans 3:21–22).

And you will see me no longer. He will not be visible on earth.

In a sentence. The Spirit would convict the world of sin, because it does not believe in Jesus, and of righteousness, because he is going to the Father, where they will see him no more.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the Spirit to convict your friends of the sin of unbelief. Only he can.

parallels.desc: raised for our justification

verseByVerse.quote: "concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world is judged. I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now."
verseByVerse.commentary:
concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world is judged. I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.

Concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world is judged. Key words. The world judged Jesus at the cross, but in fact it was Satan who was judged there (12:31). Satan’s defeat proves that judgment is real and coming for all who side with him. The Spirit convinces people that the world’s verdicts are wrong and God’s judgment is certain (Acts 17:31).

I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. They are not ready. The Spirit will teach them later. This is why the New Testament contains more than the Gospels: the apostles’ letters unfold what Jesus began to teach.

In a sentence. The Spirit would convict the world of judgment, because its ruler has been judged; and Jesus said he had more to tell them, but they could not bear it yet.

For worship. Satan is judged. Every enemy of God’s people is already condemned. Rejoice.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you.

When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth. Key words. A promise first to the apostles. “Guide” (hodēgēsei): lead along the way. “All the truth”: everything they need about Christ and the gospel. This was fulfilled in the writing of the New Testament. It is why we can trust the apostles’ teaching as God’s word.

For he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak. The Spirit doesn’t bring a different message from the Son, any more than the Son brought a different message from the Father.

And he will declare to you the things that are to come. Including the things of the new age: the meaning of the cross, the life of the church, the future hope (as in Revelation).

He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you. Key words. The Spirit’s great purpose is to glorify Christ. He shines the spotlight on Jesus, not on himself. A sure test of any ministry claiming the Spirit: does it make much of Christ?

What it does not mean. It doesn’t mean that every Christian will receive infallible guidance into all truth, or that new revelation continues today. The apostles received it, and wrote it down. The Spirit now illuminates that word for us (1 Corinthians 2:12–13).

In a sentence. Jesus said the Spirit of truth would guide them into all the truth, speaking only what he hears, declaring what is to come, and glorifying Christ by making known what is his.

On a Tuesday. When you read Scripture, ask the Spirit to show you Christ. That is his delight.

verseByVerse.quote: "All that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you. A little while, and you will see me no longer; and again a little while, and you will see me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you. A little while, and you will see me no longer; and again a little while, and you will see me.

All that the Father has is mine. Key words. A stunning claim. Everything the Father has belongs to the Son. No creature could say it. The Father, the Son and the Spirit share all things (17:10). The Spirit takes from the Son what belongs to the Father, and gives it to us: the Trinity working together for our salvation.

A little while, and you will see me no longer. His death, in a few hours.

And again a little while, and you will see me. His resurrection, three days later. Some also see a reference to his second coming.

In a sentence. Jesus said that all the Father has is his, so the Spirit would take what is his and declare it to them, and in a little while they would not see him, and then in a little while they would.

For worship. All the riches of God belong to Christ, and through the Spirit he shares them with you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–33 — Sorrow Turned to Joy: I Have Overcome the World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Puzzled, the disciples ask one another what he means by “a little while” and “going to the Father”. Knowing their question, Jesus tells them they will weep and mourn while the world rejoices, but their grief will become joy, like a woman whose pain in labour is forgotten in the joy of a new child. They grieve now, but he will see them again, and their joy no one will take away. In that day they will not need to ask him; the Father will give them whatever they ask in his name. Until now they have asked nothing in his name; they should ask and receive, so that their joy may be complete. He has spoken in figures, but soon he will speak plainly about the Father. They will ask in his name, not because he must plead for them, but because the Father himself loves them for loving and trusting his Son. He came from the Father into the world and is now leaving it to return. The disciples say that now he speaks plainly, and they believe he came from God. Jesus asks whether they really believe now. The hour has come when they will scatter, each to his home, and leave him alone; yet he is not alone, for the Father is with him. He has told them this so that in him they may have peace. In the world they will face trouble, but they should take courage: he has conquered the world.
verseByVerse.theology:
The chapter's second half turns on a claim about time. Everything Jesus promises here is stated as though it has already happened: the sorrow will turn into joy, the ruler of this world is judged, and — in the last verse — I have overcome the world, in the perfect tense, before the arrest. The disciples are being taught to live inside an outcome that is settled but not yet visible, which is the permanent situation of the church.

This is why the childbirth image governs the section. It is not a picture of pain compensated afterwards by an unrelated good, which is how providence is usually consoled about. It is a picture of pain that turns out to have been productive — the same event, read from the far end, carrying a meaning it could not disclose at the time. Applied to the cross, this is the interpretive key to the whole Gospel: the worst thing that ever happened is the thing the church sings about, and nothing had to be deleted for that to be true.

And the prayer promise sits in the middle of it for a reason. Prayer in the name of Jesus is not a technique for extracting outcomes; it is the practice of people who believe the outcome is already secured and are asking to be brought into line with it. Its stated end in verse 24 is not acquisition but fullness of joy.
verseByVerse.examples:
In the world you will have tribulation (v. 33) is the sentence to set against every version of Christianity that promises exemption. Not may, not could — will, spoken by the one person entitled to say it, on the last free evening of his life. And it stands beside in me you may have peace without contradiction, because the two prepositions name two locations and a believer is in both at once. That is why a Christian life so often feels like two contradictory reports about the same afternoon.

The pastoral use of verse 22 is worth naming: no one will take your joy from you is not a promise of cheerfulness. The joy in this passage is grounded in his seeing them, not in their managing to feel anything, which is precisely why it cannot be confiscated — nobody can reach the thing it depends on.

And verse 12 — you cannot bear them now — is the answer to the reader who suspects God is asking more than can be carried. Here is the Son measuring what he says against what eleven exhausted men can hold, and stopping short, on the one night when he had most to say and least time to say it.

verseByVerse.quote: So some of his disciples said to one another, "What is this that he says to us, 'A little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me'; and, 'because I am going to the Father'?" So they were saying, "What does he mean by 'a little while'? We do not know what he is talking about."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So some of his disciples said to one another, “What is this that he says to us, ‘A little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me’; and, ‘because I am going to the Father’?” So they were saying, “What does he mean by ‘a little while’? We do not know what he is talking about.”

What is this that he says to us? The disciples are puzzled, and whisper among themselves.

What does he mean by “a little while”? We do not know what he is talking about. An honest admission of confusion. The repetition of the phrase shows how much it bothered them. They could not imagine death and resurrection.

In a sentence. Some disciples asked one another what Jesus meant by a little while and not seeing him, and seeing him again, and going to the Father, admitting they did not understand.

On a Tuesday. It’s fine to admit you don’t understand. Bring your questions to Jesus, as they eventually did.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus knew that they wanted to ask him, so he said to them, "Is this what you are asking yourselves, what I meant by saying, 'A little while and you will not see me, and again a little while and you will see me'? Truly, truly, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus knew that they wanted to ask him, so he said to them, “Is this what you are asking yourselves, what I meant by saying, ‘A little while and you will not see me, and again a little while and you will see me’? Truly, truly, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy.

Jesus knew that they wanted to ask him. He knows their hearts.

You will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. At the cross, the disciples will mourn while his enemies celebrate.

You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy. Key words. Not replaced by joy, but turned into joy. The very thing that causes their sorrow, his death, will become the source of their joy. The cross, their grief, becomes their glory (Galatians 6:14).

In a sentence. Jesus knew what they wanted to ask, and solemnly told them they would weep while the world rejoiced, but their sorrow would turn into joy.

For worship. What brings you sorrow now, God can turn into joy. He did it at the cross.

parallels.desc: weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning

verseByVerse.quote: "When a woman is giving birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come, but when she has delivered the baby, she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy that a human being has been born into the world. So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When a woman is giving birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come, but when she has delivered the baby, she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy that a human being has been born into the world. So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.

When a woman is giving birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come. A picture used often in the Old Testament for the pains that come before God’s new age (Isaiah 26:17–19; 66:7–14). Her pain is real and intense. But it leads to new life.

But when she has delivered the baby, she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy. The joy outweighs the pain. The cross is the birth pang of the new creation.

So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice. “I will see you”: he will come to them in the resurrection (20:20).

And no one will take your joy from you. Key words. Joy grounded in the risen Christ cannot be taken away by persecution, loss or death. The apostles rejoiced after being flogged (Acts 5:41). This joy is permanent.

In a sentence. Jesus compared their sorrow to a woman in labour, who forgets the anguish for joy once her baby is born, and said that he would see them again, and they would rejoice with a joy no one could take away.

On a Tuesday. No one can take your joy in the risen Christ. Not your boss, your illness, or your enemies.

verseByVerse.quote: "In that day you will ask nothing of me. Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you. Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In that day you will ask nothing of me. Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you. Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full.

In that day you will ask nothing of me. “That day”: after the resurrection. “Ask” here may mean ask questions (as in v. 19): they will no longer be confused, because the Spirit will teach them.

Whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you. “Ask” here is the word for requests. A new way of prayer opens: directly to the Father, in the name of the Son.

Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Prayer in Jesus’ name is new, made possible by his death and exaltation as our mediator (Hebrews 4:14–16).

Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full. Answered prayer fills our joy.

In a sentence. Jesus said that in that day they would no longer question him, and whatever they asked the Father in his name, the Father would give, for they had not yet asked in his name, but should ask and receive so that their joy would be full.

For worship. You can go straight to the Father in Jesus’ name. Use that privilege today.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said these things to you in figures of speech. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures of speech but will tell you plainly about the Father. In that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have said these things to you in figures of speech. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures of speech but will tell you plainly about the Father. In that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf;

I have said these things to you in figures of speech. “Figures of speech” (paroimiai): veiled sayings, pictures (10:6). The vine, the woman in labour, the house with many rooms.

The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures of speech but will tell you plainly about the Father. After the resurrection, through the Spirit.

In that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf. Not that Jesus stops interceding (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25), but that they don’t need to think of the Father as reluctant, needing to be persuaded by the Son. The Father himself loves them (v. 27).

In a sentence. Jesus said he had spoken in figures, but would soon speak plainly about the Father, and they would ask in his name, without needing him to persuade the Father for them.

On a Tuesday. The Father doesn’t need persuading to love you. Pray with confidence.

verseByVerse.quote: "for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God. I came from the Father and have come into the world, and now I am leaving the world and going to the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God. I came from the Father and have come into the world, and now I am leaving the world and going to the Father.

For the Father himself loves you. Key words. Not because Jesus asks him to. The Father himself loves you. “Loves” here is phileō, the warm love of friendship and family. The Father is not a stern judge whom the kind Son must soften. The Father sent the Son because he loved the world (3:16).

Because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God. Their love and faith are the evidence that they belong to the Father’s family, and themselves the fruit of his love.

I came from the Father and have come into the world, and now I am leaving the world and going to the Father. Key words. The whole of Jesus’ mission in one sentence: incarnation and ascension, coming down and going back. His pre-existence with the Father, his earthly life, and his return.

In a sentence. Jesus said the Father himself loves them because they have loved him and believed he came from God, for he came from the Father into the world, and was now leaving the world and going to the Father.

For worship. The Father himself loves you. Let that sink in.

verseByVerse.quote: His disciples said, "Ah, now you are speaking plainly and not using figurative speech! Now we know that you know all things and do not need anyone to question you; this is why we believe that you came from God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His disciples said, “Ah, now you are speaking plainly and not using figurative speech! Now we know that you know all things and do not need anyone to question you; this is why we believe that you came from God.”

Ah, now you are speaking plainly. They think they finally understand.

Now we know that you know all things and do not need anyone to question you. He has answered the question they hadn’t asked aloud (v. 19). He knows their thoughts.

This is why we believe that you came from God. A real confession, but their confidence is ahead of their understanding. They will be tested within hours.

In a sentence. His disciples said he was now speaking plainly, and they knew that he knew all things, and so they believed he came from God.

On a Tuesday. Faith is real even when it’s immature. But don’t mistake a moment of clarity for strength to stand.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Do you now believe? Behold, the hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered them, “Do you now believe? Behold, the hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me.

Do you now believe? Not doubting their faith, but warning them of its weakness.

The hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered. As Zechariah foretold: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered (Zechariah 13:7; Mark 14:27, 50).

And will leave me alone. All of them would run.

Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me. Key words. The Father never leaves him (8:29). What then of his cry from the cross that God had forsaken him (Mark 15:34)? There the Son bore the Father’s judgment against our sin, and experienced the loss of the Father’s comforting presence. Yet even there the Father’s love for the Son never ceased, and the unity of the Trinity was never broken. Jesus could still say “my God” and, at the end, “Father, into your hands” (Luke 23:46).

In a sentence. Jesus asked if they now believed, warning that the hour had come when they would scatter and leave him alone, though he would not be alone, for the Father was with him.

For worship. When everyone else leaves, the Father remains. That was true for Christ, and in him it is true for you.

parallels.desc: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world.

I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. Key words. The purpose of the whole farewell discourse: peace. Not in circumstances, but “in me.” Peace is found in union with Christ.

In the world you will have tribulation. “Tribulation” (thlipsis): pressure, distress, affliction. Not “might,” but “will.” The Christian life is not trouble-free (Acts 14:22).

But take heart; I have overcome the world. Key words. “Take heart” (tharseite): be courageous. “I have overcome” (nenikēka): perfect tense, a completed victory with lasting effect. Jesus says it on the eve of the cross, as if the battle is already won. And it is. By the cross and resurrection he has defeated sin, death and Satan. His people share in his victory (1 John 5:4–5; Revelation 3:21).

In a sentence. Jesus said he had told them these things so that they would have peace in him, for in the world they would have trouble, but they should take heart, because he has overcome the world.

On a Tuesday. Trouble will come today. Take heart: Christ has already overcome the world.

parallels.desc: the victory that has overcome the world
