Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you.<sup>24</sup>Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full.<sup>25</sup>“I have said these things to you in figures of speech. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures of speech but will tell you plainly about the Father.<sup>26</sup>In that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf;<sup>27</sup>for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God.<sup>28</sup>I came from the Father and have come into the world, and now I am leaving the world and going to the Father.”<sup>29</sup>His disciples said, “Ah, now you are speaking plainly and not using figurative speech!<sup>30</sup>Now we know that you know all things and do not need anyone to question you; this is why we believe that you came from God.”<sup>31</sup>Jesus answered them, “Do you now believe?<sup>32</sup>Behold, the hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me.<sup>33</sup>I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world.”
16.overview:
Jesus warns his disciples plainly so that they will not fall away when persecution comes: they will be expelled from synagogues, and some will kill them thinking they are serving God. Sorrow fills their hearts at his going, but he tells them it is for their good, for unless he goes the Helper will not come. When the Spirit comes he will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness and judgment: sin, because they do not believe in Jesus; righteousness, because Jesus goes to the Father and is vindicated; judgment, because the ruler of this world is condemned. The Spirit of truth will guide the apostles into all the truth, declaring what is to come and glorifying Christ by taking what is his and making it known.

Then Jesus speaks of “a little while”: a little while and they will not see him, and again a little while and they will see him. The disciples are puzzled. He explains with the picture of a woman in labour, whose anguish gives way to joy when the child is born: they will grieve while the world rejoices, but he will see them again, and no one will take their joy from them. In that day they will pray to the Father in his name and receive, so that their joy may be full, for the Father himself loves them. When the disciples declare that now they understand and believe, Jesus warns that they will soon be scattered and leave him alone, yet he is not alone, for the Father is with him. His last words before his prayer are a promise for every age: “In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world.”

17.title: The High-Priestly Prayer

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — Jesus Prays for Himself, the Disciples, and All Believers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Raising his eyes to heaven, Jesus asks the Father to glorify the Son now that the hour has come, so that the Son may glorify him by giving eternal life to all the Father has given him. That life is knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent. Having finished his work on earth, Jesus asks for the glory he shared with the Father before creation. He has revealed the Father to those given him out of the world, and they have received his words and believed. He prays for them, not for the world: that the holy Father would keep them in his name and make them one; he has kept them, and none is lost except the son of destruction. The world hates them, but he asks not that they be removed from it, but guarded from the evil one, set apart by the truth of God’s word, and sent as he was sent; for them he consecrates himself. He prays too for all who will believe through their message, that they may be one as he and the Father are one, so that the world may believe and know the Father’s love. He longs for them to be with him and see his glory, and promises to keep making the Father known, so that the Father’s love and the Son himself may be in them.
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer is called the High-Priestly Prayer because it parallels the High Priest's prayer on the Day of Atonement — the one moment in the year when the high priest entered the Most Holy Place to intercede for the people. Jesus is simultaneously the priest and the sacrifice; he intercedes for his people while preparing himself for the offering that will accomplish what he prays for. His prayer for their sanctification (v. 17), protection (v. 11), joy (v. 13), and unity (v. 21-23) is the charter of the church's life.
verseByVerse.examples: That they may be one, as we are one (v. 22): the unity Jesus prays for is patterned on and derived from the inner-Trinitarian unity of Father and Son. This is not organizational uniformity or ecclesiastical merger but the living unity of love, shared purpose, and mutual indwelling. The church's unity is the Father's means of witnessing to the world (v. 21, 23): the divided church contradicts its own evangelistic witness. The prayer for unity is also the prayer for effective mission — they are inseparable in Jesus' own intercession.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had spoken these words, he lifted up his eyes to heaven, and said, "Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son that the Son may glorify you, since you have given him authority over all flesh, to give eternal life to all whom you have given him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus had spoken these words, he lifted up his eyes to heaven, and said, “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son that the Son may glorify you, since you have given him authority over all flesh, to give eternal life to all whom you have given him.

Meaning first. John 17 is often called Jesus’ high priestly prayer: he prays as the great High Priest for his people before offering himself as their sacrifice. Like the high priest who carried the names of the tribes on his heart into the holy place (Exodus 28:29), Jesus carries his people before the Father. He prays for himself (vv. 1–5), for his disciples (vv. 6–19), and for all who will believe through them (vv. 20–26). It is the longest prayer of Jesus recorded, and lets us overhear the conversation within the Trinity.

He lifted up his eyes to heaven. As at Lazarus’s tomb (11:41).

Father, the hour has come. The hour so long awaited (2:4; 12:23; 13:1).

Glorify your Son that the Son may glorify you. Key words. Not a selfish prayer. The Son asks to be glorified in his death, resurrection and exaltation, so that he can glorify the Father. Their glory is one.

Since you have given him authority over all flesh. “All flesh”: all humanity. The Son has authority over every person (Matthew 28:18).

To give eternal life to all whom you have given him. Key words. The phrase “given me” appears seven times in this prayer (vv. 2, 6 twice, 9, 11, 12, 24). The Father has given a people to the Son, and the Son gives them eternal life. His authority is universal; his saving gift is particular. This is the covenant of redemption: the Father’s gift of a people to the Son, made before the world began (v. 24; Ephesians 1:4).

In a sentence. Jesus looked up and prayed that the Father would glorify the Son in this hour, so that the Son might glorify him, since the Father had given him authority over all people to give eternal life to all the Father had given him.

For worship. If you are in Christ, you were the Father’s gift to the Son. He prayed for you on the night before he died.
verseByVerse.note: John 17 is often called Jesus’ high priestly prayer: he prays for himself, his disciples and all future believers.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do.

And this is eternal life, that they know you. Key words. The best definition of eternal life in Scripture. Not first endless existence, but knowing God. “Know” in the Bible means a personal relationship, not mere information (Jeremiah 31:34; Hosea 6:6). Eternal life begins now, the moment we come to know God, and grows for ever.

The only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. Knowing God and knowing Christ go together. Jesus puts himself alongside the only true God as the object of saving knowledge. He doesn’t deny his own deity by calling the Father the only true God; he denies the idols. The Son is included within the one true God (1:1; 1 John 5:20: “He is the true God and eternal life”).

I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do. “Accomplished” (teleiōsas): completed, finished. Jesus speaks of the cross as already done. On it he will cry, “It is finished” (19:30), the same root word.

In a sentence. Jesus said eternal life is knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent, and that he had glorified the Father on earth by finishing the work he gave him.

On a Tuesday. Eternal life is knowing God. Spend time today getting to know him better.
verseByVerse.note: “Know” in the Bible means a personal relationship, not mere information.

parallels.desc: that he understands and knows me
“It is finished”

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed. I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world. Yours they were, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed. I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world. Yours they were, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word.

Glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed. Key words. One of the clearest statements of Christ’s eternal pre-existence. Before creation, the Son shared the Father’s glory. God says he will not give his glory to another (Isaiah 42:8). So the Son is not another; he is God. In the incarnation, he veiled that glory (Philippians 2:6–7). Now he asks to return to it, in his human nature as well.

I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world. “Your name”: God’s character, all that he is. Jesus has revealed the Father to his disciples (1:18).

Yours they were, and you gave them to me. Key words. They belonged to the Father before they belonged to the Son. Chosen before they came (6:37; Ephesians 1:4).

And they have kept your word. Despite all their weakness, and the coming failures of that night, Jesus speaks well of them. He sees their faith as genuine.

In a sentence. Jesus asked the Father to glorify him with the glory he had with him before the world existed, and said he had revealed the Father’s name to those the Father gave him from the world, who were his and had kept his word.

For worship. The one who prayed for you shared the Father’s glory before the world began. And he still speaks well of his weak disciples.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now they know that everything that you have given me is from you. For I have given them the words that you gave me, and they have received them and have come to know in truth that I came from you; and they have believed that you sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now they know that everything that you have given me is from you. For I have given them the words that you gave me, and they have received them and have come to know in truth that I came from you; and they have believed that you sent me.

Now they know that everything that you have given me is from you. They recognise that Jesus’ words and works come from the Father.

For I have given them the words that you gave me. The chain of revelation: Father to Son, Son to disciples, and through them to us.

And they have received them. Faith begins by receiving God’s word.

And have come to know in truth that I came from you; and they have believed that you sent me. Knowing and believing together. The central truth of the Gospel: Jesus came from God.

In a sentence. Jesus said the disciples now knew that everything he had came from the Father, because he gave them the Father’s words, and they received them, knew he came from the Father, and believed the Father sent him.

On a Tuesday. Receive God’s words as the disciples did. Faith grows by hearing.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am praying for them. I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me, for they are yours. All mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am praying for them. I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me, for they are yours. All mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them.

I am praying for them. I am not praying for the world. Key words. Jesus’ high priestly intercession here is particular: for those the Father has given him. Not that he never prayed for unbelievers (Luke 23:34), or that we shouldn’t (1 Timothy 2:1). But his intercession as High Priest, which secures salvation, is for his own (Hebrews 7:25; Romans 8:34). His sacrifice and his intercession have the same scope. He prays for those for whom he dies, and he dies for those for whom he prays. This is one of the strongest supports for definite atonement.

But for those whom you have given me, for they are yours. Again the Father’s gift.

All mine are yours, and yours are mine. Anyone can say “all mine is yours” to God. Only the Son can say “all yours is mine” (16:15). Perfect equality.

And I am glorified in them. Christ is glorified in his people, weak as they are.

In a sentence. Jesus said he was praying not for the world but for those the Father had given him, who were the Father’s, for all that is his is the Father’s and all the Father’s is his, and he is glorified in them.

For worship. Christ prays for his own, and his prayers are always answered. He prays for you now.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them in your name, which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are one. While I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them in your name, which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are one. While I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled.

I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world. He speaks as if already gone. They will remain in a hostile world.

Holy Father, keep them in your name. Key words. “Holy Father”: only here. Holiness and fatherhood together. “Keep” (tērēson): guard, protect, preserve. “In your name”: by the power of who you are, and in loyalty to your revealed character. His first request for them is preservation. This is the basis of their perseverance.

Which you have given me. The Father has given the Son his name: the divine name (Philippians 2:9–11).

That they may be one, even as we are one. The goal of their preservation: unity, modelled on the Trinity.

I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction. “Son of destruction” describes one destined for destruction (2 Thessalonians 2:3, of the man of lawlessness). Judas. He was never one of those truly given; he was lost because he never truly belonged (6:64, 70). His loss fulfilled Scripture (Psalm 41:9; 13:18). Jesus did not fail to keep him; Judas’s end shows his own guilt and God’s sovereign purpose, both together.

In a sentence. Jesus prayed that the Holy Father would keep his disciples in his name and make them one as they are one, for while he was with them he kept them, and none was lost except the son of destruction, as Scripture foretold.

On a Tuesday. The Holy Father keeps you. Your security rests on his name, not on your strength.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of destruction” describes one destined for destruction — Judas.

verseByVerse.quote: "But now I am coming to you, and these things I speak in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves. I have given them your word, and the world has hated them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now I am coming to you, and these things I speak in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves. I have given them your word, and the world has hated them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.

That they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves. He prays aloud so that they may hear and be filled with joy (15:11). Overhearing Christ pray for you is a source of joy.

I have given them your word, and the world has hated them. The word they received sets them apart, and draws the world’s hatred.

Because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. Their origin is now from above, like his (3:3).

In a sentence. Jesus said he was speaking this in the world so that they would have his joy in full, and that he had given them the Father’s word, and the world hated them because they, like him, did not belong to it.

For worship. Christ’s joy can be yours, even when the world hates you.

verseByVerse.quote: "I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one. They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one. They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.

I do not ask that you take them out of the world. Key words. The church is not meant to withdraw from the world into isolation. They must stay in it, for their mission (v. 18).

But that you keep them from the evil one. “The evil one” (tou ponērou): Satan (1 John 5:18–19). Compare “deliver us from evil” in the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:13). The danger is not the world itself, but the evil one who works in it. The Father keeps his own from his power.

They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. In the world, but not of it.

Where Christians differ: separation from the world. Some Christians have sought holiness by withdrawing from society; others have so blended in that no difference remains. Verdict: Jesus prays for neither. His people are to live in the world, engaged in its life, but distinct in character and loyalty, kept by God from evil. Not monasteries, nor conformity, but holy presence.

In a sentence. Jesus asked not that the Father take them out of the world, but that he keep them from the evil one, since they, like him, did not belong to the world.

On a Tuesday. Your workplace is where God wants you. Ask him to keep you from the evil one there.

parallels.desc: deliver us from evil

verseByVerse.quote: "Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth. As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth. As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world.

Sanctify them in the truth. Key words. To sanctify is to set apart for God and make holy. It is both a status (set apart, 1 Corinthians 6:11) and a process (made holy, 1 Thessalonians 5:23). Jesus prays that the Father will make them holy, for their mission.

Your word is truth. Key words. God’s word is the instrument of sanctification. Not “contains truth” or “becomes truth,” but “is truth.” It is the standard of all truth. This is why Scripture is central to the Christian life. We grow in holiness as we are shaped by God’s word (Psalm 119:9, 11; Ephesians 5:26; 2 Timothy 3:16–17).

As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world. The Son’s mission is the pattern for the church’s (20:21). Sent, as he was sent, set apart, as he was set apart.

In a sentence. Jesus prayed that the Father would make them holy by the truth, for his word is truth, and said that as the Father sent him into the world, he has sent them.

For worship. God’s word is truth. Let it shape you today, and you will grow holy.
verseByVerse.note: To sanctify is to set apart for God and make holy.

parallels.desc: your law is true

verseByVerse.quote: "And for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth. I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth. I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word,

And for their sake I consecrate myself. Key words. “Consecrate” (hagiazō) is the same word as “sanctify.” Jesus was already holy. Here he means he sets himself apart for the sacrifice, as a priest consecrated an offering (Exodus 28:41; Deuteronomy 15:19). He is both priest and sacrifice, dedicating himself to death “for their sake” (hyper, in their place).

That they also may be sanctified in truth. His self-offering is what makes them holy (Hebrews 10:10, 14).

I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word. Key words. Now Jesus prays for us. Every Christian since the apostles has believed through their word, the gospel they preached and wrote down. If you believe, Jesus prayed for you by name that night.

In a sentence. Jesus said he consecrated himself for their sake, so that they too would be made holy by the truth, and that he prayed not only for them but for all who would believe in him through their word.

For worship. Jesus prayed for you, two thousand years ago, on the night before he died. Thank him.

parallels.desc: sanctified through the offering of his body

verseByVerse.quote: "that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me. The glory that you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one even as we are one,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me. The glory that you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one even as we are one,

That they may all be one. Key words. His prayer for future believers: unity.

Just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you. The model of their unity is the unity of the Trinity: distinct persons, perfect oneness of love and life.

That they also may be in us. Not just one with each other, but one in God. Christian unity is rooted in union with the Father and the Son.

So that the world may believe that you have sent me. Unity is a witness. Divided Christians make the gospel hard to believe; loving unity makes it credible.

The glory that you have given me I have given to them. The glory of the Son, revealed in his life and above all in the cross, he shares with his people.

What it does not mean. This prayer is not a call for one worldwide church organisation that ignores the truth. The unity Jesus prays for is “in us,” in the truth of the Father and the Son, and among those who “believe in me through their word” (v. 20). Unity apart from apostolic truth is not the unity he prayed for. But neither does it excuse needless division among true believers.

In a sentence. Jesus prayed that all believers would be one, as the Father and Son are in each other, and that they would be in them, so that the world would believe, and he has given them his glory so that they would be one.

On a Tuesday. Is there a believer you are at odds with? Pursue reconciliation. The world is watching, and Jesus prayed for this.

verseByVerse.quote: "I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me. Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me. Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world.

I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one. “Perfectly” (teteleiōmenoi): brought to completion. Unity grows towards its goal.

So that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me. Key words. The Father loves believers as he loves the Son. Not that we are equal to the Son, but that we are loved with the same love, because we are in him.

Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am. Key words. “I desire” (thelō): I will. Not a request but the confident will of the Son, in perfect agreement with the Father. His last request for his people: that they be with him. This is the heart of heaven (14:3).

To see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world. Heaven is seeing Christ’s glory. And here is the eternal love within the Trinity: the Father loved the Son before creation. God did not need to create to have someone to love. He is love, from all eternity (1 John 4:8).

In a sentence. Jesus prayed that they would be perfectly one, so that the world would know the Father sent him and loved them as he loved him, and willed that those the Father gave him would be with him to see his glory, given in the Father’s love before the world began.

For worship. The Son wills that you be with him and see his glory. It will surely happen.

verseByVerse.quote: "O righteous Father, even though the world does not know you, I know you, and these know that you have sent me. I made known to them your name, and I will continue to make it known, that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
O righteous Father, even though the world does not know you, I know you, and these know that you have sent me. I made known to them your name, and I will continue to make it known, that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them.

O righteous Father. “Holy Father” in v. 11, “righteous Father” here. The Father is just. He will vindicate the Son and judge the world.

Even though the world does not know you, I know you, and these know that you have sent me. Three groups: the world that doesn’t know God, the Son who knows him perfectly, and the disciples who know that the Son came from him.

I made known to them your name, and I will continue to make it known. Through the cross and resurrection, and by the Spirit.

That the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them. Key words. The prayer ends where all the purposes of God end: the love of the Father for the Son dwelling in believers, and Christ himself dwelling in them. This is salvation’s goal: to be loved with the love that flows between the Father and the Son, for ever.

In a sentence. Jesus prayed to his righteous Father that, though the world did not know him, he did, and the disciples knew he was sent; he had made the Father’s name known and would continue to, so that the Father’s love for the Son and the Son himself would be in them.

For worship. The love of the Father for the Son is in you, and Christ himself is in you. Nothing is greater than this.

Yours they were, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word.<sup>7</sup>Now they know that everything that you have given me is from you.<sup>8</sup>For I have given them the words that you gave me, and they have received them and have come to know in truth that I came from you; and they have believed that you sent me.<sup>9</sup>I am praying for them. Holy Father, keep them in your name, which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are one.<sup>12</sup>While I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled.<sup>13</sup>But now I am coming to you, and these things I speak in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves.<sup>14</sup>I have given them your word, and the world has hated them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.<sup>15</sup>I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one.<sup>16</sup>They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.<sup>17</sup>Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.<sup>18</sup>As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world.<sup>19</sup>And for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth.<sup>20</sup>“I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word,<sup>21</sup>that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me.<sup>22</sup>The glory that you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one even as we are one,<sup>23</sup>I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me.<sup>24</sup>Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world.<sup>25</sup>O righteous Father, even though the world does not know you, I know you, and these know that you have sent me.<sup>26</sup>I made known to them your name, and I will continue to make it known, that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them.”
17.overview:
Before going out to Gethsemane, Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven and prays aloud. Since the sixteenth century this has been called his “high-priestly prayer”: like the high priest on the Day of Atonement, he prays for himself, for his priests (the apostles), and for the people. It is the longest prayer of Jesus recorded, and lets us hear the Son speaking to the Father on the night before the cross.

First he prays for himself: the hour has come; may the Father glorify the Son, so that the Son may glorify him by giving eternal life to all the Father has given him. Eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent. He asks to be restored to the glory he had with the Father before the world existed. Then he prays for his disciples: he has made the Father’s name known to those given him out of the world, and kept them, losing none but the son of destruction. He does not ask that they be taken out of the world, but kept from the evil one, made holy by the truth of God’s word, and sent into the world as he was sent. Finally he prays for all who will believe through their word: that they may be one, as the Father and the Son are one, so that the world may believe; and that they may be with him where he is, to see his glory and share the Father’s love. Every Christian is named in this prayer, and Christ’s intercession continues for them in heaven (Hebrews 7:25).

18.title: The Arrest, the Denial, and the Trial Before Pilate

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–27 — Gethsemane, the Arrest, and Peter's Denial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In a garden across the Kidron, Judas arrives with soldiers and temple guards. Jesus, knowing what lies ahead, steps forward and identifies himself, and at his “I am he” they fall back to the ground. He secures his disciples’ release, so that none of those given him is lost. When Peter cuts off the ear of Malchus, the high priest’s servant, Jesus orders him to put up his sword: he will drink the Father’s cup. Bound, he is taken to Annas, father-in-law of the high priest Caiaphas. Another disciple, known to the high priest, gets Peter into the courtyard, where Peter denies to the doorkeeper that he is a disciple and warms himself by the fire. Questioned about his teaching, Jesus says he has taught openly and they should ask those who heard him. An officer strikes him, and Jesus asks for evidence of any wrong he has said. Annas sends him to Caiaphas. Asked twice more, Peter denies Jesus again, and the rooster crows.
verseByVerse.theology: I am he — ego eimi — spoken in the garden, is the same divine Name Jesus has been claiming throughout the gospel. When he says it, the soldiers fall to the ground: the mere self-identification of the Son of God is enough to flatten an armed cohort. Jesus surrenders not because he is overpowered but because he chooses to. This is the theology of the atonement in action: the Lamb who lays down his own life, the Shepherd who gives himself for the sheep. The arrest is simultaneously Jesus' most vulnerable moment and his most sovereign act.
verseByVerse.examples: Peter's denial happens at the same fire where the servants are warming themselves — the detail is vivid and specific. He denies knowing Jesus to a slave girl, to bystanders, to a relative of the man whose ear he cut off. Three denials as predicted, completed at the crowing of the rooster. Peter's failure is not moral weakness alone but the collapse of self-confident discipleship — the faith that depends on its own resources rather than on grace. His restoration (ch. 21) will be built on a different foundation.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, which he and his disciples entered. Now Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, for Jesus often met there with his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, which he and his disciples entered. Now Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, for Jesus often met there with his disciples.

Meaning first. John’s account of the arrest and trials shows Jesus in complete control. He goes out to meet his captors, they fall before him, he protects his disciples, and before Pilate he is the one who judges. Meanwhile Peter denies him three times. The King goes to the cross not as a victim, but as the Lord who lays down his life of his own accord (10:18).

He went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron. Setting and background. The Kidron Valley lies between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives, on the east side of the city. It was dry most of the year, a winter torrent. David crossed it weeping when his son Absalom rebelled and his friend Ahithophel betrayed him (2 Samuel 15:23, 30–31). The Son of David now crosses it on the night of his betrayal.

Where there was a garden. The other Gospels call it Gethsemane, “oil press” (Mark 14:32), an olive grove on the lower slope of the Mount of Olives. John alone calls it a garden. A garden, where Adam fell; a garden, where the second Adam is arrested; and a garden, where he will be buried and rise (19:41).

Now Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, for Jesus often met there with his disciples. Jesus didn’t hide. He went where Judas would find him.

In a sentence. After praying, Jesus went with his disciples across the Kidron to a garden, which Judas knew, because Jesus often met his disciples there.

For worship. Jesus went to the place where he knew he would be arrested. He went willingly, for you.
verseByVerse.note: The Kidron Valley lies between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives; it is usually dry except in the rainy season. Matthew and Mark name the garden Gethsemane.

parallels.desc: David, betrayed, crosses the Kidron weeping

verseByVerse.quote: So Judas, having procured a band of soldiers and some officers from the chief priests and the Pharisees, went there with lanterns and torches and weapons. Then Jesus, knowing all that would happen to him, came forward and said to them, "Whom do you seek?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Judas, having procured a band of soldiers and some officers from the chief priests and the Pharisees, went there with lanterns and torches and weapons. Then Jesus, knowing all that would happen to him, came forward and said to them, “Whom do you seek?”

A band of soldiers. Setting and background. The ESV notes that the “band of soldiers” was a cohort, a tenth of a Roman legion, nominally six hundred men, though a detachment may have been sent. Their presence shows the Romans were involved from the start. With them came the temple police (“officers”). A huge force to arrest one unarmed teacher.

With lanterns and torches and weapons. Under a full Passover moon. They come with their little lights to arrest the light of the world.

Then Jesus, knowing all that would happen to him, came forward. Key words. He doesn’t hide or run. He steps forward. He knows everything that will happen, and goes to meet it.

Whom do you seek? The same question he asked his first disciples (1:38), and will ask Mary at the tomb (20:15).

In a sentence. Judas came with a detachment of soldiers and temple officers, carrying lanterns, torches and weapons, and Jesus, knowing everything that would happen, stepped forward and asked whom they were looking for.

For worship. He knew all that would happen to him, and came forward. That is love.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the “band of soldiers” was a cohort, a tenth of a Roman legion — Roman troops joined with the temple police.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "Jesus of Nazareth." Jesus said to them, "I am he." Judas, who betrayed him, was standing with them. When Jesus said to them, "I am he," they drew back and fell to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They answered him, “Jesus of Nazareth.” Jesus said to them, “I am he.” Judas, who betrayed him, was standing with them. When Jesus said to them, “I am he,” they drew back and fell to the ground.

Jesus of Nazareth. They seek a man from a despised village.

Jesus said to them, “I am he.” Key words. The ESV notes that “I am he” is literally “I am” here and in verses 6 and 8. On one level, it simply means “I’m the one.” But John’s readers have heard Jesus use these words as the divine name (8:24, 28, 58). And what happens next shows the deeper meaning.

Judas, who betrayed him, was standing with them. Judas has changed sides completely.

They drew back and fell to the ground. At the name of God, the soldiers collapse. A flash of his divine majesty. They could not take him unless he let them. This is the one who has authority to lay down his life (10:18).

In a sentence. When they said they were looking for Jesus of Nazareth, he said “I am he,” and with Judas standing among them, they drew back and fell to the ground.

For worship. One word from Christ, and an armed cohort falls. He went to the cross not because he was weak, but because he was willing.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “I am he” is literally “I am” here and in verse 8 — the words of the divine name.

parallels.desc: my adversaries stumble and fall

verseByVerse.quote: So he asked them again, "Whom do you seek?" And they said, "Jesus of Nazareth." Jesus answered, "I told you that I am he. So, if you seek me, let these men go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he asked them again, “Whom do you seek?” And they said, “Jesus of Nazareth.” Jesus answered, “I told you that I am he. So, if you seek me, let these men go.”

So he asked them again, “Whom do you seek?” They pick themselves up. He asks again. He is directing his own arrest.

I told you that I am he. The third “I am.”

So, if you seek me, let these men go. Key words. The Good Shepherd protects his sheep (10:11–12). He gives himself up so that they go free. A picture of substitution: he is taken; they are released.

In a sentence. Jesus asked again whom they wanted, and when they said Jesus of Nazareth, he said he had told them he was the one, and if they were looking for him, they should let his disciples go.

For worship. “Take me, let them go.” That is what Christ said for you at the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: This was to fulfill the word that he had spoken: "Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one." Then Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the high priest's servant and cut off his right ear. (The servant's name was Malchus.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
This was to fulfill the word that he had spoken: “Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one.” Then Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the high priest’s servant and cut off his right ear. (The servant’s name was Malchus.)

This was to fulfill the word that he had spoken. Jesus’ words are fulfilled like Scripture, because they are Scripture. The word is from 17:12 (and 6:39). Their physical rescue here is a sign of his keeping them for eternal life.

Then Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it. Only John names Peter as the swordsman and Malchus as the servant. Peter acts as he promised (13:37), bravely and foolishly, against a cohort.

And struck the high priest’s servant and cut off his right ear. Probably aiming for his head. Luke adds that Jesus touched the ear and healed him (Luke 22:51), his last miracle before the cross, on an enemy.

The servant’s name was Malchus. An eyewitness detail. John knew the high priest’s household (v. 15).

In a sentence. This fulfilled Jesus’ word that he would lose none the Father gave him; then Peter drew a sword and cut off the right ear of the high priest’s servant Malchus.

On a Tuesday. Zeal without understanding does harm. Peter fought with the wrong weapons for the wrong cause. Our weapons are not fleshly (2 Corinthians 10:4).
verseByVerse.note: Only John names Peter as the swordsman and Malchus as the servant.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus said to Peter, "Put your sword into its sheath; shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?" So the band of soldiers and their captain and the officers of the Jews arrested Jesus and bound him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Jesus said to Peter, “Put your sword into its sheath; shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?” So the band of soldiers and their captain and the officers of the Jews arrested Jesus and bound him.

Put your sword into its sheath. Jesus’ kingdom doesn’t advance by the sword (v. 36; Matthew 26:52).

Shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me? Key words. The “cup” pictures the suffering and judgment the Father had appointed for him. In the Old Testament the cup is often the cup of God’s wrath (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). Jesus will drink the cup of God’s anger against sin, so that his people never have to. The other Gospels record his prayer in the garden, “remove this cup” (Mark 14:36); John gives us his resolve: shall I not drink it?

So the band of soldiers and their captain and the officers of the Jews arrested Jesus and bound him. “Captain” (chiliarchos): commander of a thousand, a senior Roman officer. They bind the one who had just floored them. He lets them.

In a sentence. Jesus told Peter to put away his sword, for he would drink the cup the Father had given him, and the soldiers, their commander and the temple officers arrested and bound him.

For worship. Christ drank the cup of wrath to the last drop. There is none left for those who are his.
verseByVerse.note: The “cup” pictures the suffering and judgment the Father had given him to bear.

verseByVerse.quote: First they led him to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. It was Caiaphas who had advised the Jews that it would be expedient that one man should die for the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
First they led him to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. It was Caiaphas who had advised the Jews that it would be expedient that one man should die for the people.

First they led him to Annas. Setting and background. Annas had been high priest from AD 6 to 15; five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office after him. He was the real power behind the throne. The Romans had deposed him, but many Jews still regarded him as the true high priest, since the office was meant to be for life. Only John records this preliminary hearing.

For he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. The family controlled the temple and its lucrative trade, the very trade Jesus had disrupted (2:13–16).

It was Caiaphas who had advised the Jews that it would be expedient that one man should die for the people. John reminds us of 11:49–52. The verdict was decided before the trial.

In a sentence. They took Jesus first to Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas, the high priest that year, who had advised that one man should die for the people.

On a Tuesday. Jesus faced a rigged trial with a predetermined verdict. When you face injustice, he knows.
verseByVerse.note: Annas had been high priest from AD 6 to 15; five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office after him, and he remained the power behind it. Only John records this first hearing.

parallels.desc: the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter followed Jesus, and so did another disciple. Since that disciple was known to the high priest, he entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest, but Peter stood outside at the door. So the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the servant girl who kept watch at the door, and brought Peter in.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon Peter followed Jesus, and so did another disciple. Since that disciple was known to the high priest, he entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest, but Peter stood outside at the door. So the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the servant girl who kept watch at the door, and brought Peter in.

Simon Peter followed Jesus. Brave, after the others had fled (Mark 14:50).

And so did another disciple. The “other disciple” is often thought to be the beloved disciple, John himself (20:2). How a Galilean fisherman was known to the high priest is uncertain: perhaps through business (supplying fish), or family connections (some traditions say John was of priestly descent).

He entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest. A large house with a central courtyard. Annas and Caiaphas may have shared the residence.

But Peter stood outside at the door. Until the other disciple brings him in, and into temptation.

In a sentence. Peter and another disciple followed Jesus, and the other, known to the high priest, went into the courtyard and then spoke to the girl at the door and brought Peter in.

For worship. Following Jesus into danger is good; following him in your own strength is dangerous. Ask for his strength.
verseByVerse.note: The “other disciple” is often thought to be the beloved disciple, John.

verseByVerse.quote: The servant girl at the door said to Peter, "You also are not one of this man's disciples, are you?" He said, "I am not." Now the servants and officers had made a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were standing and warming themselves. Peter also was with them, standing and warming himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant girl at the door said to Peter, “You also are not one of this man’s disciples, are you?” He said, “I am not.” Now the servants and officers had made a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were standing and warming themselves. Peter also was with them, standing and warming himself.

You also are not one of this man’s disciples, are you? The Greek form expects the answer no. An easy question to answer wrongly. “Also”: like the other disciple.

He said, “I am not.” Key words. The contrast is deliberate. Inside, Jesus says, “I am” (vv. 5, 6, 8). Outside, Peter says, “I am not” (ouk eimi). The man who drew a sword against a cohort is undone by a servant girl’s question.

A charcoal fire, because it was cold. Jerusalem, high in the hills, can be cold on spring nights. “Charcoal fire” (anthrakia) appears only here and in 21:9, where the risen Jesus cooks breakfast and restores Peter beside another charcoal fire. The smell may have taken Peter back to this night.

Peter also was with them, standing and warming himself. Standing with the enemies of Jesus.

In a sentence. The girl at the door asked Peter if he was one of Jesus’ disciples, and he said he was not, and stood with the servants and officers warming himself at a charcoal fire.

On a Tuesday. Denials often begin with small questions in ordinary places. Be ready to say “I am” when asked about Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Jerusalem, high in the hills, can be cold on spring nights. John mentions a charcoal fire again when Peter is restored.

verseByVerse.quote: The high priest then questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching. Jesus answered him, "I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where all Jews come together. I have said nothing in secret."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The high priest then questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching. Jesus answered him, “I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where all Jews come together. I have said nothing in secret.

The high priest then questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching. Annas, called high priest by courtesy. He fishes for evidence: how many followers, what doctrine? Perhaps looking for a charge of sedition or false teaching.

I have spoken openly to the world. Jesus has no secret movement or hidden doctrine.

I have always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where all Jews come together. I have said nothing in secret. Not that he never taught privately (chapters 13–17), but that his teaching was public, with nothing to hide (Isaiah 45:19).

In a sentence. When the high priest questioned him about his disciples and teaching, Jesus answered that he had always spoken openly in synagogues and the temple and said nothing in secret.

For worship. Christ’s gospel is public truth, not a secret society. Proclaim it openly.

parallels.desc: I did not speak in secret

verseByVerse.quote: "Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me what I said to them; they know what I said." When he had said these things, one of the officers standing by struck Jesus with his hand, saying, "Is that how you answer the high priest?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me what I said to them; they know what I said. When he had said these things, one of the officers standing by struck Jesus with his hand, saying, “Is that how you answer the high priest?”

Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me. Setting and background. Under Jewish law, a case should be established by witnesses, not by forcing the accused to testify against himself. Jesus calls for a proper trial.

One of the officers standing by struck Jesus with his hand. “Struck” (rhapisma): a slap, perhaps with a rod. The first blow. Illegal and humiliating.

Is that how you answer the high priest? Showing off to his master.

In a sentence. Jesus told the high priest to ask those who heard him, and an officer slapped him, asking if that was how he answered the high priest.

For worship. The hand that made the officer’s hand was struck by it. He bore it for us.

parallels.desc: you shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me?" Annas then sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered him, “If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me?” Annas then sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.

If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me? Calm and dignified. Jesus does not literally turn the other cheek here (Matthew 5:39), but neither does he retaliate. He appeals to justice. Turning the other cheek doesn’t mean silence before injustice; it means refusing revenge.

Annas then sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest. To the official high priest and the council, for the formal trial, which the other Gospels describe (Mark 14:53–65). John passes over it.

In a sentence. Jesus asked the officer to testify to any wrong he had said, or explain why he struck him if it was right, and Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas.

On a Tuesday. You can speak up for justice without hitting back. Jesus did.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. So they said to him, "You also are not one of his disciples, are you?" He denied it and said, "I am not." One of the servants of the high priest, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, asked, "Did I not see you in the garden with him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. So they said to him, “You also are not one of his disciples, are you?” He denied it and said, “I am not.” One of the servants of the high priest, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, asked, “Did I not see you in the garden with him?”

Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. John cuts between Jesus and Peter: Jesus standing firm inside, Peter falling outside.

He denied it and said, “I am not.” The second denial.

A relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off. Another eyewitness detail. The danger is real: this man saw him with the sword.

Did I not see you in the garden with him? The Greek expects the answer yes.

In a sentence. As Peter warmed himself, others asked if he was one of Jesus’ disciples, and he denied it; then a relative of Malchus asked whether he had not seen him in the garden with Jesus.

For worship. Peter warmed himself at the world’s fire while his Lord was struck. How often we do the same. Thank God for his forgiveness.

verseByVerse.quote: Peter again denied it, and at once a rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter again denied it, and at once a rooster crowed.

Peter again denied it. The third denial. The other Gospels say he swore and called down curses (Mark 14:71).

And at once a rooster crowed. Exactly as Jesus said (13:38). Luke adds that the Lord turned and looked at Peter, and he went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61–62). John says nothing of Peter’s tears here, but he will tell of his restoration (21:15–19). Three denials will be met by three questions of love.

Judas and Peter. Both failed Jesus that night. Judas betrayed him and despaired; Peter denied him and repented. The difference was not in the size of their sin, but in what they did with it, and above all in Jesus’ prayer for Peter (Luke 22:32). Peter was one of those given to the Son; Judas was not.

In a sentence. Peter denied Jesus a third time, and immediately a rooster crowed.

On a Tuesday. If you have denied Christ, don’t despair like Judas. Weep like Peter, and come back. He restores.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–40 — The Trial Before Pilate: What Is Truth?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At daybreak Jesus is taken to the Roman governor’s headquarters. His accusers stay outside to avoid defilement before eating the Passover, so Pilate comes out to them. They give no charge but insist he is a criminal; told to judge him by their own law, they say they are not allowed to execute anyone, fulfilling Jesus’ word about the kind of death he would die. Inside, Pilate asks Jesus if he is the King of the Jews. Jesus asks whether that is Pilate’s own question. Pilate retorts that he is no Jew; Jesus’ own people handed him over. Jesus answers that his kingdom does not come from this world, or his followers would fight. Pilate presses: so he is a king? Jesus says he was born to testify to the truth, and those who belong to the truth listen to him. Pilate asks what truth is, then goes out and declares him not guilty, offering to release him by the Passover custom. The crowd shouts for Barabbas, a bandit, instead.
verseByVerse.theology: Are you the King of the Jews? is the question Pilate must answer, and his ironic placard — THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS — will become the most accurate theological statement of the passion narrative. Jesus' kingdom is not from this world: it does not advance by the sword (as Peter demonstrated), does not require political coercion, does not depend on earthly armies. It advances by truth — by the witness of the one who is the truth, received by those who are of the truth. Pilate's question — What is truth? — is asked by the man standing in front of the answer.
verseByVerse.examples: The Barabbas exchange is the gospel in miniature: the guilty goes free, the innocent is condemned. Barabbas is released while the Son of the Father is crucified. He is a robber and insurrectionist — exactly the kind of person Jesus' opponents had accused Jesus of being. The crowd chooses the wrong son. In choosing Barabbas, they choose the kind of liberation they wanted — political, violent — and reject the liberation they needed — spiritual, sacrificial.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they led Jesus from the house of Caiaphas to the governor's headquarters. It was early morning. They themselves did not enter the governor's headquarters, so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the Passover. So Pilate went outside to them and said, "What accusation do you bring against this man?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they led Jesus from the house of Caiaphas to the governor’s headquarters. It was early morning. They themselves did not enter the governor’s headquarters, so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the Passover. So Pilate went outside to them and said, “What accusation do you bring against this man?”

To the governor’s headquarters. The governor’s headquarters is the praetorium: either Herod’s palace on the west side of the city, or the Antonia Fortress beside the temple. Pilate, governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36, normally lived in Caesarea, but came to Jerusalem at feasts to keep order.

It was early morning. Roman officials began work at dawn.

They themselves did not enter the governor’s headquarters, so that they would not be defiled. Setting and background. Entering a Gentile house was thought to make a Jew ritually unclean, unfit to eat the Passover. The irony is crushing: they scrupulously avoid ritual defilement while plotting the murder of an innocent man (Matthew 23:24).

But could eat the Passover. This raises a famous question. The other Gospels present the Last Supper as a Passover meal (Mark 14:12–16). Here, the Passover seems still to come. Where Christians differ. Some say John has moved the date for theological reasons, so that Jesus dies as the lambs are slaughtered; others that different groups followed different calendars. Verdict: “eat the Passover” can refer to the whole seven-day feast of Unleavened Bread, which was also called Passover (Luke 22:1), including the festal offering eaten on the next day (2 Chronicles 30:22). The Last Supper was a Passover meal, and the leaders here wished to stay clean for the feast’s continuing meals. The Gospels do not contradict one another.

What accusation do you bring against this man? Pilate starts a formal Roman trial.

In a sentence. At dawn they took Jesus from Caiaphas to the governor’s headquarters but would not go in, to avoid defilement before eating the Passover, so Pilate came out and asked what charge they brought against him.

For worship. They kept themselves clean for the Passover while delivering the true Passover Lamb to death. Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7).
verseByVerse.note: The governor’s headquarters is the praetorium. Entering a Gentile’s house would make them ritually unclean for the festival.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "If this man were not doing evil, we would not have delivered him over to you." Pilate said to them, "Take him yourselves and judge him by your own law." The Jews said to him, "It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They answered him, “If this man were not doing evil, we would not have delivered him over to you.” Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and judge him by your own law.” The Jews said to him, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.”

If this man were not doing evil, we would not have delivered him over to you. They don’t name a charge. They expect Pilate to take their word for it.

Take him yourselves and judge him by your own law. Pilate doesn’t want to be involved in a religious quarrel.

It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death. Setting and background. Rome kept the power of capital punishment for itself in Judea. The Jewish leaders could not legally execute (though stonings sometimes happened in mob violence, as with Stephen, Acts 7). They want Jesus dead, and only Rome can do it. Now they show their real goal.

In a sentence. They told Pilate they would not have brought him if he were not doing evil, and when Pilate told them to judge him by their own law, they said they were not allowed to put anyone to death.

On a Tuesday. Unbelief often hides its real aims. Ask God to show you the true motives of your heart.
verseByVerse.note: Rome kept the power of capital punishment for itself in Judea.

parallels.desc: Stephen stoned by a mob

verseByVerse.quote: This was to fulfill the word that Jesus had spoken to show by what kind of death he was going to die. So Pilate entered his headquarters again and called Jesus and said to him, "Are you the King of the Jews?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This was to fulfill the word that Jesus had spoken to show by what kind of death he was going to die. So Pilate entered his headquarters again and called Jesus and said to him, “Are you the King of the Jews?”

This was to fulfill the word that Jesus had spoken to show by what kind of death he was going to die. Setting and background. Stoning was the Jewish penalty for blasphemy; being “lifted up” meant crucifixion, the Roman penalty (3:14; 12:32–33). By handing him to Rome, the leaders ensure he will be crucified, fulfilling his word. And being hanged on a tree meant being under God’s curse (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). He became a curse for us.

Are you the King of the Jews? Key words. The charge is now political. Luke says they accused him of forbidding tribute to Caesar and claiming to be Christ a king (Luke 23:2). In Greek, Pilate’s “you” is emphatic: You? This beaten, bound man? A king?

In a sentence. This fulfilled Jesus’ words about the kind of death he would die, and Pilate went back inside and asked him if he was the King of the Jews.

For worship. Even the manner of his death was foretold. Nothing happened by accident; it was all for us.
verseByVerse.note: Stoning was the Jewish penalty for blasphemy; being “lifted up” pointed to Roman crucifixion.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you about me?" Pilate answered, "Am I a Jew? Your own nation and the chief priests have delivered you over to me. What have you done?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered, “Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you about me?” Pilate answered, “Am I a Jew? Your own nation and the chief priests have delivered you over to me. What have you done?”

Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you about me? Jesus asks what Pilate means. If Pilate means a political rebel king, the answer is no. If he means the Messiah, the answer is yes.

Am I a Jew? Contempt. Why would a Roman care about Jewish religious ideas?

Your own nation and the chief priests have delivered you over to me. What have you done? Pilate wants a simple answer.

In a sentence. Jesus asked whether Pilate said this himself or had been told it, and Pilate retorted that he wasn’t a Jew; Jesus’ own people had handed him over, so what had he done?

On a Tuesday. Pilate thought Jesus’ claims had nothing to do with him. He was wrong. They have everything to do with us all.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world." Then Pilate said to him, "So you are a king?" Jesus answered, "You say that I am a king. For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world — to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered, “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world.” Then Pilate said to him, “So you are a king?” Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king. For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world — to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice.”

My kingdom is not of this world. Key words. Not that his kingdom has nothing to do with this world, but that it does not come from it, or work the way the world’s kingdoms do. Its source is heaven. Its power is truth, not swords.

If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting. The proof: he stopped Peter fighting.

But my kingdom is not from the world. Its origin is God.

So you are a king? Pilate seizes on the word.

You say that I am a king. A cautious yes. He is a king, though not in Pilate’s sense.

For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world. Born, and came: a man born, and one who came from elsewhere. Incarnation in a phrase.

To bear witness to the truth. His kingdom is the reign of truth. He conquers by testimony.

Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice. His subjects are those who hear him, as the sheep hear the shepherd (10:27). An invitation even to Pilate.

Where Christians differ: the kingdom and the state. Some have sought to establish Christ’s kingdom by political power or force; others have concluded that faith has nothing to say to public life. Verdict: Christ’s kingdom advances by the word and Spirit, not by the sword. The church must not use the state’s weapons to spread the gospel. Yet Christ is king over all, and his truth addresses rulers too, as here.

In a sentence. Jesus said his kingdom is not of this world, or his servants would fight, and when Pilate asked if he was a king, he said he was born and came into the world to testify to the truth, and everyone who is of the truth listens to his voice.

For worship. Christ is King, and his kingdom comes through truth. Listen to his voice.

parallels.desc: the good confession before Pontius Pilate

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate said to him, "What is truth?" After he had said this, he went back outside to the Jews and told them, "I find no guilt in him. But you have a custom that I should release one man for you at the Passover. So do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate said to him, “What is truth?” After he had said this, he went back outside to the Jews and told them, “I find no guilt in him. But you have a custom that I should release one man for you at the Passover. So do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?”

What is truth? Key words. Cynical, weary, or dismissive. Pilate doesn’t wait for an answer. The irony: the Truth is standing in front of him (14:6). Francis Bacon wrote: “What is truth? said jesting Pilate, and would not stay for an answer.” Many still ask the question without wanting the answer.

I find no guilt in him. The first of three times Pilate declares Jesus innocent (19:4, 6). The judge declares him innocent, and still sentences him. The innocent dies for the guilty.

But you have a custom that I should release one man for you at the Passover. The custom is not recorded outside the Gospels, but is consistent with Roman practice of clemency at festivals.

Do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews? Pilate tries to wriggle out, and mocks the leaders with the title.

In a sentence. Pilate asked what truth is, then went out and told the Jews he found no guilt in Jesus, and offered to release the King of the Jews to them under their Passover custom.

On a Tuesday. Don’t ask “What is truth?” and walk away. Stay for the answer: it is Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: They cried out again, "Not this man, but Barabbas!" Now Barabbas was a robber.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They cried out again, “Not this man, but Barabbas!” Now Barabbas was a robber.

Not this man, but Barabbas! Key words. Setting and background. Mark says Barabbas had committed murder in an insurrection (Mark 15:7). His name means “son of the father” (bar abba). Some early manuscripts of Matthew call him Jesus Barabbas (Matthew 27:16–17). The guilty son of a father goes free; the innocent Son of the Father dies. Barabbas is the first person whose life was saved by Jesus’ death in a literal sense. He is a picture of every sinner: guilty, condemned, and set free because Jesus took his place.

Now Barabbas was a robber. “Robber” (lēstēs): bandit, insurrectionist, the word used of the thieves in 10:1, 8. They chose the robber over the Good Shepherd.

In a sentence. They shouted for Barabbas instead of Jesus, though Barabbas was a robber.

For worship. You are Barabbas. Jesus took your place, and you walked free.
verseByVerse.note: Mark says Barabbas had committed murder in an insurrection; “robber” was often used for violent rebels.

18.text: <sup>1</sup>When Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, which he and his disciples entered.<sup>2</sup>Now Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, for Jesus often met there with his disciples.<sup>3</sup>So Judas, having procured a band of soldiers and some officers from the chief priests and the Pharisees, went there with lanterns and torches and weapons.<sup>4</sup>Then Jesus, knowing all that would happen to him, came forward and said to them, “Whom do you seek?”<sup>5</sup>They answered him, “Jesus of Nazareth.” Jesus said to them, “I am he.” Judas, who betrayed him, was standing with them.<sup>6</sup>When Jesus said to them, “I am he,” they drew back and fell to the ground.<sup>7</sup>So he asked them again, “Whom do you seek?” And they said, “Jesus of Nazareth.”<sup>8</sup>Jesus answered, “I told you that I am he. So, if you seek me, let these men go.”<sup>9</sup>This was to fulfill the word that he had spoken: “Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one.”<sup>10</sup>Then Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the high priest’s servant and cut off his right ear. (The servant’s name was Malchus.)<sup>11</sup>So Jesus said to Peter, “Put your sword into its sheath; shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?”<sup>12</sup>So the band of soldiers and their captain and the officers of the Jews arrested Jesus and bound him.<sup>13</sup>First they led him to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.<sup>14</sup>It was Caiaphas who had advised the Jews that it would be expedient that one man should die for the people.<sup>15</sup>Simon Peter followed Jesus, and so did another disciple. Since that disciple was known to the high priest, he entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest,<sup>16</sup>but Peter stood outside at the door. So the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the servant girl who kept watch at the door, and brought Peter in.<sup>17</sup>The servant girl at the door said to Peter, “You also are not one of this man’s disciples, are you?” He said, “I am not.”<sup>18</sup>Now the servants and officers had made a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were standing and warming themselves. Peter also was with them, standing and warming himself.<sup>19</sup>The high priest then questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching.<sup>20</sup>Jesus answered him, “I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where all Jews come together. I have said nothing in secret.<sup>21</sup>Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me what I said to them; they know what I said.”<sup>22</sup>When he had said these things, one of the officers standing by struck Jesus with his hand, saying, “Is that how you answer the high priest?”<sup>23</sup>Jesus answered him, “If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me?”<sup>24</sup>Annas then sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.<sup>25</sup>Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. So they said to him, “You also are not one of his disciples, are you?” He denied it and said, “I am not.”<sup>26</sup>One of the servants of the high priest, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, asked, “Did I not see you in the garden with him?”<sup>27</sup>Peter again denied it, and at once a rooster crowed.<sup>28</sup>Then they led Jesus from the house of Caiaphas to the governor’s headquarters. It was early morning. They themselves did not enter the governor’s headquarters, so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the Passover.<sup>29</sup>So Pilate went outside to them and said, “What accusation do you bring against this man?”<sup>30</sup>They answered him, “If this man were not doing evil, we would not have delivered him over to you.”<sup>31</sup>Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and judge him by your own law.” The Jews said to him, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.”<sup>32</sup>This was to fulfill the word that Jesus had spoken to show by what kind of death he was going to die.<sup>33</sup>So Pilate entered his headquarters again and called Jesus and said to him, “Are you the King of the Jews?”<sup>34</sup>Jesus answered, “Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you about me?”<sup>35</sup>Pilate answered, “Am I a Jew? Your own nation and the chief priests have delivered you over to me. What have you done?”<sup>36</sup>Jesus answered, “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world.”<sup>37</sup>Then Pilate said to him, “So you are a king?” Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king. For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world— to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice.”<sup>38</sup>Pilate said to him, “What is truth?” After he had said this, he went back outside to the Jews and told them, “I find no guilt in him.<sup>39</sup>But you have a custom that I should release one man for you at the Passover. So do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?”<sup>40</sup>They cried out again, “Not this man, but Barabbas!” Now Barabbas was a robber.
18.overview:
John’s account of the arrest and trials shows Jesus not as a victim but as the one in control. In the garden across the Kidron, when soldiers and temple police come with Judas, Jesus steps forward and asks whom they seek; at his “I am he” they fall to the ground. He protects his disciples, rebukes Peter’s sword, and goes willingly to drink the cup his Father has given him. Bound, he is taken first to Annas, the former high priest and power behind the office, and questioned about his teaching, while outside in the courtyard Peter, warming himself at a charcoal fire, denies three times that he is a disciple, and the rooster crows.

At dawn he is brought to Pilate, the Roman governor. The Jewish leaders will not enter the praetorium, lest they be defiled before Passover, while they hand over the true Passover Lamb to be killed. Pilate moves in and out between the accusers outside and the prisoner inside. To his question, “Are you the King of the Jews?”, Jesus answers that his kingdom is not of this world; he came to bear witness to the truth, and everyone who is of the truth listens to his voice. Pilate replies, “What is truth?”, declares Jesus innocent, and offers to release him for Passover; the crowd demands Barabbas instead. The judge is on trial before the truth, and fails.

19.title: The Crucifixion and Burial of Jesus

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Crown of Thorns and the Cross
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pilate has Jesus flogged, and the soldiers mock him as king with a crown of thorns and a purple cloak, striking him. Pilate brings him out to the crowd to show he finds no fault, and presents him: “Behold the man!” The chief priests demand crucifixion. When they add that he claimed to be God’s Son, Pilate becomes more afraid and questions Jesus, who first stays silent, then tells him that his authority comes from above, and the one who delivered Jesus bears greater guilt. Pilate seeks to free him, but the leaders threaten that this would make him no friend of Caesar. At noon on the day of Preparation, seated on the judgment seat at the Stone Pavement, Pilate offers them their king; they cry for his death and declare Caesar their only king, and Pilate gives him up. Jesus carries his cross to Golgotha and is crucified between two others, beneath Pilate’s trilingual notice, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews”, which Pilate refuses to alter.
verseByVerse.theology: Behold the man (v. 5) and Behold your King (v. 14) are Pilate's two presentations of Jesus to the crowd — each one a deeper truth than Pilate knows. Ecce Homo is the great statement of the incarnation: here is humanity in its representative, here is the man who is also the king. Pilate intends mockery and irony; the Spirit intends revelation. The crown of thorns (the curse of Gen. 3:18 placed on the head of the one who came to bear the curse), the purple robe (borrowed royalty that will soon be stripped), and the reed scepter — all are parodies of kingship that are simultaneously truths about the king who reigns from the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: They crucified him, and with him two others — one on either side (v. 18): the king flanked by his 'court,' the condemned alongside the condemned, the innocent among the guilty. The inscription in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek — the languages of religion, law, and culture — makes the proclamation universal: in every language, beside a road just outside the city, in the full light of Passover day, the truth is declared. The chief priests want it changed to 'he said he was king'; Pilate refuses: What I have written, I have written.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pilate took Jesus and flogged him. And the soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head and arrayed him in a purple robe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
