Then Pilate took Jesus and flogged him. And the soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head and arrayed him in a purple robe.

Meaning first. John 19 tells of Jesus’ sentence, crucifixion, death and burial. John presents the cross as the King’s enthronement: crowned, robed, proclaimed king in three languages, lifted up. And it is the Passover sacrifice: he dies as the lambs are prepared, no bone broken, sprinkled with hyssop. At the centre stands his cry: It is finished. The work of salvation is complete.

Then Pilate took Jesus and flogged him. Setting and background. Roman flogging used a whip weighted with bone or metal. It tore the flesh to ribbons, and sometimes killed the prisoner before crucifixion. Pilate may have hoped that this would satisfy the crowd, so he could release Jesus (Luke 23:16, 22). Isaiah foretold it: by his stripes we are healed (Isaiah 53:5).

And the soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head. A mock crown, perhaps from a thorny plant, painful and humiliating. Thorns were part of the curse on the ground after Adam’s sin (Genesis 3:18). The King bears the curse on his head.

And arrayed him in a purple robe. Purple was the colour of royalty, made from costly dye. Perhaps an old soldier’s cloak. They dress him as a king to mock him.

In a sentence. Pilate had Jesus flogged, and the soldiers made a crown of thorns, put it on his head, and dressed him in a purple robe.

For worship. The King of glory wore thorns for us. By his wounds we are healed.
verseByVerse.note: Roman flogging used a whip weighted with bone or metal. Purple was the colour of royalty.

verseByVerse.quote: They came up to him, saying, "Hail, King of the Jews!" and struck him with their hands. Pilate went out again and said to them, "See, I am bringing him out to you that you may know that I find no guilt in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They came up to him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” and struck him with their hands. Pilate went out again and said to them, “See, I am bringing him out to you that you may know that I find no guilt in him.”

Hail, King of the Jews! A parody of “Hail, Caesar!” The soldiers mock him with the truth.

And struck him with their hands. Repeatedly, in the Greek.

That you may know that I find no guilt in him. The second declaration of innocence (18:38). Pilate’s plan: show them a broken man, no threat to anyone.

In a sentence. The soldiers mocked him as King of the Jews and struck him, and Pilate brought him out to show the people that he found no guilt in him.

On a Tuesday. They mocked him as king; one day every knee will bow to him as King (Philippians 2:10). Bow now, gladly.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. Pilate said to them, "Behold the man!" When the chief priests and the officers saw him, they cried out, "Crucify him, crucify him!" Pilate said to them, "Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no guilt in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Jesus came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. Pilate said to them, “Behold the man!” When the chief priests and the officers saw him, they cried out, “Crucify him, crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no guilt in him.”

So Jesus came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. Bloodied, crowned, robed.

Behold the man! Key words. In Latin, Ecce homo, the title of countless paintings. Pilate means: look at this pitiful man; is he a threat? But John hears more. Here is the man: the true human being, the second Adam, the Son of Man (Daniel 7:13), suffering for all. God’s verdict on humanity and his answer to it stand in one figure.

Crucify him, crucify him! The chief priests and officers lead the shout. Pity doesn’t move them.

Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no guilt in him. The third declaration of innocence. A taunt: Pilate knows they can’t legally crucify.

In a sentence. Jesus came out wearing the thorns and the robe, and Pilate said, “Behold the man!”, but the chief priests and officers shouted for him to be crucified, and Pilate said they could crucify him themselves, for he found no guilt in him.

For worship. Behold the man: crowned with thorns, for you. Look at him long.

parallels.desc: no beauty that we should desire him

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews answered him, "We have a law, and according to that law he ought to die because he has made himself the Son of God." When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jews answered him, “We have a law, and according to that law he ought to die because he has made himself the Son of God.” When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid.

We have a law, and according to that law he ought to die. The law against blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16).

Because he has made himself the Son of God. Key words. The real charge comes out. Not sedition, but his claim to be the Son of God (5:18; 10:33). They have understood his claim exactly. The only question is whether it is true.

When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid. “Even more”: he was already uneasy. Matthew says his wife had warned him of a dream (Matthew 27:19). Romans believed in sons of gods, divine men who walked among mortals. What if this man really was one?

In a sentence. The Jews answered that by their law he should die for claiming to be the Son of God, and Pilate became even more afraid.

On a Tuesday. The question that frightened Pilate is the question for us all: is he the Son of God?

parallels.desc: whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death

verseByVerse.quote: He entered his headquarters again and said to Jesus, "Where are you from?" But Jesus gave him no answer. So Pilate said to him, "You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He entered his headquarters again and said to Jesus, “Where are you from?” But Jesus gave him no answer. So Pilate said to him, “You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?”

Where are you from? Key words. Not his hometown; Pilate knows that (Luke 23:6–7). He means: who are you, really? Where do you come from? The great question of John’s Gospel (7:27–28; 8:14; 9:29).

But Jesus gave him no answer. Like the lamb led to slaughter that opens not its mouth (Isaiah 53:7). Pilate had already heard the truth (18:37) and brushed it aside. Jesus will not cast pearls before swine.

Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you? Pilate falls back on his power. He thinks he holds Jesus’ life in his hands.

In a sentence. Pilate went back in and asked Jesus where he came from, and when Jesus did not answer, reminded him he had authority to release or crucify him.

For worship. Christ was silent before his judge, so that we might have something to say before ours: he died for me.

parallels.desc: he opened not his mouth

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above. Therefore he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin." From then on Pilate sought to release him, but the Jews cried out, "If you release this man, you are not Caesar's friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered him, “You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above. Therefore he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin.” From then on Pilate sought to release him, but the Jews cried out, “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar.”

You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above. Key words. All human authority is delegated by God (Romans 13:1). Pilate is not ultimately in control. God is, and has ordained this hour (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). Jesus is the one truly in charge of this trial.

Therefore he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin. Probably Caiaphas, or Judas, or the leaders as a group. They knew the Scriptures and the evidence. Pilate is guilty, but less so. There are degrees of sin (Luke 12:47–48).

From then on Pilate sought to release him. He tries harder.

If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Setting and background. “Friend of Caesar” was an honorary title for loyal officials. Pilate’s record was poor; he had offended the Jews several times, and the emperor Tiberius was suspicious and quick to punish disloyalty. A report to Rome could end his career, or his life.

Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar. The threat works.

In a sentence. Jesus told Pilate his authority came from above, and those who handed him over had the greater sin; Pilate then tried to release him, but the Jews shouted that if he did, he was no friend of Caesar, for anyone claiming to be king opposes Caesar.

On a Tuesday. Whatever authority you hold was given you from above. Use it as one who will give an account.
verseByVerse.note: “Friend of Caesar” was an honorary title for loyal officials; the threat was that Pilate would be reported to the emperor.

parallels.desc: there is no authority except from God

verseByVerse.quote: So when Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called The Stone Pavement, and in Aramaic Gabbatha. Now it was the day of Preparation of the Passover. It was about the sixth hour. He said to the Jews, "Behold your king!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called The Stone Pavement, and in Aramaic Gabbatha. Now it was the day of Preparation of the Passover. It was about the sixth hour. He said to the Jews, “Behold your king!”

He brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat. The judgment seat was the raised platform from which a Roman official gave formal sentence (bēma). The Greek could even mean that Pilate sat Jesus on the judgment seat, in mockery. Either way, the irony is that Jesus is the true Judge (5:22, 27).

At a place called The Stone Pavement, and in Aramaic Gabbatha. An eyewitness detail. “Gabbatha” may mean a raised place.

Now it was the day of Preparation of the Passover. Key words. “Day of Preparation” (paraskeuē) was the regular term for Friday, the day of preparing for the Sabbath (v. 31; Mark 15:42). “Of the Passover”: Friday of Passover week. Jesus dies on the afternoon of the day the lambs were traditionally connected with the feast. John wants us to see that Jesus is the Passover Lamb (1:29).

It was about the sixth hour. About noon by Jewish reckoning. Mark says he was crucified at the third hour, about 9 a.m. (Mark 15:25). Some suggest John used Roman reckoning (from midnight, so 6 a.m.); others that both are approximations of a morning-to-midday span, with no clocks to be precise. The difference is no contradiction for people who told time by the sun’s position.

Behold your king! Pilate mocks the Jews. He speaks the truth.

In a sentence. Pilate brought Jesus out and sat on the judgment seat at the Stone Pavement, Gabbatha; it was the day of Preparation of the Passover, about noon, and he said, “Behold your king!”

For worship. Behold your King: bleeding, mocked, condemned, and reigning.
verseByVerse.note: The judgment seat was the raised platform from which a Roman official gave judgment. The ESV notes that the sixth hour was about noon; Mark gives the third hour for the crucifixion — times were approximate and may be reckoned differently.

verseByVerse.quote: They cried out, "Away with him, away with him, crucify him!" Pilate said to them, "Shall I crucify your King?" The chief priests answered, "We have no king but Caesar." So he delivered him over to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They cried out, “Away with him, away with him, crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Shall I crucify your King?” The chief priests answered, “We have no king but Caesar.” So he delivered him over to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus,

Away with him, away with him, crucify him! Total rejection.

Shall I crucify your King? Pilate twists the knife.

We have no king but Caesar. Key words. A shocking statement from the chief priests of Israel. God was Israel’s king (Judges 8:23; 1 Samuel 8:7; Psalm 5:2), and they longed for the Messiah, the son of David, to rule. Now, to get rid of Jesus, they renounce both. At the Passover, which celebrated deliverance from a pagan king, they bow to Caesar. In rejecting Jesus they reject God.

So he delivered him over to them to be crucified. “To them”: to their will. Roman soldiers carried it out (v. 23).

In a sentence. They shouted for him to be taken away and crucified, and when Pilate asked if he should crucify their King, the chief priests answered that they had no king but Caesar, so he handed him over to be crucified.

On a Tuesday. Whom do you serve as king? If not Christ, then some Caesar. Choose your King.

parallels.desc: they have rejected me from being king over them

verseByVerse.quote: And he went out, bearing his own cross, to the place called The Place of a Skull, which in Aramaic is called Golgotha. There they crucified him, and with him two others, one on either side, and Jesus between them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he went out, bearing his own cross, to the place called The Place of a Skull, which in Aramaic is called Golgotha. There they crucified him, and with him two others, one on either side, and Jesus between them.

And he went out, bearing his own cross. Setting and background. Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution. The upright post usually stood there already. The other Gospels tell us Simon of Cyrene was made to carry it, probably after Jesus collapsed (Mark 15:21). John stresses that Jesus went out carrying it himself, perhaps recalling Isaac carrying the wood up Mount Moriah for his own sacrifice (Genesis 22:6). “Went out”: outside the city, as the sin offering was burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27; Hebrews 13:12).

To the place called The Place of a Skull, which in Aramaic is called Golgotha. Perhaps a rocky hill shaped like a skull, or a place of execution. “Calvary” comes from the Latin calvaria, skull. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre probably marks the site, just outside the city wall of that time.

There they crucified him. Key words. John says it in a few words. Crucifixion was the most cruel and shameful death Rome could inflict, reserved for slaves and rebels. Nails were driven through wrists and feet; the victim died slowly of exhaustion and suffocation, often over days. Cicero said the very word “cross” should be far from a Roman citizen’s thoughts. This is how the Son of God died.

And with him two others, one on either side, and Jesus between them. Numbered with the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12). The other Gospels call them robbers or criminals.

In a sentence. Jesus went out carrying his own cross to the Place of a Skull, Golgotha, where they crucified him between two others.

For worship. He went out carrying the cross for you, to the place of shame, and was counted among sinners.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution; Simon of Cyrene was later made to carry it. Golgotha is Aramaic for “skull.”

parallels.desc: Isaac carries the wood

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate also wrote an inscription and put it on the cross. It read, "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews." Many of the Jews read this inscription, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Aramaic, in Latin, and in Greek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate also wrote an inscription and put it on the cross. It read, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.” Many of the Jews read this inscription, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Aramaic, in Latin, and in Greek.

Pilate also wrote an inscription and put it on the cross. The charge was usually written on a board (titulus) and carried before the condemned man or hung around his neck, then nailed to the cross.

Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews. Key words. The charge was meant to mock and warn: this is what happens to would-be kings. But it proclaims the truth. On the cross, Jesus is enthroned as King. The Latin initials INRI (Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum) appear on many crucifixes.

It was written in Aramaic, in Latin, and in Greek. Aramaic was the local language, Latin the language of Roman rule, Greek the common language of the empire. The King is announced to the whole world: in the language of religion, of government, and of culture.

In a sentence. Pilate put an inscription on the cross, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews,” which many read, since it was near the city and written in Aramaic, Latin and Greek.

For worship. The cross proclaims him King in every language. Let your tongue add its own.
verseByVerse.note: Aramaic was the local language, Latin the language of Roman government, Greek the common language of the eastern empire.

verseByVerse.quote: So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, "Do not write, 'The King of the Jews,' but rather, 'This man said, I am King of the Jews.'" Pilate answered, "What I have written, I have written."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, “Do not write, ‘The King of the Jews,’ but rather, ‘This man said, I am King of the Jews.’” Pilate answered, “What I have written, I have written.”

Do not write, “The King of the Jews,” but rather, “This man said, I am King of the Jews.” The chief priests are humiliated. The sign says that the Jews’ king has been crucified.

What I have written, I have written. Key words. Pilate, who could not stand up to them for justice, now stands firm out of spite. But God overrules: the truth stays on the cross. Like Caiaphas (11:51), Pilate testified to the truth without meaning to. God’s word stands written.

In a sentence. The chief priests asked Pilate to change the sign to say that Jesus only claimed to be King, but Pilate answered that what he had written, he had written.

On a Tuesday. God can use even stubborn and spiteful people to declare his truth. He is never defeated.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–42 — The Death and Burial of Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The soldiers divide Jesus’ clothes in four and cast lots for his seamless tunic, fulfilling the psalm. Near the cross stand his mother, her sister, Mary the wife of Clopas and Mary Magdalene; Jesus entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple, who takes her into his home. Knowing his work is complete, Jesus says he is thirsty, to fulfil Scripture, and is given sour wine on a hyssop branch. Then he says, “It is finished,” bows his head and gives up his spirit. Because the Sabbath of Passover week is near, the leaders ask Pilate to have the legs of the crucified broken and the bodies removed. The soldiers break the legs of the two others, but finding Jesus already dead, one pierces his side with a spear, and blood and water flow out. The eyewitness testifies truthfully so that readers may believe; these things fulfilled the Scriptures that none of his bones would be broken and that they would look on the one they pierced. Joseph of Arimathea, a secret disciple, gets Pilate’s permission to take the body, and Nicodemus brings about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes. They wrap the body with the spices in linen, as Jews bury, and, because it is the day of Preparation and the tomb is near, lay him in a new tomb in a garden by the place of crucifixion.
verseByVerse.theology: It is finished is the single most important word of the gospel. It announces a completed action whose effects are permanent: the work of redemption is done, accomplished, complete — it does not require addition, continuation, or supplement. Every subsequent act of piety, every religious effort, every moral striving — none adds to what is finished on the cross. Salvation is received, not achieved; accepted, not earned.
verseByVerse.examples: The beloved disciple who stood at the cross (with Mary, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the wife of Clopas) is the model of discipleship under pressure: present where the cost is highest, faithful where the others fled. He sees the blood and water from the soldier's spear — the sign that Jesus is truly dead, truly human, truly sacrificed — and testifies that what he saw is true. His testimony is the foundation of the gospel that will go to the world.

verseByVerse.quote: When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier; also his tunic. But the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom, so they said to one another, "Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it shall be." This was to fulfill the Scripture which says, "They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots." So the soldiers did these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier; also his tunic. But the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom, so they said to one another, “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it shall be.” This was to fulfill the Scripture which says, “They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.” So the soldiers did these things.

They took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier. The four shares suggest a squad of four soldiers; the clothes of the condemned were the executioners’ perk. Jesus was crucified naked, the final humiliation.

But the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom. The inner garment. Some note that the high priest’s robe was woven in one piece (Exodus 28:32; Josephus says the same). Jesus dies as our High Priest. Others have seen the unity of the church. John doesn’t explain; he points to the fulfilment of Scripture.

This was to fulfill the Scripture. Psalm 22:18. Psalm 22 begins “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” and describes in astonishing detail a man surrounded by mockers, with pierced hands and feet, his bones on display, his garments divided. Written a thousand years earlier, before crucifixion was invented. The soldiers, without knowing it, carried out the script.

So the soldiers did these things. Every detail, even the gambling of soldiers, was under God’s hand.

In a sentence. After crucifying Jesus, the soldiers divided his clothes into four shares and cast lots for his seamless tunic, fulfilling the Scripture about dividing his garments and casting lots for his clothing.

For worship. He was stripped of everything, so that we might be clothed in his righteousness.
verseByVerse.note: The four shares suggest a squad of four soldiers; the clothes of the condemned went to them.

parallels.desc: they divide my garments among them

verseByVerse.quote: but standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, "Woman, behold, your son!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
but standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, “Woman, behold, your son!”

But standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. Probably four women: his mother; her sister (perhaps Salome, mother of James and John, Mark 15:40; Matthew 27:56, which would make John Jesus’ cousin); Mary the wife of Clopas; and Mary Magdalene, from whom Jesus had cast seven demons (Luke 8:2). The men had fled; the women stayed. Simeon’s prophecy to Mary is fulfilled: a sword will pierce your own soul too (Luke 2:35).

When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby. John, too, came back.

Woman, behold, your son! Key words. “Woman” is not cold but respectful, as at Cana (2:4). In his agony, Jesus provides for his mother. As the eldest son, it was his duty. His brothers did not yet believe (7:5). He entrusts her to the beloved disciple. Even on the cross, he keeps the fifth commandment.

Where Christians differ: Mary at the cross. Roman Catholic teaching sees here Mary made the spiritual mother of all believers, and sometimes speaks of her as co-redemptrix, sharing in Christ’s saving work. Verdict: the plain meaning is that a loving son provides a home for his widowed mother. Christ alone is the Redeemer, and his sacrifice needs no human partner (1 Timothy 2:5; Hebrews 10:14). Mary is honoured as a believer and the mother of our Lord, but she is not a mediator. This also suggests that Mary had no other sons who believed at that time, but it doesn’t prove she had no other sons at all (Mark 6:3).

In a sentence. His mother, her sister, Mary wife of Clopas and Mary Magdalene stood by the cross, and when Jesus saw his mother and the disciple he loved, he told his mother that this was now her son.

On a Tuesday. Even in agony, Jesus cared for his mother. Look after your parents, especially in their need.

parallels.desc: a sword will pierce your own soul

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to the disciple, "Behold, your mother!" And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home. After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, said (to fulfill the Scripture), "I thirst."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he said to the disciple, “Behold, your mother!” And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home. After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, said (to fulfill the Scripture), “I thirst.”

Behold, your mother! A new family formed at the cross: the family of believers, bound by Christ.

And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home. John cared for Mary from then on. Tradition says she later lived with him in Ephesus.

After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished. Key words. “Finished” (tetelestai): the same word as v. 30. Everything the Father gave him to do was complete, except his final words and death.

Said (to fulfill the Scripture), “I thirst.” Psalm 69:21: for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink; and Psalm 22:15: my tongue sticks to my jaws. The creator of the waters, the giver of living water (4:14; 7:37), thirsts. His humanity was real, and so was his suffering. He thirsted that we might never thirst.

In a sentence. Jesus told the disciple that Mary was now his mother, and he took her to his home; then, knowing that all was finished, Jesus said “I thirst,” to fulfil Scripture.

For worship. The fountain of living water cried “I thirst” so that you might drink and never thirst again.

parallels.desc: my tongue sticks to my jaws

verseByVerse.quote: A jar full of sour wine stood there, so they put a sponge full of the sour wine on a hyssop branch and held it to his mouth. When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, "It is finished," and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A jar full of sour wine stood there, so they put a sponge full of the sour wine on a hyssop branch and held it to his mouth. When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, “It is finished,” and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.

A jar full of sour wine stood there. Cheap, vinegary wine (oxos), the soldiers’ drink. Not the drugged wine he refused earlier (Mark 15:23).

On a hyssop branch. Hyssop was the plant used to sprinkle the blood of the Passover lamb on the doorposts (Exodus 12:22), and in purification (Psalm 51:7). A small, bushy plant; some think a long stalk is meant, or that John chose the word to show Jesus as the Passover Lamb. The point is theological: the Lamb’s blood is applied.

It is finished. Key words. One word in Greek: tetelestai. Perfect tense: finished, and remaining finished. It was used on receipts in the papyri to mean “paid in full.” Not “I am finished,” but “It is finished”: the work the Father gave him (4:34; 17:4). The sacrifice for sin is complete. The debt is paid. The prophecies are fulfilled. Nothing can be added to it, and nothing needs to be.

And he bowed his head and gave up his spirit. He bowed his head, as one lying down to rest; then gave up his spirit. Not that his life was taken from him: he gave it up (10:18). Luke records his last words, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit” (Luke 23:46).

Where Christians differ: what happened at the cross? Some say Christ’s death was mainly an example of love, or a victory over evil powers, and reject the idea that he bore God’s punishment for our sin. Verdict: Christ’s death was a victory and an example, but at its heart it was penal substitution: he bore the penalty of our sins in our place (Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24). That is why “It is finished” can mean “paid in full.” Nor does the Mass repeat or re-present the sacrifice; it was offered once for all, finished (Hebrews 9:25–28; 10:10–14).

In a sentence. They lifted a sponge of sour wine on hyssop to his mouth, and when Jesus had received it, he said “It is finished,” bowed his head and gave up his spirit.

For worship. It is finished. Add nothing to it. Rest in it.
verseByVerse.note: Hyssop was the plant used to sprinkle the blood of the Passover lamb. “It is finished” is a cry of completion, not defeat.

parallels.desc: a bunch of hyssop

verseByVerse.quote: Since it was the day of Preparation, and so that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a high day), the Jews asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away. So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who had been crucified with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since it was the day of Preparation, and so that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a high day), the Jews asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away. So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who had been crucified with him.

So that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath. Setting and background. The law forbade leaving a hanged body overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22–23); the coming Sabbath made it urgent. The Romans often left bodies on crosses for days as a warning, but in Judea they respected Jewish custom.

For that Sabbath was a high day. The Sabbath of Passover week, especially solemn.

That their legs might be broken. Breaking the legs (crurifragium) with a heavy mallet sped death: the victim could no longer push up to breathe and suffocated quickly. Brutal mercy.

So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first, and of the other. Both criminals still lived.

In a sentence. Since it was the day of Preparation and the next Sabbath was a high day, the Jews asked Pilate to have the legs broken and the bodies removed, and the soldiers broke the legs of the two crucified with Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Even the timing of Jesus’ death and burial was bound up with God’s law and calendar. Nothing was random.
verseByVerse.note: The law forbade leaving a hanged body overnight; the coming Sabbath made it more urgent. Breaking the legs stopped a crucified man pushing up to breathe and hastened death.

parallels.desc: his body shall not remain all night on the tree

verseByVerse.quote: But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water.

When they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. Jesus died quickly, after about six hours. Pilate was surprised (Mark 15:44). He had given up his spirit.

But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear. To make sure. The Roman soldier was trained to confirm death.

And at once there came out blood and water. Key words. Physically, this has been explained as blood and watery fluid from around the heart or lungs, proof that he was truly dead. This answers those who later claimed Jesus only appeared to die, or merely fainted. But John also sees a sign. Blood and water: the blood of atonement and the water of cleansing and life (7:38–39; 1 John 5:6–8). Many church fathers saw here the gospel’s two great gifts, forgiveness and the Spirit, and pictures of the Supper and baptism. Zechariah 13:1 promised a fountain opened for sin and uncleanness.

In a sentence. When they came to Jesus and found him already dead, they did not break his legs, but a soldier pierced his side with a spear, and blood and water flowed out at once.

For worship. From his pierced side flowed blood to cleanse and water to give life. Come to the fountain.

parallels.desc: the water and the blood
a fountain opened for sin

verseByVerse.quote: He who saw it has borne witness — his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth — that you also may believe. For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: "Not one of his bones will be broken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who saw it has borne witness — his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth — that you also may believe. For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: “Not one of his bones will be broken.”

He who saw it has borne witness — his testimony is true. Key words. John himself, the beloved disciple, standing at the cross (v. 26), insists he saw it. This is eyewitness testimony, sworn as in court (21:24). The Christian faith rests on historical events, seen and reported.

That you also may believe. The purpose of the whole Gospel (20:31).

Not one of his bones will be broken. The Passover lamb’s bones were not to be broken (Exodus 12:46; Numbers 9:12). Psalm 34:20 says the same of the righteous sufferer. Jesus is the true Passover Lamb, whose blood saves from judgment. Paul says: Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7).

In a sentence. The eyewitness has given true testimony so that readers may believe, for these things fulfilled the Scripture that none of his bones would be broken.

For worship. Behold the Lamb of God (1:29), his bones unbroken, his blood shed for you.
verseByVerse.note: The Passover lamb’s bones were not to be broken.

parallels.desc: he keeps all his bones

verseByVerse.quote: And again another Scripture says, "They will look on him whom they have pierced." After these things Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate gave him permission. So he came and took away his body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And again another Scripture says, “They will look on him whom they have pierced.” After these things Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate gave him permission. So he came and took away his body.

They will look on him whom they have pierced. From Zechariah 12:10, where the Lord says that the house of David and the people of Jerusalem will look on me, on him whom they have pierced, and mourn for him as for an only child. Notice: in Zechariah, it is the Lord himself who is pierced. God was pierced at Golgotha. Some looked in mockery; many will look in repentance and faith (Revelation 1:7).

Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews. Setting and background. Arimathea was a town of Judea. Joseph was a member of the council who had not agreed to its decision (Luke 23:50–51), and a rich man (Matthew 27:57). Fulfilling Isaiah 53:9: with a rich man in his death.

Asked Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus. A bold act. Mark says he “took courage” (Mark 15:43). The secret disciple comes into the open at the moment when following Jesus seemed most hopeless. The cross, which scattered the twelve, brought out the secret believers.

In a sentence. Another Scripture says they will look on the one they pierced; afterwards Joseph of Arimathea, a secret disciple out of fear, asked Pilate for Jesus’ body, and with permission took it away.

On a Tuesday. If you have been a secret disciple, the cross calls you into the open. Take courage, like Joseph.
verseByVerse.note: Arimathea was a town of Judea. Joseph was a member of the council.

parallels.desc: they look on me, on him whom they have pierced

verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night, came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight. So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night, came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight. So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews.

Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night. The man who came in the dark (3:2) now comes in the light. His journey from night to day is complete.

A mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight. The ESV notes that the weight is literally a hundred Roman pounds, about 75 English pounds or 34 kilograms. An enormous amount, fit for a king’s burial (2 Chronicles 16:14). Myrrh was a fragrant resin; aloes, a fragrant wood powder. They didn’t embalm the body, but covered and surrounded it with spices to honour it and mask the smell of decay.

So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices. Strips of linen wound around the body, with spices between. Compare Lazarus (11:44).

As is the burial custom of the Jews. Not Egyptian embalming, but Jewish burial.

In a sentence. Nicodemus, who had once come by night, brought about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes, and they wrapped Jesus’ body in linen with the spices, according to Jewish custom.

For worship. Two rich men gave a king’s burial to the crucified King. Give him your best, too.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the weight is literally a hundred Roman pounds — a quantity fit for a royal burial. Myrrh and aloes were aromatic spices laid with the linen wrappings.

parallels.desc: King Asa laid on a bier filled with spices
myrrh at his birth

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid. So because of the Jewish day of Preparation, since the tomb was close at hand, they laid Jesus there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid. So because of the Jewish day of Preparation, since the tomb was close at hand, they laid Jesus there.

Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden. Another garden. Eden was lost in a garden; the King is buried in one; and in this garden he will rise, and Mary will think him the gardener (20:15). The new creation begins in a garden.

And in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid. Matthew says it was Joseph’s own tomb, cut in the rock (Matthew 27:60). “New”: no other body there, so there could be no confusion about whose body was missing on Sunday.

So because of the Jewish day of Preparation, since the tomb was close at hand, they laid Jesus there. Time was short before the Sabbath began at sunset. The tomb was near.

Why the burial matters. “He was buried” is part of the gospel (1 Corinthians 15:4). It proves he truly died. And his burial sanctifies the graves of his people: he has lain where we will lie, and has come out.

In a sentence. In a garden near the place of crucifixion there was a new tomb where no one had been laid, and because of the day of Preparation and since it was close, they laid Jesus there.

On a Tuesday. When you stand at a believer’s grave, remember the garden tomb. Christ has been there, and it could not hold him.

parallels.desc: with a rich man in his death

19.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Pilate took Jesus and flogged him.<sup>2</sup>And the soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head and arrayed him in a purple robe.<sup>3</sup>They came up to him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” and struck him with their hands.<sup>4</sup>Pilate went out again and said to them, “See, I am bringing him out to you that you may know that I find no guilt in him.”<sup>5</sup>So Jesus came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. Pilate said to them, “Behold the man!”<sup>6</sup>When the chief priests and the officers saw him, they cried out, “Crucify him, crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no guilt in him.”<sup>7</sup>The Jews answered him, “We have a law, and according to that law he ought to die because he has made himself the Son of God.”<sup>8</sup>When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid.<sup>9</sup>He entered his headquarters again and said to Jesus, “Where are you from?” But Jesus gave him no answer.<sup>10</sup>So Pilate said to him, “You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?”<sup>11</sup>Jesus answered him, “You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above. Therefore he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin.”<sup>12</sup>From then on Pilate sought to release him, but the Jews cried out, “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar.”<sup>13</sup>So when Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called The Stone Pavement, and in Aramaic Gabbatha.<sup>14</sup>Now it was the day of Preparation of the Passover. It was about the sixth hour. He said to the Jews, “Behold your King!”<sup>15</sup>They cried out, “Away with him, away with him, crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Shall I crucify your King?” The chief priests answered, “We have no king but Caesar.”<sup>16</sup>So he delivered him over to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus,<sup>17</sup>and he went out, bearing his own cross, to the place called The Place of a Skull, which in Aramaic is called Golgotha.<sup>18</sup>There they crucified him, and with him two others, one on either side, and Jesus between them.<sup>19</sup>Pilate also wrote an inscription and put it on the cross. It read, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.”<sup>20</sup>Many of the Jews read this inscription, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Aramaic, in Latin, and in Greek.<sup>21</sup>So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, “Do not write, ’The King of the Jews,’ but rather, ’This man said, I am King of the Jews.’”<sup>22</sup>Pilate answered, “What I have written I have written.”<sup>23</sup>When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier; also his tunic. But the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom,<sup>24</sup>so they said to one another, “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it shall be.” This was to fulfill the Scripture which says, “They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.” So the soldiers did these things,<sup>25</sup>but standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.<sup>26</sup>When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, “Woman, behold, your son!”<sup>27</sup>Then he said to the disciple, “Behold, your mother!” And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home.<sup>28</sup>After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, said (to fulfill the Scripture), “I thirst.”<sup>29</sup>A jar full of sour wine stood there, so they put a sponge full of the sour wine on a hyssop branch and held it to his mouth.<sup>30</sup>When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, “It is finished,” and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.<sup>31</sup>Since it was the day of Preparation, and so that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a high day), the Jews asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away.<sup>32</sup>So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who had been crucified with him.<sup>33</sup>But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs.<sup>34</sup>But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water.<sup>35</sup>He who saw it has borne witness— his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth— that you also may believe.<sup>36</sup>For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: “Not one of his bones will be broken.”<sup>37</sup>And again another Scripture says, “They will look on him whom they have pierced.”<sup>38</sup>After these things Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate gave him permission. So he came and took away his body.<sup>39</sup>Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night, came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight.<sup>40</sup>So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews.<sup>41</sup>Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid.<sup>42</sup>So because of the Jewish day of Preparation, since the tomb was close at hand, they laid Jesus there.
19.overview:
John tells the crucifixion as the hour of Jesus’ glory and the fulfilment of Scripture. Pilate has Jesus flogged, and the soldiers mock him with a crown of thorns and a purple robe. Pilate presents him to the crowd, “Behold the man!”, three times declares him innocent, and tries to release him; but when the leaders accuse Jesus of claiming to be Son of God, and threaten Pilate that releasing a rival king is disloyalty to Caesar, the governor gives way. At noon on the day of Preparation for the Passover, when the lambs were being slaughtered, Pilate hands him over, and the chief priests declare, “We have no king but Caesar.” Jesus carries his own cross to Golgotha and is crucified between two others under a sign in Aramaic, Latin and Greek: “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.”

From the cross Jesus entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple. Knowing that all was now finished, he says, “I thirst,” and receiving sour wine, says, “It is finished,” bows his head and gives up his spirit. To hasten death before the Sabbath, the soldiers break the legs of the others, but finding Jesus already dead they pierce his side, and blood and water flow out. John, the eyewitness, insists that his testimony is true, and that these things fulfilled Scripture: not a bone of the Passover lamb was broken, and they will look on the one they pierced. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, secret disciples until now, bury him with a king’s quantity of spices in a new tomb in a garden. The work God gave him to do is complete.

20.title: The Resurrection

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Empty Tomb and Mary's Encounter with the Risen Lord
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before dawn on Sunday Mary Magdalene finds the stone moved and runs to Peter and the beloved disciple, fearing the body has been stolen. Racing to the tomb, they find the grave-clothes lying in place and the head cloth folded apart; the beloved disciple sees and believes, though they do not yet understand the Scriptures. Mary stays weeping, sees two angels, and then Jesus, whom she mistakes for the gardener until he speaks her name. He tells her not to cling to him but to tell his brothers that he is ascending to his Father and theirs, his God and theirs. She brings the disciples the news: she has seen the Lord.
verseByVerse.theology: The resurrection appearances in John are structured around recognition: the beloved disciple sees and believes from the evidence of the linen cloths; Mary recognizes Jesus when he calls her name (the Good Shepherd and the sheep who knows his voice, 10:3); Thomas recognizes Jesus when invited to touch the wounds. Each recognition is different, calibrated to each person's need and capacity. This is the risen Lord — the same person, now transformed, who meets each disciple where they are.
verseByVerse.examples: Mary Magdalene is the first witness to the resurrection, commissioned by the risen Lord to tell the disciples: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God. The announcement is simultaneously personal (my Father) and covenantal (your Father) — the resurrection makes the disciples' relationship to the Father the same as Jesus' own. The first gospel proclamation after the resurrection is spoken by a woman who was weeping at a tomb and heard her name called by the one she thought was dead. This is how the gospel always comes: to those who have not ceased to love the crucified Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: Now on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb. So she ran and went to Simon Peter and the other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved, and said to them, "They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb. So she ran and went to Simon Peter and the other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved, and said to them, “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him.”

Meaning first. John 20 tells of the resurrection: the empty tomb, the risen Jesus meeting Mary, the disciples, and Thomas. Each meeting moves from grief, fear or doubt to faith and joy. The chapter ends with the Gospel’s purpose: these things are written so that you may believe. The resurrection is not a myth or a feeling; it is a historical event, attested by witnesses, which changes everything.

Now on the first day of the week. The first day of the week is Sunday. From then on, Christians gathered on the first day, the Lord’s Day (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10). The day of resurrection became the day of worship. It is the first day of the new creation.

Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark. The other Gospels mention other women too (Mark 16:1); her “we” in v. 2 shows she was not alone. Darkness outside, and in her heart.

And saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb. Not rolled away so that Jesus could get out, but so that the witnesses could get in.

They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him. Her first thought: grave robbers, or the authorities. Resurrection doesn’t cross her mind. The witnesses didn’t expect it, which makes their testimony more believable: they were not people who saw what they wanted to see.

In a sentence. Early on Sunday, while still dark, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb, found the stone removed, and ran to tell Peter and the beloved disciple that someone had taken the Lord’s body.

For worship. Every Lord’s Day celebrates this morning. Gather with joy.
verseByVerse.note: The first day of the week is Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter went out with the other disciple, and they were going toward the tomb. Both of them were running together, but the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Peter went out with the other disciple, and they were going toward the tomb. Both of them were running together, but the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first.

So Peter went out with the other disciple. Peter, despite his denials, is still with the disciples, and runs.

The other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first. A vivid, almost humorous eyewitness detail, probably because John was younger. An invented story would have no reason to include it.

In a sentence. Peter and the other disciple ran together to the tomb, and the other disciple outran Peter and got there first.

On a Tuesday. Run to Christ, whatever your past failures. Peter did.

parallels.desc: Peter runs to the tomb

verseByVerse.quote: And stooping to look in, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in. Then Simon Peter came, following him, and went into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And stooping to look in, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in. Then Simon Peter came, following him, and went into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there,

Stooping to look in, he saw the linen cloths lying there. Tomb entrances were low. “Lying” (keimena): lying flat, in place.

But he did not go in. Perhaps from awe, or reluctance to defile himself.

Then Simon Peter came, following him, and went into the tomb. Peter, characteristically, goes straight in.

He saw the linen cloths lying there. “Saw” (theōrei): looked carefully, studied.

In a sentence. The other disciple bent down and saw the linen cloths but did not go in; then Peter arrived, went in, and saw the cloths lying there.

For worship. Look carefully at the evidence. It points to a risen Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: and the face cloth, which had been on Jesus' head, not lying with the linen cloths but folded up in a place by itself. Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;
verseByVerse.commentary:
and the face cloth, which had been on Jesus’ head, not lying with the linen cloths but folded up in a place by itself. Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;

And the face cloth, which had been on Jesus’ head, not lying with the linen cloths but folded up in a place by itself. Key words. Grave robbers would not have unwrapped the body and left the costly linen and spices; they would have taken everything, or the body wrapped. And they would not have folded the face cloth. The orderly state of the grave clothes shows that the body was not stolen. Some take “folded” (entetuligmenon) to mean rolled up, keeping its shape where the head had been. Either way, it looked as if the body had simply passed out of the wrappings. Compare Lazarus, who came out still bound (11:44).

Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed. Key words. The first to believe in the resurrection, before he had seen the risen Lord. What he saw convinced him: not an angel, not Jesus himself, but the empty grave clothes. He believed Jesus had risen. Blessed are those who have not seen (v. 29).

In a sentence. They saw the face cloth folded up by itself apart from the linen, and the other disciple went in, saw, and believed.

On a Tuesday. The empty tomb is a fact of history that no rival explanation has ever accounted for. Let it strengthen your faith.
verseByVerse.note: Grave robbers would not have unwrapped the body and left the cloths neatly behind.

verseByVerse.quote: for as yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead. Then the disciples went back to their homes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
for as yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead. Then the disciples went back to their homes.

For as yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead. Key words. They believed because of what they saw, not yet because of Scripture. Later, they understood that the Old Testament foretold it (Psalm 16:10; Isaiah 53:10–12; Luke 24:25–27, 44–46; Acts 2:24–32; 1 Corinthians 15:4). “Must” (dei): it was necessary, part of God’s plan.

Then the disciples went back to their homes. Probably where they were staying in Jerusalem.

In a sentence. They did not yet understand from Scripture that he must rise from the dead, and the disciples went back home.

For worship. The resurrection was not plan B. It was written. Read the Scriptures with the risen Christ in view.

parallels.desc: you will not let your holy one see corruption

verseByVerse.quote: But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb, and as she wept she stooped to look into the tomb. And she saw two angels in white, sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and one at the feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb, and as she wept she stooped to look into the tomb. And she saw two angels in white, sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and one at the feet.

But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb. The disciples leave; Mary stays. Her love keeps her at the grave.

She saw two angels in white, sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and one at the feet. Like the two cherubim at either end of the mercy seat on the ark of the covenant (Exodus 25:18–22), where the blood of atonement was sprinkled. The place where Jesus lay is the true mercy seat (Romans 3:25). Mary doesn’t seem to realise they are angels.

In a sentence. Mary stood weeping outside the tomb, and stooping to look in, saw two angels in white sitting where Jesus’ body had lain, one at the head and one at the feet.

On a Tuesday. Mary stayed when others left. Love lingers. Linger near Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to her, "Woman, why are you weeping?" She said to them, "They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him." Having said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them, “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.” Having said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus.

Woman, why are you weeping? A gentle question. There is no need to weep.

They have taken away my Lord. “My Lord”: personal, devoted. She still thinks of a dead body.

She turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus. The risen Jesus was not always recognised at first (Luke 24:16; John 21:4). His resurrection body was the same body, with its wounds (v. 20), but transformed. And her eyes were full of tears, and she wasn’t expecting him.

In a sentence. The angels asked why she was weeping, and she said someone had taken her Lord, and then she turned and saw Jesus standing there, but did not recognise him.

For worship. Sometimes Jesus is standing beside us in our grief, and we don’t recognise him. Look again.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?" Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, "Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away." Jesus said to her, "Mary." She turned and said to him in Aramaic, "Rabboni!" (which means Teacher).
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.” Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to him in Aramaic, “Rabboni!” (which means Teacher).

Whom are you seeking? The question of 1:38 and 18:4. Not “what,” but “whom.”

Supposing him to be the gardener. An understandable mistake, and a profound one. He is the gardener of the new creation, the second Adam in the garden (19:41).

Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away. Love that doesn’t calculate. How would she carry a body wrapped in seventy-five pounds of spices?

Jesus said to her, “Mary.” Key words. One word, her name. The Good Shepherd calls his own sheep by name, and they know his voice (10:3–4). She recognises him at once.

She turned and said to him in Aramaic, “Rabboni!” “Rabboni” is Aramaic for “my teacher,” a warm and respectful form of “rabbi.” She uses the name she always used. She doesn’t yet grasp all that he now is.

In a sentence. Jesus asked why she wept and whom she sought, and thinking he was the gardener, she asked where he had put the body; then Jesus said her name, “Mary,” and she turned and said to him in Aramaic, “Rabboni!”

For worship. The risen Lord knows your name. He calls you by it.
verseByVerse.note: “Rabboni” is Aramaic for “my teacher,” a warm and respectful address.

parallels.desc: he calls his own sheep by name

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Do not cling to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father; but go to my brothers and say to them, 'I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.'" Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, "I have seen the Lord" — and that he had said these things to her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to her, “Do not cling to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father; but go to my brothers and say to them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’” Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord” — and that he had said these things to her.

Do not cling to me. Key words. “Do not cling to me” means the old relationship cannot simply resume. She has grabbed hold of him, as if never to let go. Not “do not touch me” (the old translation), but “stop holding on to me.” He hasn’t come back to the old life in Galilee. A new relationship is coming, by the Spirit, after he ascends.

For I have not yet ascended to the Father. He is on his way. There will be time with him; but there is a task now.

But go to my brothers. Key words. “My brothers”: for the first time, Jesus calls his disciples brothers. After the cross, they are members of his family, children of his Father (Hebrews 2:11–12).

I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God. Notice: not “our Father,” but “my Father and your Father.” His sonship is unique and eternal; theirs is by adoption, through him. And yet he shares his Father with them. The cross has made it possible.

Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord.” The first witness to the risen Christ was a woman, at a time when women’s testimony was not accepted in Jewish courts. No one inventing a story would have chosen her. She is sometimes called the apostle to the apostles.

In a sentence. Jesus told Mary to stop clinging to him, since he had not yet ascended, but to tell his brothers that he was ascending to his Father and theirs, his God and theirs, and Mary went and told the disciples, “I have seen the Lord.”

On a Tuesday. God is your Father because he is Christ’s Father. Go and tell someone: I have seen the Lord.
verseByVerse.note: “Do not cling to me” means the old relationship cannot simply resume; he is going to the Father.

parallels.desc: not ashamed to call them brothers

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–31 — Appearances to the Disciples and to Thomas
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: That Sunday evening, with the doors locked for fear of the authorities, Jesus comes and stands among the disciples, greets them with peace, and shows them his hands and side, and they rejoice. He sends them as the Father sent him, breathes on them and tells them to receive the Holy Spirit; whoever’s sins they forgive are forgiven, and whoever’s they retain are retained. Thomas, absent, refuses to believe unless he touches the wounds. Eight days later Jesus comes again through locked doors and invites Thomas to touch and believe. Thomas responds, “My Lord and my God!” Jesus calls blessed those who believe without seeing. Jesus did many other signs, John says, but these are written so that readers may believe he is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name.
verseByVerse.theology: Peace be with you (vv. 19, 21, 26): three times in this section Jesus speaks this word. The resurrection peace is not the absence of the disciples' fear but the presence of the risen Lord. He shows them his hands and his side — the wounds are still present, the marks of the passion carried into the resurrection body. The resurrection does not erase the cross; it vindicates it, glorifies it, makes it permanently the ground of peace. The scars of Jesus in his resurrection body are the permanent declaration that the atonement is real and its benefits are everlasting.
verseByVerse.examples: Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed (v. 29): the beatitude of all post-apostolic faith. Every Christian since the first generation believes on the basis of testimony rather than sight — on the word of those who were there, preserved in the Scripture the Spirit inspired, applied by the Spirit who illuminates. Thomas's faith required the visible wounds; blessed are those who trust the testimony about the wounds. This is where the fourth gospel places us: in the company of the blessed who believe without seeing.

verseByVerse.quote: On the evening of that day, the first day of the week, the doors being locked where the disciples were for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them and said to them, "Peace be with you." When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the evening of that day, the first day of the week, the doors being locked where the disciples were for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them and said to them, “Peace be with you.” When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord.

On the evening of that day, the first day of the week. Easter Sunday evening.

The doors being locked where the disciples were for fear of the Jews. Frightened men behind locked doors, expecting arrest.

Jesus came and stood among them. Locked doors don’t stop him. His resurrection body is real, physical, but not limited as ours are (1 Corinthians 15:42–44).

Peace be with you. Key words. “Peace be with you” was the ordinary Hebrew greeting, shalom. But from the risen Lord, to the men who deserted him, it is far more. Not a rebuke, but peace: the peace he promised (14:27; 16:33), now won by the cross (Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:14–17).

He showed them his hands and his side. Proof: the same Jesus, the one who was crucified. His wounds remain in his glorified body, the eternal marks of his love (Revelation 5:6).

Then the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord. Sorrow turned to joy, as he promised (16:20–22).

In a sentence. That Sunday evening, with the doors locked for fear, Jesus came and stood among the disciples and said, “Peace be with you,” showed them his hands and side, and they were glad to see the Lord.

For worship. The risen Christ comes to his frightened people with peace, and shows his wounds. Rejoice.
verseByVerse.note: “Peace be with you” was the ordinary Hebrew greeting, shalom — now full of meaning.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them again, "Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you." And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, "Receive the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them again, “Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you.” And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit.”

Peace be with you. Again: peace for them, and now peace for their mission.

As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you. Key words. John’s Great Commission. The Son’s mission becomes the church’s mission (17:18). Sent as he was sent: to make the Father known, to serve, to suffer, and to bring people to God.

And when he had said this, he breathed on them. Key words. Breathing on them recalls God breathing life into Adam (Genesis 2:7), the same Greek verb in the Greek Old Testament (emphysaō), and Ezekiel’s vision of the Spirit breathing life into dry bones (Ezekiel 37:9). A new creation begins.

Receive the Holy Spirit. How does this relate to Pentecost (Acts 2)? Where Christians differ. Some see this as John’s version of Pentecost; others as a separate, partial gift. Verdict: this is a real gift, but also an acted promise, preparing the disciples for the full outpouring at Pentecost fifty days later, when Jesus had ascended (7:39; 16:7; Acts 1:4–5, 8). The Spirit was given to them here, and poured out in power there. Both show that the Spirit comes from the risen Christ.

In a sentence. Jesus gave them peace again and said that as the Father sent him, he was sending them, and then breathed on them and told them to receive the Holy Spirit.

For worship. You are sent as Christ was sent, with his peace and his Spirit. Go.
verseByVerse.note: Breathing on them recalls God breathing life into Adam.

parallels.desc: the breath of life
come, O breath

verseByVerse.quote: "If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld." Now Thomas, one of the twelve, called the Twin, was not with them when Jesus came.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld. Now Thomas, one of the twelve, called the Twin, was not with them when Jesus came.

If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld. Key words. The Greek perfect tense says: they have already been forgiven, they have already been withheld. The disciples do not create forgiveness; they announce what God has already done. By preaching the gospel, they declare forgiveness to all who believe, and declare that those who refuse remain in their sins (Matthew 16:19; 18:18; Acts 2:38; 13:38–39).

Where Christians differ: who forgives sins? Roman Catholic teaching sees here the institution of the sacrament of penance, giving priests power to absolve sins in confession. Verdict: only God forgives sins (Mark 2:7). The words are given to the disciples as a group, and their exercise in Acts is the preaching of the gospel: forgiveness is proclaimed to all who repent and believe. Every Christian who declares the gospel speaks with this authority. Church discipline also applies it (1 Corinthians 5:4–5; 2 Corinthians 2:7–10). There is no special priestly power to absolve.

Now Thomas, one of the twelve, called the Twin, was not with them when Jesus came. We are not told why.

In a sentence. Jesus said that if they forgave anyone’s sins, they were forgiven, and if they withheld it, it was withheld; but Thomas, one of the Twelve, was not with them.

On a Tuesday. When you tell a friend that God forgives all who trust Christ, you speak with Christ’s authority. Say it with confidence.

verseByVerse.quote: So the other disciples told him, "We have seen the Lord." But he said to them, "Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and place my finger into the mark of the nails, and place my hand into his side, I will never believe." Eight days later, his disciples were inside again, and Thomas was with them. Although the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said, "Peace be with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the other disciples told him, “We have seen the Lord.” But he said to them, “Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and place my finger into the mark of the nails, and place my hand into his side, I will never believe.” Eight days later, his disciples were inside again, and Thomas was with them. Although the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.”

We have seen the Lord. The same testimony as Mary’s (v. 18).

Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails. Nails were driven through the hands (or wrists) and feet. The word for hand could include the wrist.

And place my hand into his side, I will never believe. “Never” (ou mē): the strong negative. Thomas wants physical proof. He is not a cynic, but a realist who will not accept something so great on hearsay. His doubt, recorded honestly, adds to the evidence: the disciples were not credulous.

Eight days later. The next Sunday, counting inclusively. The disciples gathered again on the first day of the week.

Although the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.” The same greeting, for Thomas.

In a sentence. The others told Thomas they had seen the Lord, but he said he would never believe unless he saw and touched the nail marks and his side; a week later, with Thomas present and the doors locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.”

For worship. Christ came back for the one who doubted. He is patient with honest doubters.
verseByVerse.note: Nails were driven through the hands (or wrists) and feet.

parallels.desc: they have pierced my hands and feet

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to Thomas, "Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side. Do not disbelieve, but believe." Thomas answered him, "My Lord and my God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he said to Thomas, “Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side. Do not disbelieve, but believe.” Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”

Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side. Jesus knows exactly what Thomas said, though he wasn’t visibly there. He offers Thomas exactly what he asked for.

Do not disbelieve, but believe. Literally “do not become unbelieving, but believing.”

Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!” Key words. The climax of John’s Gospel. We are not told that Thomas touched him; seeing was enough. Thomas makes the highest confession in the Gospels: Jesus is Lord and God. The Gospel began, “the Word was God” (1:1); it ends with a disciple calling Jesus “my God.” And Jesus accepts it. A devout Jew, whose creed was “the Lord our God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4), calls Jesus “my Lord and my God.” “My”: personal faith.

Where Christians differ. Some, such as Jehovah’s Witnesses, suggest Thomas was exclaiming in surprise, like an oath, or addressing the Father. Verdict: the Greek says Thomas answered “him,” Jesus; and a Jew would never use God’s name as an exclamation (the third commandment). It is a confession, addressed to Jesus, and Jesus commends it in the next verse. Jesus is God.

In a sentence. Jesus told Thomas to put his finger in the nail marks and his hand in his side, and not to doubt but believe, and Thomas answered, “My Lord and my God!”

For worship. Make Thomas’s confession your own: my Lord and my God.

parallels.desc: my God and my Lord

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed." Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to him, “Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.” Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book;

Have you believed because you have seen me? Not a rebuke, but a statement.

Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed. Key words. The last beatitude of the Gospels, and it is for us. Every believer since the apostles has believed without seeing (1 Peter 1:8). We are not second-class believers; Jesus calls us blessed. Our faith rests on the testimony of those who saw (v. 31; 1 John 1:1–3).

Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book. John has been selective (21:25).

In a sentence. Jesus told Thomas that he believed because he had seen, but blessed are those who believe without seeing; and Jesus did many other signs not written in this book.

For worship. If you believe without having seen, Jesus calls you blessed.

parallels.desc: though you do not now see him, you believe in him

verseByVerse.quote: but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.

But these are written so that you may believe. Key words. The purpose statement of the whole Gospel. The signs are selected and written for faith. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “may continue to believe.” The difference matters little: John writes both to bring people to faith and to strengthen those who believe.

That Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. The content of faith. Jesus, the man from Nazareth, is the Christ, the promised Messiah of Israel, and the Son of God, sharing the Father’s nature. Martha confessed it (11:27); Thomas confessed it in its fullest form (v. 28).

And that by believing you may have life in his name. The result of faith: life, eternal life, now and for ever (3:16; 17:3). “In his name”: through who he is and what he has done.

In a sentence. These signs are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and by believing have life in his name.

For worship. This is why the Gospel was written: for you to believe and live. Do you?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “may continue to believe.”

20.text: <sup>1</sup>Now on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb.<sup>2</sup>So she ran and went to Simon Peter and the other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved, and said to them, “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him.”<sup>3</sup>So Peter went out with the other disciple, and they were going toward the tomb.<sup>4</sup>Both of them were running together, but the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first.<sup>5</sup>And stooping to look in, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in.<sup>6</sup>Then Simon Peter came, following him, and went into the tomb.
