He saw the linen cloths lying there,<sup>7</sup>and the face cloth, which had been on Jesus’ head, not lying with the linen cloths but folded up in a place by itself.<sup>8</sup>Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;<sup>9</sup>for as yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead.<sup>10</sup>Then the disciples went back to their homes.<sup>11</sup>But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb, and as she wept she stooped to look into the tomb.<sup>12</sup>And she saw two angels in white, sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and one at the feet.<sup>13</sup>They said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them, “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.”<sup>14</sup>Having said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus.<sup>15</sup>Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.”<sup>16</sup>Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to him in Aramaic, “Rabboni!” (which means Teacher).<sup>17</sup>Jesus said to her, “Do not cling to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father; but go to my brothers and say to them, ’I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’”<sup>18</sup>Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord”—and that he had said these things to her.<sup>19</sup>On the evening of that day, the first day of the week, the doors being locked where the disciples were for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them and said to them, “Peace be with you.”<sup>20</sup>When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord.<sup>21</sup>Jesus said to them again, “Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you.”<sup>22</sup>And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit.<sup>23</sup>If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld.”<sup>24</sup>Now Thomas, one of the twelve, called the Twin, was not with them when Jesus came.<sup>25</sup>So the other disciples told him, “We have seen the Lord.” But he said to them, “Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and place my finger into the mark of the nails, and place my hand into his side, I will never believe.”<sup>26</sup>Eight days later, his disciples were inside again, and Thomas was with them. Although the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.”<sup>27</sup>Then he said to Thomas, “Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side. Do not disbelieve, but believe.”<sup>28</sup>Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”<sup>29</sup>Jesus said to him, “Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”<sup>30</sup>Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book;<sup>31</sup>but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.
20.overview:
On the first day of the week, while it is still dark, Mary Magdalene finds the stone rolled away and runs to tell Peter and the beloved disciple that the body has been taken. The two run to the tomb; the beloved disciple arrives first, looks in, and sees the linen cloths lying there; Peter goes in and sees the head cloth folded by itself. The beloved disciple goes in, sees, and believes. Mary stays weeping outside, sees two angels, then turns and sees Jesus, whom she takes for the gardener, until he calls her by name. He sends her to tell his brothers that he is ascending to his Father and their Father, to his God and their God. A woman becomes the first witness of the resurrection.

That evening Jesus stands among the disciples behind locked doors, shows them his hands and side, and gives them peace. As the Father sent him, so he sends them; he breathes on them and says, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” and gives them authority to declare sins forgiven or retained. Thomas is absent and refuses to believe without touching the wounds. A week later Jesus appears again and invites him to do so; Thomas answers with the highest confession in the Gospels, “My Lord and my God!” Jesus pronounces a blessing on all who will believe without seeing. John then states the purpose of his book: these signs are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and by believing have life in his name.

21.title: The Restoration of Peter and the Beloved Disciple

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Breakfast on the Shore: Restoration and Commission
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: By the Sea of Tiberias, Peter and six other disciples spend a fruitless night fishing. At dawn a stranger on the shore tells them to cast the net on the right side, and the catch is too great to haul in. The beloved disciple realises it is the Lord; Peter plunges into the water to reach him. On the shore Jesus has a fire of coals with fish and bread; the net, holding 153 large fish, is unbroken, and Jesus serves them breakfast. Afterwards he asks Peter three times whether he loves him, and each time, as Peter affirms his love, commissions him to feed and care for his flock. He foretells that in old age Peter will be bound and led where he would not choose, the death by which he would glorify God, and calls him to follow. When Peter asks about the beloved disciple, Jesus says that even if he wills him to remain until he returns, that is not Peter’s concern: Peter must follow. John corrects the rumour this started, identifies the beloved disciple as the author whose testimony is true, and closes by saying that the world could not hold the books needed to record all that Jesus did.
verseByVerse.theology: The threefold restoration of Peter — Do you love me? / Feed my sheep — is the most pastoral moment in the gospel. Three questions match three denials; three commissions match three failures. The charcoal fire (the same as 18:18) brings the smell of the denial back to Peter's senses; the same kind of fire is now the fire of restoration. Jesus does not ignore the failure or pretend it did not happen; he names it by re-enacting the scene in reverse. The gospel's answer to failure is not silence but renewed commission — the broken shepherd is restored to shepherd the flock.
verseByVerse.examples: The beloved disciple as the witness who wrote these things (v. 24): the gospel stakes its authority on eyewitness testimony. This is not mythology or legend but the account of one who was there — who saw the water turned to wine, stood at the cross, ran to the empty tomb, and watched Jesus break bread on the shore. The testimony is true because the witness is trustworthy; the witness is trustworthy because the one he testifies to is the resurrection and the life. The gospel ends not with a doctrine but with a person: if everything were written, the world itself could not contain the books. The Word is larger than any book.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples by the Sea of Tiberias, and he revealed himself in this way. Simon Peter, Thomas (called the Twin), Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples by the Sea of Tiberias, and he revealed himself in this way. Simon Peter, Thomas (called the Twin), Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.

Meaning first. John 21 is an epilogue. John 20 ended with the purpose of the book; now John adds a final scene in Galilee. It shows the risen Lord providing for his disciples, restoring Peter after his denials, commissioning him to shepherd the flock, foretelling his death, and correcting a rumour about John. It tells us that the risen Christ cares for failures, calls them to serve, and gives each his own path.

Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples by the Sea of Tiberias. The Sea of Tiberias is the Sea of Galilee, named after the city Herod Antipas built on its shore in honour of the emperor Tiberius. Jesus had told them he would meet them in Galilee (Mark 16:7). “Revealed himself” (ephanerōsen): showed himself, made himself known.

Simon Peter, Thomas (called the Twin), Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others. Seven disciples. Nathanael came from Cana, where Jesus did his first sign (2:1–11). “The sons of Zebedee”: James and John, named only here in John’s Gospel, John characteristically hiding himself.

In a sentence. Jesus showed himself again to the disciples at the Sea of Tiberias, where Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, the sons of Zebedee and two others were together.

For worship. The risen Christ comes to his people in their ordinary places. Look for him there.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Tiberias is the Sea of Galilee. Nathanael came from Cana; the sons of Zebedee are James and John.

parallels.desc: he is going before you to Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter said to them, "I am going fishing." They said to him, "We will go with you." They went out and got into the boat, but that night they caught nothing. Just as day was breaking, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon Peter said to them, “I am going fishing.” They said to him, “We will go with you.” They went out and got into the boat, but that night they caught nothing. Just as day was breaking, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.

I am going fishing. Some see Peter giving up and returning to his old trade. More likely he is simply doing something useful while they wait. Fishermen needed to eat.

They went out and got into the boat, but that night they caught nothing. Setting and background. Fishing on the lake was done at night, when the fish came near the surface and couldn’t see the nets. A wasted night, as at their first calling (Luke 5:5).

Just as day was breaking, Jesus stood on the shore. As at the tomb, at dawn.

Yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus. In the half-light, about a hundred yards away.

In a sentence. Peter went fishing with the others, but they caught nothing all night, and at daybreak Jesus stood on the shore, though they did not recognise him.

On a Tuesday. Some nights of labour bring nothing. At daybreak, Christ is on the shore.
verseByVerse.note: Fishing on the lake was done at night.

parallels.desc: we toiled all night and took nothing

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "Children, do you have any fish?" They answered him, "No." He said to them, "Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some." So they cast it, and now they were not able to haul it in, because of the quantity of fish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them, “Children, do you have any fish?” They answered him, “No.” He said to them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” So they cast it, and now they were not able to haul it in, because of the quantity of fish.

Children, do you have any fish? “Children” was a friendly way of addressing men, like “lads.” The Greek form expects the answer no.

Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some. A strange instruction to experienced fishermen. But they obey.

And now they were not able to haul it in, because of the quantity of fish. A miracle, recalling their first calling, when Jesus said they would be fishers of men (Luke 5:4–10). Their mission will be fruitful only by his word. Without him, they catch nothing (15:5); with him, more than they can haul.

In a sentence. Jesus asked if they had caught anything, and when they said no, told them to cast the net on the right side, and they caught so many fish they could not haul it in.

For worship. Fruit in Christ’s work comes from his word, not our skill. Cast your net where he says.
verseByVerse.note: “Children” was a friendly way of addressing men.

parallels.desc: the first great catch

verseByVerse.quote: That disciple whom Jesus loved therefore said to Peter, "It is the Lord!" When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea. The other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from the land, but about a hundred yards off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That disciple whom Jesus loved therefore said to Peter, “It is the Lord!” When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea. The other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from the land, but about a hundred yards off.

It is the Lord! Key words. John, quick to perceive, as at the tomb (20:8). He sees the sign and knows.

He put on his outer garment, for he was stripped for work. Fishermen worked in a loincloth or a short tunic. Peter dresses before meeting the Lord, out of respect.

And threw himself into the sea. Peter, quick to act, as always. He can’t wait. John sees first; Peter reaches him first.

About a hundred yards off. The ESV notes that the distance is literally two hundred cubits, about 100 yards or 90 metres.

In a sentence. The disciple Jesus loved told Peter, “It is the Lord!”, and Peter put on his outer garment and jumped into the sea, while the others brought the boat in, dragging the net, about a hundred yards from shore.

On a Tuesday. Some see Christ first; others run to him first. Both are gifts. Learn from John’s insight and Peter’s eagerness.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the distance is literally two hundred cubits.

verseByVerse.quote: When they got out on land, they saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread. Jesus said to them, "Bring some of the fish that you have just caught."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they got out on land, they saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread. Jesus said to them, “Bring some of the fish that you have just caught.”

They saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread. Key words. John mentions a charcoal fire only here and at Peter’s denial (18:18). It is deliberate. Peter denied his Lord beside one charcoal fire; he will be restored beside another. Jesus had already prepared breakfast, before they brought their catch. The risen Lord serves his disciples, as he did at the supper (13:4–5).

Bring some of the fish that you have just caught. He invites them to add what they have caught to what he has provided. In his work, he provides, and also uses what we bring.

In a sentence. On land they saw a charcoal fire with fish and bread already cooking, and Jesus told them to bring some of the fish they had caught.

For worship. The risen Lord cooked breakfast for his tired, failing disciples. He still provides for his own.
verseByVerse.note: John mentions a charcoal fire only here and at Peter’s denial.

verseByVerse.quote: So Simon Peter went aboard and hauled the net ashore, full of large fish, 153 of them. And although there were so many, the net was not torn. Jesus said to them, "Come and have breakfast." Now none of the disciples dared ask him, "Who are you?" They knew it was the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Simon Peter went aboard and hauled the net ashore, full of large fish, 153 of them. And although there were so many, the net was not torn. Jesus said to them, “Come and have breakfast.” Now none of the disciples dared ask him, “Who are you?” They knew it was the Lord.

Full of large fish, 153 of them. Many symbolic meanings have been proposed for 153; the plainest is that an eyewitness remembered the count. Fishermen counted their catch to share it out. Augustine and Jerome offered symbolic readings (Jerome said there were 153 kinds of fish, standing for all nations), but none is convincing. The precise number points to an eyewitness, and the great catch points to the worldwide mission.

And although there were so many, the net was not torn. In Luke 5:6, the nets began to break. Here they hold. Some see a picture of the church: gathering all kinds of people, and not torn apart.

Come and have breakfast. An invitation to fellowship.

None of the disciples dared ask him, “Who are you?” They knew it was the Lord. Something about him was different, and yet they knew. Awe and certainty together.

In a sentence. Peter hauled the net ashore full of 153 large fish, yet it did not tear, and Jesus invited them to breakfast, and none dared ask who he was, for they knew it was the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Come and have breakfast with Jesus. Start each day in fellowship with him.
verseByVerse.note: Many symbolic meanings have been proposed for 153; the plainest point is that someone counted — a detail from an eyewitness.

parallels.desc: their nets were breaking

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and so with the fish. This was now the third time that Jesus was revealed to the disciples after he was raised from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and so with the fish. This was now the third time that Jesus was revealed to the disciples after he was raised from the dead.

Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and so with the fish. As he did at the feeding of the five thousand by the same lake (6:11). The host serves his guests. Luke tells us the risen Jesus also ate (Luke 24:42–43): his body was real.

This was now the third time that Jesus was revealed to the disciples after he was raised from the dead. The third appearance to the group of disciples in John (20:19, 26). There were others (1 Corinthians 15:5–8).

In a sentence. Jesus took the bread and fish and gave them to the disciples, the third time he had appeared to them after rising from the dead.

For worship. The risen Lord still feeds his people, by his word and at his table.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had finished breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, "Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?" He said to him, "Yes, Lord; you know that I love you." He said to him, "Feed my lambs." He said to him a second time, "Simon, son of John, do you love me?" He said to him, "Yes, Lord; you know that I love you." He said to him, "Tend my sheep."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had finished breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.” He said to him a second time, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Tend my sheep.”

Simon, son of John. Not “Peter,” the rock, but his old name, as at his first meeting with Jesus (1:42). Peter has not been a rock.

Do you love me more than these? Key words. “More than these” probably means more than the other disciples love me, since Peter had boasted that even if all fell away, he would not (Mark 14:29). Some take it as more than these things: the boats, nets and fish. The first is more likely. Jesus gently probes his pride.

Yes, Lord; you know that I love you. Peter no longer compares himself with others. He appeals to Jesus’ knowledge.

Agapaō and phileō. Jesus asks with agapaō the first two times; Peter answers with phileō each time; the third time Jesus uses phileō. Some see great significance: Jesus asks for the highest love, Peter can only offer friendship love, and Jesus comes down to Peter’s level. But John uses the two words interchangeably elsewhere (both are used of the Father’s love for the Son, 3:35; 5:20), and he varies other words in this passage too (lambs and sheep, feed and tend). The main point is the threefold question, not the variation.

Feed my lambs. Key words. Peter’s restoration is also his commission. The flock is “my” lambs: they belong to Christ, not to Peter. The shepherd must feed them, with the word of God.

Tend my sheep. “Tend” (poimaine): shepherd, care for, guide, protect. Feeding and leading.

In a sentence. After breakfast Jesus asked Simon son of John whether he loved him more than these, and twice Peter said Jesus knew he loved him, and Jesus told him to feed his lambs and tend his sheep.

For worship. Love for Christ shows itself in care for his people. Whom can you feed today?
verseByVerse.note: “More than these” probably means more than the other disciples love me — Peter had claimed he would never fall away.

parallels.desc: shepherd the flock of God

verseByVerse.quote: He said to him the third time, "Simon, son of John, do you love me?" Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, "Do you love me?" and he said to him, "Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you." Jesus said to him, "Feed my sheep. Truly, truly, I say to you, when you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted, but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, “Do you love me?” and he said to him, “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep. Truly, truly, I say to you, when you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted, but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go.”

He said to him the third time. Key words. Three questions mirror Peter’s three denials. Each denial is answered by a confession of love. Jesus doesn’t pretend the denials didn’t happen; he heals them.

Peter was grieved. The third time stung. It reminded him of his threefold failure.

Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you. Peter throws himself on Jesus’ knowledge. He can’t prove his love by his record; only Jesus can see his heart (2:24–25).

Feed my sheep. Restored and recommissioned. Failure is not the end of service.

When you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted. Youthful independence.

But when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go. “Stretch out your hands” was an early Christian way of describing crucifixion. Tradition says Peter was crucified in Rome under Nero, around AD 64–68, and asked to be crucified upside down, feeling unworthy to die as his Lord did. Peter had said he would lay down his life for Jesus (13:37); now Jesus says he will.

Where Christians differ: Peter and the papacy. Roman Catholic teaching sees this passage, with Matthew 16:18, as Christ giving Peter primacy over the whole church, passed on to the bishops of Rome. Verdict: this is the restoration of a fallen apostle, not the founding of an office. Peter calls himself a “fellow elder” (1 Peter 5:1) and tells all elders to shepherd the flock (1 Peter 5:2). Paul opposed him to his face (Galatians 2:11). The New Testament says nothing of Peter’s successors. All pastors are under-shepherds of the one Chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:4).

In a sentence. When Jesus asked a third time, Peter was hurt, and said Jesus knew everything and knew he loved him; Jesus told him to feed his sheep, and foretold that when he was old, others would bind him and lead him where he did not want to go.

On a Tuesday. Your past failure does not disqualify you from Christ’s service. He restores, and sends.
verseByVerse.note: Three questions mirror Peter’s three denials. “Stretch out your hands” was an expression used of crucifixion; early Christian tradition says Peter was crucified in Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: This he said to show by what kind of death he was to glorify God. And after saying this he said to him, "Follow me." Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the one who also had leaned back against him during the supper and had said, "Lord, who is it that is going to betray you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This he said to show by what kind of death he was to glorify God. And after saying this he said to him, “Follow me.” Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the one who also had leaned back against him during the supper and had said, “Lord, who is it that is going to betray you?”

This he said to show by what kind of death he was to glorify God. Key words. Peter’s death would glorify God. A martyr’s death is not a defeat but a way of honouring God (Philippians 1:20). By the time John wrote, Peter had died.

Follow me. Key words. Where it began (1:43; Mark 1:17), it ends. The whole Christian life in two words. Follow, all the way, even to a cross.

Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them. John, following too.

The one who also had leaned back against him during the supper. John reminds us who he is (13:23–25).

In a sentence. Jesus said this to show the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God, and told him to follow him; Peter turned and saw the disciple Jesus loved following them.

For worship. “Follow me.” Answer him again today.

verseByVerse.quote: When Peter saw him, he said to Jesus, "Lord, what about this man?" Jesus said to him, "If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Peter saw him, he said to Jesus, “Lord, what about this man?” Jesus said to him, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!”

Lord, what about this man? Very human. Having just heard of his own death, Peter wants to know about John’s.

If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? Key words. Jesus will not satisfy Peter’s curiosity. Each disciple has his own path, appointed by the Lord. Comparison is a trap.

You follow me! “You” is emphatic. Mind your own call. Jesus’ will for John is not Peter’s business.

In a sentence. When Peter saw John and asked about him, Jesus answered that if he wanted John to remain until he came, that was not Peter’s concern: Peter must follow him.

On a Tuesday. Stop comparing your path with others’. What is that to you? You follow him.

verseByVerse.quote: So the saying spread abroad among the brothers that this disciple was not to die; yet Jesus did not say to him that he was not to die, but, "If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?" This is the disciple who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things, and we know that his testimony is true.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the saying spread abroad among the brothers that this disciple was not to die; yet Jesus did not say to him that he was not to die, but, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?” This is the disciple who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things, and we know that his testimony is true.

So the saying spread abroad among the brothers that this disciple was not to die. The rumour may have spread because the beloved disciple lived to a great age. Tradition says John lived in Ephesus until the reign of Trajan, around AD 98, the last of the apostles.

Yet Jesus did not say to him that he was not to die. John corrects the rumour carefully, quoting Jesus’ exact words. A lesson in handling Scripture: pay attention to what is actually said, not what people think it says.

This is the disciple who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things. Key words. The author identifies himself: the beloved disciple. The Gospel is eyewitness testimony.

And we know that his testimony is true. “We”: probably the elders of the church at Ephesus, or John’s circle, who knew him and endorsed his Gospel. They vouch for him.

In a sentence. A rumour spread that this disciple would not die, but Jesus had not said that, only “if I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?”; and this disciple is the one who testifies and wrote these things, and his testimony is true.

For worship. The Gospel you hold is true testimony from one who leaned on Jesus’ breast. Trust it.
verseByVerse.note: The rumour may have spread because the beloved disciple lived to a great age. Verse 24 identifies him as the author of the Gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there are also many other things that Jesus did. Were every one of them to be written, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there are also many other things that Jesus did. Were every one of them to be written, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.

Now there are also many other things that Jesus did. John has told us only a selection (20:30).

Were every one of them to be written, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written. Key words. A deliberate exaggeration, a common ancient way of saying “countless.” But there is truth in it. The person and work of Jesus are inexhaustible. If the Word through whom all things were made (1:3) became flesh, then the world itself is too small to hold the full account of him.

What it does not mean. It doesn’t mean that we need other sources, traditions or revelations to know Jesus truly. What is written is enough to believe and have life (20:31). The Scriptures are sufficient, though not exhaustive.

In a sentence. Jesus did many other things, so many that if each were written down, the world could not hold the books.

For worship. You will never come to the end of Jesus. Eternity will not exhaust him. Keep learning of him.

21.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples by the Sea of Tiberias, and he revealed himself in this way.<sup>2</sup>Simon Peter, Thomas (called the Twin), Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.<sup>3</sup>Simon Peter said to them, “I am going fishing.” They said to him, “We will go with you.” They went out and got into the boat, but that night they caught nothing.<sup>4</sup>Just as day was breaking, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.<sup>5</sup>Jesus said to them, “Children, do you have any fish?” They answered him, “No.”<sup>6</sup>He said to them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” So they cast it, and now they were not able to haul it in, because of the quantity of fish.<sup>7</sup>That disciple whom Jesus loved therefore said to Peter, “It is the Lord!” When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea.<sup>8</sup>The other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from the land, but about a hundred yards off.<sup>9</sup>When they got out on land, they saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread.<sup>10</sup>Jesus said to them, “Bring some of the fish that you have just caught.”<sup>11</sup>So Simon Peter went aboard and hauled the net ashore, full of large fish, 153 of them. And although there were so many, the net was not torn.<sup>12</sup>Jesus said to them, “Come and have breakfast.” Now none of the disciples dared ask him, “Who are you?” They knew it was the Lord.<sup>13</sup>Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and so with the fish.<sup>14</sup>This was now the third time that Jesus was revealed to the disciples after he was raised from the dead.<sup>15</sup>When they had finished breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.”<sup>16</sup>He said to him a second time, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Tend my sheep.”<sup>17</sup>He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, “Do you love me?” and he said to him, “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.<sup>18</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, when you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted, but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go.”<sup>19</sup>(This he said to show by what kind of death he was to glorify God.) And after saying this he said to him, “Follow me.”<sup>20</sup>Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the one who also had leaned back against him during the supper and had said, “Lord, who is it that is going to betray you?”<sup>21</sup>When Peter saw him, he said to Jesus, “Lord, what about this man?”<sup>22</sup>Jesus said to him, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!”<sup>23</sup>So the saying spread abroad among the brothers that this disciple was not to die; yet Jesus did not say to him that he was not to die, but, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?”<sup>24</sup>This is the disciple who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things, and we know that his testimony is true.<sup>25</sup>Now there are also many other things that Jesus did. Were every one of them to be written, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.
21.overview:
After the conclusion of chapter 20, John adds an epilogue set by the Sea of Galilee. Seven disciples go fishing with Peter and catch nothing all night. At dawn a figure on the shore tells them to cast the net on the right side, and they cannot haul it in for the number of fish. The beloved disciple recognises him: “It is the Lord!” Peter throws himself into the water. On the beach Jesus has a charcoal fire burning with fish and bread, and invites them to breakfast; the net holds 153 large fish and is not torn.

Beside that charcoal fire, the same kind as the one where Peter denied him, Jesus asks Peter three times, “Do you love me?”, and three times commissions him: “Feed my lambs… Tend my sheep… Feed my sheep.” Peter, grieved at the third question, answers, “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.” Jesus foretells that Peter will one day be bound and led where he does not want to go, signifying the death by which he would glorify God, and says, “Follow me.” When Peter asks about the beloved disciple, Jesus replies that this is not his concern: “You follow me!” John corrects a rumour that the beloved disciple would not die, identifies him as the author of the Gospel, and closes by saying that if everything Jesus did were written, the world could not hold the books. The Gospel ends not with failure but with a forgiven disciple, a renewed calling and the command to follow.
